title: PRBench: Large-Scale Expert Rubrics for Evaluating High-Stakes Professional Reasoning
human_time: ~30-90 min per task: open-ended legal/finance analysis a JD/CFA would draft against ~18-criterion rubrics; estimated, paper doesn't state.
frontier_score: GPT-5 / GPT-5 Pro lead; best 0.39 (Finance) and 0.37 (Legal) on Hard subsets, 0.51/0.50 on full set
one_line: 1,100 expert-authored legal & finance tasks scored against 19,356 weighted rubric criteria by an LLM judge.
notes: ~30% of tasks carry multi-turn context but the model only writes the final response, so classified single-turn. Headline eval is tool-free (web-search/code-interpreter runs are ablations, all <=0.40).
placement_reason: Built to measure the messy, open-ended legal and finance work people actually pay credentialed professionals for (JD/CFA-authored tasks), because saturating academic benchmarks say nothing about high-stakes professional competence — an occupational-domain probe, with domain content (law, finance) rather than explicit economic valuation as the design core.

title: MedExpQA: Multilingual Benchmarking of Large Language Models for Medical Question Answering
human_time: ~1-2 min per multiple-choice clinical-case vignette (137-token case + 80-token options, MIR-exam style); explaining the answer in full would take longer but only the answer letter is graded.
frontier_score: Zero-shot RAG-7 (best automatic condition): 37.9% avg accuracy (4 models x 4 languages), barely above no-grounding's 35.6% and far below the 82.2% full-gold-explanation upper bound
one_line: The first multilingual (Spanish/English/Italian/French) medical exam QA benchmark pairing MC questions with physician-written gold explanations, isolating reasoning from retrieval quality.
notes: 622 documents/language x 4 = 2,488 total (test split 125/language = 500). tool_access=[search-retrieval] because the dek foregrounds the RAG-vs-no-grounding comparison (MedRAG BM25+MedCPT at k=7/32) as a headline condition, alongside gold-explanation (tool-free) conditions used to define upper bounds; classified on the RAG condition per FinanceBench precedent. MIRAGE (Xiong et al. 2024, source of the MedRAG baseline this paper's RAG conditions run) is a real second ancestor but isn't yet in the taxonomy or this batch, so omitted from lineage. Medium confidence: family placement (A2 exam vs D2 occupational) is a judgment call -- no clinician-panel/free-text-harm framing here (unlike Med-PaLM/HealthBench), so classified with the plain knowledge-exam family instead.
placement_reason: Built on Spain's own MIR medical licensing exam (CasiMedicos), scored by first-character answer-letter match -- a knowledge-exam capability probe extended to multilingual and reasoning-vs-retrieval axes, not a clinical-deployment rehearsal: unlike Med-PaLM/HealthBench (D2), there is no clinician-rated free-text safety/harm panel here, and the paper's own conclusion admits explanation quality isn't graded at all, only which letter was chosen.

title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
group: Gray Swan AI / UK AI Security Institute
human_time: Each behavior requires a coherent sequence of 2-8 dependent tool calls -- comparable to a few minutes of human task-planning and execution with the same tools.
frontier_score: Under a universal jailbreak template: GPT-4o's harm score rises to 72.7% (from 48.4% no-attack); best-of-5 sampling pushes Mistral Large 2 to 90.8%
one_line: 440 (110 base x4 presentation variants) explicitly malicious multi-step agentic tasks across 11 harm categories against 104 synthetic proxy tools, scored by hand-written rubrics that only count success if the agent stays capable enough to actually finish the harmful task.
notes: A 132-task private split was never exposed to public LLM APIs and is evaluated only on a non-logging Azure deployment -- a genuine private-holdout defense, unusually strong for a jailbreak benchmark (the 264-task public split remains fully exposed).
placement_reason: Built to measure whether chatbot-era refusal training transfers to tool-calling agents, and specifically to close a measurement gap in prior jailbreak evals: a jailbreak that suppresses refusal but leaves the model too incoherent to finish the harmful task looks 'successful' on a refusal-only metric, so AgentHarm's harm score is conditioned on retained task-completing competence via a matched benign-task control. The object is attack surface / agent compliance under attack, not model skill -- the E1 case.

title: VQA: Visual Question Answering
human_time: Seconds per item: one short question about one image; 89% of answers are a single word and humans hit 83.3% at a glance.
frontier_score: Best 2015 model 58.16% open-ended / 63.09% multiple-choice (test-standard) vs 83.30% human
one_line: Free-form questions about images graded by consensus string match against 10 human answers; ~0.76M questions on COCO.
notes: Saturation judged from own knowledge: v1 was retired for balanced VQA v2 and modern multimodal models exceed the 2015 human-model gap. items_count is total questions; eval test splits are a subset. Held-out test-standard/test-reserve eval server = private-holdout.
placement_reason: Born as an 'AI-complete' perception probe: can a model answer a free-form question about an image, replacing ungradeable captioning with a quantitative multimodal recognition/understanding task — a classic vision+language capability benchmark of the ImageNet/COCO era.

title: Have LLMs Advanced Enough? A Challenging Problem Solving Benchmark For Large Language Models
human_time: Roughly 1-3 min per JEE-Advanced item at standard exam pacing (515 problems across a multi-hour exam).
frontier_score: GPT-4 + CoT + Self-Consistency@8: 38.9% overall (2023); GPT-4 zero-shot 30.9%
one_line: 515 pre-engineering Physics/Chemistry/Math problems from 8 years of India's IIT JEE-Advanced exam, with JEE's own partial-credit and negative-marking rules carried through to the metric.
notes: Diagnostic comparison (Figure 2) against MMLU-STEM and MATH is the explicit basis for the C1 placement and the de-saturates lineage edges.
placement_reason: Explicitly built because 'popular reasoning benchmarks... were running out of headroom' - the paper's own diagnostic shows GPT-4 solving >80% of MMLU-STEM and ~60% of MATH but only ~20-42% of JEEBench's three subjects, sourcing from a real, high-stakes human entrance exam (~5% acceptance) whose own scoring rubric (partial credit, negative marking) is carried through wholesale; durable headroom (38.9% best score) is the stated design goal, matching the C1 pattern (OlympiadBench's direct peer), not a rebuild of one saturated predecessor (B3).

title: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health
human_time: Minutes per item: read a ~2.6-turn health chat and compose one thorough reply; physicians wrote their own responses in-session.
frontier_score: o3: 0.60 overall; 0.32 on HealthBench Hard
one_line: 5,000 open-ended health conversations graded against 48,562 physician-written rubric criteria by a validated GPT-4.1 judge.
notes: Provenance borderline: physicians authored the rubrics and scenario specs but an LM pipeline generated most dialogues (synthetic-generated is defensible). Single-turn since the model only answers the final user message. 0.60 sits right at the open/closing boundary; Hard subset (0.32) is open. Canary string also shipped, but private holdout is the stronger defense.
placement_reason: Framed explicitly around whether a model is safe to put in front of a patient — realistic multi-turn health conversations replacing saturated USMLE-style multiple choice, with physician-written rubrics as ground truth; clinical-deployment readiness, the canonical D2 case the taxonomy itself names.

title: Program Synthesis with Large Language Models
human_time: Short, one-sentence problems; not stated.
frontier_score: 137B-parameter model: 59.6% solve rate (80 samples); modern frontier models exceed 90%
one_line: A crowd-sourced benchmark of 974 short, one-sentence Python problems isolating natural-language-to-code synthesis from the narrative competitive-programming style of contemporaries like APPS and Codex/HumanEval.
notes: Alongside HumanEval, one of the two canonical basic-code-synthesis benchmarks; heavily memorized by modern LLMs, prompting EvalPlus's MBPP+ hardened-test successor.
placement_reason: HumanEval's sibling: the same natural-language-to-short-function synthesis task, built independently and crowd-sourced rather than hand-authored, giving the field two convergent basic code-synthesis benchmarks from the same year.

title: Vending-Bench: A Benchmark for Long-Term Coherence of Autonomous Agents
human_time: Human baseline: one participant ran the same task for 5 hours through a chat interface, with no prior knowledge of the environment beyond the prompt.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet $2,217.93 mean net worth (best), beating the $844.05 human baseline, but every model has runs that spiral into unproductive 'meltdown' loops
one_line: LLM agents run a simulated vending-machine business for 20M+ cumulative tokens (from a 30K-token window); Sonnet and o3-mini beat a human baseline on average net worth but every model has meltdown runs uncorrelated with memory filling (Pearson 0.167).
notes: No fixed item/question count -- it's a single persistent environment run 5x per model/condition, so items_count left null. domain_primary=tool-use for the domain-api business-management tools (email, pricing, inventory) the agent operates; safety is secondary for the paper's explicit dual-use framing (autonomous capital/resource acquisition as an AI-risk-relevant capability). contamination_defense=procedural: the paper's own critique section states risk is 'low by construction' because the simulated economy, supplier replies, and demand are all LLM-generated at runtime rather than drawn from a fixed test set. Family choice (A5 over A7/G-anything) is a judgment call -- no dedicated 'long-horizon coherence' family exists; A5 fits because the headline construct is operating a persistent interactive environment (a simulated business) end-to-end, the same shape as AppWorld/OSWorld, just stretched over hundreds of simulated days.
placement_reason: Isolates whether an agent can operate a persistent interactive environment (a simulated vending-machine business, via email/pricing/inventory tools and a sub-agent) coherently once the run stretches to hundreds of simulated days and 20M+ tokens -- the same environment-operation shape as AppWorld/OSWorld, not a communication probe (A7, coordination isn't scored) or a tool-selection probe (A6, the tool roster is fixed and small); the paper's contribution is showing this capability degrades independent of context-window limits.

title: LongBench: A Bilingual, Multitask Benchmark for Long Context Understanding
human_time: Average context 6,711 words (EN) / 13,386 characters (ZH) — a few minutes for a human to read the relevant span and answer.
frontier_score: GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k leads at 44.7% overall (mid-2023 models); a truncation ablation confirms genuine context use for GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k/ChatGLM2-6B-32k but not Vicuna-v1.5-7B-16k; a without-context control shows 31.7 F1 on HotpotQA with zero context, exposing memorization contamination on 3 of 21 datasets.
one_line: The first bilingual (EN/ZH) benchmark testing whether LLMs genuinely use a long context rather than merely accept one — 21 datasets across 6 task categories, with a truncation ablation and a without-context memorization control built into the evaluation itself.
notes: Superseded quickly by its own successor (LongBench v2) and by 100k-1M-token models; saturation='closing' reflects that the paper's own 4k-32k regime is now the easy end of the problem, per the explainer's bottom line, even though the original 2023 scores were far from ceiling.
placement_reason: Tests whether a model can parse and retrieve from a long document — reading comprehension, retrieval, multi-hop QA, summarization, and code completion over 6-14k-word contexts — the A1 pattern (cf. Long Range Arena, NaturalQuestions, BEIR in the existing taxonomy), not a wall-durability claim (no expert-curated ceiling) or a construct audit of an existing metric.

title: LongBench v2: Towards Deeper Understanding and Reasoning on Realistic Long-context Multitasks
human_time: Human experts search the source document and answer within a 15-minute cap; most correct answers land in the 5-10 minute band.
frontier_score: GPT-4o (direct answer): 50.1%; o1-preview (extended reasoning): 57.7%, vs. a 53.7% human-expert baseline (25% random floor)
one_line: 503 human-annotated, human-reviewed multiple-choice questions across six long-context task families (8k-2M words) engineered to resist retrieval shortcuts; human experts average only 53.7% within 15 minutes, and only o1-preview's extended reasoning clears that bar.
notes: The natural predecessor/parent, the team's own LongBench v1 (bai-2023-longbench), is a papers.json node but not yet in this taxonomy, so no lineage edge is added per the instructions; dynasty label kept regardless since the relationship is real and well-documented in the explainer. The paper's own memorization probe (zero-context answering) shows single-doc-QA and code-repo scores stay well above the random floor -- a residual contamination signal the authors flag but don't further quantify.
placement_reason: The team's own prior benchmark is explicitly distrusted here: extractive QA is 'easily handled by modern long-context models and RAG systems, as evidenced by their perfect recall in Needle-in-a-Haystack' -- LongBench v2 rebuilds the same long-context-understanding construct with a harder, human-reviewed, retrieval-resistant multiple-choice format (dual automated+manual difficulty gates) to restore discriminative headroom, the canonical B3 desaturation-sequel move on the same construct, not a new one.

title: PHYRE: A New Benchmark for Physical Reasoning
human_time: Not reported - the paper explicitly flags the absence of a human or animal AUCCESS baseline as a gap despite its own introduction comparing physical reasoning across humans, capuchins, chimps, and crows; a single ball/pair-of-balls placement decision would plausibly take a human seconds to a minute of visual reasoning per attempt.
frontier_score: Best 2019 agent (DQN-O, online-updating) 56.2%+-10.5 AUCCESS cross-template on PHYRE-B / 39.6%+-11.1 on PHYRE-2B; the same DQN architecture reaches 77.6%/67.8% within-template (templates seen in training); no human baseline reported
one_line: 5,000 single-action 2D physics puzzles (2 action tiers x 25 templates x 100 tasks each) scored by AUCCESS, a log-weighted area under the success-vs-attempts curve rewarding sample-efficient, intervention-based solving.
notes: Domain/family placement is a judgment call (see the batch-wide RL/robotics vocabulary-gap note on wang-2019-mbrl-benchmark). Unlike its RL/robotics siblings in this batch, PHYRE's own title and framing ('physical reasoning', explicit comparison to human/animal cognition) support 'reasoning' as domain_primary more directly than a forced fallback.
placement_reason: An intervention benchmark, not a static puzzle: an agent must act on a deterministic 2D physics world (place one or two balls) through up to 100 attempts to cause a goal state, observing outcomes and adapting - task_shape=interactive-env places it with A5's 'operate an interactive environment' pattern over A3's static checkable-puzzle framing, even though its content (physics, not web/computer use) again sits outside this family's usual exemplars.

title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
human_time: ~10-30 min per task for a human: multi-server lookup/orchestration workflows (mean 9.8 tool calls, 2.55 servers); estimated from task descriptions.
frontier_score: Muse Spark (Meta) 82.2% Pass@0.75, mean coverage 86.2%; open GLM-5.1 at 75.6%
one_line: 1,000 agentic tasks over 36 live MCP servers and 220 real tools, scored by an answer-centric claims rubric per task.
notes: tool_access lists code-exec and search-retrieval because the MCP server pool includes code executors/cli and search servers, all exposed via MCP. Prompts are single-turn but execution is a full agent loop, so interactive-env. 500/500 public/private split = private-holdout.
placement_reason: Asks whether agents can discover, select, and orchestrate real MCP tools across servers under distractor noise — 1,000 tasks over 36 live MCP servers where tool discovery and multi-server sequencing is the skill being probed; a textbook MCP tool-use suite.

title: The Hanabi Challenge: A New Frontier for AI Research
human_time: Roughly the length of one Hanabi hand: a full 2-5-player game runs several minutes of turn-based hint/play/discard decisions.
frontier_score: ACHA (~20B self-play steps) reaches 22.73 (2P) declining to 16.80 (5P), below hand-coded bots at every player count beyond two; independently-trained agents scoring >20/25 in self-play collapse to near-zero when paired with an unfamiliar same-algorithm-trained partner.
one_line: Purely cooperative, imperfect-information card game (Hanabi, 2-5 players) packaged with self-play and ad-hoc-team evaluation regimes and an open-source Hanabi Learning Environment; billions of self-play RL steps still underperform hand-coded bots and collapse near-zero against unfamiliar partners.
notes: No BENCH_DOMAINS value cleanly fits cooperative multi-agent card-game reasoning; 'reasoning' (the paper's own framing: reading a partner's intent from constrained hints, a theory-of-mind-adjacent skill) is the closest available. items_count is null -- this is a configurable game environment (2-5 player counts, 14 evaluated agents), not a fixed enumerable item set.
placement_reason: A turn-based interactive-environment probe of cooperative multi-agent coordination under genuine imperfect information and a scarce shared communication resource -- agents must operate the game's constrained action space (hint/play/discard) to coordinate, the archetypal interactive-operation construct (A5); its central result (ad-hoc-team collapse) is about coordination robustness in an operated environment, not exam-style knowledge or open dialogue.

title: τ2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
human_time: A customer-support-style task (retail/airline/telecom) requiring a handful of dialogue turns and tool calls from both agent and user; minutes per task, no stated human baseline.
frontier_score: Frontier LLMs clearing 56-79% pass^1 on retail/airline drop to 34-49% on the new telecom domain; removing the user (single-control) recovers 18-25 points
one_line: τ-bench's sequel gives the simulated user its own tools and database in a formalized Dec-POMDP, adding a telecom domain (114 of 2,285 possible tasks); frontier LLMs clearing up to 79% pass^1 on retail/airline collapse to 34-49% on telecom, and the drop is mostly about coordinating with a user, not raw reasoning.
notes: items_count=279 sampled tasks total across retail (115) + airline (50) + telecom (114); telecom alone composes from 2,285 possible task instantiations.
placement_reason: Direct sequel to τ-bench, keeping its tool-agent-user interaction construct but making the user a second first-class tool-user (dual control) instead of a text-only instruction source -- still the same 'orchestrate tools under a written policy while extracting intent from a human' skill, now measurably harder because the user can also act and err.

title: API-BLEND: A Comprehensive Corpora for Training and Benchmarking API LLMs
human_time: Under a minute per utterance to identify the right API(s) and parameters for a single- or multi-intent request; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: 4 of 5 API-BLEND-fine-tuned models (Falcon-40B/MPT-30B/LLaMA-2-7B/StarCoder-15B) beat ToolLLaMA-2-7B and Lynx-7B on every weighted OOD metric
one_line: Five human-annotated dialogue/semantic-parsing corpora repurposed into API-call training data, held against five out-of-distribution tool-benchmark test suites.
notes: items_count (11,976) is a lower bound: it sums the stated test-split sizes of the six paper-authored datasets (SeqSGD/SeqMultiWOZ/SeqATIS/SeqSNIPS/SeqTopV2/SeqToolQA); the four off-the-shelf OOD suites' (ToolBench/ToolLLM/API-Bank/ToolAlpaca) exact item counts aren't stated in the explainer.
placement_reason: Builds a held-out, cross-corpus OOD test suite (ToolLLM/API-Bank/ToolBench/ToolAlpaca plus the new SeqToolQA) to ask whether tool-calling skill generalizes past the exact corpus it was tuned on — a tool-orchestration capability question (detect the API, fill slots, sequence calls), not a grader-hardening paper: API-BLEND doesn't repair a broken metric of an existing benchmark, its own exact-match F1 protocol is new.

title: MedHELM: Holistic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Medical Tasks
human_time: One real clinical task (discharge summary, triage message, billing code, referral note) from a 121-task taxonomy -- minutes for a clinician per task.
frontier_score: DeepSeek R1 (66% win-rate) and o3-mini (64%, highest macro-average at 0.77) lead nine frontier LLMs
one_line: A clinician-validated taxonomy (29 clinicians, 96.7% category agreement) of 5 categories/22 subcategories/121 real clinical tasks, mapped onto a 35-benchmark suite (17 existing, 5 reformulated, 13 new -- 12 EHR-based) and graded by exact-match or a clinician-checked 3-model LLM jury (ICC=0.47 vs. clinician-clinician's 0.43).
notes: items_count=121 tasks (the taxonomy's leaf nodes); the underlying 35 benchmarks each carry their own item counts, not summed here (same convention as BIG-Bench/HELM). 14 of the 35 component benchmarks are held private specifically to keep them out of future LLM training data, hence private-holdout despite 14 others being fully public.
placement_reason: Applies HELM's define-taxonomy/build-suite/define-metrics recipe (transplants-method-of liang-2022-helm) to a single occupation -- clinical practice -- rather than spanning many domains the way HELM itself does; explicitly critiques HealthBench for modeling the LLM as acting alone with no task taxonomy, and builds coverage of the actual clinical workday (documentation, triage, billing, research) instead of exam accuracy, the canonical D2 occupational-competence-suite shape.

title: The Arcade Learning Environment: An Evaluation Platform for General Agents
human_time: Up to 5 minutes real-time per episode (18,000-frame cap); the paper's own evaluation unit.
frontier_score: UCT planning (perfect emulator model) beats all learners on 49/55 games (e.g. 290,700 on Asterix vs. the best learner's 987); best learning agent beats R/C/P baselines on 40/55 games.
one_line: A common interface to hundreds of independently-authored Atari 2600 games with a disjoint train/test split — the benchmark platform pre-LLM deep RL was built on.
notes: No domain in the controlled vocabulary covers 'games'; classified multimodal (primary observation is the raw pixel screen) with reasoning as secondary (strategic play/planning). Saturation from own knowledge (Agent57, 2020, exceeded the human baseline on all games of the later-canonized 57-game Atari list; this paper's own 55-game list and normalization scheme were both superseded, as the explainer's own critique documents).
placement_reason: The title itself calls ALE 'An Evaluation Platform for General Agents': a single interface exposing hundreds of independently-authored Atari games, with a disjoint 5-train/50-test protocol built specifically so 'general competency' has to be demonstrated on held-out tasks rather than claimed — an interactive-environment capability probe (A5's own definition: 'operate an interactive environment'), not a training sandbox. Distinguished from F1-reward-factories (where OpenAI Gym, ALE's direct descendant in this batch, lands): ALE's whole Section 4 is a proposed *evaluation* methodology (three ways to normalize and aggregate scores across incomparable games) with no equivalent training-oriented apparatus, whereas Gym explicitly declines to specify any evaluation protocol at all.

title: SUPER: Evaluating Agents on Setting Up and Executing Tasks from Research Repositories
human_time: Upwork-hired experts ($30-40/hr) solved each task end-to-end within a 4-hour cap (extended to 6h case-by-case) -- real repo setup, dependency debugging, and configuration work, even though the target scripts themselves run CPU-only under 10 minutes.
frontier_score: SWE-Agent+GPT-4o: 16.3%+-2.1% Expert-set Accuracy (36.8% Landmarks); 46.1% Accuracy on the 152 Masked sub-problems (74.9% Landmarks)
one_line: Agents set up and execute real experiments from 45 low-profile (median 14-star) ML/NLP research repos, graded by outcome-based Accuracy plus partial-credit Landmarks; 152 Masked sub-problems and 604 auto-generated tasks extend the set.
notes: items_count=801 sums three differently-built sets (45 Expert + 152 Masked + 604 Auto); the paper's own two headline numbers (16.3%/46.1%) are Expert/Masked only. Complexity is a judgment call: task runtime is capped under 10 minutes, but real solve time (setup, dependency fixes) runs up to hours per the Upwork cap.
placement_reason: Built to test whether an agent can set up AND execute a real experiment from a deliberately obscure, under-documented research repository end-to-end (install deps, configure, run, report a metric) -- median 14 GitHub stars vs. 9,632-35,309 for its named comparators (DS-1000, SWE-bench, ML-Bench), forcing genuine comprehension over pattern-matching a famous repo. Open-ended research-workflow execution is the A8 case; not A4 (SWE-bench-style fix inside a pre-configured repo) or A5 (a built interactive environment), since SUPER's 'environment' is an arbitrary, uncurated GitHub repository.

title: Large-scale Simple Question Answering with Memory Networks
human_time: Seconds per question: a factoid question answerable from a single KB fact.
frontier_score: Best MemNN config 62.1-63.9% path-level accuracy on SimpleQuestions test (no prior published baseline exists to compare against); 41.2-42.2% F1 on WebQuestions.
one_line: 108,442 human-written questions each paired to a single supporting Freebase fact — an order of magnitude larger than the era's WebQuestions.
notes: No external baseline exists in the original paper for SimpleQuestions itself (explicitly stated), so the 62-64% path-accuracy frontier_score is only comparable across the authors' own MemNN variants. Saturation from own knowledge (single-fact KB retrieval is straightforward for modern retrieval-augmented/LLM systems).
placement_reason: A single-fact knowledge-base retrieval probe — read a natural-language question, retrieve the one Freebase fact that answers it — the same 'recognize, parse, retrieve' family A1 already houses SQuAD and TriviaQA under; the paper's own headline concern (does a model trained on one QA source generalize to another) is a generalization study built on top of the capability construct, not a re-framing of what the score measures.

title: A large annotated corpus for learning natural language inference
human_time: Seconds per pair: read two short sentences (14 and 8 tokens on average) and pick entailment/contradiction/neutral.
frontier_score: Best 2015 models: 78.2% (lexicalized feature classifier), 77.6% (100d LSTM); modern models >90%
one_line: 570K crowd-written sentence pairs labeled entailment/contradiction/neutral - the corpus that made neural NLI trainable.
notes: items_count is the 10K test split of the 570,152-pair corpus. Saturation partly from own knowledge (modern models >91%; community treats SNLI as solved and artifact-ridden). Reasoning secondary since entailment is inference, though rubric files NLI under language.
placement_reason: Built to make entailment learnable and measurable at scale — 570K labeled sentence pairs so neural models could finally be trained and tested on natural language inference; the archetypal NLU parse/entail capability corpus (named in the family definition).

title: OpenAI Gym
human_time: Not applicable in the usual sense — no fixed human-performance task; RL agents interact with environments over many training episodes.
frontier_score: No benchmark scores — an infrastructure/interface release; PPO, TRPO, DQN, A3C and most subsequent deep-RL papers report scores using it purely as the environment layer.
one_line: A versioned reset()/step() interface wrapping a growing RL environment suite (Atari, MuJoCo, Go, algorithmic tasks) — the substrate deep RL trained and reported against for years.
notes: This is an infrastructure/interface paper, not a scored benchmark — it ships zero baselines and zero held-out test set, and explicitly favors sample-complexity over final-performance reporting. Classified F1-reward-factories over A5-embodied-operation because the paper's own framing (env.step/reset training loop, no evaluation apparatus, versioned specifically for repeated training runs) matches the training-sandbox pattern of MLGym/Reasoning Gym far more than the eval-protocol pattern of the web-agent benchmarks in A5. domain_primary is a judgment call — no vocabulary term covers 'general RL control/games/robotics'; classified multimodal since most bundled environments (Atari, MuJoCo, VizDoom) are pixel/sensor observation tasks. items_count is null by design — the suite is deliberately open-ended and grew even during the paper's own writing.
placement_reason: The paper is explicit that this ships no evaluation apparatus at all — 'no held-out test set to report,' an explicit preference for sample-complexity (training efficiency) over final-performance reporting, and a design that 'only provides an abstraction for the environment, not the agent' so agents can be trained against it in whatever style researchers choose. That is F1's definition verbatim (a generator/sandbox meant to be trained on, training as the explicit primary use) rather than A5's (an environment an agent is *evaluated* operating) — the field's overwhelming actual use of Gym was as the substrate for training DQN/TRPO/PPO-style agents via millions of environment steps, not as a fixed benchmark score to report.

title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
human_time: Seconds per item: one frontal portrait, one binary gender label.
frontier_score: Overall accuracy 87.9-93.7% (Microsoft best at 93.7%), but darker-female error up to 34.7% (IBM)
one_line: Skin-type-and-gender-balanced face benchmark (PPB) exposing intersectional error gaps in commercial gender classifiers.
notes: Audit paper; classified artifact is the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark. Fairness/bias auditing has no taxonomy bucket, so 'safety' secondary is an imperfect fit. Provenance: images harvested from official parliament portraits (real-work-mined) with expert dermatologist labeling. Saturated per the 2019 follow-up showing vendors patched the gaps; the audit is treated as historical.
placement_reason: Points at the measurement apparatus, not a skill: shows aggregate accuracy on skin-tone-skewed benchmarks certifies systems that fail one in three darker-skinned women, making demographic disaggregation the headline — the canonical construct audit (named in the family definition).

title: nuScenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous driving
human_time: Seconds per item: one 3D box detection/track prediction against a keyframe sampled from a driving scene.
frontier_score: Best 2019 external leaderboard submission (Megvii, lidar) reaches NDS 63.3% / mAP 52.8%; best image-only submission (MonoDIS) reaches NDS 38.4% / mAP 30.4%, well behind lidar.
one_line: 1,000 twenty-second scenes with the first full 360deg AV sensor suite (6 cameras, 5 radars, 1 lidar): 1.4M 3D boxes across 23 classes, plus NDS/sAMOTA composite metrics using center-distance matching instead of IoU so small objects don't score 0 AP by construction.
notes: Provenance is a judgment call: raw sensor data is purpose-collected by a dedicated driving campaign (not crowdsourced, not exam-derived, not synthetic) -- classified real-work-mined as the closest fit (real-world driving activity, distinct from crowdsourced photo/text collection). Saturation ('closing') reflects own knowledge that nuScenes detection leaderboard NDS scores rose substantially in the years after this paper (well past the reported 63.3%), though the 1:10,000 long-tail class imbalance the paper itself flags as unsolved likely still limits full saturation. contamination_defense reflects the leaderboard/external-submission structure described in the paper, though no explicit description of submission-frequency limits or a private/public split protocol is given.
placement_reason: A perception capability probe for autonomous driving -- 3D object detection and tracking from a full 360-degree multi-sensor rig, scored via a metric (NDS) purpose-built to correct IoU's small-object bias -- recognize-and-localize is the headline skill tested, not vehicle control, so A1 rather than an interactive-operation family despite the driving-domain framing.

title: Can It Edit? Evaluating the Ability of Large Language Models to Follow Code Editing Instructions
human_time: A few minutes per problem for an experienced Python dev to write/verify a small edit (avg 42.5→49.8 lines, Levenshtein diff 302 chars); not stated exactly by the paper.
frontier_score: GPT-4 63.33/51.95 pass@1 (descriptive/lazy); fine-tuned EditCoder-33B reaches 55.90/42.33, beating GPT-3.5-Turbo on descriptive
one_line: 105 hand-written Python code-editing problems (210 with paired descriptive/lazy instructions), scored pass@1 against a hidden test suite.
notes: domain_secondary instruction-following reflects the paper's central descriptive-vs-lazy instruction-sensitivity finding, not just code correctness; grading is pass@1 against a hidden test suite (programmatic), not a fuzzy exact-match.
placement_reason: Asks whether a model can correctly transform existing code given a natural-language instruction, checked pass@1 against a hidden test suite exactly like HumanEval/MBPP — a program-synthesis question with an added instruction-phrasing axis, not primarily a communication/instruction-following benchmark (A7): the graded deliverable is code correctness, not conversational compliance, and the paper's own comparison set (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-Bench) is entirely A4's family.

title: SemEval-2017 Task 1: Semantic Textual Similarity Multilingual and Crosslingual Focused Evaluation
human_time: Seconds per pair: read two short sentences and rate similarity on a 0-5 scale.
frontier_score: ECNU best overall (avg. Pearson r=0.7316 across tracks 1-5); on the STS-B test split, ECNU 81.0 vs. sentence-embedding baselines InferSent 75.8, GloVe 40.6.
one_line: 8,628 sentence pairs (STS Benchmark) scored 0-5 for semantic similarity — the fixed sentence-embedding yardstick nearly every paper since (InferSent...SimCSE) reports against.
notes: Saturation ('saturated') is supported by the explainer's own critique: the same 1,379-pair test split has been reported against essentially unchanged for eight-plus years and is the default sentence-embedding yardstick even after transformer-era encoders substantially closed the 2017 gap.
placement_reason: Scores graded semantic similarity between two sentences on a fixed 0-5 scale — a parse/understand-meaning capability construct matching A1's SNLI precedent (both descend from the same 'can a model judge sentence-pair semantic relationship' probe family); STS-B's own sentence pool is explicitly re-paired from SNLI. Not B4, despite this survey's own critique flagging real construct-validity gaps (Table 12's failure modes, the 0.41 STS-vs-MT-quality correlation): the *original paper* frames its contribution as consolidating five fragmented years of STS data into one fixed, citable artifact, not as an audit exposing an existing benchmark's score to mean something else.

title: LexGLUE: A Benchmark Dataset for Legal Language Understanding in English
human_time: Most items are per-provision/per-sentence classification or a 5-way CaseHOLD MCQ (~1-10 min); long ECtHR/SCOTUS judgment-prediction cases push toward 30+ min but are the minority of items.
frontier_score: Legal-BERT leads the harmonic-mean aggregate at 70.8 macro-F1 / 78.9 micro-F1 (UNFAIR-ToS ~96 micro-F1, LEDGAR ~88)
one_line: GLUE-for-law: seven English legal-NLU classification/QA datasets unified behind one micro/macro-F1 leaderboard.
notes: Borderline domain: tasks are classic NLU classification (language) but over legal expert material - filed as professional (law) per the LegalBench precedent, language secondary. items_count is the approximate combined test splits (~23.9K); saturation judged in the fine-tuning era the explainer reports.
placement_reason: Born as the 'GLUE for law': seven English legal-NLU tasks (judgment prediction, contract clauses, legal QA) unified behind one leaderboard to test whether models can do practitioner-relevant legal work. The task style is GLUE-like NLU (A1 pull), but the content is wholly occupational — law and contracts, expert-curated, explicitly favoring legal expertise where SuperGLUE excluded it — and D2's occupational-content-beats-framing rule places legal/contract competence suites (LegalBench-style, which LexGLUE is the direct ancestor of) here.

title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
human_time: Paper's own complexity annotation for an ML engineer today: 30% Low (<2 h), 50% Medium (2-10 h), 20% High (>10 h) - typical instance is several hours.
frontier_score: o1-preview + AIDE earns a medal in 16.9% of competitions (pass@1), 34.1% at pass@8
one_line: 75 hand-ported Kaggle competitions where agents do end-to-end ML engineering, medal-graded against real human leaderboards.
notes: Contamination: the paper runs honest probes (familiarity r=-0.24, obfuscation 8.5->8.4) but ships no structural defense - all data is public Kaggle, so none-public. Anti-cheat (Dolos plagiarism, log analyzer) is rule enforcement, not contamination defense.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can an agent do machine-learning engineering end-to-end?' — read an open-ended problem, prepare data, train, debug, budget compute, iterate autonomously over 24 hours, anchored to real Kaggle human leaderboards. This is open-ended knowledge work executed end-to-end, the literal A8 exemplar (MLE-bench-style). The safety/autonomy-dial framing is motivation, not the measured object; the headline is agent skill at ML engineering.

title: NegotiationToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind on Negotiation Surrounding
human_time: One truncated conversation round (avg. 42.2-token turns) answered across 7 questions (3 desire, 3 belief, 1 intention); a few minutes for a human, matching the CS-grad human baseline.
frontier_score: Best model trails human annotators by 27.85 (desire) to 48.98 (intention) points across three mental-state axes, even with chain-of-thought
one_line: Real human-to-human negotiation dialogues (CaSiNo) annotated for desire/belief/intention at every round, testing whether LLMs track a negotiating partner's evolving mental state -- not synthetic Sally-Anne templates.
notes: Domain is a least-bad fit: BENCH_DOMAINS has no theory-of-mind slot, so classified social-moral per the survey's established convention (theory-of-mind/social-cognition papers go here) even though the tested construct is mental-state tracking accuracy, not moral judgment. items_count = 13.8K questions across 395 dialogues / 2,380 rounds / 4,618 utterances. Desire/belief are newly annotated (Fleiss kappa 79%); intention labels are inherited from CaSiNo's own strategy annotations. Real ancestors (FANToM, ToMi) exist as graph nodes but aren't yet in this taxonomy or my batch, so lineage is empty despite the paper explicitly building against them.
placement_reason: The headline is a capability verdict, not an audit or hazard measure: even with CoT, the best of six 2023-era LLMs trails human annotators by 28-49 points at tracking a negotiating partner's desire/belief/intention round-by-round in a real dialogue -- a conversational mental-state-tracking probe extending LoCoMo's memory-across-sessions framing to mental-state coherence within a single real negotiation, A7's territory rather than E3's moral-judgment-quality (no values/ethics content here) or D3's human-in-the-loop collaboration (both parties are dataset dialogue, not a live human partner).

title: JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
human_time: One behavior yields one ~150-token response (harmful or refused); a human writing a comparable how-to would take a few minutes.
frontier_score: Prompt+RS (strongest attack) hits 89-93% ASR on 3 of 4 models and still 78% on GPT-4, at ~2-3 queries avg; no defense uniformly stops it (8-25% ASR survives Erase-and-Check)
one_line: 100-behavior open jailbreak-robustness benchmark (JBB-Behaviors) with a human-validated open judge (Llama-3-70B) and a public leaderboard for attacks and defenses.
notes: 100 harmful + 100 matched-benign behaviors (the benign set is a built-in over-refusal check, not counted in items_count). 55% of behaviors original to this paper, 27% from TDC/HarmBench, 18% from AdvBench -> aggregated. Judge chosen from 6 candidates against a 300-example human-labeled set (Llama-3-70B: 90.7% agreement, open-weight, statistically tied with GPT-4's 90.3%).
placement_reason: Standardizes the incomparable jailbreak-ASR literature into one artifact repository, harm taxonomy, and judge -- the measured object is attack success / robust refusal (risk), not skill, the same territory as HarmBench. Narrower scope than HarmBench (4 models, adaptive-attack and multimodal explicitly out) but sharper judge-selection rigor (a human-labeled ground truth actually used to pick among 6 judge candidates); not B2, since no single prior benchmark's grader is being hardened -- it standardizes a fragmented field, the same E1 role as its own named exemplar.

title: Microsoft COCO Captions: Data Collection and Evaluation Server
human_time: ~30-60s per image to write one descriptive caption, per the AMT instruction set (>=8 words, literal, present-tense).
frontier_score: No model scores reported; human-vs-human agreement ceiling given instead — CIDEr-D 0.854, BLEU-4 0.217, METEOR 0.252 at the standard 5-reference setting.
one_line: Five human captions per COCO image plus a hidden-test-set evaluation server, standardizing BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE/CIDEr-D scoring across captioning papers.
notes: The paper itself reports zero model scores (only human-vs-human agreement), so frontier_score is the human ceiling, not a model number. Saturation ('saturated') is inferred from own knowledge — n-gram-overlap captioning metrics on COCO are widely treated as gamed/near-ceiling, and the field moved to CLIPScore-style reference-free metrics, a shift the explainer's own critique documents.
placement_reason: Standardizes the captioning capability probe (generate a natural-language description of an image) that was previously fragmented across incomparable per-paper eval setups — the classic image-to-language perception/generation construct A1 already houses (VQA, COCO itself); the eval-server and CIDEr-D modification are instrumentation in service of measuring that construct, not a meta-evaluation study of grading itself (no judge/grader is the object being tested — human-vs-human agreement is reported as a ceiling, not audited as a construct).

title: MedDialog: A Large-scale Medical Dialogue Dataset
human_time: A multi-turn doctor-patient consultation - reading the patient's history/symptoms and composing an appropriate multi-turn medical reply would take a human minutes; these are crawled real consultations, not benchmark items with one designed answer.
frontier_score: No capability leaderboard - internal ablation only: MedDialog-CN pretraining improves perplexity (53.3 to 13.7) and BLEU-2 (5.7% to 7.8%) on the CovidDialog-CN transfer task, and raises human-rated human-likeness from 2.57 to 3.29 (ceiling 3.78)
one_line: A crawled patient-doctor consultation corpus (3.4M Chinese / 257K English dialogues per the EMNLP camera-ready) built to pretrain medical dialogue generation and transfer it to low-resource tasks like COVID-19 consultation.
notes: LIKELY MIS-TAG, flagged for the survey author/critic: this paper's primary contribution is a crawled pretraining corpus plus a transfer-learning demonstration (fine-tune on a tiny 1,088-dialogue COVID set), not a graded evaluation benchmark - the explainer's own critique notes there is 'no human evaluation... on the full MedDialog-CN benchmark itself,' only on the small downstream transfer task. This looks like a training dataset that merely enables a downstream task, which the survey's own membership rubric (Procedure D) excludes. items_count uses the EMNLP camera-ready's CN figure (3,407,494); the arXiv v2 body text states a materially different, internally-inconsistent 1,145,231 for the same release, per the explainer's own critique - a real, unresolved discrepancy in the source paper, not a transcription choice made here.
placement_reason: The paper's own stated purpose is a pretraining corpus for medical dialogue generation plus a transfer-learning demonstration (fine-tune on the tiny CovidDialog-CN set) - training on the corpus, not scoring against a fixed graded benchmark, is the explicit primary use, matching F1's 'generators and sandboxes meant to be trained on' definition; the paper reports no human evaluation on the full corpus itself, only on the downstream transfer task, reinforcing that MedDialog functions as training fuel rather than an evaluation instrument.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
human_time: Each item is one self-contained function from a docstring at easy software-interview difficulty - a few minutes for a competent programmer.
frontier_score: Codex-S 12B: 37.7% pass@1, 77.5% oracle pass@100 (paper-era); community now treats HumanEval as solved
one_line: HumanEval: 164 hand-written Python problems graded by executing hidden unit tests; origin of pass@k and execution grading.
notes: Problems were hand-written to avoid training overlap - creation-time hygiene, but the set shipped fully public with no holdout, so none-public (explainer notes it later leaked into corpora). Saturation call uses community consensus beyond the file's 2021 numbers.
placement_reason: HumanEval's birth question is 'can a code-specialized GPT actually write correct programs?' — 164 hand-written function-synthesis problems graded by executing hidden unit tests, with the headline being Codex's pass rates (28.8% pass@1). The execution-grading + pass@k methodology is a huge side contribution, but the paper's claim is about model skill at writing code, making it the founding A4 capability probe.

title: FinQA: A Dataset of Numerical Reasoning over Financial Data
human_time: One question over a single filing page with a <=5-step arithmetic chain; experts wrote ~2 questions/page at ~$35/hr (~3-4 min/question), so answering is a few minutes for an analyst.
frontier_score: FinQANet (RoBERTa-large): 61.24% execution accuracy vs 91.16% for human finance experts
one_line: 8,281 expert-written numerical-reasoning questions over real S&P 500 filings, each with a gold executable arithmetic program.
notes: Domain judged by the work's nature (financial-analyst reasoning) -> professional, math secondary. items_count is the test split (1,147 of 8,281 total). Headline execution accuracy is numeric exact-match; program accuracy adds a symbolic-equivalence programmatic check. Saturation: explainer says modern LLMs 'largely closed' the 30-point gap but quotes no modern number - closing, from own knowledge.
placement_reason: Asks whether models 'could do an analyst's actual job': multi-step numerical reasoning over real S&P 500 earnings filings, with questions only CPAs/MBAs could write and a finance-expert human ceiling (91.16%) as the bar. The measured skill is checkable arithmetic-program reasoning (A3 pull), but the set is defined by professional financial-analysis competence — D2's occupational-content-beats-framing rule and its FinanceBench-style family (which FinQA founded) place it here.

title: A Benchmark for Automatic Medical Consultation System: Frameworks, Tasks and Datasets
human_time: A few minutes to read and label one consultation; the corpus averages roughly 40 utterances per dialogue (164,731 utterances / 4,116 dialogues) -- a full pediatric telemedicine session, not a single turn.
frontier_score: Best per task: ERNIE-Health NER F1 91.24, DAC Acc 82.37; HRL DDP DX-Acc 0.556 vs. a 0.706 perfect-symptom-collector upper bound
one_line: 4,116 real Chinese pediatric-telemedicine consultations (164,731 utterances), annotated at token/utterance/dialogue level and packaged into five shared-split tasks spanning NER through diagnosis-oriented dialogue policy.
notes: Occupational medical-domain benchmark like its sibling CBLUE (which it cites and reuses baselines from, e.g. MC-BERT). DDP's patient simulator is a lookup function over gold-labeled symptom data, not a language-based patient, so DX-Acc/SX-Rec measure policy-learning over structured slots rather than a full doctor-patient interaction loop. Table 4's ERNIE-Health NER recall (2.82) is very likely a transcription error inconsistent with its own reported F1/precision, per the explainer's critique.
placement_reason: Real pediatric telemedicine consultations (Muzhi, 10 diseases) packaged into the sub-tasks an automatic medical-consultation system needs -- NER, dialogue-act classification, symptom inference, report generation, diagnosis policy -- occupational clinical-consultation competence, the same design center as CBLUE and Med-PaLM/MultiMedQA; the individual sub-tasks look like A-family skills (NER, classification) but the professional-domain content and shared clinical-consultation framing place the whole benchmark in D2.

title: ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery
human_time: Each task's gold solution averages 58.6 lines of domain-specific Python (bio/chem/geo/psych); a domain expert with the paper's own reference approach in hand needs on the order of tens of minutes to reproduce it.
frontier_score: Claude-3.5-Sonnet + Self-Debug + expert knowledge: 34.3% Success Rate (32.4% without knowledge); OpenAI o1-preview reaches 42.2% as a cost-unmatched reference (10x the API cost)
one_line: 102 tasks distilled from 44 peer-reviewed papers across four sciences, each reduced to one verifiable, execution-graded Python program with built-in shortcut/contamination countermeasures (dropped test points, dummy labels).
notes: Two concrete, targeted contamination/shortcut mitigations (random test-point removal; dummy placeholder test labels) are built directly into the data, motivated by an observed real shortcut (OpenHands reading ground-truth labels) -- among the stronger such stories in this batch, though still classified none-public since neither is a live-refresh or holdout mechanism.
placement_reason: Built as a direct rebuttal to end-to-end 'AI automates science' claims (e.g. The AI Scientist): isolates individual, verifiable steps of real data-driven discovery workflows sourced from actual peer-reviewed code rather than grading a whole generated paper -- open-ended scientific knowledge work executed end-to-end, the A8 case; distinguished from CORE-Bench by targeting novel analysis-code production rather than reproducing a paper's own already-written code.

title: T-Eval: Evaluating the Tool Utilization Capability of Large Language Models Step by Step
human_time: Under a minute per micro-decision (next thought/tool/parameter) for a human annotator judging one step against the gold path; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4 86.4 Overall (Dec 2023 snapshot); best open model Qwen-72B 71.4
one_line: Six separately-graded tool-use sub-abilities (plan/reason/retrieve/understand/instruct/review), scored step-by-step against a frozen, human-verified gold solution path.
notes: tool_access set to domain-api since T-Eval's 15 hand-curated tools span generic domains (Research/Travel/Entertainment/Web/Life/Financials); grading blends Sentence-BERT-based PLAN scoring and strict JSON exact-match, both rule-based (not LLM-judged), hence programmatic as primary.
placement_reason: Decomposes 'can an LLM use tools' into six inspectable sub-abilities graded against a frozen gold path — a fine-grained tool-orchestration capability probe (à la Gorilla/API-Bank, which it explicitly critiques for grading only outcomes or single-step calls), not a grader-hardening paper: T-Eval doesn't rebuild another benchmark's broken metric, it decomposes a capability into six of its own.

title: ToMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models
human_time: A minute or two per question: read a short social vignette and answer one MCQ; the paper's 20-student human baseline needed no extra tutorial.
frontier_score: Human 85.4% (task view) / 86.1% (ability view) vs. best model GPT-4-1106 75.3%; gap widens to 16.2 points under the paper's own coherent test
one_line: 2,860 bilingual multiple-choice questions across 8 psychology-grounded ToM tasks and 31 ATOMS abilities, written entirely from scratch.
placement_reason: Asks whether a model can infer another's emotions/beliefs/intentions from an original social vignette — a from-scratch capability probe explicitly engineered to avoid the memorization risk of recombined psychology inventories (its own Appendix A shows GPT-4 reciting the Sally-Anne scenario verbatim when asked with no context), not an audit of an existing ToM benchmark's grading or construct.

title: ACEBench: Who Wins the Match Point in Tool Usage?
human_time: Normal/Special items are single or short-chain API calls (seconds); Agent items run genuine multi-turn sandbox dialogues against mobile-app/food-delivery/banking/travel scenarios -- minutes each for a human with the same tools.
frontier_score: GPT-4o: 85.4% overall (93.0% Special, 63.8% Agent); best open-source model Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct: 79.6%, ahead of five of seven closed-source models tested
one_line: 2,000 Chinese/English-parallel tool-use items split into Normal (clean instructions, AST-matched), Special (broken/irrelevant instructions, graded on defect detection), and Agent (multi-turn sandbox execution) regimes, all scored deterministically without an LLM judge.
notes: task_shape=interactive-env reflects the Agent category's genuine multi-turn, stateful sandbox (the paper's most distinctive contribution), even though the Normal and Special categories -- the large majority of the 2,000 items -- are single-shot function-call generation. Models fine-tuned specifically for tool-calling (Watt-Tool-8B, xLAM-7B-r, Hammer2.1) collapse on Special (down to single digits for three of four), rarely even detecting that an instruction is broken.
placement_reason: Explicitly built to check more boxes than prior tool-use benchmarks at once (LLM-free grading, robustness to broken instructions, interactivity, atomic-parameter isolation, personalization) -- by the paper's own comparison table, no prior benchmark (MetaTool, API-Bank, BFCL, tau-bench, HammerBench) checks more than two; the Special category specifically tests whether a model recognizes a bad tool call rather than blindly executing it -- tool selection/sequencing competence under both clean and adversarial-instruction conditions, the A6 case.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Answering and Explaining Challenging Medical Questions
human_time: Several minutes per item: read a real clinical case or USMLE-style vignette and choose/justify an answer; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4 drops from 78.63% (MedQA-4) to 66.23% (Medbullets-4) and 53.33% (JAMA, 4-choice)
one_line: 1,524 real JAMA Clinical Challenge cases + 308 post-2022 Medbullets USMLE-style questions, both with expert explanations, scored on answer accuracy and explanation quality.
notes: provenance expert-authored covers both sources (JAMA's editorial Clinical Challenge cases and Medbullets' USMLE-style question bank), neither of which is raw real-work-mined or a literal licensing exam (Medbullets mimics USMLE Step 2/3 but isn't the real exam).
placement_reason: Tests whether a model can both answer and *explain* real, difficult clinical cases and post-cutoff USMLE-style questions — professional-domain competence with an explanation-quality axis MedQA/MedMCQA never had, the canonical occupational-probe pattern (à la Med-PaLM/HealthBench) rather than a raw A2 knowledge-exam recall test, since the paper's own novel contribution is scoring explanations, not just answers.

title: RoboTwin 2.0: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark with Strong Domain Randomization for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
human_time: One bimanual manipulation task (e.g. a pick-and-place or tool-use routine) -- a couple of minutes for a person; the 'subject' being scored is a trained policy, not a zero-shot LLM.
frontier_score: Domain-randomized synthetic pretraining lifts RDT/Pi0 by +31.9%/+29.3% relative over their released-pretrained baselines; 10 real demos + 1,000 synthetic trajectories add a 24.4-point average real-robot success-rate gain
one_line: An MLLM-driven, self-repairing code-generation pipeline plus five axes of domain randomization turn a 731-object asset library into 50 dual-arm manipulation tasks and 100,000+ synthetic trajectories across 5 embodiments; the paper's own ablations show the randomization itself, not just more synthetic data, drives sim-to-real robustness gains.
notes: domain_primary=multimodal per this batch's convention for robotics/manipulation (BENCH_DOMAINS has no robotics slot); least-bad fit, noted per instructions. contamination_defense=procedural: each scene is generated fresh via 5 axes of randomization (clutter, background, lighting, height, language) rather than drawn from a fixed set, similar to AndroidWorld's seeded-parameterization defense. Kingdom judgment call: the title and headline result both center on the DATA GENERATOR (100,000+ trajectories) driving policy-training gains (RDT/Pi0 sim-to-real numbers), with the 50-task Easy/Hard suite riding on top as the evaluation apparatus -- the same 'generator whose primary use is training' shape as MLGym/Reasoning Gym, not a pure environment-operation probe like OSWorld/AppWorld (A5) where no training-data-generation claim is the headline.
placement_reason: The paper's headline empirical claim is about training data, not a leaderboard: domain-randomized synthetic pretraining (not merely more synthetic data) measurably improves sim-to-real policy robustness for RDT and Pi0, and the object shipped is explicitly a 'Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark' where the generator is named first -- the F1 reward-factory pattern (a sandbox meant to be trained on, with evaluation riding along), not a pure capability probe.

title: EmbodiedEval: Evaluate Multimodal LLMs as Embodied Agents
human_time: Expert demonstrations average 10.72 steps per episode; the non-expert human baseline reaches 97.26% success through the same interface, a task of a few minutes each.
frontier_score: GPT-4o: 25.00% Success / 32.42% Goal-condition Success (best of 19 evaluated MLLMs) vs. a 97.26% non-expert human baseline; Random agent: 5.49%
one_line: 328 tasks across 125 3D scenes and 5 categories (navigation, object interaction, social interaction, attribute QA, spatial QA), scored via a discrete candidate-action interface; the best of 19 MLLMs (GPT-4o) reaches just 25.00% success against a 97.26% non-expert human baseline.
notes: The paper itself is internally inconsistent about its own size (Dataset Statistics/Figure 4 say 328 tasks, the Limitations section says 327); 328 used per the more prominent statement. tool_access=domain-api reflects the simulator's structured action-selection interface (LEGENT), not real code execution or an external API. provenance=synthetic-generated reflects that a large share of scenes/tasks are LLM-generated (GPT-3.5/Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini-1.5-Flash) then expert-reviewed -- the paper does not discuss the resulting contamination risk of evaluating GPT-4-family and Gemini models against a benchmark partly built by GPT-3.5/Claude/Gemini.
placement_reason: Purpose-built to test MLLMs as embodied decision-makers inside a real interactive 3D simulator across navigation, object interaction, social interaction, and QA -- checking every box (scene diversity, task diversity, MLLM-native discrete action space, egocentric vision) a comparison table shows no predecessor (ALFRED, BEHAVIOR, OpenEQA, EQA-MX) checks all of at once -- the direct A5 case: operate an interactive environment via egocentric vision.

title: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference
human_time: A typical battle is a short open-ended chat prompt (~95 tokens, avg 1.3 turns) - answering well takes a human a few minutes.
one_line: Live crowdsourced arena: users prompt two anonymous models, vote the winner; Bradley-Terry turns ~240K votes into an Elo leaderboard.
notes: Task shape: real-user dialogue averaging 1.3 turns - mostly single-turn in practice but multi-turn by design. No fixed item set (243,329 conversations at the paper's snapshot), so items_count null; relative leaderboard with no ceiling -> saturation not-applicable.
placement_reason: The contribution is not a task set but an evaluation protocol: live anonymous pairwise battles, Bradley-Terry ranking with multiplicity-corrected confidence intervals, active sampling, and anomaly detection — machinery for turning crowd human preference into a leaderboard. Built explicitly against the static ground-truth benchmark paradigm (frozen, contaminated, no ground truth for open-ended chat). The named G2 exemplar.

title: MoReBench: Evaluating Procedural and Pluralistic Moral Reasoning in Language Models, More than Outcomes
human_time: One 44-393-word dilemma answered with a thorough reasoned trace hitting ~23 criteria - roughly 15-30 min for an expert (validation experts wrote such traces by hand).
frontier_score: Models satisfy 72.0-85.5% of harmlessness criteria (best 85.5%, GPT-5-mini) but only up to 65.1% of logical-process criteria (Qwen3-235B)
one_line: 1,000 moral dilemmas graded on the reasoning process via 23,018 philosopher-written weighted criteria scored by an LLM judge.
notes: Secondary safety: 41.4% of scenarios are AI-safety-flavored Moral Agent dilemmas and harmlessness is a scored dimension. A 150-scenario MoReBench-Theory sibling is excluded from items_count. Saturation is a judgment call from per-dimension 48-85% satisfaction rates - roughly 'closing' but the metric has no clean ceiling.
placement_reason: Grades the quality of moral reasoning itself: 1,000 dilemmas with 23,018 philosopher-written criteria scoring whether a model's thinking trace surfaces the right considerations and weighs pluralistic values — the object is moral/ethical judgment quality, the named E3 exemplar. The rubric-grading machinery (G3 flavor) is instrumentation in service of measuring the values construct, not the contribution's object.

title: On the Measure of Intelligence
human_time: Not explicitly timed - three high-IQ humans solved every task without practice or verbal explanation; grid puzzles (up to 30x30 cells, ~3.3 demonstration pairs on average) plausibly take a human several minutes each, longer for harder tasks.
frontier_score: ARC ships as 1,000 tasks (400 train / 400 public eval / 200 private eval); no baseline model scores are reported in this launch paper; every task was solved by at least one of 3 informal high-IQ human solvers; the corpus later saturated under heavy test-time-compute approaches, prompting the 2025 successor ARC-AGI-2
one_line: 1,000 visual abstraction/reasoning grid puzzles (400 train / 400 public eval / 200 private eval) built on explicit 'Core Knowledge' priors, introduced alongside a formal Kolmogorov-complexity definition of intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency rather than raw task performance.
notes: Kingdom/family placement (C2 vs a plain A3 capability-probe reading) is a genuine judgment call - see placement_reason. Saturation 'saturated' is directly textual: the explainer's own critique states ARC 'has itself become a target for exactly the buy performance with unlimited resources pattern' and needed a 2025 successor (ARC-AGI-2) once it 'saturated under heavy test-time-compute approaches.'
placement_reason: Explicitly designed to resist the 'buy skill with unlimited priors/compute' failure mode the paper's own formalism diagnoses (chess/Go/Dota moonshots): a private 200-task holdout, Core Knowledge priors instead of learnable/expert domain facts, and binary exact-grid-match scoring that is trivial to verify but was, for years, hard for any system to pass - closer to C2's 'hard to solve, engineered easy to verify' than C1's expert-exam framing, since ARC deliberately avoids expert/acquired knowledge in favor of near-universal human priors; the durable-difficulty design goal (later validated when ARC itself needed ARC-AGI-2) is a frontier-wall case, not a plain capability probe.

title: Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge
human_time: Seconds per item: one grade-school multiple-choice science question (3-5 options).
frontier_score: Best 2018 baseline (DGEM) reaches 27.11% on the Challenge Set, inside the paper's own +/-2.5% 95% CI around the 25.02% random-guess floor -- effectively chance; Easy Set scores land 50-65%.
one_line: 7,787 real grade-school science questions split into an Easy Set (5,197) and a Challenge Set (2,590), defined operationally as questions both an IR solver and a PMI solver answer incorrectly -- every 2018 baseline stays within noise of random guessing on Challenge.
notes: items_count uses the Challenge Set (2,590), the subset the benchmark is named for and the one every later citation reports against; the Easy Set (5,197) exists alongside it. Saturation is from own knowledge -- the explainer's own numbers show 2018 baselines at chance, but ARC-Challenge is now a standard, largely-solved component of modern LLM eval suites.
placement_reason: Real standardized-test science questions partitioned by construction into an Easy Set two simple retrieval baselines already solve and a Challenge Set neither can -- an exam-conditions knowledge probe (A2, exam-derived provenance) whose entire design exists to rule out the retrieval shortcuts that make a knowledge exam trivial rather than genuinely hard.

title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
human_time: Grade-school word problems of 2-8 steps; a competent adult solves one in roughly 1-5 minutes (the rubric's own L2 exemplar).
frontier_score: frontier models exceeded 95% within a couple of years (paper-era best: 175B verifier ~55% vs ~33% finetuned)
one_line: 8.5K human-written grade-school math word problems (1K test) graded by final-answer match; the default math-reasoning yardstick.
notes: Provenance from own knowledge: problems written by contracted Surge AI workers (quality-controlled crowdworkers), not domain experts; explainer only says 'human-written'. The paper's own eval injects calculator annotations that override arithmetic at test time, but standard benchmark use is pure text-in/text-out, so tool_access=none.
placement_reason: Born to ask 'can LMs do multi-step grade-school math word problems yet?' — checkable final answers in a deliberate difficulty sweet spot between toy sets and the then-intractable MATH; headline is model solve rate on the skill (plus the verifier method).

title: XNLI: Evaluating Cross-lingual Sentence Representations
human_time: Seconds per pair: read a translated premise/hypothesis pair and pick entailment/contradiction/neutral.
frontier_score: TRANSLATE-TEST (BiLSTM-max) beats every other method in all 15 languages: 70.7% Spanish down to 59.3% Urdu vs. a 73.7% English ceiling; the paper's own aligned multilingual-encoder method (X-BiLSTM) trails by up to 6 points.
one_line: MultiNLI-style dev/test sentence pairs professionally translated into 14 more languages (112,500 pairs, 15 languages total) to benchmark cross-lingual NLI transfer strategies -- translate-then-classify beat every multilingual sentence-encoder alignment method tested, in every language.
notes: Zero-shot mBERT/XLM/XLM-R evaluation on the same test sets became standard within a couple of years and pushes accuracy well past the paper's own numbers; treated as saturated. Provenance is crowdsourced for the underlying English content (7,500 pairs collected via the identical MultiNLI pipeline); the translation step itself has no separate category in the controlled vocabulary.
placement_reason: The first large sentence-level, human-validated NLI capability probe extended across 15 languages -- testing whether cross-lingual transfer strategies can do genuine three-way entailment outside English -- a straightforward entailment capability benchmark (A1's named exemplar construct, extended multilingually), distinct from the later audit (MultiLoKo) that questions whether translate-the-benchmark construction measures real cross-lingual understanding.

title: MuTual: A Dataset for Multi-Turn Dialogue Reasoning
group: Microsoft Research Asia / Zhejiang University / Westlake University
human_time: Seconds per item: read a short (4.7-turn avg) dialogue and pick the best of four candidate next utterances; three NLP experts set the human ceiling.
frontier_score: Best 2020 model RoBERTa (individual scoring) 71.3% Test R@1 vs. 93.8% 3-expert human ceiling; TF-IDF barely clears the 25% random floor at 27.9%
one_line: 8,860 Chinese-exam-derived four-candidate next-utterance-selection items testing multi-turn dialogue reasoning (intention/multi-fact/situation/attitude/algebraic), not surface matching.
notes: Task shape is multi-turn dialogue context with a single next-response selection, hence 'multi-turn' over 'single-turn' despite the model emitting one classification. Saturation judged from own knowledge: this is a 4-way MC dialogue-reasoning task well within frontier-LLM reach, not benchmarked against modern LLMs in the paper itself (pre-LLM, 2020).
placement_reason: Rewrites Chinese English-exam listening-comprehension items into a response-selection task explicitly built to demand tracking intentions, multi-fact combination, and situational inference across a conversation, not just language-model fluency — a conversational-reasoning capability probe (A7) rather than A3's context-free logic puzzles, since the object being measured is dialogue-context reasoning specifically.

title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
human_time: One borderline prompt, one answer-or-refuse decision; the graded refusal judgment takes a human seconds (a full helpful answer might take a minute or two).
frontier_score: Llama-3.1-70B 3.0% over-refusal on Hard-1K (lowest in study); GPT-4o 6.7%; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 43.8%
one_line: 80K auto-generated borderline-benign prompts (plus Hard-1K and ~600 toxic) measuring over-refusal vs safety across models.
notes: Grading: headline Hard-1K/Toxic numbers use a GPT-4 refusal judge (no per-item rubric -> llm-judge); the full 80K uses keyword refusal matching, which I coded as programmatic. Contamination_defense=procedural is borderline: the released 80K is a static public set, but the fully automated Mixtral+ensemble pipeline is shipped and pitched as re-runnable to regenerate fresh borderline prompts. Saturation 'closing': best models sit within a few points of the ~1.8% label-noise floor on over-refusal, but the joint safe-AND-helpful objective is unsolved (Spearman 0.89 trade-off) and the Claude family still refuses heavily.
placement_reason: The instrument points at what safety scores really mean: 'safe' models buy safety by refusing benign prompts (Spearman 0.89 coupling). Headline finding is about the safety construct's validity, not a new skill — the canonical over-refusal audit.

title: The PASCAL Recognising Textual Entailment Challenge
human_time: Seconds per pair: read a short text and hypothesis (usually one or two sentences) and judge entailment.
frontier_score: Best 2005 system (Perez, Madrid) 0.700 accuracy / 0.782 cws; most systems clustered 50-60% accuracy, at or below a naive always-true baseline (f=0.67).
one_line: 1,367 hand-annotated text-hypothesis pairs across 7 application settings defining Recognising Textual Entailment as a shared task — direct ancestor of SNLI/MultiNLI/GLUE.
notes: Provenance is genuine multi-source aggregation across 7 application settings (IR, comparable documents, reading comprehension, QA, IE, MT, paraphrase acquisition), not a single collection method. Saturation judged from own knowledge (modern entailment models trivially exceed the reported 50-60% band; RTE was folded unmodified into GLUE/SuperGLUE and is long since solved there).
placement_reason: Defines a generic three-way entailment-recognition construct and ships the first shared benchmark for it — the archetypal NLU parse/entail capability corpus, matching A1's own SNLI/MultiNLI precedent (RTE is their direct, explicitly-cited ancestor). Not B-audit: this is the founding artifact establishing the construct, not a later paper exposing that an existing entailment score means something else.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
human_time: Typical user task is an office chore (summarize emails and forward, make a bank transfer, book travel) a human finishes in a few minutes with the same tools.
frontier_score: best agents hijacked in <25% of cases under the strongest generic attack (~8% with a detector); benign utility <66%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet best trade-off
one_line: Stateful gym of 70 tools/97 tasks/629 injection cases testing tool-using agents against indirect prompt injection, scored by Python state checks.
notes: Environments and tasks hand-built by the ETH authors (dummy data LLM-generated then manually inspected) -> expert-authored. Contamination defense: fully synthetic data and an extensible attack/defense framework mitigate staleness, but nothing fits private-holdout/live-refresh, so none-public. Saturation 'open' reads the security+utility joint objective; ASR alone has no clean ceiling.
placement_reason: Built to measure attack surface: indirect prompt injection hijacking tool-using agents, scored on attacker success (ASR) vs utility. The object is risk — agent hijacking and defenses — not a new skill; explicitly fixes InjecAgent's single-shot setting.

title: ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database
human_time: Recognizing the object category in one image takes a human seconds (fine-grained synsets like Burmese cat a bit longer).
one_line: 3.2M web-crawled, MTurk-verified images over 5,247 WordNet synsets; the dataset whose ILSVRC descendant defined deep-learning-era vision.
notes: The 2009 paper is a construction report with no test split or model baselines; I classified the artifact it ships (the labeled database, consumed as label-match classification, per the downstream ILSVRC protocol). Explainer quotes no model scores (99.7% is labeling precision), so frontier_score=null, but saturation=saturated from own knowledge: ILSVRC surpassed human top-5 error and retired in 2017. items_count is the database size at publication, not a fixed eval set.
placement_reason: Born to ask whether data-hungry models could do general visual object recognition at all — the classic perception probe, and the taxonomy's own A1 exemplar. A construction report whose scale+cleanliness+hierarchy defined the recognition-benchmark era.

title: Mind2Web: Towards a Generalist Agent for the Web
human_time: Tasks average 7.3 actions (book a flight leg, filter Netflix comedies, like a tweet) - a few minutes each for a human web user.
frontier_score: best step SR 52.0% (MindAct Flan-T5XL, Cross-Task); whole-task success <=7.1%, GPT-4 2.0%
one_line: 2,350 crowd-annotated high-level tasks on 137 real websites, graded on cross-task/-website/-domain generalization of web agents.
notes: task_shape is borderline: conceptually a web-agent action loop (so interactive-env), but the official eval replays cached snapshots teacher-forced with oracle history - the environment never reacts to the model's own actions. grading_all includes proxy-metric for Operation F1 (token-F1 on typed values). items_count = 1,341 test tasks across the three splits (2,350 total incl. 1,009 train). Saturation judged from the explainer's 2023 numbers; later multimodal agents score higher but end-to-end whole-task success remained far from ceiling.
placement_reason: Born to ask 'can one agent operate ANY real website from a high-level instruction?' — the environment/agentic task (137 unsimplified sites, generalization splits) is the contribution; headline is agent step/task success on operating the web.

title: SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?
human_time: Multi-file enterprise changes averaging 107 LOC across 4.1 files; the paper says a professional takes hours to days - typical instance sits in the hours band.
frontier_score: Claude Sonnet 4.5 43.6% Pass@1 on the public set; best on private commercial repos Opus 4.1 17.8%
one_line: 1,865 human-verified multi-file issue-resolution tasks from copyleft and purchased commercial repos, hardening SWE-bench against saturation and contamination.
notes: Tasks mined from real commit histories (plus purchased startup codebases) with heavy human augmentation of problem statements/requirements/interfaces - primary provenance stays real-work-mined. Strongest shipped defense is the 858-task private held-out set plus the 276 never-public commercial set (private-holdout); the public tier's copyleft argument is legal, not empirical. An LLM judge is used only for failure analysis, not scoring.
placement_reason: Framed head-on against SWE-bench Verified's saturation (>70%, 161/500 trivial edits) and contamination: same issue-resolution construct rebuilt with copyleft/purchased repos and multi-file tasks to restore headroom (<45%) and discriminative power.

title: Jacquard: A Large Scale Dataset for Robotic Grasp Detection
human_time: Seconds per item: a robot-grasp rectangle predicted for one RGB-D scene of a single object.
frontier_score: AlexNet trained on Jacquard reaches 72.42% SGT accuracy (simulated replay) vs. 42.76% for the same architecture trained on Cornell; 78.43% real-robot grasp success (28 objects) vs. 60.46% Cornell-trained.
one_line: 1.1M physics-simulated grasp rectangles across 11k ShapeNet objects (54k rendered RGB-D images), 46-137x the Cornell Grasping Dataset by axis, evaluated by physically replaying a predicted grasp (SGT) rather than matching a rectangle geometrically.
notes: domain_primary has no closer fit in the controlled vocabulary -- there is no 'robotics'/'embodied' domain, so multimodal (the CV-adjacent perception-and-action task) is the least-bad option, matching how the taxonomy treats other pure-CV benchmarks.
