Saturation set to not-applicable: no modern tracked frontier score exists for this exact 2D-rectangle construct -- the field moved to GraspNet-1Billion's 6-DoF, real-sensor, cluttered-scene paradigm before headroom on Jacquard's own metric visibly closed. items_count uses images (54k); the paper's headline '1.1M grasps' is annotation volume, not the per-item evaluation unit.
placement_reason: A grasp-location perception probe -- from a single RGB-D image, predict where a gripper should grasp -- graded by replaying that one prediction physically (SGT) rather than the model taking a sequence of actions itself; the tested skill is single-shot visual localization (parse the scene, output a five-parameter rectangle), the same construct as detection/pose estimation, so A1 rather than an interactive-environment family.

title: TRAIL: Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization
human_time: Paper's own annotation numbers: 30-40 minutes per trace ($12.66) for expert annotators to find/classify errors in one trace.
frontier_score: Gemini-2.5-Pro: 11% joint accuracy (18% GAIA / 5% SWE-Bench)
one_line: 148 expert-annotated OpenTelemetry agent traces; LLM judges must classify and locate 841 errors inside multi-million-token structured logs.
notes: Traces are freshly generated by running agents (organic induced errors) then expert-annotated - provenance called expert-authored on the gold labels, but arguably synthetic-generated on the trace side. Freshness is incidental, not a shipped defense, hence none-public. Long-context is co-primary in practice (scores anti-correlate with input length; 3/8 models exceed context).
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can an LLM debug another agent's trace?' — its contribution is a step-level error taxonomy (reasoning/system-execution/planning) plus expert-annotated traces for evaluating other systems' outputs, i.e. a trace-debugging taxonomy / judge benchmark, not a new task skill.

title: The Second Conversational Intelligence Challenge (ConvAI2)
human_time: Seconds per turn within a 4-6-turn Mechanical Turk chat, rated afterward on a 1-4 engagingness scale.
frontier_score: Automatic-metrics winner Hugging Face (perplexity 16.28, Hits@1 80.7, F1 19.5) placed second in the Mechanical Turk round; Lost in Conversation won the grand prize on engagingness (3.11/4 vs. 2.68); a fixed nonsense reply scored F1 19.6, beating every real competitor's F1.
one_line: NeurIPS 2018 competition benchmarking 23 open-domain chatbots on a Persona-Chat-based hidden test set (100 fresh personas, 6,634 examples); the automatic-metrics winner lost the human-judged grand prize, and a meaningless fixed reply outscored every competitor's F1.
notes: Kingdom placement is a genuine judgment call: ConvAI2 is built on the same capability task as PersonaChat (A7), but its own throughline and lasting citation value is the documented divergence between automatic dialogue metrics and human judgment on the same 23 systems -- classified as a meta-evaluation protocol paper (G2) rather than a capability leaderboard. Saturation not-applicable: a one-time competition snapshot, and the paper itself falsifies its own F1 metric mid-report.
placement_reason: The paper's own throughline is not 'who won' but what happened when automatic dialogue metrics and human judgment were run side by side on the same 23 systems: the automatic-metrics sweep winner lost the human-judged grand prize, and F1 was falsified in passing by a nonsense fixed reply -- a competition-format evaluation-protocol case study (G2, alongside Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench), not primarily a chatbot capability leaderboard.

title: Few-NERD: A Few-shot Named Entity Recognition Dataset
human_time: Seconds per sentence: read a ~61-token Wikipedia paragraph and tag entity mention spans against the 66-type schema -- no human baseline is run through the same harness (a gap the critique flags).
frontier_score: Fully-supervised BERT-Tagger: 67.13 F1 (SUP) vs. 91.34 on CoNLL'03; best few-shot baseline (ProtoBERT) tops out at 58.79 F1 in its easiest setting (INTER, 5-way 5~10-shot)
one_line: 188,238 Wikipedia sentences hand-annotated with an 8-coarse/66-fine entity-type hierarchy, purpose-built (not re-split from an existing corpus) to test fine-grained few-shot NER.
notes: Provenance is a large managed annotation team (70 trained annotators + 10 experts, quality-gated per batch) over Wikipedia text located via FIGER distant supervision -- closer to a paid crowd-labeling pipeline than either casual crowdsourcing or a handful of domain experts; filed as crowdsourced for lack of a closer vocabulary value. Every FEW-NERD-specific result (SUP row, all three few-shot tables) was silently re-run between arXiv v1 and v6 with no erratum; this page's numbers follow the current v6.
placement_reason: Squarely a recognize/parse capability probe -- can a tagger correctly locate and type entity spans -- extending the classic NER lineage (CoNLL'03, OntoNotes) to a fine-grained 66-type schema purpose-built for few-shot evaluation; headline is model skill (67.13 F1 supervised, 58.79 F1 best few-shot) against a much finer label space, not an audit of an existing grader or a durability wall.

title: Evaluating Prerequisite Qualities for Learning End-to-End Dialog Systems
human_time: Seconds per exchange: short factual/recommendation dialog turns built largely from templates.
frontier_score: MemN2N: QA 79.3 hits@1 (a dedicated QA system reaches 90.7), Recs 28.6 hits@100, QA+Recs 81.7 hits@10, Reddit 29.2 hits@10.
one_line: Four automatically-scored movie-domain dialog tasks (QA, recommendation, combined, Reddit chit-chat) testing prerequisite skills beyond fluent chit-chat.
notes: Saturation inferred from the explainer's own contamination note (OMDb/MovieLens/Reddit are public data very likely in modern pretraining corpora, letting a modern model answer Task 1 from memorized knowledge rather than the supplied KB) rather than from a directly reported post-2016 frontier score.
placement_reason: Four ranking-based dialog tasks (QA, recommendation, combined, chit-chat) built specifically to test 'prerequisite qualities' beyond fluent chit-chat — factual recall, personalization, multi-turn context use — matching A7's communication-skill definition and its existing conversation-domain members (LoCoMo, MSC).

title: DeepResearch Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Deep Research Agents
human_time: Paper frames deep-research agents as compressing 'hours of desk research into minutes'; each PhD-level task yields an analyst-grade cited report - several hours for a human expert.
frontier_score: Gemini-2.5-Pro Deep Research: RACE Overall 48.88 (111.21 effective citations; Perplexity DR leads citation accuracy at 90.24%)
one_line: 100 expert-written PhD-level deep-research tasks (50 EN/50 ZH); web-research agents graded on report quality (RACE) and citation trustworthiness (FACT).
notes: RACE uses judge-generated adaptive criteria with dynamic weights against a reference report - classified rubric-judge; FACT's per-claim binary support verdicts are llm-judge. Scores are relative to a Gemini-written reference (0.5 = parity), so saturation is not-applicable: read rankings, not a ceiling. Task mix grounded in 44,019 real user queries but items themselves are expert-authored.
placement_reason: Framed at birth as the first end-to-end benchmark for Deep Research Agents — long-form multi-source research synthesis grounded in real user demand; the headline is model performance at open-ended knowledge work, exactly the deep-research-suite slot of A8.

title: DROP: A Reading Comprehension Benchmark Requiring Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs
human_time: A minute or two per item: read a Wikipedia passage (often with dense numeric detail) and perform a discrete operation -- addition, counting, sorting, comparison -- across it.
frontier_score: Best 2019 baseline (BERT) reached 32.7% F1 vs. 96.4% human performance (six authors); the paper's own NAQANet model reaches 47.0% F1, though roughly 14 points of that gain reflects a training-data asymmetry (span-extraction baselines had to drop the 45% of questions with non-span answers).
one_line: 96,567 crowdsourced reading-comprehension questions over ~7,000 Wikipedia passages, collected with a live adversarial BiDAF baseline in the loop so every question had to beat it -- 2019 SOTA (BERT) reached only 32.7% F1 against 96.4% human performance.
notes: Modern LLMs score far above the 2019 baselines on DROP (a standard component of LLM eval suites); saturated is from own knowledge, the explainer only reports 2019-era numbers.
placement_reason: Built specifically to break span-extraction's 'find the answer verbatim' shortcut by requiring discrete symbolic operations (addition, counting, sorting, comparison) chained across a paragraph, with a live adversarial baseline gating every submitted question -- a closed-form, checkable-answer reasoning probe (A3) layered on reading comprehension, not plain retrieval.

title: AlpacaFarm: A Simulation Framework for Methods that Learn from Human Feedback
human_time: 805 short single-turn chat instructions (self-instruct/Vicuna/Koala style) - a few minutes each for a human to answer well.
frontier_score: GPT-4: 79.0% simulated / 69.8% human win-rate vs Davinci-003
one_line: Simulated-annotator RLHF sandbox whose eval artifact is an 805-prompt pairwise win-rate benchmark vs Davinci-003, judged by a noisy 13-LLM pool.
notes: Eval-methodology paper - classified the shipped artifact (805-prompt win-rate eval + simulated-annotator pool, the AlpacaEval precursor). Prompts are recombined from prior public instruction sets, hence aggregated. Human grading appears in the validation loop (Mhuman), not the headline metric. Win-rate vs the fixed Davinci-003 reference is effectively saturated/superseded (length-controlled AlpacaEval replaced it).
placement_reason: The contribution is a simulator: a noisy pool of LLM annotators that generates unlimited cheap pairwise preference feedback so RLHF/LPF methods can be trained and tuned in a $70 sandbox — the canonical RLHF-sandbox reward factory; training on the generated signal is the explicit primary use.

title: Evaluating Attribution in Dialogue Systems: The BEGIN Benchmark
human_time: Seconds to under a minute per item: read a knowledge snippet, prior turn, and one generated response, then apply the three-way attribution label -- annotators reached >95% majority-vote precision at this pace.
frontier_score: Best-scoring metric (adversarially-trained NLI classifier, T5 backbone) tops out at 45.9% test macro-F1 vs >95% human majority-vote precision
one_line: 12,288 machine-generated dialogue turns hand-labeled fully-attributable/generic/not-attributable, built to audit eight automatic attribution metrics rather than rank the dialogue systems that produced them.
notes: Meta-evaluation benchmark: the subject under test is the eight automatic metrics, not the four dialogue systems that generated the labeled pool. Only the NLI-classifier family gets a real quantitative P/R/F1 score against the human labels (Table 2), so grading_primary is filed as exact-match (classifier label vs. human majority-vote label); the other seven metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/F1/BERTScore/BARTScore/BLEURT/Q2) are checked only by visual score-distribution overlap, not a uniform protocol.
placement_reason: BEGIN's own stated goal is 'to determine to what extent current evaluation metrics fulfill their purpose' -- a diagnostic set purpose-built to audit NLG attribution metrics against human labels, not a leaderboard for the dialogue systems that produced the pool; squarely the G3 grader-benchmark pattern (cf. FActScore, JudgeBench) rather than an A-family capability probe of the underlying dialogue systems, which the paper explicitly disclaims ranking.

title: FaithDial: A Faithful Benchmark for Information-Seeking Dialogue
human_time: Seconds to a minute per turn: read the knowledge snippet and Wizard response, then judge (or rewrite) whether it's faithful, generic, or hallucinated -- independent validators reproduced the majority-vote label at 90% (BEGIN) / 81% (VRM) F1.
frontier_score: T5+InfoNCE (FaithDial-trained): 1.4% Critic-flagged hallucination in-domain; human-judged hallucination falls from 55.8% (WoW-trained T5) to 23.2% (FaithDial-trained T5)
one_line: A curated, turn-by-turn rewrite of Wizard of Wikipedia -- every hallucinated or uncooperative Wizard turn edited to be faithful to the same knowledge snippet -- moving WoW's own audited 20.9% faithful-turn rate to a validated 94.4%, with the gains transferring zero-shot to CMU-DoG and TopicalChat.
notes: A construct-audit-and-repair paper: it first re-measures WoW's own hallucination rate (only 20.9% of turns faithful, per the companion audit) and then ships the fixed corpus as the artifact -- the audit result and the benchmark are the same paper's two faces. Every faithfulness number ultimately traces back to a small (10-worker), self-referential annotation pipeline (the same BEGIN taxonomy both builds and re-validates it), per the explainer's critique; the out-of-domain zero-shot transfer (Table 8) is the strongest independent evidence the faithfulness gain isn't just fitting the annotators' own conventions.
placement_reason: Points at the measurement/training substrate, not a skill: exposes that WoW's gold 'knowledge-grounded' responses are only 20.9% actually faithful (71.4% hallucinated/partially so) -- so any model trained or scored against WoW's references is being taught and measured against a corrupted construct -- and ships the corrected dataset as the fix, the same audit-then-repair move as Gender Shades exposing what an accuracy score was really hiding, not a fresh A7 conversation-ability probe of an unaudited construct.

title: Measuring and Improving Consistency in Pretrained Language Models
human_time: Seconds per cloze item: fill in a masked-token fact ('Homeland originally aired on [MASK]') from a restricted per-relation candidate set.
frontier_score: Best 2021 model (BERT-large): 61.1% Consistency, 48.1% Accuracy, only 29.5% Consistent-Acc (correct AND self-agreeing) -- a KL-divergence consistency loss improves held-out Consistency by 5.8 pts but showed no measurable gain on a downstream SQuAD-paraphrase transfer test
one_line: 328 human-vetted paraphrase cloze patterns across 38 relations testing whether a masked LM gives the same (not necessarily correct) answer to differently-phrased versions of the same fact -- best model agrees with itself only 61.1% of the time.
notes: 'Human agreement' quality check (95.5%/98.3%) is agreement-with-the-authors'-own-label after re-annotating disagreements, not independent blind inter-annotator agreement -- a real, disclosed measurement-quality caveat. Saturation 'open': the underlying self-consistency-under-paraphrase problem remains broadly unsolved even though this specific cloze-restricted-candidate-set paradigm predates and doesn't directly transfer to generative-LLM consistency evals.
placement_reason: Points at what a 'knows the fact' accuracy score from LAMA-style probing actually means: a model can be consistently WRONG or correct-but-self-contradicting, so accuracy alone doesn't establish the model stores a stable fact rather than pattern-matching a phrasing -- headline finding is about the knowledge-probing construct's validity, the same B4 slot TruthfulQA occupies for 'knows the answer' more broadly, not a new capability skill.

title: HiL-Bench (Human-in-Loop Benchmark): Do Agents Know When to Ask for Help?
human_time: 150 SWE-Bench Pro repo issues (hours each for an engineer) + 150 BIRD SQL tasks (tens of minutes); typical instance ~1 hour including blocker clarification.
frontier_score: GPT-5.5: 29% combined pass@3, 53% Ask-F1
one_line: 300 SWE/SQL tasks seeded with hidden blockers; measures whether agents know when to call ask_human(), via spam-proof Ask-F1 plus pass@3.
notes: Base tasks come from SWE-Bench Pro/BIRD but the tested content (1,131 expert-injected, multiply-audited blockers) is expert-authored - aggregated is the runner-up call. Grading: pass@3 is programmatic (tests/execution); Ask-F1 relevance is adjudicated by a frozen Llama-3.3-70B semantic judge (97/91 validated), hence llm-judge in grading_all. Secondary 'reasoning' covers the metacognitive uncertainty-detection skill the benchmark isolates. 200 public / 100 private held-out tasks.
placement_reason: Built to measure selective escalation — whether an agent knows when to ask the human for help mid-task — with the human explicitly kept in the loop via ask_human(); a mixed-initiative collaboration rehearsal (the family's named exemplar), motivated by enterprise-pilot failure rates.

title: MMTEB: Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark
human_time: Not applicable in the usual sense -- MMTEB scores embedding models automatically; a human doing one classification/STS/bitext item would need seconds, one retrieval query over a corpus a couple of minutes.
frontier_score: A 560M-parameter multilingual-e5-large-instruct beats billion-parameter Mistral-based embedders (GritLM-7B, e5-mistral-7b-instruct) on MTEB(Multilingual)/MTEB(Indic); GritLM-7B still leads MTEB(Europe)
one_line: A GitHub-coordinated, 87-contributor expansion of MTEB from 58 datasets/112 languages to 400+ datasets (500+ tasks) across 250+ languages, plus a redundancy-pruned English suite that reproduces the original ranking (Spearman 0.90) from ~2% of the documents.
notes: items_count left null -- MMTEB is a collection of 500+ tasks each with its own item count, not a single test set (same convention as BEIR/HELM). grading_primary judgment call: scoring spans nDCG@10 (retrieval), accuracy (classification), clustering V-measure and STS Spearman correlation -- coded programmatic (all rule-based/automatic) with proxy-metric secondary for the correlation-style subtask metrics, rather than BEIR's own (inconsistent) exact-match coding. domain_primary=language rather than BEIR's long-context, since MMTEB is a superset spanning classification/clustering/STS/reranking/summarization, not just retrieval; long-context kept secondary for the retrieval/long-document component.
placement_reason: Same construct as its parent (BEIR-style: can a model's learned text representation generalize zero-shot across tasks and languages), broadened rather than fixed -- the gap is coverage (58->400+ datasets, 112->250+ languages, 8->10 task types) and evaluation cost, not a saturated ceiling, so it's the A1 capability-suite exemplar taken multilingual, not a B3 desaturation sequel or a G1 general-purpose panorama (it stays scoped to one capability: embedding quality).

title: MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs
human_time: Each item is a self-contained riddle/grammar/cultural-math question with a word-or-phrase answer - a few minutes for a native-speaker expert.
frontier_score: o3-pro (high): 49.00% - no model clears 50%
one_line: 1,055 natively-authored (not translated) French/Spanish/Chinese reasoning questions across linguistic, wordplay, cultural, and cultural-math categories.
notes: Grading call: answers are short objective gold strings, but equivalence is checked by a GPT-4.1 judge (>95% human agreement, Scott's Pi 0.88) - classified exact-match in spirit with llm-judge as the matching mechanism. Adversarial 3-of-5-models-fail filter builds in the low ceiling and is not a contamination defense; set is public on Hugging Face.
placement_reason: A capability probe of natively-grounded reasoning — linguistic puzzles, wordplay/riddles, cultural reasoning, and culturally-grounded math, each with a short objective checkable answer; framed against translated benchmarks (MGSM) and exam ports, so the role is 'can models reason natively in-language yet', not a wall or an exam port.

title: GraspNet-1Billion: A Large-Scale Benchmark for General Object Grasping
human_time: Seconds per grasp: a single 6-DoF grasp-pose prediction on one RGB-D scene, scored online against a physical force-closure computation rather than a fixed label.
frontier_score: Proposed network AP 27.56/29.88 (Seen), 26.11/27.84 (Unseen), 10.55/11.51 (Novel) (RealSense/Kinect) — Novel AP roughly 38% of Seen AP for every method tested
one_line: 97,280 real RGB-D images over 190 cluttered scenes, densely labeled with ~1.1B analytically force-closure-scored 6-DoF grasp poses, graded online rather than against a fixed label set.
notes: No 'robotics' domain exists in the controlled vocabulary; 'multimodal' (RGB-D visual + physical pose output) is the closest fit. Complexity reflects one grasp decision, not a full manipulation episode. items_count uses the image count (97,280); the headline '1 billion' is a count of scored grasp candidates, not images/objects/scenes (91 objects, 190 scenes).
placement_reason: Perceive an RGB-D scene and produce a structured, physically-checkable 6-DoF grasp prediction — a parse-and-produce capability probe (A1) whose real methodological contribution is replacing a fixed, necessarily-incomplete hand-labeled grasp set with online force-closure scoring, not an interactive multi-step manipulation loop (A5) since each prediction is a single-shot pose, not a rollout.

title: MMDialog: A Large-scale Multi-turn Dialogue Dataset Towards Multi-modal Open-domain Conversation
human_time: A multi-turn social-media reply with an optional image; roughly 1-2 min per turn for a human, not stated directly in the paper.
frontier_score: Divter (generation) 61.85 MM-Relevance / DE++ (retrieval) 68.91 MM-Relevance (2023, sole baseline per task)
one_line: 1.08M real multi-turn social-media dialogues with 1.53M images (88x PhotoChat), scored by a new CLIP-based aligned precision/recall metric, MM-Relevance.
notes: Provenance judged 'real-work-mined' (scraped real social-media conversations, filtered) rather than 'user-traffic', since it's not live AI-system usage logs but a one-time crawl of an unnamed platform's public posts. Grading is fully automatic (BLEU/ROUGE/Inception Score/MM-Relevance); the paper's own human-correlation study (Pearson 0.40/0.29) is metric validation, not eval-time grading, so kept out of grading_all. items_count = 10,000 test dialogues.
placement_reason: The headline construct is conversational capability under a genuinely multi-modal, image-anywhere dialogue structure ('can a model generate/retrieve the right text-and-image response in a real social conversation') — matching A7's 'follow instructions, converse, clarify' pattern (the same family as MSC/LoCoMo), not an audit of an existing grader (MM-Relevance is a new metric this paper introduces, not a fix to one) or a deployment/hazard probe.

title: MRQA 2019 Shared Task: Evaluating Generalization in Reading Comprehension
human_time: A few minutes per item: read a passage (up to 800 tokens) and extract an answer span; passage genres range from news, Wikipedia, and textbooks to speech transcripts.
frontier_score: Best 2019 submission (D-Net, an XLNet+ERNIE2.0 ensemble) 72.5 macro-F1 across 12 held-out domains vs 61.8 organizer BERT-Large baseline; per-domain range from 37.4-53.9 F1 (RACE) to 81.3-89.0 F1 (RelationExtraction, near-saturated even at baseline)
one_line: 18 existing QA datasets reformatted into one extractive schema and split into 6 training-only / 6 dev-shown / 6 fully-hidden out-of-domain sets, scoring 10 teams' systems purely on out-of-domain transfer F1 from a fixed training pool.
notes: items_count is the combined Split II + Split III held-out test example count (15,017); Split I (6 training datasets) has no held-out test portion of its own. grading_primary 'proxy-metric' matches the SQuAD/HotpotQA span-F1 convention already established in this taxonomy, distinct from the discrete-label 'exact-match' bucket used for aggregated classification suites like GLUE/XTREME.
placement_reason: An aggregation of 18 pre-existing extractive-QA datasets behind one shared schema and protocol, explicitly built to test out-of-domain reading-comprehension transfer rather than in-domain accuracy - the GLUE-style aggregated capability-probe pattern (A1), even though the shared task's own meta-analysis (in-/out-of-domain scores strongly correlated) complicates the generalization construct it set out to isolate.

title: Video-MME: The First-Ever Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark of Multi-modal LLMs in Video Analysis
human_time: Videos run 11 seconds to 1 hour; the paper's own 'certificate length' (minimum span a human needs to verify an answer) has medians of 26s/165s/891s for short/medium/long videos.
frontier_score: Gemini 1.5 Pro leads at 75.0% overall (frames-only); best open-source model (VILA-1.5 34B) manages 59.0%
one_line: 900 real YouTube videos (11s-1hr) across 6 domains/30 subfields, with subtitles and audio as first-class inputs -- video's counterpart to the static-image perception suites.
notes: 2,700 QA pairs (3 MCQs/video) over 900 videos; items_count uses the video count as the benchmark's primary unit. Annotators with vision-language research experience both write and cross-check questions, and any question Gemini 1.5 Pro can answer from text alone (<15% accuracy threshold) is sent back for revision -> expert-authored.
placement_reason: Explicitly framed as closing video's counterpart to the static-image perception suites (MMBench/MMMU) that dominated multimodal eval to that point -- accuracy-graded recognition/reasoning/synthesis MCQs over real video, the video-domain instance of A1's recognize/parse/retrieve mandate (VQA/ImageNet's own family), not an audit or hazard probe.

title: Baby Intuitions Benchmark (BIB): Discerning the goals, preferences, and actions of others
human_time: Watch an 8-trial familiarization sequence plus a paired expected/unexpected test-video pair (a few tens of seconds of video per trial) and judge which outcome is more surprising; no new infant/adult behavioral data collected in this paper.
frontier_score: Three passively-trained baselines clear chance on obstacle/efficiency tasks (74-99%) but land at or below chance on Preference (26.3-48.3%) and Multi-agent binding (48.2-50.3%), collapsing on the blocking-barrier instrumental-action sub-task (47.1-62.9%)
one_line: A five-family violation-of-expectation video benchmark adapted directly from infant-cognition experiments; three passively-trained neural baselines sit at or below chance on two of five task families.
notes: items_count is the 5x1,000-episode evaluation set (5 task families x 1,000 episodes each); 28,000 background-training episodes are separate. Contamination_defense 'none-public': the generator is procedural but the released test videos are a static public set, not regenerated per-query. Domain 'social-moral' is the closest available label for infant-style theory-of-mind/goal-inference reasoning -- no dedicated social-cognition domain exists in the controlled vocabulary.
placement_reason: Adapts developmental-psychology violation-of-expectation experiments so a machine's 'surprise' rating is checkable against how infants actually attend to the same events -- treating theory-of-mind/goal inference as an extension of perceiving and parsing an agent's hidden mental state from purely observed behavior (A1), since the model never acts in an environment, only rates pre-rendered video pairs.

title: MCP-RADAR: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Evaluating Tool Use Capabilities in Large Language Models
human_time: Tasks are single operations or short chains (send an email, file op, terminal command, tool-assisted math/web lookup) - minutes each for a human with the same tools.
frontier_score: Gemini 2.5 Pro best overall (Email 82.5%, Terminal 59.9%, Web 29.8%; ~57% cross-domain average)
one_line: 507 MCP tool-use tasks across six domains (math, web, email, calendar, files, terminal), graded by exact-match answers/operations plus turn-level call validity.
notes: Provenance split: ~300 Fuzzy tasks are template-generated per tool (synthetic primary); the 214 math/web Precise tasks are adapted from prior academic datasets (aggregated minority). The Gemini-Flash 'answerable without tools' filter targets memorization but isn't one of the listed contamination defenses. Saturation borderline: email ~82% closing but web <30% and best cross-domain average sits under 60% - called open.
placement_reason: The first benchmark built around the Model Context Protocol: 507 tasks asking whether models can select and parameterize the right MCP tool across six domains — a tool-selection/sequencing capability probe (MCP suite), with the syntax-vs-semantics tool-choice gap as the headline.

title: RefactorBench: Evaluating Stateful Reasoning in Language Agents Through Code
human_time: ~5 min/task: the paper's own human baseline gave a proficient developer 5 minutes per task with an IDE (solved 87%).
frontier_score: SWE-agent + Claude-3.5-Sonnet (descriptive) 35%; state-aware GPT-4 agent 38/100 vs human 87%
one_line: 100 handcrafted multi-file Python refactoring tasks probing coding agents' stateful reasoning, graded by AST unit tests.
notes: Reference solutions are withheld (only AST tests released), but tasks live in public repos and the task set is public, so contamination_defense = none-public. Paper notes reasoning-model agents already solve 'many more' tasks, so 'open' reflects the quoted 2024-era panel.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can coding agents do multi-file refactoring — stateful reasoning across a long edit trajectory?', a skill SWE-bench-style bug-fixing filtration leaves untested. The headline is model performance on a repo-level code-editing skill (22% vs human 87%), so it is a capability probe in the repo-level SWE family, not an environment contribution (A5) or an audit of SWE-bench's scores (B).

title: The GEM Benchmark: Natural Language Generation, its Evaluation and Metrics
human_time: Minutes per item: produce/rate a short generated text (summary, data-to-text description, simplified sentence, or a schema-driven dialogue turn) across 11 datasets and 18 languages.
frontier_score: Reported numbers are small-model (T5-60M/BART-139M) validation-split baselines ahead of the actual ACL 2021 shared task -- explicitly not final test-set results, with no single leaderboard score by design
one_line: A 56-author 'living benchmark' packaging 11 NLG datasets across 18 languages, ten types of adversarial challenge sets, and an interactive multi-metric exploration tool, refusing a single leaderboard number by design.
notes: items_count left null: an aggregated 11-dataset suite the paper's own text states inconsistently as ranging '5k to 500k' in one place and '5,000 to 1.5M' in another, though Table 1 itself tops out at 594k -- a real internal inconsistency worth flagging rather than resolving with a single hand-picked number. Saturation 'not-applicable': GEM explicitly rejects a single-score ceiling in favor of a parallel-coordinates multi-metric exploration tool.
placement_reason: Explicitly built because NLG never got NLU's GLUE/SuperGLUE-style shared evaluation surface, and argues no single number can capture generation quality -- a holistic, multi-metric aggregation of the NLG eval landscape (G1, the same slot HELM and BIG-bench occupy) plus a maintained-over-time process (dataset/metric review, challenge sets, data cards), not a fixed capability test.

title: GenEval: An Object-Focused Framework for Evaluating Text-to-Image Alignment
human_time: Seconds per templated prompt-image pair for a Mechanical Turk annotator to judge correct/incorrect (6,000 annotations across 1,200 images, 5 annotators each).
frontier_score: GenEval reaches 83.4% agreement with human annotators (vs. an 87.8% inter-annotator ceiling), beating the best CLIPScore backbone (79.8%) specifically on counting/position/attribute-binding; best T2I model (IF-XL) scores 0.61 overall but only 0.13-0.35 on position/attribute-binding.
one_line: An off-the-shelf object-detector-based (Mask2Former, no finetuning) verdict engine for text-to-image alignment across 6 compositional tasks (553 templated prompts), replacing CLIPScore's single similarity score with a per-element correct/incorrect trace validated on 6,000 human annotations.
notes: Domain_secondary='reasoning' reflects that GenEval's real edge over CLIPScore concentrates on the three tasks needing the most compositional reasoning (counting, position, attribute binding). The explainer flags that the paper's own Figure 3 and adjoining prose quote two different CLIPScore backbones without saying so (an 8.9-point vs. a 22-point counting gap) — doesn't affect classification but tempers confidence in the exact quoted comparison numbers.
placement_reason: The contribution is a verdict engine, not a T2I capability probe: an off-the-shelf detector plus zero-shot color classifier replacing CLIPScore's single similarity number with a per-element correct/incorrect trace, explicitly validated against 6,000 human annotations — the object is which automated grader tracks human judgment on compositional alignment, the G3 pattern for a non-text modality (cf. FActScore, min-2023). Not A1: the six task categories exist to stress the grading pipeline's coverage, not to rank T2I models as the headline finding.

title: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI
human_time: Research-mathematician-level problems; the paper reports professional mathematicians (some problem authors) needing hours to days per problem.
frontier_score: Every frontier LLM solved fewer than 2% of problems at publication
one_line: Hundreds of original, unpublished mathematics problems written and vetted by 60+ research mathematicians, checked by automated verification rather than human proof-grading — every frontier LLM solved fewer than 2% at publication.
notes: Kept as a private holdout by design, explicitly to prevent the contamination that saturated MATH/GSM8K; the direct successor once those benchmarks closed.
placement_reason: MATH and GPQA both closed within a couple of years of release; FrontierMath is the next summit — research-mathematician-authored problems held as a private holdout specifically so the wall can't be climbed by memorization.

title: Audio MultiChallenge: A Multi-Turn Evaluation of Spoken Dialogue Systems on Natural Human Interaction
human_time: A few minutes: listen to a 3-8-turn conversation (~2 min of audio on average) and compose the final-turn response satisfying its ~3.8 rubrics.
frontier_score: Gemini 3 Pro Preview (Thinking): 54.65% APR (82.54% ARS)
one_line: 452 unscripted multi-turn spoken dialogues with 1,712 atomic rubrics testing voice models on natural human conversation.
notes: Provenance is borderline: tasks are recorded by vetted Scale AI human contributors guided by agentic blueprints (65% blueprint-leveraged) with multi-stage QC — could arguably be crowdsourced. Fresh Dec-2025 original recordings give low leakage risk, but no formal holdout mechanism is described, hence none-public. Grading is fixed-context on the final turn, transcript-only.
placement_reason: The gap is that voice benchmarks score single-turn synthetic speech while the capability people actually use — extended, spontaneous multi-turn conversation — was untested in audio. It extends the text MultiChallenge multi-turn axes (memory, instruction retention, self-coherence) into speech and adds Voice Editing: a multi-turn conversation-competence probe ported to a new modality, squarely A7.

title: Virology Capabilities Test (VCT): A Multimodal Virology Q&A Benchmark
human_time: A lab-troubleshooting scenario (sometimes with an image) plus 4-10 true/false statements to identify exactly; human experts got 15-30 minutes with internet access per question.
frontier_score: o3 (Apr '25): 43.8% accuracy, outperforming 34 of 36 matched expert virologists (94th percentile); every reasoning model tested beat the median expert (22.1%)
one_line: 322 lab-troubleshooting virology questions written by 68 PhD-level virologists (multiple-response format, Google-proof filtered); o3 outscores 94% of matched expert virologists, a direct dual-use capability signal for biosecurity governance.
notes: Complexity is a borderline L2/L3 call: the 15-30 min human-expert time sits above typical L2-minutes items but below hour-scale L3 tasks (kept L2-minutes for consistency with similarly-timed benchmarks like AppWorld). Shares a co-author (Dan Hendrycks) and mission with WMDP, though VCT tests troubleshooting Q&A accuracy directly rather than WMDP's unlearning-target framing.
placement_reason: Explicitly built as a dual-use hazardous-knowledge proxy for AI governance -- 'expert-level virology troubleshooting ability is inherently dual-use... deciding what governance an AI capability needs first requires being able to measure whether that capability has arrived' -- the same object as WMDP (has the dangerous capability arrived), not a science-knowledge exam (A2) where the point is breadth of recall rather than a hazard signal.

title: Making the V in VQA Matter: Elevating the Role of Image Understanding in Visual Question Answering
human_time: Seconds per item: one short question about one of two visually similar images; matches VQA v1's per-item cost.
frontier_score: Best 2016 model (MCB) 54.22% on the balanced val set (vs. 60.36% on the original unbalanced val); the language-only ablation falls to 41.40%.
one_line: Balances VQA by pairing every question with two visually similar images with different answers — ~1.1M pairs forcing models to actually use the image.
notes: contamination_defense and saturation mirror antol-2015-vqa's own classification (private-holdout eval server; long since saturated by modern VLMs), since VQA v2 is the same held-out-test-server protocol applied to a rebalanced item set.
placement_reason: The paper's stated goal is explicitly a validity claim, not a new skill: VQA v1's headline accuracy partly measured language-prior exploitation ('do you see a...' answered 'yes' scores 87% blind), not genuine image understanding — 'a leaderboard that state-of-the-art VQA models climb by exploiting language priors gives a false signal.' Per-question answer balancing is the audit instrument (matching B4's own construct-audit pattern, e.g. TruthfulQA, OR-Bench, which likewise ship a new dataset as part of exposing what a score really means), not a harder version of the same skill for its own sake.

title: ManiSkill2: A Unified Benchmark for Generalizable Manipulation Skills
human_time: A few minutes per manipulation episode (pick-place, peg insertion, soft-body pour) for a human teleoperator; not stated directly, but demonstration trajectories are short-horizon.
frontier_score: DAPG+PPO: 0.94-0.95 on pick-and-place (PickCube/StackCube) but <=0.04 on all three precision-assembly tasks at default clearances (2023)
one_line: 20 manipulation task families (soft-body, precision assembly, pick-and-place, mobile/articulated) with 2,000+ objects and a render-server architecture reaching ~2,500 FPS visual-RL sample collection.
notes: items_count = 20 task families, not the much larger per-family episode/demonstration count (4M+ frames total, unevenly distributed); no single 'items' total is a better fit for a task-family-organized suite like this one, matching the LEV/complexity convention for task-count benchmarks.
placement_reason: The contribution is the ENVIRONMENT plus systems infrastructure (multi-controller demonstration conversion, a shared-GPU render server) across 20 manipulation task families with real contact-physics grasping (explicitly built against prior benchmarks' 'abstract grasp') — a capability probe asking whether a policy can operate physically simulated manipulation with real dynamics, matching A5's pattern (the direct SAPIEN-ManiSkill lineage predecessor of LIBERO/BEHAVIOR-1K's peers), not an audit or hazard/deployment framing.

title: CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
human_time: ~1 minute: the filter explicitly keeps only problems 'a good programmer could solve in about a minute' without scratch memory.
frontier_score: GPT-4 + CoT: 74.8% (input) / 81.9% (output) pass@1
one_line: 800 short Python functions; predict output from input (CRUXEval-O) or input from output (CRUXEval-I), execution-checked.
notes: Complexity sits at the L1/L2 boundary (~1 min by design). The generate-and-filter recipe is re-runnable for harder future versions, but the shipped set is fixed and public, so not 'procedural'. Explainer notes the 2023 panel is dated and the ceiling is almost certainly higher now, hence 'closing'.
placement_reason: Primary framing is a missing skill: no public benchmark tested whether a model can READ code and predict execution (output/input prediction), the foundation under debugging and repair — exactly the 'code-execution reasoning' named in A4. The famous distillation finding (HumanEval gains don't transfer) gives it a B4-audit flavor, but that is a result, not the construct: the benchmark itself is an execution-grounded capability probe built against HumanEval's blind spot.

title: HallusionBench: An Advanced Diagnostic Suite for Entangled Language Hallucination and Visual Illusion in Large Vision-Language Models
human_time: Seconds per yes/no question about an image.
frontier_score: GPT-4V leads at 31.42% question-pair accuracy (28.79% under the GPT-4 judge); every one of 12 open-source models scores below the 15.60% random-chance baseline; GPT-4V's lead vanishes on Hard (edited-image-only) accuracy, where several smaller open models and even random chance score higher.
one_line: 1,129 yes/no questions over 346 images (181 hand-edited) built as control-pair triples (original / edited / no-image) so a fixed decision tree — not human judgment — attributes each wrong answer to language hallucination or visual illusion.
notes: Placed in B4 over A1 because the paper's own gap section is an explicit construct-validity critique of prior hallucination benchmarks (POPE, M-HalDetect, GAVIE) — a single accuracy/F1 number conflates two mechanistically distinct failures with no counterfactual to separate them; the decision-tree attribution mechanism is the headline contribution, not raw VQA accuracy. The explainer flags real, checkable contradictions between the paper's own prose and its own tables (the abstract's 'below 16%' claim vs. Claude 3's 21.76%; a 'beats Random Choice' claim vs. two models' own sub-random qAcc) — noted for medium confidence on exact quoted numbers, though the B4 classification itself doesn't depend on those errors.
placement_reason: The gap section is an explicit construct-validity critique: existing hallucination benchmarks (POPE, M-HalDetect, GAVIE) collapse two mechanistically different failures — over-trusting prior knowledge vs. misreading the image — into one accuracy/F1 number with no counterfactual to tell them apart. HallusionBench's control-pair-plus-decision-tree construction exists to attribute *why* a model failed, the canonical B4 move (cf. TruthfulQA exposing 'knows the answer' isn't truthfulness), not to rank raw multimodal perception (A1).

title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models
human_time: Well under a minute typical: most items are short binary/classification questions on a clause or brief fact pattern; rule-application explanations take a lawyer a few minutes.
frontier_score: GPT-4 (balanced-acc): rule-conclusion 89.9, issue-spotting 82.9, rule-recall 59.2
one_line: 162 legal-reasoning tasks hand-built by 40 legal professionals, organized by the IRAC framework, scored by balanced accuracy.
notes: 162 tasks across 36 corpora; total instance count not stated, so items_count = null. Grading is mostly exact-match balanced accuracy, with multi-label F1 (proxy-metric) and manual human grading of rule-application 'analysis' by one law-trained grader. Leakage openly acknowledged (Appendix D maps prior web availability) but no defense shipped. Saturation mixed by category (89.9 conclusion vs 59.2 rule-recall) — 'closing' on balance.
placement_reason: The taxonomy's own D2 exemplar ('LegalBench-style'). Born of the mid-2023 question 'can LLMs draft briefs, review contracts, help close the access-to-justice gap?' — professional-domain legal competence, expert-authored (40 legal professionals) and organized by the lawyers' own IRAC typology so scores translate to practice. Occupational content beats the 'can models do the skill' surface framing per the tie-break.

title: StableToolBench: Towards Stable Large-Scale Benchmarking on Tool Learning of Large Language Models
human_time: Minutes per query: a multi-step tool-use trajectory reproducing ToolBench's own task set; not stated (this paper's contribution is infrastructure, not new human-timed items).
frontier_score: GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613+DFS leads at 63.0±1.1 Solvable Pass Rate (Average); ToolLLaMA-v2 trails at 46.6±1.7
one_line: ToolBench's 1,100 queries re-scored against a cache-then-LLM-simulate virtual API server and a majority-voted solvable-task gate, replacing its decaying live RapidAPI layer.
notes: provenance synthetic-generated describes this paper's own contribution (the cache-then-LLM-simulate response layer); the underlying 1,100 test queries are inherited unchanged from ToolBench (qin-2023-toolllm). contamination_defense doesn't cleanly map to this paper's actual concern (evaluator/infrastructure stability, not text leakage) — none-public is the closest available bucket.
placement_reason: The named B2 case for tool-use: ToolBench's live RapidAPI layer decays (55.6% of endpoints no longer succeed) and its GPT-3.5 solvability/win judge swings 6+ points run to run on identical inputs. StableToolBench keeps ToolBench's queries and tools but rebuilds the broken measurement apparatus itself (a cache-then-simulate virtual API server, a majority-voted solvability gate, a single GPT-4 judge) — EvalPlus's grader-hardening pattern applied to a live-infrastructure benchmark rather than a static test suite, not a new capability probe since no new task is added.

title: Beyond Seeing: Evaluating MLLMs on Tool-Enabled Image Perception, Transformation, and Reasoning
human_time: Minutes: human reference solutions need fewer than five tool calls — inspect/crop/enhance an image, maybe compute or search, then answer.
frontier_score: GPT-5-think: 18.68% APR (0.4712 ARS)
one_line: 1,204 expert tasks where MLLMs must crop/edit/enhance images with tools to answer, graded on 7,777 weighted rubrics.
notes: Tool set: python_image_processing + python_interpreter (code-exec), web_search + browser_get_page_text (search-retrieval; text fetch, not interactive browsing), calculator + historical_weather (domain-api). Original contributor images and a >=2-of-3-models-fail admission filter lower leakage, but no holdout mechanism is described. The 18.68% floor is partly a selection artifact (only tasks that broke 2 of 3 reference models are admitted).
placement_reason: The frontier skill is 'think WITH images': deciding when and how to invoke a six-tool API (crop/edit/brighten, calculator, search) and fold results back into reasoning — tasks never name the tool, so tool selection/sequencing is what's probed, and tool-use proactivity is the dividing line in the results. Positioned explicitly against static visual-QA (A1-style MMMU/MathVista) and against trivial-crop tool benchmarks (GTA, m&m's), it is a tool-orchestration capability probe in the visual domain.

title: Benchmarking the Spectrum of Agent Capabilities
group: Google Research (Brain Team) / University of Toronto
human_time: Not stated per-episode, but 5 human experts played 100 recorded episodes total; only 5 of those 100 unlocked all 22 achievements, so a full run plausibly takes many minutes.
frontier_score: Best 2021 baseline (DreamerV2): 10.0% +/- 1.2 score vs. 50.5% +/- 6.8 for 5 human experts
one_line: A procedurally generated 2D open-world survival game scored by 22 difficulty-weighted achievements in a single 1M-step budget -- the best 2021 RL baseline reaches 10.0% vs. 50.5% for human experts.
notes: items_count is the 22 named achievements the geometric-mean score is computed over. contamination_defense filed as procedural: every episode's 64x64 world is freshly generated via OpenSimplex noise, so an agent cannot memorize a fixed layout. Baselines are not equal-effort (DreamerV2 is the sole author's own prior architecture, kept at Atari defaults but given extra capacity; only Rainbow was specifically re-tuned), per the explainer's critique.
placement_reason: A single fast procedurally generated environment standing in for a whole RL benchmark suite, scored by a difficulty-weighted geometric mean over 22 achievements -- the archetypal 'can an agent operate this interactive world' capability probe (crafting/survival/combat), headline being the wide gap to human experts (10.0% vs 50.5%), not a grader audit or occupational-domain probe.

title: Hi-ToM: A Benchmark for Evaluating Higher-Order Theory of Mind Reasoning in Large Language Models
human_time: A few minutes to read a multi-chapter narrative (up to 26+ lines) and answer a nested-belief multiple-choice question.
frontier_score: GPT-4-32k leads at 58.99% overall standard accuracy (Claude-instant 46.00%, Guanaco-65B 32.17%, GPT-3.5-turbo 31.50%); the stricter cumulative joint accuracy collapses to roughly 0.15-0.2 by order 3-4 in 3-chapter stories, worse under deceptive communication.
one_line: Sally-Anne-style narrative QA pushing Theory-of-Mind evaluation to a full 0th-4th-order belief ladder on the same story, with optional deceptive agent communication, generated from a large randomized component pool (30 rooms x 37 objects x 39 containers x 40 agents).
notes: items_count left null — the explainer gives per-order/per-condition breakdowns (1-3 chapters x with/without deception x vanilla/CoT prompting) but never states a single total story or question count. domain_secondary includes social-moral as the closest available vocabulary slot for theory-of-mind/social-cognitive reasoning, though the taxonomy has no dedicated ToM domain. Placed in A3 (capability-depth extension) rather than B4 (contrast with FANToM, same batch, placed in B4) because Hi-ToM's own framing is 'push order depth past the 1st/2nd-order ceiling,' not a measurement-validity critique of how prior ToM benchmarks are scored.
placement_reason: Extends Sally-Anne-style ToM QA (ToM-QA, ToMi) directly from their 1st/2nd-order ceiling to a full 0th-4th-order belief ladder with checkable MC ground truth — a capability-depth extension along a closed-form, exact-match-gradeable recursive-reasoning axis, not a critique of how ToM had been measured (contrast FANToM, same batch, B4).

title: OlympiadBench: A Challenging Benchmark for Promoting AGI with Olympiad-Level Bilingual Multimodal Scientific Problems
human_time: ~10-40 min for a strong human on a typical competition/Gaokao item; hardest IMO/IPhO problems run to hours.
frontier_score: GPT-4V: 17.97% avg (21.70 math / 10.74 physics) on the 2024 panel
one_line: 8,476 olympiad-level bilingual multimodal math/physics free-response problems with automatic answer-equivalence grading.
notes: Grading straddles exact-match and programmatic: final-answer equivalence via SymPy symbolic checking + numeric tolerance; the 21% theorem-proving slice has no auto-grader (manual sampling only, hence 'human' in grading_all). Quoted 2024 numbers are open (17.97%), but the explainer says later work treats it as a saturating sub-benchmark under reasoning models — 'closing' reflects the current frontier. PDF-to-markdown sourcing is best-effort leakage mitigation, not a shipped defense.
placement_reason: Explicitly built because GSM8K/MATH were saturating ('increasingly surmounted'): draws from IMO/IPhO/Gaokao so 'the pinnacle of human intellectual achievement becomes the measuring stick' and the gap to humans is 'wide enough to track progress for years' — durable headroom is the stated design goal, the wall framing C1 names for olympiad-level sets (GPT-4V at 17.97% confirms). Not B3: it is not a rebuild of one saturated benchmark but a new bilingual-multimodal summit exam.

title: WebVoyager: Building an End-to-End Web Agent with Large Multimodal Models
human_time: ~2-5 min per task for a human (find/read info on a public site); agent capped at 15 steps.
frontier_score: WebVoyager (GPT-4V backbone) 59.1% task success on 643 tasks, human eval
one_line: Live-web agent benchmark: 643 open-ended tasks on 15 real sites, scored by human/GPT-4V trajectory judgment.
notes: Tasks are GPT-4 self-instruct generated, human-verified -> synthetic-generated. Live-web drift is incidental, tasks fixed/public -> none-public. Saturation from outside knowledge (later agents report ~87-90%+ and treat it as solved, though 2025 audits dispute judge inflation); explainer quotes only the 2024 59.1%.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can an agent operate the real live web end-to-end?' — the gap attacks text-only inputs and simplified simulators/static snapshots (MiniWoB, WebShop, Mind2Web), contributing a 643-task benchmark on 15 live sites plus an LMM trajectory judge; the interactive web environment is the contribution, so A5.

title: AdvancedIF: Rubric-Based Benchmarking and Reinforcement Learning for Advancing LLM Instruction Following
human_time: ~10-30 min to write one response satisfying 6-20 layered constraints over the given conversation.
frontier_score: GPT-5 (full thinking) 77.9 overall; Gemini 3 Pro 74.7
one_line: 1,645 expert-written prompts with human rubrics testing complex, multi-turn, and system-prompt instruction following.
notes: Task shape borderline: 1,243 of 1,645 items are multi-turn dialogs, but the context is fixed and only the final-turn response is graded -> classed single-turn. Set was unreleased at publication (release promised), so no shipped defense -> none-public.
placement_reason: Headline claim is about the skill: advanced instruction following (6+ constraints, multi-turn carried context, system-prompt steerability) is unsolved — frontier models top out at 75-78% on 1,645 human-expert prompts/rubrics; IFEval-style IF probing extended, so A7 despite the companion RIFL training pipeline.

title: Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations
human_time: Seconds per item: classify one (corrupted) image into one of 1,000 ImageNet classes.
frontier_score: mCE fell from 100.0 (AlexNet, defining baseline) to 76.7 (ResNet-50) purely from clean-accuracy gains; Relative mCE, which isolates corruption-specific damage, rose slightly (100.0 to 105.0) -- a decade of architecture progress bought essentially zero dedicated corruption robustness.
one_line: IMAGENET-C (15 corruptions x 5 severities) and IMAGENET-P (10 temporal perturbation types) applied to the 50,000-image ImageNet validation set, normalized against an AlexNet baseline into mCE/mFR metrics -- absolute error fell with a decade of architecture progress, but Relative mCE (isolating corruption-specific damage) got slightly worse.
notes: items_count is the base ImageNet validation set (50,000 images); each is evaluated across 75 corrupted conditions (15 types x 5 severities) for IMAGENET-C alone. Saturation ('open') reflects the paper's own headline finding that dedicated (relative) corruption robustness has not improved despite absolute-accuracy progress; a 2020 follow-up (Taori et al.) found little transfer from this synthetic-corruption robustness to natural distribution shift, reinforcing that the underlying construct remains open.
placement_reason: Its central finding isn't a new capability -- it's that clean-ImageNet-accuracy progress (AlexNet to ResNet-50) bought almost no *dedicated* corruption robustness once baseline accuracy gains are normalized away (Relative mCE actually rose slightly): exposing that 'accuracy' and 'robustness' are different constructs the field's single clean-accuracy leaderboard had been conflating -- the textbook construct audit (B4), one family over from recht-2019-imagenet-generalize's adaptive-overfitting finding on the same base dataset.

title: Aligning AI With Shared Human Values
human_time: Seconds to ~1 min: read a short scenario (occasionally 1-6 paragraphs) and give a binary/comparative moral judgment.
frontier_score: ALBERT-xxlarge (fine-tuned) 71.0% Test / 47.9% Hard Test (2020)
one_line: 130K+ everyday scenarios testing whether models predict consensus moral judgments across five ethical frameworks.
notes: Provenance mixed: qualification-gated MTurkers wrote most tasks, long commonsense items scraped from Reddit -> crowdsourced. Utilitarianism's pairwise ranking still scores against fixed labels -> exact-match. Saturated per the explainer's own critique (modern models near-ceiling zero-shot, contaminated since 2020).
placement_reason: Built to answer 'does a model even know what humans broadly consider right and wrong?' — 130K scenarios scoring moral verdicts across justice, deontology, virtue, utilitarianism, and commonsense; the object is moral/ethical judgment quality, and ETHICS is the taxonomy's named E3 exemplar.

title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
human_time: Under a minute per 4-option exam question for a knowledgeable human; hardest professional items a few minutes.
frontier_score: GPT-3 175B few-shot 43.9% avg (2020, best in paper)
one_line: 57-subject four-option multiple-choice exam of pretraining world knowledge, from elementary to professional level.
notes: items_count (14,042 test questions) from outside knowledge, not stated in the explainer. Saturation from outside knowledge: frontier models score ~88-90%+ and the community treats MMLU as retired (MMLU-Pro/GPQA built to escape it); the explainer quotes only 2020 numbers.
placement_reason: Zero/few-shot 57-subject exam measuring how much world knowledge pretraining actually instills — graded like human exams from elementary to professional level; the canonical A2 exemplar. Its anti-saturation motive targets a NEW construct (knowledge, not GLUE's NLU), so responds-to rather than B3.

title: Measuring Coding Challenge Competence With APPS
human_time: Typical interview-tier problem ~20-30 min for a competent programmer; competition tier can take 1+ hours.
frontier_score: GPT-Neo 2.7B (fine-tuned) 3.90% strict acc Introductory (2021); cited Codex 12B 25% @1000 samples
one_line: 10,000 coding-challenge problems in three difficulty tiers, graded by executing Python against hidden test cases.
notes: Complexity sits on the L2/L3 line (competition tier is hours; typical interview item ~20-30 min). BLEU is reported only to debunk it, so not in grading_all. Saturated call is outside knowledge: community retired APPS (contamination + supersession by LiveCodeBench/SWE-bench; frontier reasoning models handle competition-level problems); the explainer's own 2021 numbers are near zero. items_count = 5,000 test problems of 10,000 total.
placement_reason: Asks 'can a model turn an arbitrary natural-language spec into working code?' — 10,000 difficulty-tiered problems graded by executing Python against 131,777 hidden tests, replacing BLEU with functional correctness; APPS is a named A4 exemplar.

title: CUAD: An Expert-Annotated NLP Dataset for Legal Contract Review
human_time: At 5-10 min/page and contracts up to 150 pages, finding one category's clauses in a contract runs ~30 min to hours.
frontier_score: DeBERTa-xlarge 44.0% Precision @ 80% Recall (47.8 AUPR), 2021
one_line: 510 SEC contracts with 13,101 expert-labeled clauses across 41 categories; extractive span-finding for legal review.
notes: Grading: Jaccard>=0.5 word-overlap span match feeding AUPR/P@R is token-overlap -> proxy-metric, not exact-match. Provenance: real EDGAR contracts, expert-annotated (expert-authored is arguable). items_count is annotated clauses, not (contract x label) test queries (~4.2K). 'Open' rests on 2021 encoder numbers; no modern-LLM results quoted and the benchmark is little-tracked now.
placement_reason: Probes a real professional job — clause-finding in commercial contract review ($500-900/hr lawyer work, ~$2M of expert annotation) — asking whether NLP transfers to expert domains; occupational legal content beats the extractive-QA format, and contracts/law are D2's named territory.

title: Natural Adversarial Examples
human_time: Seconds per item: a single real photograph, 200-class classification; the paper's own graduate-student annotators estimate ~90% human accuracy, confirming the images are solvable even though they fool every tested model.
frontier_score: DenseNet-121 collapses from >=90% (standard ImageNet) to ~2% on IMAGENET-A; best in-paper model (DeiT-base, a ViT) 28.2% acc / 24.8% AUPR (IMAGENET-O) - still far from solved even at launch
one_line: 7,500 real, unmodified photos (IMAGENET-A) adversarially filtered against a fixed ResNet-50 ensemble to expose shared classifier blind spots, plus a 2,000-image OOD-detection companion (IMAGENET-O).
notes: items_count is IMAGENET-A's own count (the slug/short-label artifact); IMAGENET-O's 2,000 images are a separate companion set. Saturation 'saturated' is directly textual: the paper's own critique section states 'subsequent large vision-language and foundation models are widely known to score much higher on IMAGENET-A than anything reported here.'
placement_reason: Standard ImageNet accuracy had saturated (>=90% for ordinary classifiers) so this paper restores real headroom via active adversarial filtration of real photos rather than a passive fresh resample - collapsing DenseNet-121 from >=90% to ~2%, a far steeper reset than a simple i.i.d. re-draw. Distinguished from B1 (recht-2019-imagenet-generalize, a passive resample testing overfitting to the original test set) by being adversarially curated rather than independently sampled.

title: The Many Faces of Robustness: A Critical Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Generalization
human_time: Seconds per item: classify one art/cartoon/sculpture/embroidery/etc. rendition image into one of 200 ImageNet classes; no human baseline is actually run in the paper.
frontier_score: 2020 baseline ResNet-50: 63.9% ImageNet-R error; best combo (DeepAugment+AugMix) 53.2%; modern augmentation/pretraining has closed much of this gap without fully saturating the hardest rendition styles
one_line: 30,000 Flickr-mined art/cartoon/sculpture/embroidery renditions of 200 ImageNet classes, headlining a 4-dataset battery showing no single robustness intervention helps everywhere.
notes: Classified by the paper's headline meta-finding, not just the ImageNet-R artifact: the real contribution is exposing that 'robustness' isn't one scalar (self-attention/pretraining help ImageNet-C but not ImageNet-R/DFR; augmentation helps ImageNet-R/C but not DFR/SVSF/ImageNet-A) — a construct audit of prior single-benchmark robustness claims, including the paper's own critique that ImageNet-R's 200-class subset is itself a curated worst-case slice, not a representative rendition sample.
placement_reason: The paper's real payload is accusing prior single-benchmark robustness claims of construct-validity failure and then proving it with a 4-6-dataset grid where no intervention (scale, self-attention, pretraining, augmentation) wins everywhere — 'robust' is not a scalar a model either has or lacks. That meta-finding, not the ImageNet-R artifact alone, is what the paper is actually measuring, the textbook B4 case alongside OR-Bench's over-refusal audit.

title: Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset
human_time: Paper's own human study: 20 problems in 1 hour (no calculator), i.e. ~3 min per problem for strong humans; competition items typically take a few minutes each.
frontier_score: o1-/R1-class systems report 90%+ on the MATH test set (2024-25); paper-era best was GPT-2 1.5B at 6.9%
one_line: 12,500 competition-math problems (5,000 test) with worked solutions, graded by exact match on a single boxed final answer.
notes: items_count is the 5,000-problem test set (12,500 total incl. train). Explainer explicitly names contamination as the dominant caveat: public AMC/AIME problems mirrored on AoPS, no defense shipped.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can models genuinely solve competition math yet?' — prior math benchmarks were either near-solved plug-and-chug or formal-prover suites, so MATH built 12,500 exactly-gradable boxed-answer competition problems where frontier models scored 3-7%. Headline is model skill on checkable math; the canonical A3 exemplar.

title: Teaching Machines to Read and Comprehend
human_time: ~1-3 min to read one news article and fill in the blanked entity from its own summary sentence.
frontier_score: Impatient Reader 63.8% CNN / Attentive Reader 69.0% Daily Mail test accuracy vs. a symbolic frame-semantic baseline's 40.2%/35.5%.
one_line: ~1M entity-anonymized cloze questions built automatically from CNN/Daily Mail articles and their bullet-point summaries — the first million-scale RC training corpus.
notes: Saturation is explicitly supported by the explainer: Chen, Bolton & Manning (2016) showed a tuned model was already near the effective ceiling within a year, and the dataset's own construction (heavy reliance on entity salience) caps its real difficulty.
placement_reason: The founding automatically-constructed cloze reading-comprehension corpus — ground every answer in the document via entity anonymization — squarely A1's 'recognize, parse, entail, retrieve' definition, and the direct methodological ancestor SQuAD (already A1 in this taxonomy) responds to.

title: Constructing A Multi-hop QA Dataset for Comprehensive Evaluation of Reasoning Steps
human_time: A few minutes per question: read up to four Wikipedia paragraphs, chain two facts through a bridge entity, and produce both an answer span and the supporting evidence triples.
frontier_score: Same pre-BERT baseline model scores lower on 2WikiMultiHopQA joint EM/F1 (9.22/26.76) than on HotpotQA (10.97/40.52) despite comparable ~91% human answer-F1 ceilings; evidence-generation EM near-zero for every 2020 model tested
one_line: 192,606 multi-hop QA items built from the intersection of Wikipedia summaries and Wikidata, adding an explicit evidence chain of (subject, relation, object) triples that HotpotQA's sentence-level supporting facts didn't provide.
notes: Provenance is template-generated (799 compositional + 62 bridge-comparison + smaller sets) over a closed vocabulary, flagged in the critique as a real memorization/shortcut risk with no template-holdout evaluation reported. Saturation 'closing': modern retrieval-augmented LLMs handle multi-hop answer EM/F1 far better than the pre-BERT 2020 baseline, but the strict-exact-match evidence-triple sub-task (alias-sensitive) likely still shows real headroom.
placement_reason: Pairs Wikipedia paragraphs with Wikidata triples so multi-hop question answering can be graded not just on the final span but on an explicit, checkable evidence chain -- a retrieve-and-entail capability probe (A1, the family that explicitly names 'retrieve') rather than a grader-hardening fix to HotpotQA itself, since 2WikiMultiHopQA is a new dataset with its own construction, not a patch to HotpotQA's existing scoring.

title: RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?
human_time: Tasks run 4K-128K tokens (retrieval, multi-hop variable tracing, aggregation, QA); a human manually tracing a variable chain through a 128K-token haystack would take well over an hour, though the 4K condition is minutes.
frontier_score: Of 17 models claiming 32K+ context, only ~half clear a fixed 32K effective-length threshold; GPT-4 (claimed 128K) effective only to 64K, GradientAI/Llama3-70B (claimed 1M) effective only to 16K
one_line: Synthetic long-context suite (retrieval variants, multi-hop variable tracking, aggregation, QA) at 4K-128K tokens, defining a model's 'effective context length' rather than trusting its claimed one.
notes: items_count = 500 generated examples per task per length (13 representative tasks x 6 lengths tested; no single fixed total across the whole grid, so 500 is the per-task-per-length figure). The effective-length threshold is defined relative to Llama2-7B's own 4K score (85.6%) -- the paper's own Limitations flag this as an arbitrary reference point.
placement_reason: Follows Long Range Arena's precedent (A1's named exemplar) of a synthetic, dial-the-difficulty capability probe: independently controllable length and complexity isolate whether a model can actually retrieve, trace, and aggregate over its context window rather than pattern-match a single needle -- a parse/retrieve capability stress test, not an audit of an existing benchmark's grader (B) or a durability wall built to resist near-term saturation (C, since RULER's own numbers show most models already fail it today).

title: XTREME: A Massively Multilingual Multi-task Benchmark for Evaluating Cross-lingual Generalization
human_time: Seconds per item for classification/tagging tasks (XNLI, PAWS-X, POS, NER); QA span answers (XQuAD/MLQA/TyDiQA) take a bit longer to read a passage - a mix, mostly well under a minute per item.
frontier_score: Best 2020 model (XLM-R Large) 68.2 avg across 9 tasks (vs mBERT 59.8), but well below the human reference wherever available (79.2 vs 92.8 XNLI, 60.8 vs 82.3 EM on XQuAD, 73.8 vs 97.0 POS)
one_line: 9 existing cross-lingual NLU tasks (XNLI, PAWS-X, POS, NER, XQuAD, MLQA, TyDiQA-GoldP, BUCC, Tatoeba) bundled into one zero-shot transfer protocol across 40 languages / 12 language families: fine-tune on English only, evaluate everywhere else.
notes: items_count left null - 9 tasks across 40 languages with heterogeneous per-task/per-language sizes and no single stated combined total (same treatment as GLUE). Saturation 'closing' is inferred (own knowledge, modern multilingual LLMs likely close much of the human gap on classification/QA sub-tasks though structured-prediction tasks like POS/NER may lag); the explainer only quotes 2020 numbers.
placement_reason: The GLUE/SuperGLUE playbook explicitly ported to cross-lingual transfer ('do for cross-lingual transfer what GLUE and SuperGLUE did for English', quoting the paper) - nine pre-existing recognize/parse/entail/retrieve tasks aggregated behind one zero-shot English-to-40-languages protocol, the direct multilingual analogue of GLUE's own A1 exemplar role in this taxonomy.

title: TIFA: Accurate and Interpretable Text-to-Image Faithfulness Evaluation with Question Answering
group: University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI
human_time: Writing/rating one short text-to-image prompt and judging faithfulness takes a human a couple of minutes; not stated directly.
frontier_score: Stable Diffusion v2.1: 82.0 TIFA(mPLUG) average, best of 7 generators tested (2023); explainer notes current T2I models are 'far past the ceiling this study measured'
one_line: Decomposes a text-to-image prompt into GPT-3-generated, UnifiedQA-filtered QA pairs, then scores faithfulness as VQA-model accuracy on them — beating CLIPScore's human-correlation by nearly 2x.
notes: grading_primary judged 'rubric-judge' (per-element QA-pair decomposition verified by a model, the FActScore/atomic-fact pattern) over 'llm-judge' (no single holistic model judgment) or 'exact-match' (each item is a VQA call, not a bare label match) - a close call. Saturation 'saturated' rests on the explainer's own 2026 read that current T2I models are far past this benchmark's 2023 ceiling, not on a number quoted in the paper itself.
placement_reason: The contribution is a WAY of grading: decompose a T2I prompt into per-element QA pairs, verify each against the generated image with an off-the-shelf VQA model, and validate the resulting score against human faithfulness judgment (Spearman rho up to 0.597 vs. CLIPScore's 0.332) — the FActScore pattern (atomic decomposition + automated verifier validated against humans) ported to image faithfulness; the 7-model TIFA v1.0 leaderboard is a demonstration of the metric, not the paper's point, matching G3's named pattern.

title: InfiAgent-DABench: Evaluating Agents on Data Analysis Tasks
human_time: A few minutes for a data analyst to explore one CSV and compute the closed-form answer; not stated exactly by the paper.
frontier_score: GPT-4-0613 78.99% accuracy on the full 34-model/agent leaderboard; best non-agent open/code LLM Qwen-72B-Chat 59.92%
one_line: 257 real-CSV data-analysis questions rewritten into closed-form, exact-match-gradable form via a constraints+format-prompting pipeline.
notes: A6 (tool orchestration via a code-exec sandbox in a ReAct loop) chosen over A4 (single-shot program synthesis) because the paper's own framing is the full plan-code-execute-iterate loop, not one-shot code generation; A4 is the reasonable rival call. Also over A5 (mutable environment) since there's no persistent stateful world, only CSV files plus a sandbox.
placement_reason: Asks whether an agent can plan, write, and iterate on Python code inside a live sandbox to answer a closed-form data-analysis question — the tool being orchestrated is a code interpreter in a ReAct loop, closer to GAIA/Gorilla-style tool orchestration than a single-shot A4 code-synthesis task (no iterative execution loop) or an A5 mutable-world environment (no persistent stateful world, just CSV files and a sandbox).

title: Labeled Faces in the Wild: A Database for Studying Face Recognition in Unconstrained Environments
human_time: Seconds per pair: two face photos, one same/different judgment.
frontier_score: No baseline in the original report; field converged from DeepFace 97.35% (2014, ~human parity 97.53%) to ArcFace 99.83% (2019) on the View 2 protocol.
one_line: 13,233 web news-photo faces of 5,749 people with a strict unseen-pair-matching protocol — the decade-defining unconstrained face-verification benchmark.
notes: The original report ships zero accuracy numbers of its own; frontier_score summarizes the field's later View-2 trajectory as quoted in the explainer. contamination_defense=none-public is the paper's own explicit admission (View 2 test pairs are published, relying on researcher discipline, not a technical barrier).
placement_reason: A pure capability-probe database-and-protocol paper: can an unconstrained face-verification algorithm decide if two never-before-seen photos are the same person, under a rigorously specified View 1/View 2 protocol — the classic perception probe of the pre-deep-learning CV era, the direct forerunner of the ImageNet/COCO-style A1 entries already in the taxonomy.

title: MetaTool Benchmark for Large Language Models: Deciding Whether to Use Tools and Which to Use
human_time: Seconds per query to read a short user request and a candidate tool list, then pick zero/one/two tools; a 240-response human study puts people at 96% CSR on the hardest (reliability) sub-task.
frontier_score: ChatGPT leads tool-usage awareness at 74.85% accuracy/77.81% F1 zero-shot; on the reliability sub-task (correct tool deliberately absent from the candidate list), 7 of 8 models score under 10% CSR (ChatGPT 50.35%), vs. 96% for humans.
one_line: 21,127 LLM-generated queries (ToolE, from 390 real OpenAI-plugin tools) decomposing 'should I use a tool' (awareness) from 'which tool' (selection under four stress conditions: similar choices, scenario shift, forced hallucination, multi-tool), scored via Correct Selection Rate across 8 LLMs.
notes: The explainer flags the paper's own stated 8-model roster ('including Baichuan2') not matching what actually appears in every results table — doesn't affect classification.
placement_reason: Decomposes the ReAct tool-use loop's first two decisions — whether a tool is needed at all, and which one — into dedicated, separately-scored tasks (awareness F1; CSR under four selection-stress conditions) — the canonical A6 tool-selection capability probe, distinguished from A5 by testing the decision layer in isolation rather than an embodied multi-step environment.

title: MLAgentBench: Evaluating Language Agents on Machine Learning Experimentation
human_time: Improving a starter ML model by 10% on a real dataset (edit code, train, iterate) is a multi-hour job for an ML engineer; agents were capped at 50 actions / 5 hours per run.
frontier_score: Claude 3 Opus agent: 37.5% average success rate (100% on house-price, 0% on BabyLM/parkinsons/fathomnet/vectorization)
one_line: 13 ML-experimentation tasks where an LM agent reads, edits, and executes training code to beat a starter baseline by 10%.
notes: Provenance is a mix: most tasks reframe prior benchmark datasets (CIFAR-10, IMDb, ogbn-arxiv, CLRS, BabyLM) plus real Kaggle challenges, so 'aggregated' over 'real-work-mined' is a judgment call. Contamination defense is post-cutoff Kaggle sourcing by design, but only for 4 of 13 tasks and not continuously refreshed.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can an LM agent close the full ML experimentation loop on its own?' — read files, edit training code, execute, read the metric, iterate — with an automatic evaluator. First testbed for agentic ML-engineering work, the progenitor of the MLE-bench/MLGym/PaperBench line; squarely research-execution capability.

title: CRMArena: Understanding the Capacity of LLM Agents to Perform Professional CRM Tasks in Realistic Environments
human_time: Nine day-to-day CRM tasks (case routing, policy checks, trend spotting) across three personas -- a few minutes each for a working service agent/analyst/manager with the same system access.
frontier_score: o1 with hand-crafted function-calling tools: 64.3% overall (57.7% under ReAct without hand-built tools, using only general-purpose SOQL/SOSL access)
one_line: 9 CRM tasks across 3 personas (service agent/analyst/manager), run against a real Salesforce sandbox populated by an LLM-synthesized, schema-faithful, expert-validated dataset (90% of 10 domain experts rated it realistic); even the best agent clears only 64.3%, and hand-crafted function-calling tools help strong models but actively hurt weaker ones.
notes: Kingdom/family is a genuine judgment call between D2-occupational-probes (professional CRM competence) and A6-tool-orchestration (its own stated comparators are WorkBench/WorkArena/tau-bench, all tool-orchestration benchmarks, and its headline finding -- function-calling tools help strong models, hurt weak ones -- is about tool-selection mechanics rather than domain-knowledge competence). Classified A6 to mirror the tau-bench precedent (a near-identical customer-service, tool-agent-user benchmark already classified A6/tool-use in this taxonomy).
placement_reason: Built to test whether an agent can select and sequence the right SOQL/SOSL queries and function-calling tools across a genuinely complex enterprise schema (16 objects, 1.31 dependencies/object vs. WorkBench's near-zero and WorkArena's 0.86) to complete real CRM tasks -- a tool-orchestration capability probe in a higher-fidelity environment than its named comparators (WorkBench, WorkArena, tau-bench), the A6 case; not D2, since the headline finding is about tool-selection mechanics, not domain-knowledge competence per se.

title: DA-Code: Agent Data Science Code Generation Benchmark for Large Language Models
human_time: Reference solutions average 85 lines of code across 5.7 files per task (data wrangling, ML modeling, or SQL+Python EDA); a competent data analyst with the same noisy multi-file workspace needs on the order of 30-60 minutes.
frontier_score: GPT-4 + DA-Agent: 30.5% Total (48.4% ML / 24.6% EDA); DA-Agent's own scaffold beats OpenDevin (26.2), AutoGen (18.6), and X-Agent (6.7) under identical GPT-4 on a 100-task subset
