one_line: 500 data-science tasks (data wrangling / ML / exploratory analysis) inside a Docker sandbox with fused Bash/Python/SQL actions across an average 5.7 noisy multi-file resources per task, graded by executing the output (table/chart/ML-score matching) rather than string similarity.
notes: Family placement (A5 vs. A6 tool-orchestration vs. A8 research-execution) is a genuine judgment call: DA-Code's own Table 1 explicitly frames its contribution as adding a 'Controllable Executable Environment' plus a planning requirement that DS-1000/Arcade/DA-Bench lack, which is the A5 (operate an interactive environment) definition rather than A6's external-tool-selection framing or A8's open-ended-research-workflow framing. Domain=tool-use (secondary coding) mirrors AppWorld's precedent for the same style of sandboxed, multi-file agentic coding benchmark. No contamination discussion in the paper despite mining Kaggle/GitHub for 'timely' data; the worked example itself uses a widely-reproduced public Kaggle churn dataset.
placement_reason: Built explicitly against single-file, no-execution-environment code benchmarks (DS-1000, Arcade): DA-Code's contribution is the environment itself -- a noisy, multi-file Docker sandbox an agent must explore and operate via fused Bash/Python/SQL actions to plan and execute a real data workflow, graded by executing the resulting state rather than matching text -- the A5 case (paralleling AppWorld's app-environment operation), not A4 (single-file completion, no execution loop) or A6 (external tool/API selection rather than an owned sandbox).

title: VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models
human_time: Seconds to compare a pair of short generated video clips on one dimension; the human study collected thousands of pairwise comparisons per dimension via a 5-step QA labeling process.
frontier_score: Best per-model scores don't dominate across dimensions — VideoCrafter posts the highest Dynamic Degree (89.72%) but the lowest of all 4 models on every one of the 4 temporal-consistency dimensions, while LaVie/CogVideo show the reverse; automatic-vs-human Spearman correlation ranges 0.6073 (Color) to 0.9980 (Motion Smoothness), computed over just 4 models per dimension.
one_line: 16 disentangled video-generation-quality dimensions (Video Quality x Video-Condition Consistency), each scored by a purpose-built automatic detector (DINO/CLIP/ViCLIP/RAFT/LAION-aesthetic/MUSIQ/GRiT/UMT/Tag2Text) and checked against human pairwise preference — though the human-alignment check itself aggregates to just 4 points (models) per dimension.
notes: Placed in G3 (metric-validation protocol) rather than A-capability for the same reason as EvalCrafter and GenEval in this batch: the paper's contribution and central validation claim are about which automatic metric tracks human judgment per dimension, not a T2V capability leaderboard per se — though VBench does also report a 4-model leaderboard as a secondary output. items_count left null: the paper's own text hedges 'around 100 prompts' per dimension (actual per-dimension counts range in the 70s-100s across 16 dimensions) plus a separate 800-prompt, 8-category content suite, with no single stated grand total. The explainer flags that Figure 5's human-alignment correlation is computed over only 4 data points (models) per dimension despite resting on thousands of pairwise comparisons, and that the 4 evaluated models were sampled under mismatched conditions (resolution, and CogVideo alone scored on machine-translated Chinese prompts) — doesn't affect classification but tempers confidence in exact quoted correlations.
placement_reason: The contribution is a metric-validation protocol: 16 disentangled dimensions, each with its own purpose-built automatic detector, independently checked against large-scale human pairwise preference (Spearman's rho per dimension) — replacing the single opaque FID/FVD/IS/CLIPSIM number the field had been trusting. The headline finding (VideoCrafter 'cheats' consistency via near-static video, exposed only by disentangling dimensions) is about what a single video-quality score hides, the G3 pattern shared with GenEval/EvalCrafter in the same batch, not a capability ranking.

title: MultiLoKo: a multilingual local knowledge benchmark for LLMs spanning 31 languages
human_time: Closed-form short-answer factoid questions from popular Wikipedia pages; a native speaker who knows the fact answers in seconds.
frontier_score: Gemini 2.0 Flash 34.4 average EM (dev), Llama 3.1 405B 34.3, GPT-4o 34.0 -- even the easiest languages cap below 50 EM
one_line: 31-language benchmark of 500 locally-sourced Wikipedia knowledge questions per language, made fully parallel via translation.
notes: Provenance is borderline: recruited native-speaker annotators with multi-pass QC (SQuAD-style) -- professional annotators rather than domain experts, so crowdsourced over expert-authored. Secondary 'language' because the design explicitly separates language proficiency from knowledge. Blind frequency-split test set behind an external submission service = private-holdout.
placement_reason: The gap targets the measurement apparatus: dominant 'multilingual' benchmarks are English translated, so multilingual-in-surface-only. The 2x2 parallel design (Locality Effect, Mother Tongue Effect) exists to quantify how translate-from-English distorts which languages look hard (up to 22-point swings) — the meta-finding about the construct is the durable headline, not the EM leaderboard.

title: FinanceBench: A New Benchmark for Financial Question Answering
human_time: A financial analyst locating a figure in a 10-K/10-Q and computing a metric from it: roughly 5-15 minutes per question.
frontier_score: GPT-4-Turbo: 19% correct on the realistic shared vector store; 79% in long-context; 85% with oracle evidence
one_line: Open-book financial QA: expert (question, answer, evidence) triplets over 361 real SEC filings, graded by human review.
notes: Tool access varies by configuration (closed-book none, vector-store retrieval, long-context, oracle); the headline realistic setup is RAG retrieval. Only 150 of 10,231 cases are public (and all graded numbers come from those 150). Saturation call is borderline: realistic-RAG headline is 19% (open) but best realistic long-context config hits 79%, so 'closing' on late-2023 models.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'is a model good enough to trust on a live, high-stakes analyst desk?' — ecological validity over real SEC filings is the explicit design bet, against FinQA/TAT-QA's handed-passage setup. Professional-domain finance competence with deployment-readiness framing; the taxonomy's named D2 exemplar.

title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
human_time: LeetCode/AtCoder contest problems bucketed Easy/Medium/Hard; a competent competitive programmer solves a typical one in ~10-30 minutes.
frontier_score: GPT-4-Turbo 39.7 Pass@1 on LCB-Easy code generation (paper snapshot, early 2024)
one_line: Live, release-date-stamped contest-coding benchmark grading generation, self-repair, code execution, and test-output prediction.
notes: Self-repair supplies execution feedback in the prompt but there is no agentic loop, so single-turn with no tool access. Execution/test-output-prediction scenarios grade by value equality (exact-match); headline is unit-test execution. 511 problems total, 349 in the contamination-safe main comparison. The canonical live-refresh benchmark. Saturation judged from the explainer's 2024 numbers; later reasoning models score much higher on newer rolling windows (own knowledge, not from text).
placement_reason: Unsaturability by construction is the stated point: problems are continuously scraped from live contests, time-stamped, and models scored only on post-cutoff items, turning contamination from a worry into a measurement. Live refresh as the core design is the C3 definition — and it is the taxonomy's named exemplar.

title: RLBench: The Robot Learning Benchmark & Learning Environment
human_time: Not reported - this preprint contains zero learned-agent or human results; episode lengths for the underlying tasks run roughly 100-1000 simulator timesteps (short pick-place tasks up to longer multi-stage tasks like 'empty dishwasher').
one_line: 100 hand-designed robot-manipulation tasks on a shared Franka Panda scene, with unlimited motion-planner-generated demonstrations per task; proposes a 'v1.0' few-shot challenge protocol but reports zero learned-agent results itself.
notes: Domain is a forced fallback (see wang-2019-mbrl-benchmark's note). saturation/frontier_score are 'not-applicable'/null because this preprint is unusual even for the batch: it is a pure benchmark-and-toolkit proposal with literally zero learned-agent or human results in the arXiv v1 text (confirmed by the explainer's own critique), so there is no performance data to judge saturation against at all.
placement_reason: A shared, scalable robot-manipulation task suite (100 tasks, one scene/interface, infinite scripted demos) built explicitly to replace ad hoc, per-paper task sets in manipulation research - the clearest 'operate an interactive environment' case in this batch's RL/robotics cluster, even though its domain content is physical robotics rather than the family's usual web/computer-use exemplars.

title: DiscoveryWorld: A Virtual Environment for Developing and Evaluating Automated Scientific Discovery Agents
human_time: Normal/Challenge tasks run to 1000 simulator steps; the 11 Upwork-recruited human scientists tested on them post 66% completion / 55% knowledge scores at a task-scale (not quick-pass) time budget.
frontier_score: Zero-shot GPT-4o agents complete at best 38% of Easy and 18% of Challenge tasks (ReAct), and discover at best 34% of gold knowledge on Easy (Hypothesizer), collapsing to <=10% at Challenge for every agent -- vs. 66% completion / 55% knowledge for 11 human scientists on Normal/Challenge alone
one_line: 120-task virtual laboratory (8 science themes x 3 difficulty tiers x 5 seeds) scoring the full ideation-experimentation-analysis-conclusion discovery loop on three separate axes rather than one pass/fail number.
notes: 10 additional unit-test themes isolate basic environment competency from discovery skill (Procedure/Completion only, no Knowledge axis) and aren't counted in items_count. Knowledge axis judged by GPT-4o (llm-judge) against gold yes/no questions; the scorer also supports human grading, used for the human baseline (human in grading_all). Completion and Procedure are scored automatically by the simulator itself (programmatic).
placement_reason: Built explicitly against pick-and-place environments with one implied correct plan (ALFRED, MiniGrid) and open-ended-but-unincentivized play worlds (NetHack, MineDojo) to force the full discovery cycle -- notice an anomaly, form a hypothesis, design a measurement, reach a conclusion -- across 8 real scientific domains; the open-ended-knowledge-work mandate LAB-Bench names for A8, made interactive rather than single-turn.

title: Critical Foreign Policy Decisions (CFPD)-Benchmark: Measuring Diplomatic Preferences in Large Language Models
human_time: Reading a paragraph-length IR dilemma with deliberately balanced options and choosing a course of action: a minute or two per item for an IR-literate reader.
one_line: Measures foreign-policy dispositions, not correctness: 400 expert IR scenarios expanded to 66k forced-choice questions with no answer key.
notes: No ground truth by design, so several dimensions are judgment calls: domain_primary 'social-moral' (value/political preference probe) with 'safety' secondary for escalation propensity; grading is forced-choice extraction (guided decoding for open models = exact-match; closed-model free text manually encoded = human); saturation not-applicable since the output is a preference distribution. items_count is the 66,473 expanded questions (400 base scenarios). Dataset withheld -- private by design.
placement_reason: Built for a domain with no answer key: it grades what models PREFER (escalation, intervention, cooperation, alliance leanings) and how advice shifts by country advised, as a warning against national-security deployment bias. The object is latent value/judgment disposition and country-conditional bias, not skill — political-judgment kin of ETHICS/disagreement probes; escalation-propensity edges toward E2 but the instrument measures preference dispersion, not unsafe-action capability.

title: Adversarial Examples for Evaluating Reading Comprehension Systems
human_time: ~10-30s longer than the underlying SQuAD item: read one extra distractor sentence and re-locate the answer span.
frontier_score: ADDSENT drops 16 published SQuAD readers from 75.4% to 36.4% avg. F1; ADDANY drives the four development models to 6.7% avg.; a matched human control drops only 92.6%→89.2% under ADDONESENT.
one_line: ADDSENT/ADDANY: one human-approved distractor sentence appended to a SQuAD paragraph collapses 16 published readers from 75.4% to 36.4% F1.
notes: contamination_defense='procedural' is a judgment call: the adversarial sentences are generated adaptively per target model via black-box query access (not a fixed static test set), which structurally resists memorization the way procedural generation does, though the vocabulary term is more commonly used for infinite-generator benchmarks (e.g. Reasoning Gym) than for adaptive perturbation attacks — flagged as the closest available fit. items_count is left null: the explainer doesn't state the exact size of the SQuAD dev subset the adversarial attacks were run against.
placement_reason: The paper's entire contribution is a demonstration that SQuAD's F1 leaderboard 'was never measuring language understanding in the first place — it was measuring something closer to lexical overlap detection': one human-approved distractor sentence collapses 16 published readers from 75.4% to 36.4% F1 while a matched human control barely moves. That is B4's 'expose that a score means something else' verbatim — the paper is squarely an eval-rigor critique with a shipped diagnostic instrument (the Adv(f) metric and ADDSENT/ADDANY generators), not a new capability skill.

title: MedAgentBench: A Realistic Virtual EHR Environment to Benchmark Medical LLM Agents
human_time: Each task is a single clinical lookup, aggregation, or order (e.g. a lab value, a medication order) -- a few minutes of equivalent clinician EHR navigation, capped at 8 agent rounds.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2: 69.67% overall (85.33% Query); Gemini-1.5 Pro leads Action SR at 71.33% despite trailing overall
one_line: 300 physician-written tasks (150 read-only query, 150 state-changing action) testing whether LLM agents can read and propose writes to a FHIR-compliant virtual EHR built from 100 real, de-identified Stanford patients (785,207 records) with synthetic identities layered on top.
notes: contamination_defense=private-holdout is a judgment call: the underlying clinical content is drawn from Stanford's private STARR warehouse (not public pretraining data), but the benchmark suite/code is released publicly on GitHub, and the paper doesn't state whether the 300 reference solutions ship in that release. Action-task grading checks only the correctness of the proposed POST payload, never a verified database write (the harness deliberately never applies POSTs, to avoid a ~90s per-task environment reboot) -- a passing Action score shows a well-formed write request, not a confirmed state change.
placement_reason: Explicitly built to move medical LLM evaluation past saturated static exam QA (MedQA/MedMCQA) toward whether an agent can actually operate a real EHR through the same FHIR interoperability standard a hospital's own system exposes -- reading labs, aggregating vitals, ordering tests/meds -- professional clinical-deployment competence grounded in real (de-identified) patient records, the D2 case.

title: Know Me, Respond to Me: Benchmarking LLMs for Dynamic User Profiling and Personalized Responses at Scale
human_time: Given up to 60 sessions (~1M tokens) of interaction history plus an in-situ query, pick the response option matching the user's current state -- a few minutes to locate the relevant thread for a human.
frontier_score: Frontier models (GPT-4.5, GPT-4.1, Gemini-1.5-Flash) reach ~52% overall accuracy on 4-way MC (25% = chance); below chance on the hardest query type (proactively suggesting something new)
one_line: Personas whose preferences evolve over up to 60 sessions/1M tokens of synthetic chat history; ~6,000 in-situ 4-way-MC queries test whether a model tracks and applies the user's current (not outdated) state -- frontier models land near 52%, below the 25% floor on the hardest query type.
notes: grading_primary=exact-match for the main discriminative 4-way MC setting; a secondary generative setting (log-probability scoring, open-weight models only) is proxy-metric.
placement_reason: Isolates three sub-abilities of conversational personalization -- internalize traits, track how they evolve, and apply the current (not stale) state -- explicitly distinguished in the paper's own comparison table from static-preference benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, PrefEval all show 'No update' or at most one); a conversational-memory capability probe, the same A7 family as its own named comparators.

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
human_time: Gold patches average 1.7 files / 32.8 lines in 438K-line repos with multi-point edits; a competent engineer needs roughly 1-4 hours per issue.
frontier_score: Claude 3 Opus 3.79% (BM25, 2023); agent scaffolds pushed models past 40-50% within a year
one_line: 2,294 real GitHub issues: patch a Python repo so its hidden fail-to-pass unit tests pass — execution-graded SWE.
notes: Task_shape/tool_access reflect canonical agentic use; the paper's own 2023 baselines were single-turn retrieval-augmented generation with no tools. Contamination: date-split analysis is a probe and 'continually refreshable' a design claim, but the shipped 2,294 set is fully public. Saturation call leans on the explainer's 40-50% scaffold numbers plus own knowledge (SWE-bench Verified now ~70%+).
placement_reason: Born to ask 'can models resolve real GitHub issues?' after HumanEval-style function puzzles saturated — repo-level patch generation graded by hidden unit tests, a one-shot code-writing capability probe (the agentic-environment era it later spawned came after birth). A4 explicitly covers repo-level SWE work.

title: PubMedQA: A Dataset for Biomedical Research Question Answering
human_time: ~1-3 min per item: a trained human (MD candidate) reads a structured PubMed abstract (minus its conclusion) and answers yes/no/maybe; a single annotator reaches 78.0% accuracy under the reasoning-required setting.
frontier_score: Best 2019 model (multi-phase BioBERT) 68.08% accuracy / 52.72% macro-F1 vs 78.00%/72.19% single-human (reasoning-required); majority-class baseline 55.20%/23.71%
one_line: 1,000 expert-annotated yes/no/maybe questions built from PubMed's own question-titled, structured-abstract articles (plus 61.2k unlabeled and 211.3k rule-labeled training instances); best BioBERT model reaches 68.1% vs a 78.0% single-human ceiling.
notes: items_count is PQA-L, the expert-labeled evaluated subset; PQA-U (61,200 unlabeled) and PQA-A (211,300 rule-labeled) are additional training-only pools, not part of the graded benchmark. Provenance 'expert-authored' reflects PQA-L specifically (two MD-candidate annotators); the paper also ships synthetic and unlabeled subsets used only for pretraining. Saturation 'closing' is inferred (own knowledge) from modern LLMs' general strength on biomedical-literature QA; the explainer only reports 2019 numbers.
placement_reason: A held-out-conclusion reading-comprehension/entailment task over real biomedical research abstracts - infer a paper's own yes/no/maybe verdict from its stripped abstract, the same recognize/parse/entail pattern as SQuAD/HotpotQA/MedNLI, transplanted onto a scientific-literature domain rather than a novel occupational-workflow (D2) or knowledge-exam (A2) framing.

title: What Disease does this Patient Have? A Large-scale Open Domain Question Answering Dataset from Medical Exams
human_time: Minutes per item: read a patient vignette or fact-lookup question (avg 116.6 tokens for USMLE) and pick the right diagnosis/next-step from 4 options; no human baseline is reported in the paper.
frontier_score: Best 2020 baseline (BioBERT-Large / RoBERTa-Large-WWM-EXT) 36.7% USMLE / 70.1% MCMLE test vs. 25% chance; modern frontier LLMs score well above 85% on USMLE-style MedQA, far surpassing this retrieve-then-read-era ceiling
one_line: 61,097 real medical-board-exam questions (USMLE/MCMLE/TWMLE) paired with a 12.7M-token textbook corpus for open-domain retrieval-and-reasoning — now the default 'can this model practice medicine' benchmark.
notes: tool_access is search-retrieval since MedQA is explicitly an OpenQA (retrieve-then-read) setting requiring evidence retrieval from the paired textbook corpus, even though modern usage typically skips retrieval and answers from parametric knowledge. Saturation judged from own knowledge given the paper predates the LLM-benchmarking era.
placement_reason: Sourced directly from real medical licensing exams specifically because generic reading-comprehension benchmarks had saturated and tested only 'elementary or middle school level knowledge' — professional medical-domain content is the design core, and per the occupational-content-beats-framing rule (the same one that places LexGLUE and Med-PaLM, MedQA's own direct descendant, in D2) the exam-question format doesn't override that the object being measured is clinical competence.

title: MMToM-QA: Multimodal Theory of Mind Question Answering
human_time: A minute or so per question: watch the relevant portion of a household-activity video (up to ~4,000 frames total) plus read the paired text, then pick one of two options; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: Human 93.0% multimodal accuracy; GPT-4V 44.0% (near chance); the paper's own BIP-ALM baseline reaches 76.7%
one_line: 600 binary-choice belief/goal questions over 134 procedurally-generated household-activity videos, requiring fusion of video and text world-state to answer.
notes: domain_primary multimodal reflects the video+text fusion design that is the paper's actual contribution; social-moral is the least-bad ToM-domain fit per project convention (no dedicated theory-of-mind slot in BENCH_DOMAINS) and is used only as a secondary here.
placement_reason: Forces a model to fuse video and text to infer a hidden belief/goal — a multimodal perception-and-inference capability probe in VQA's own family (this taxonomy's A1 precedent for vision+language capability tests), not a hazard/deployment/audit paper: no measurement-instrument flaw is exposed and no professional domain is rehearsed, just whether the model can read implicit state from multimodal narrative.

title: TriviaQA: A Large Scale Distantly Supervised Challenge Dataset for Reading Comprehension
human_time: ~1-2 min per question: a trivia question plus an ~2,895-word (avg.) retrieved evidence document.
frontier_score: 2017 BiDAF baseline 40.3% EM / 45.7% F1 on Wikipedia dev vs. human 79.7%; now saturated and used as an easy closed-book factual-recall check for LLMs (SimpleQA, BrowseComp).
one_line: 95,956 trivia-enthusiast-authored questions with evidence retrieved afterward from Wikipedia/web — decoupling question authorship from evidence to force real reasoning.
notes: Saturation is explicitly stated in the explainer's own critique ('TriviaQA was effectively saturated within a few years... SimpleQA (2024) calls TriviaQA now saturated').
placement_reason: A reading-comprehension/knowledge-retrieval capability probe in the same mold as SQuAD (A1's own exemplar) — read retrieved evidence and answer a factoid question — decoupling question authorship from evidence gathering to force genuine cross-sentence reasoning rather than lexical-overlap pattern matching; not a construct audit of an existing score (the paper introduces a new construction methodology rather than exposing what SQuAD's or CNN/DM's score actually measures, even though it explicitly responds to both papers' shortcut limitations).

title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
human_time: Not stated in aggregate; the 9 constituent benchmarks range from short web-QA tasks (AssistantBench, minutes) to multi-file SWE-bench issue fixes and CORE-Bench Hard research-replication tasks (hours).
frontier_score: No single frontier score (a Pareto leaderboard); Gemini 2.0 Flash is Pareto-optimal on 7 of 9 benchmarks despite being the cheapest model tested, while the priciest model (Claude Opus 4.1) lands on the accuracy-cost frontier in only 1 of 9
one_line: A standardized harness, three-axis (model x scaffold x benchmark) Pareto-frontier leaderboard, and LLM-aided log analysis across 21,730 rollouts on 9 agent benchmarks — explicitly framed as 'HELM's agent-era counterpart' — showing reasoning effort rarely helps and that identical accuracy scores can hide catastrophic agent behavior.
notes: items_count=null (mirrors HELM's own null): HAL is a leaderboard-of-leaderboards with no fixed item set of its own; 21,730 rollouts across 9 benchmarks/9 models/~$40,000 compute is the scale figure, noted in one_line instead. saturation='not-applicable' mirrors Arena-Hard's own call for a live, relative, cost-vs-accuracy Pareto artifact rather than a single-ceiling score. grading_all includes llm-judge for the Docent log-analysis layer (a six-part rubric over 1,634 of the 21,730 rollouts, ~7.5%) — the page's critique flags this coverage gap and the lack of a reported precision/recall for Docent's own judgments as the paper's weakest-evidenced claim. contamination_defense='none-public': HAL catches a real scaffold-level leakage bug (a TAU-bench few-shot prompt containing real eval examples) via log analysis, but that's incidental discovery, not a shipped ongoing defense (mirrors TRAIL's same 'freshness is incidental' convention).
placement_reason: HAL's own framing is explicit — 'HELM's agent-era counterpart' — building the standardized harness, cross-model/cross-scaffold/cross-benchmark comparability, and Pareto-frontier aggregation that agent evaluation lacked, exactly HELM's move (a holistic aggregation framework, not a new task) transplanted from static LM benchmarks to interactive agent rollouts; distinguished from any single capability benchmark it wraps (GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, etc.) because HAL contributes no new task itself, only the measurement infrastructure and cross-cutting cost/behavior analysis layered on top of them.

title: BIG-Bench Extra Hard
human_time: A single reasoning puzzle (temporal, spatial, causal, logical-deduction, sports-knowledge, etc.), now with ~6x longer inputs and more distractors than BBH -- a few minutes per item.
frontier_score: Best general-purpose model: 9.8% harmonic-mean accuracy; best reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini, high): 44.8%
one_line: Replaces every one of BBH's 23 saturated tasks (90%+ SOTA) with a harder analogue, semi-adversarially tuned until two Gemini reference models score below 70%; the best general-purpose model manages 9.8% harmonic-mean accuracy.
notes: items_count = 22 tasks x 200 + Disambiguation QA x 120 = 4,520 (a 460-item 'BBEH Mini' subset also ships). Provenance=aggregated: several tasks adapt wholesale from other published benchmarks (Linguini, SportQA, a SpatialLLMEval-derived task, MoCa/Kiciman causal items) alongside newly constructed ones.
placement_reason: Explicit like-for-like reconstruction of a saturated benchmark: keeps BBH's 23-task skeleton (the reasoning-skill coverage that made it useful) and swaps in a harder version of each task, semi-adversarially tuned against reference models until headroom is restored -- the named B3 pattern, not a new capability probe from scratch.

title: Are You Smarter Than A Sixth Grader? Textbook Question Answering for Multimodal Machine Comprehension
group: Allen Institute for AI / University of Washington
human_time: ~1-3 min per question: a middle-school science lesson (text + diagram) plus a multiple-choice question.
frontier_score: Best 2017 baseline near-random on Text True/False (50.4% vs. 50.0% floor); best Text MC 32.9% (vs. 22.7% random); best Diagram MC 31.3% (vs. 25.0% random).
one_line: 1,076 CK-12 middle-school science lessons (diagrams+text) paired with 26,260 multiple-choice questions — a bounded-knowledge multimodal machine-comprehension testbed.
notes: A2 (not A1) placement follows the same pattern as its direct descendant ScienceQA (already in the taxonomy as A2-knowledge-exams, domain=science): a grade-school curriculum multiple-choice exam, multimodal because the curriculum bundles diagrams with text, is squarely a knowledge-exam construct. Saturation ('open') reflects the huge headroom the paper's own 2017 baselines show (near-random on True/False); no later frontier score is discussed in the explainer.
placement_reason: A grade-school-curriculum multiple-choice exam (CK-12 lessons + workbook/quiz questions), multimodal because the curriculum bundles diagrams with text — matching A2's 'recall and apply knowledge under exam conditions' far more than A1's open-ended reading-comprehension framing, and placed identically to its own direct descendant ScienceQA (already A2-knowledge-exams, domain=science, in this taxonomy). Not A5: nothing here is an interactive environment an agent operates, it's a static multiple-choice exam.

title: FANToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
group: Allen Institute for AI / University of Washington / CMU / Seoul National University
human_time: A few minutes to read a multi-turn small-talk conversation (13.8 turns avg, short-context condition) and answer several belief/awareness questions about it.
frontier_score: GPT-4 0613 (June) hits 73.3% on BeliefQ[Choice] alone but only 12.3% on the strict ALL aggregate (26.6% with chain-of-thought), vs. humans' 87.5% ALL; ChatGPT and Falcon-40B collapse to ~0% ALL despite 53-54% on BeliefQ[Choice] alone.
one_line: 256 LLM-generated multiparty conversations with real information asymmetry (characters leave and rejoin) converted to ~10.3K questions across six converging formats about the same fact, scored by a strict all-six-correct (ALL*) conjunction that catches 'illusory' theory of mind — passing one question format while failing an equivalent one.
notes: Placed in B4 rather than A3 (unlike Hi-ToM in the same batch) because FANToM's own problem statement is explicitly a measurement-validity critique — invoking psychology's non-merging/mentalizing criteria and diagnosing 'illusory ToM' (a model that answers one question format correctly while failing a differently-shaped equivalent) — not a capability-depth extension. items_count=10,317 sums the seven per-question-type counts the explainer states (1,415+1,415+703+703+703+2,689+2,689); the paper's own prose rounds this to 'roughly 10K.'
placement_reason: Explicitly a measurement-validity critique, invoking psychology's non-merging and mentalizing criteria to argue prior ToM benchmarks are gameable by pattern-matching or self-projection. The diagnostic instrument — six differently-shaped questions about the same fact, scored only if a model is coherent across all six (ALL*) — exists to expose 'illusory ToM,' the canonical B4 move, not depth of belief-order capability (contrast Hi-ToM, A3, in the same batch).

title: The BiGGen Bench: A Principled Benchmark for Fine-grained Evaluation of Language Models with Language Models
human_time: One instance is a single system-message + input generation task (e.g. a math rationale, a ToM dialogue response); a few minutes to answer well.
frontier_score: Best single-evaluator human correlation: GPT-4-Turbo r=0.623 (majority vote across 5 judges: 0.627); open Prometheus-2-BGB 8x7B reaches 0.607, matching GPT-4-1106 (0.597) and beating Claude-3-Opus (0.578)
one_line: 765 test instances across 9 capabilities, each scored against a bespoke instance-specific 5-point rubric rather than a generic helpfulness scale -- shown to correlate with human judgment better than coarse-grained or FLASK-style domain rubrics.
notes: Domain is a judgment call: the benchmark spans 9 capabilities (instruction following, grounding, planning, reasoning, refinement, safety, theory of mind, tool usage, multilingual) with no single natural primary, so 'reasoning' is used as the broad catch-all per the BIG-bench precedent. ~Half of the final 765 instances are GPT-4-0125-expanded from human-written seeds, then human cross-validated -> synthetic-generated. 103 response LMs are evaluated, but frontier_score above is the judge-validity number (the paper's real headline claim), since the object being benchmarked is the grading protocol itself.
placement_reason: The headline claim is about the grading protocol, not any response model's skill: instance-specific rubrics correlate with human judgment better than MT-Bench-style coarse criteria or FLASK's fixed domain criteria, validated with 3,236 human ratings across five candidate judge LMs -- a judge/rubric-granularity validation study, G3's territory (FActScore's role: 'a way of evaluating'), not G1's holistic aggregation of pre-existing scattered tasks (BiGGen Bench's 77 tasks are original, not a compendium like HELM/BIG-bench).

title: MedExQA: Medical Question Answering Benchmark with Multiple Explanations
human_time: One MCQ + explanation from a licensed allied-health board exam (biomedical engineering, clinical lab science, clinical psychology, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology); a few minutes to answer and justify.
frontier_score: GPT4_0125: 78.8% chat-based MCQ accuracy (only MCQ figure reported for GPT models) and 32.79 AVG explanation-quality score, both benchmark highs; best open-source logits accuracy is Med42-70B at 72.0%, but every logits-scored model collapses on Speech Language Pathology (best 33.1%, SOLAR)
one_line: 965-question medical QA benchmark across five allied-health specialties absent from MMLU/MedQA/MedMCQA, pairing every question with two independently-styled reference explanations so generation-quality metrics can score against multiple references instead of one.
notes: 940-question test set (25-question few-shot dev set held out). grading_primary=proxy-metric because the benchmark's own headline contribution is enabling multi-reference BLEU/ROUGE-L/METEOR/BERTScore explanation grading (Pearson-with-human correlation rises 0.9347->0.9385 with the second reference); MCQ classification accuracy (exact-match) and a 25-question human eval (0/0.5/1 rubric) are both also reported.
placement_reason: Built from allied-health board-style mock exams (biomedical engineering, clinical lab science, clinical psychology, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology) that MMLU/MedQA/MedMCQA don't cover, scored primarily by MCQ accuracy against a 60%-pass-mark source -- a knowledge-exam capability probe extending coverage and reference-explanation richness, same family as MedExpQA/MMLU/MedQA, not a deployment rehearsal (no clinician panel or dialogue simulation, unlike Med-PaLM/AgentClinic).

title: Pick-a-Pic: An Open Dataset of User Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation
human_time: A single click choosing between two already-generated images; seconds per vote for a casual web-app user.
frontier_score: PickScore: 70.5% +/- 0.142 preference-prediction accuracy (beats disclosed human-expert baseline 68.0%, 2023); Elo correlation with real users 0.790 vs. HPS v1 0.670 / ImageReward 0.492 / CLIP-H 0.313
one_line: A live public web app turns real T2I users into an open, half-million-pair (growing) preference dataset; PickScore, a CLIP-H scorer trained on it, is proposed as the field's replacement for FID.
notes: Kingdom judged G2 (live preference-collection platform, the Chatbot Arena analog: ever-growing live user traffic, no fixed ceiling on the dataset, Elo-correlation demonstration) rather than F1 (no gradient-based generator training is attempted in this paper - Section 6's re-ranking is inference-time best-of-N selection, not weight fine-tuning). saturation 'not-applicable' follows Chatbot Arena's precedent for the open/live collection, though the paper's separate fixed 500-example test-set accuracy metric could alternatively support 'open' - a genuine judgment call. items_count = the fixed 500-example test set behind the headline 70.5% accuracy number, not the larger (583,747, growing to 1M+) live dataset.
placement_reason: A live, open web-app preference-collection PLATFORM (real users picking between generated images, dataset still growing past the paper's own snapshot) that yields both an open dataset and a proposed replacement evaluation metric (PickScore), validated by Spearman correlation against human model-rankings (0.917) and Elo-correlation against real users (0.790) - the G2 pattern (live preference collection + ranking protocol as the contribution, the T2I analog of Chatbot Arena), not a training-signal generator like ImageReward's ReFL, which this paper doesn't attempt.

title: FORTRESS: Frontier Risk Evaluation for National Security and Public Safety
human_time: One single-turn adversarial (or benign-twin) prompt -> one response; reading and answering/refusing takes a few minutes.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet most robust: ARS 14.09 (but ORS 21.80); o3 balanced at ARS 17.20 / ORS 7.80
one_line: 500 expert adversarial NSPS prompts + benign twins; rubric-panel-graded risk (ARS) vs over-refusal (ORS) on CBRNE/terror/crime.
notes: items_count = 500 public adversarial prompts, each with a benign twin (1,010 adversarial total; ~510 held private as the contamination holdout). ARS uses per-item 4-7-question rubrics voted by a 3-judge panel (rubric-judge); ORS uses a single holistic GPT-4o-mini judge (llm-judge). 'Open': best models remain far from ideal ARS~0/ORS~0 and the two trade off.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'do safeguards hold when an adversary actually asks?' — 500 expert-mined single-turn jailbreak prompts on CBRNE/terrorism/financial-crime plus benign twins for over-refusal. The object is safeguard robustness under attack (explicitly contrasted with WMDP's plainly-posed knowledge probes), squarely a jailbreak/refusal attack-surface instrument.

title: WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts
human_time: Seconds per item for the fastest datasets (classify one tumor patch or camera-trap photo); minutes for others (wheat-head detection, satellite-imagery wealth estimation) -- varies widely across the 10 datasets.
frontier_score: Standard ERM shows a real ID-OOD gap on all 10 datasets (7.2 to 36.2 points on percentage metrics); CORAL/IRM/Group DRO fail to close the gap on 8 of 10 and sometimes widen it (IRM drops RxRx1 from 29.9 to 8.2)
one_line: Ten curated real-world distribution-shift datasets (hospitals, camera traps, molecular scaffolds, satellite imagery) proving that off-the-shelf domain-generalization/subpopulation-shift methods mostly fail to close the ID-OOD gap synthetic-shift benchmarks like ImageNet-C never captured.
notes: items_count left null: WILDS is a 10-dataset suite (6,515 to 539,502 examples per dataset) with no single item pool, unlike a fixed-size single-domain benchmark. The paper is unusually candid about its own soft spots (Camelyon17's single-held-out-hospital variance, protocol heterogeneity across the 5 ID-comparison methods used, algorithms run outside their intended shift regime) -- itself part of what makes it a strong construct audit.
placement_reason: The whole contribution is showing that standard in-distribution accuracy overstates real deployment robustness -- curated real (not synthetic) shifts across 10 domains, each cleared through a real-drop/real-relevance/solvable-in-principle bar, explicitly built in response to synthetic-shift benchmarks (ImageNet-C, and DeepFashion Remixed from 'Many Faces of Robustness') whose robustness gains 'need not transfer' to real deployment shift -- a measurement-validity audit (B4), not a fixed-task capability probe.

title: VisualWebArena: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Realistic Visual Web Tasks
human_time: Human baseline 88.7% task success; paper doesn't report a per-task time.
frontier_score: Best VLM agent (GPT-4V + Set-of-Marks): 16.4% success vs. 88.7% human ceiling
one_line: A 910-task benchmark extending WebArena with genuinely visually-grounded web tasks across Classifieds, Shopping, and Reddit sites — the best VLM agent reaches 16.4% success against an 88.7% human ceiling.
notes: Direct extension of WebArena adding visual grounding as a first-class requirement, not just a text-accessibility-tree shortcut.
placement_reason: WebArena's visual-grounding sequel: the same persistent-website, functional-correctness design, but tasks are specifically constructed so a text-only accessibility-tree agent cannot solve them without seeing the page.

title: MobileWorld: Benchmarking Autonomous Mobile Agents in Agent-User Interactive and MCP-Augmented Environments
human_time: Not stated; individual UI actions are quick, but MobileWorld's tasks run a right-skewed 27.8-step average (vs. AndroidWorld's 14.3), with a second mode near 45-50 steps, so the longer multi-app tasks likely push past AndroidWorld's minutes-scale norm for a human.
frontier_score: GPT-5 + UI-Ins-7B leads at 51.7% overall (54.0% GUI-Only, 62.2% User-Interaction, 51.6% MCP); best end-to-end GUI model (Doubao-1.5-UI-TARS) reaches only 20.9%
one_line: 201-task, 20-app mobile GUI benchmark replacing AndroidWorld's saturated single-app tasks with long-horizon cross-app workflows, agent-user clarification dialogue, and MCP tool invocation, scored deterministically via self-hosted app backends; the best system reaches only 51.7% success.
notes: confidence=medium: the page's critique finds the SOTA agentic framework's grounding model (UI-Ins-7B) shares essentially the same author roster as MobileWorld itself, released two months earlier from the same lab, while every end-to-end competitor is fully external — an unflagged asymmetry; it also shows the 'Overall' SR formula appears to silently score untested Interaction/MCP tasks as failures for models excused from having those action spaces (working backward from GUI-Owl-7B's numbers confirms this), inflating the agentic-vs-end-to-end gap; and the two novel categories (40-45 tasks each) carry no run-to-run variance reporting. contamination_defense='none-public': no canary, live-refresh, or private-holdout mechanism is disclosed for the released 201-task set.
placement_reason: Ships a new interactive environment for operating a real phone — self-hosted deterministic app backends (Mattermost/Mastodon/Mall4Uni stand-ins for apps it can't authenticate into), a POMDP-over-screenshots task format, and a new action space (ask_user, mcp_call) — the same 'can an agent operate this device' question AndroidWorld asks, extended with genuinely new action types rather than only harder items of the identical format; kept out of B3-desaturation-sequels because, unlike a same-format headroom-restoring sequel (MMLU→MMLU-Pro), MobileWorld adds two structurally new task families (clarification dialogue, MCP tool calls) that AndroidWorld's action space couldn't even attempt, matching A5's own precedent for environment-expanding sequels (VisualWebArena vs. WebArena).

title: ContractNLI: A Dataset for Document-level Natural Language Inference for Contracts
human_time: One item = read a full NDA (~2,254 tokens avg) and judge one policy hypothesis plus mark evidence spans — several minutes.
frontier_score: DeBERTa-xlarge + CUAD transfer: NLI acc .892, evidence mAP .936 (contradiction F1 only .405)
one_line: 607 NDAs x 17 fixed policy hypotheses: document-level entail/contradict/not-mentioned plus evidence-span identification.
notes: Professional-vs-language primary is borderline: it is classic NLI machinery, but the work is real legal contract review over real NDAs, so classified by the work's nature. items_count = 607 docs x 17 hypotheses (~10.3K pairs; test = 123 docs, ~2.1K pairs). Evidence mAP treated as exact-match against gold span sets. Saturation: headline acc .892 reads closing, but the hard contradiction/negation-by-exception subclass is wide open.
placement_reason: The gap opens on professional contract review as costly, hand-done paid work (Fortune-1000 firms hold 20-40k contracts) and reframes it as document-level NLI so policy violations can be flagged automatically. Occupational content (contracts/law, ancestral to LegalBench) beats the NLI task-framing per the tie-break, so D2 over A1.

title: Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images
human_time: Seconds per image: single-object classification among 10 or 100 classes.
frontier_score: Best 2009 result (backprop net initialized from unwhitened-RBM features): 64.84% CIFAR-10 test accuracy; modern CNNs exceed 99%.
one_line: 10/100-class labeled subsets (6,000/600 images per class) carved from 80M web images — the default small-image classification sandbox of the deep-learning era.
notes: Provenance is a judgment call: labels came from paid student labelers (not an MTurk-style crowd), each submission personally verified by the author — closer to a small trained team than a broad crowd platform, but classified 'crowdsourced' for consistency with ImageNet's web-image-plus-human-verification pattern. Saturation from own knowledge (CIFAR-10.1 independent resample found consistent accuracy drops; modern models exceed 99%).
placement_reason: CIFAR-10/100 are label-and-classify image benchmarks in the ImageNet/COCO mold — the report's real headline contribution (RBM/DBN generative modeling) is a historical footnote, but the two datasets it ships as evaluation material are the enduring artifact, and their construct (recognize an object class in a small image) is squarely A1's perception-probe definition.

title: Refusal-Trained LLMs Are Easily Jailbroken As Browser Agents
human_time: Each behavior is a short browser task (send an email, register an account, post content) — a human completes one in a few minutes; agents get a 10-step cap.
frontier_score: GPT-4o agent: 74% ASR direct-ask, 100% under attack ensemble; most robust agent (Claude 3 Opus) still 41%
one_line: 100 harmful browser-agent behaviors on synthetic + live sites testing whether chat refusal training survives agentic framing.
notes: ASR judged by a GPT-4o classifier (HarmBench-style, holistic — no per-item rubric); synthetic-site action listeners log actions but do not grade. Provenance mixed: 46 original red-team-authored, 54 adapted from HarmBench/AIR-Bench (partly aggregated). 'Open' read from the defender's side: even the most robust agent is jailbroken 41% of the time under ensemble attack.
placement_reason: Built to test whether chat refusal training survives the agentic setting: 100 harmful browser behaviors on sandboxed websites, headline = attack success rate jumping 12%->74%->100% under transferred jailbreaks. Browser-agent red-teaming / refusal-of-harmful-web-actions is a named E1 exemplar; the object is risk, not skill.

title: LongLaMP: A Benchmark for Personalized Long-form Text Generation
human_time: One item is completing an email, writing an abstract/review/Reddit post in a specific user's voice, conditioned on their retrieved writing history; a few minutes to draft a comparable paragraph.
frontier_score: Personalization gains range 5.7%-128% across metrics vs. non-personalized generation, averaging 30.21% ROUGE-1 / 47.5% ROUGE-L; Email Completion gains most (up to 169% ROUGE-L), Review Writing least (low single digits)
one_line: Extends LaMP's short-form personalization benchmark to full paragraphs -- email completion, abstract generation, review writing, Reddit posts -- retrieval-augmented from a user's own writing history, scored against what that user actually wrote.
notes: No single unified item count: four tasks x two splits each (e.g. Email Completion user-split: 3,286 train/958 val/823 test; Review Writing user-split: 14,745 train/1,822 test). Built from four pre-existing real-world corpora (Avocado Email, AMiner citation network, Amazon Reviews, Reddit TL;DR) -> aggregated. The Email task's source (Avocado) is a private, confidentiality-controlled corpus chosen specifically to avoid pretraining leakage, but the other three tasks are fully public with no stated defense, so contamination_defense is called none-public overall.
placement_reason: Moves LLM personalization past LaMP's title/headline-length outputs into full paragraphs across four real use cases, testing whether a model holds a consistent voice and stays on-topic for 100+ tokens while conditioning on a specific user's retrieved history -- an extension of A7's tailor-output-to-the-partner mandate to long-form personalized writing, not a tool-orchestration (A6) or retrieval-capability (A1) paper, since retrieval is instrumentation for personalization, not the measured skill.

title: The Open Images Dataset V4: Unified image classification, object detection, and visual relationship detection at scale
human_time: Seconds per item: verify a candidate image-level label, or draw a box via extreme-clicking (avg. 7.4s/box).
frontier_score: No single headline leaderboard score (a construction/methodology paper); own baselines show detection mAP rising monotonically with training-set size up to the full 14.6M-box subset, and image-level label recall audited at only 43-59% against expert re-annotation (vs. COCO's quoted 83%).
one_line: 9.18M Creative-Commons Flickr images unified across image classification (30.1M labels, 19,794 classes), detection (15.4M boxes, 600 classes, 17.4x COCO's box count), and visual-relationship detection (374,768 triplets) on the same images, with a custom mAP_OI metric built for non-exhaustive labeling.
notes: Saturation set to open given the paper's own acknowledged 1:10,000 class-imbalance long tail and 43-59% label recall -- substantial, unresolved coverage gaps by the authors' own audit, not a benchmark near any ceiling.
placement_reason: A large-scale perception capability probe unifying classification, detection, and visual-relationship recognition on one image pool so cross-task and joint training become testable -- the canonical A1 perception/parsing construct at unprecedented scale, plus a metric (mAP_OI) purpose-built for its own non-exhaustive labeling rather than a new reasoning or interaction skill.

title: Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research
human_time: One item = find (or decline to find) a long+short answer in a full Wikipedia page for one real query — roughly 1-3 minutes of scanning.
frontier_score: Paper-era best: 55.0 long-answer F1 vs single human 73.4 and super-annotator ceiling 87.2
one_line: 307K real Google queries paired with full Wikipedia pages; extract long + short answers or abstain, scored vs a human ceiling.
notes: Language-vs-knowledge primary is borderline: real info-seeking world-knowledge queries, but the shipped task is doc-grounded extraction in the SQuAD lineage -> language, with knowledge and long-context (full-page input, retrieval lineage: DPR/BEIR) secondary. Provenance: queries mined from real search logs (user-traffic) with crowd annotation. Saturated call uses post-paper knowledge (BERT-era+ models approached the 87.2 ceiling; community treats the original task as retired) — the explainer itself only quotes pre-BERT 55 F1. items_count = test split (7,842); 307K train + 7.8K dev.
placement_reason: Born to replace back-written, artifact-leaking reading-comprehension sets (SQuAD already superhuman) with 307k real search queries over full Wikipedia pages — headline is the human-machine gap on genuine information-seeking span extraction/retrieval, the canonical A1 parse-and-extract construct.

title: DS-1000: A Natural and Reliable Benchmark for Data Science Code Generation
human_time: Problems average 140 words with 3.6-line reference solutions; a fluent data scientist solves one in a few minutes.
frontier_score: Codex-002 (Insertion) 43.3% pass@1 — 2022 best, since 'cleared comfortably' by modern models per the explainer
one_line: 1,000 StackOverflow data-science problems across 7 Python libraries, execution-graded and perturbed to defeat memorization.
notes: Contamination: ships a genuine one-time perturbation defense (>half of problems modified from their StackOverflow sources) that doesn't fit the taxonomy buckets — the set is static and public with no holdout/refresh, so none-public with this caveat. Grading combines execution tests and AST surface-form constraints, both programmatic. Saturation uses own knowledge that modern models score well above 43.3%.
placement_reason: Asks 'can models write real data-science code?' — 1,000 StackOverflow-sourced pandas/numpy/etc. problems, execution-graded with a reliable multi-criteria metric and perturbed against memorization; headline is Codex-002 at 43.3%. DS-1000 is a named A4 exemplar; the contamination defence is a design feature, not the headline claim, so A4 over B1.

title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
human_time: Not applicable — the 'subject' being tested is a reward model, not a human or generalist LLM.
frontier_score: 80+ reward models scored; wide spread across chat/chat-hard/safety/reasoning subsets, no model near-ceiling on all four
one_line: A common benchmark and evaluation codebase for reward models — the classifiers and DPO checkpoints that decide what counts as a better answer during RLHF — exposing a wide, previously invisible gap between classifier-trained and DPO-derived reward models.
notes: Dual-tagged benchmarks+evaluations: it is both a named leaderboard (a survey of benchmarks would cite it) and the field's first standard evaluation codebase for an entire model class (reward models) that had none before.
placement_reason: Reward models are themselves graders (they decide which of two responses is better during RLHF); RewardBench is the benchmark that tests the graders, aggregating chat, reasoning, safety, and legacy preference subsets into one leaderboard — the reward-model peer of JudgeBench's LLM-judge testing.

title: LAB-Bench: Measuring Capabilities of Language Models for Biology Research
human_time: A few minutes per typical item (read a figure, compute a sequence task, retrieve a finding); the 41 CloningScenarios take a biologist 10-60 min but are the tail, not the median.
frontier_score: models cluster at low absolute accuracy (~0.2-0.35); Claude 3.5 Sonnet only matches/edges humans on TableQA
one_line: 2,457-question multiple-choice benchmark of practical biology-research tasks: lit search, figure/table reading, DB lookup, protocol troubleshooting, sequence/cloning.
notes: domain_primary=science per rubric (LAB-Bench named there); multimodal secondary because FigQA/TableQA (~531 items) are caption-less images. Provenance is a split: LitQA/SuppQA/Fig/Table/Protocol/Cloning are expert-authored but SeqQA+DbQA (~1,400 of 2,457) are program-generated, so 'synthetic-generated' is a defensible alternative; called expert-authored on the benchmark's headline identity. tool_access=[none] because the eval was explicitly tool-free even though the tasks are designed to be tool-dependent. Headline metric is MC accuracy (exact-match); the open-response rerun grading mechanism is not specified in the text.
placement_reason: The gap explicitly rejects MMLU/GPQA-style exams ('real biology research is a workflow, not a quiz') and probes whether frontier models can do the work of research: literature search, figure/table reading, database lookup, protocol troubleshooting, DNA/protein and cloning tasks. It is the named exemplar of A8-research-execution (open-ended scientific knowledge work).

title: Revisiting the Evaluation of Theory of Mind through Question Answering
human_time: Seconds per item: short bAbI-style synthetic stories (few sentences) with a single object-location question; quick for a human to read and answer, though false-belief items require explicitly tracking what another agent has/hasn't observed.
frontier_score: Best 2019 model (EntNet) 66.8% joint accuracy on ToMi overall, but only 54.95% on first-order false-belief pairs and 36.55% on second-order false-belief pairs specifically (MemNN/RelNet far lower, 10.4-17.8%); no human ceiling reported
one_line: Fixes ToM-bAbi's leaky three-template story generator (perfectly solvable by a four-rule lexical hack with zero belief modeling) with a single randomized generator plus distractors, and a stricter joint-accuracy protocol scoring all six question types per story together.
notes: items_count left null - dataset size and train/test split counts are absent from the paper's own six-page main text (deferred to unincluded supplementary material, per the explainer's own critique). Saturation 'saturated' is an own-knowledge inference (modern LLMs generally handle short synthetic bAbI-style reasoning well), not a number in the explainer.
placement_reason: ToM-bAbi's three rigid story templates leak the answer through pure lexical/positional cues (a hand-written four-rule solver with zero belief modeling reaches 100%); ToMi rebuilds the same construct (false-belief theory-of-mind QA) with a randomized generator and a stricter joint-accuracy metric that restores real headroom (44.3-66.8% joint accuracy, collapsing further to 10.4-54.95% on false-belief pairs specifically) - the diagnose-and-rebuild pattern that places HellaSwag/WinoGrande/MultiNLI here, not a plain new capability probe.

title: DailyDialog: A Manually Labelled Multi-turn Dialogue Dataset
human_time: Seconds per turn: a short daily-life conversational reply (avg. 14.6 tokens/utterance); the paper reports no human evaluation of generated replies at all.
frontier_score: Best 2017 baseline: feature-based retrieval BLEU-4 0.194 vs. gold; generation ties at BLEU-4 0.009 across three architectures (plain HRED, label-conditioned Attn-Seq2Seq, label-conditioned HRED) -- no human evaluation was run.
one_line: 13,118 human-written, single-session, multi-turn daily-life dialogues manually double-labeled with 4-class dialog acts and 7-class Ekman emotions -- a compact, topic-coherent alternative to noisy social-media dialogue corpora.
notes: Provenance is a judgment call: dialogues are scraped from English-learner practice websites (templated, pedagogically-written scenarios) rather than either organic real-world conversation or crowdsourced chit-chat, so 'real-work-mined' is an approximation -- closest available category to 'mined from an existing real source' though the source is itself synthetic teaching content. Saturation set to not-applicable: the paper's own generation/retrieval numbers (BLEU-4 up to 0.194) are explicitly flagged by the authors as weak signals with no human validation, and the corpus is used today mainly as a dialog-act/emotion resource rather than via one tracked frontier score. domain_secondary includes social-moral for the emotion-tagging axis, though the mini-benchmark itself scores generation quality, not emotion classification.
placement_reason: Built to give conversational models a clean, topic-coherent, dual-labeled (dialog-act + emotion) alternative to sprawling Switchboard/OpenSubtitles transcripts or noisy Twitter/Weibo post-reply pairs, then benchmarks next-utterance retrieval/generation against it -- a conversational-capability probe (A7), not a knowledge or reasoning test.

title: BEHAVIOR-1K: A Benchmark for Embodied AI with 1,000 Everyday Activities and Realistic Simulation
human_time: ~10-30 min estimated per household activity (e.g. 'wash the floor', 'clean after a party'); not stated directly in the paper.
frontier_score: Action-primitive RL (+history): 0.42-0.88 success across 3 hand-picked activities; end-to-end visuomotor RL 0.00 (2022)
one_line: 1,000 household activities (909 top-ranked by a 1,461-respondent preference survey, 91 from BEHAVIOR-100), simulated in a new fluid/deformable/thermal-capable engine, OmniGibson.
notes: domain_primary 'multimodal' follows the ImageNet/COCO precedent for vision-centric benchmarks; BENCH_DOMAINS has no dedicated 'robotics/embodied' slot. tool_access 'none' since the primitive action space (pick/place/push/navigate) is the task's native interface, not an external tool in the LLM-agent sense the vocabulary was built for (a judgment call, flagged for the merge).
placement_reason: The contribution is the ENVIRONMENT: a survey-grounded 1,000-activity household task set instantiated in a new simulator (OmniGibson) built because prior engines couldn't realistically simulate the fluids/deformables/thermal effects 'over half' the activities require — an embodied-operation capability probe (can an agent operate a photorealistic household simulation), matching the A5 pattern (Mind2Web/WebArena/OSWorld's physical-world analog), not an audit or deployment rehearsal.

title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
human_time: One dialogue turn requiring an API call (weather, calendar, search) takes a human a couple of minutes with the right tool; not stated directly in the paper.
frontier_score: GPT-4: 60.24% overall accuracy (2023); GPT-3.5-turbo 47.16%; fine-tuned Lynx-7B 39.58%
one_line: A runnable, three-tier (Call / Retrieve+Call / Plan+Retrieve+Call) tool-use benchmark of 73 hand-implemented APIs and 314 annotated dialogues, grounded in 500 user interviews.
notes: task_shape judged 'multi-turn' (314 annotated dialogues over a real, stateful backend) rather than 'interactive-env'; a defensible alternative given the runnable, state-changing nature of the API calls. provenance covers the classified EVAL artifact (hand-built 314-dialogue set, $8/dialogue annotation); the separate 1,888-dialogue TRAINING set is synthetic-generated via a 5-agent pipeline, noted but not the classified facet. The paper's own comparison table cites ToolLLM/Gorilla, but those postdate this paper's arXiv date (2023-05/07 vs. this paper's 2023-04), so they are excluded from lineage to avoid a reversed-chronology edge.
placement_reason: A runnable, three-tier tool-orchestration benchmark grounded in 500 user interviews, testing whether a model can select and sequence real, stateful APIs (Call / Retrieve+Call / Plan+Retrieve+Call) — the A6 headline skill, matching ToolLLM/Gorilla's family; its second half (a 5-agent synthetic training-data pipeline) is a reward/training-data contribution, but the classified artifact is the hand-built eval benchmark itself.

title: Can LLM Already Serve as A Database Interface? A BIg Bench for Large-Scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQLs
human_time: A skilled analyst writes one SQL query (avg 30.9 tokens, ~1 JOIN) over a dirty schema in ~5-15 min; simple items faster, challenging (10%) longer.
frontier_score: GPT-4 54.89% execution accuracy vs 92.96% human experts (hidden test, oracle knowledge)
one_line: Large-scale text-to-SQL benchmark: 12,751 questions over 95 dirty real-world databases (33GB) with hand-annotated evidence and the VES efficiency metric.
notes: Text-to-SQL = coding (SQL synthesis); knowledge secondary because external-knowledge grounding (worth ~+20 pts) is the paper's headline bottleneck. Grading is execution-result match against gold = programmatic. tool_access=[none] because the base eval is text (schema+question+evidence)->SQL with no execution feedback to the model; a domain-api reading is possible for agentic variants (DIN-SQL). Provenance is borderline: databases are real-work-mined (Kaggle) but the NL-question/SQL pairs are written by vetted crowds -> called crowdsourced. Saturation=closing: published best is 54.89% (~59% of the 92.96% ceiling, borderline open) but the explainer states agentic pipelines have since closed much of the gap.
placement_reason: A text-to-SQL benchmark ('Can LLM serve as a database interface?') whose headline is model execution accuracy on generating correct/efficient SQL over dirty real-world databases. A4 explicitly names text-to-SQL; framing is a capability probe, not economic/deployment realism, so it stays in A4 rather than D.

title: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
human_time: A single yes/no visual-object-presence judgment; a few seconds for a human looking at the image.
frontier_score: InstructBLIP leads at 88.73% accuracy / 89.29 F1 (Random, MSCOCO, 2023); three of five LVLMs answer 'Yes' to 95.37-100% of questions, F1 near the 66.67 constant-Yes floor
one_line: Replaces CHAIR's prompt-sensitive free-form caption parsing with closed-form yes/no polling (random/popular/adversarial negative sampling), 20x more stable across prompt rewordings.
notes: provenance 'synthetic-generated': the base images/ground-truth objects are drawn from existing datasets (MSCOCO/A-OKVQA/GQA) unchanged, but the polling QUESTIONS themselves - the evaluated items - are newly constructed via a template + rule-based negative-sampling algorithm, not merely repackaged from an existing item pool.
placement_reason: The gap is that CHAIR's free-form caption parsing is a broken grader for LVLM hallucination - its CHAIR_I score swings from 14.8 to 30.2 (and flips model rankings) on two semantically-identical prompt rewordings. POPE replaces it with a closed-form yes/no polling protocol needing no caption parser, empirically 20x more stable (CV 1.16% vs. 23.2%) - the measurement apparatus is the headline finding, matching EvalPlus's named B2 pattern (harden a broken grader of an existing construct) rather than introducing a new hallucination construct or skill.

title: From Crowdsourced Data to High-Quality Benchmarks: Arena-Hard and BenchBuilder Pipeline
human_time: Answering one hard open-ended prompt (Python/SQL/logic-puzzle style) takes minutes to tens of minutes; single-turn, no ground truth.
one_line: Automated pipeline (BenchBuilder) mining crowd chat logs into Arena-Hard-Auto: 500 hard open-ended prompts, LLM-judged pairwise vs a baseline, tracking Chatbot Arena.
notes: Grades new models via pairwise GPT-4-Turbo judge (5-pt Likert, CoT, no per-item rubric) = llm-judge; the 7 quality indicators are for prompt selection, not answer grading. saturation=not-applicable: it is a Bradley-Terry win-rate leaderboard vs a fixed baseline, no ceiling (frontier_score null). Provenance=user-traffic (prompts mined from live Chatbot Arena/WildChat queries); 'crowdsourced' is a near-synonym here. contamination_defense is the biggest judgment call: the BenchBuilder pipeline enables refresh BY DESIGN (live-refresh) but the released 500-prompt artifact is static/public with no defense, so 'none-public' is defensible for what people download.
placement_reason: BenchBuilder mines Chatbot Arena logs for the hardest prompts to build Arena-Hard-Auto, whose headline is restoring discriminative power/separability (87.4% of pairs) that saturated benchmarks like MT-Bench lost. The schema lists 'Arena-Hard vs MT-Bench' as the canonical B3-desaturation-sequels example; its object is the measurement apparatus, not a new skill.

title: Embodied Agent Interface: Benchmarking LLMs for Embodied Decision Making
human_time: Household tasks average 8.76 (VirtualHome) to 14.6 (BEHAVIOR) action steps each -- a few minutes of equivalent human planning/execution per task.
frontier_score: o1-preview leads BEHAVIOR's average module success rate (74.9% vs. 64.2% runner-up Claude-3.5 Sonnet); Claude-3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro tie for the VirtualHome lead (65.7% each, edging out o1-preview's 64.4%)
one_line: A shared linear-temporal-logic representation splits embodied decision making into four separately-graded modules (goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, transition modeling) across BEHAVIOR and VirtualHome, replacing a single success/fail number with a named error taxonomy.
notes: domain_primary follows the batch convention (multimodal for robotics/embodied tasks) as a least-bad fit: the paper's main 180-run sweep is entirely over abstract text/state representations, not images -- vision is tested only in a 2-metric side experiment (Appendix K). task_shape=single-turn because each module produces its complete output in one call (a full LTL goal or full action trajectory), which is then executed non-interactively for scoring -- unlike AgentBench/AppWorld's live round-by-round loop, the closest comparable A5 members. items_count=126 is the 26 VirtualHome + 100 BEHAVIOR task names; grounded goal instances run far higher (801 VirtualHome goals, 673 BEHAVIOR goals, up to 4,164 grounded variants per task via BDDL quantifiers). No repeated-sampling variance is reported despite several 1-2 point 'wins' in the headline table.
placement_reason: Formalizes 'can an LLM run a household robot' into four isolable, ground-truth-swapped modules so a failure can be attributed to goal interpretation vs. action sequencing vs. transition modeling rather than a single opaque success/fail -- the object measured is the model's own embodied-planning capability (broken into diagnostic sub-scores), the A5 case; distinguished from a G3 grader-benchmark since nothing here grades another system's free-form output, it grades the model under test directly against ground truth.

title: Long-context LLMs Struggle with Long In-context Learning
human_time: Demonstration sets run 2K-50K tokens (up to 174 classes x up to 5 examples each); a human would need well over an hour to internalize a 50K-token, 174-class demonstration set before classifying one held-out instance.
frontier_score: On the hardest task (Discovery, 174 classes), every open-source model and 3 of 4 frontier API models score at or near zero; best result anywhere is Gemini-1.5-Pro's 14.0% vs. 87.4% for a fully fine-tuned classifier on the same labels
one_line: Repurposes extreme-label in-context classification (28-174 classes, up to 50K-token demonstration sets) as a long-context stress test that can't be solved by local retrieval alone.
notes: items_count = 500 test examples per dataset (6 datasets, each swept across up to 5 'rounds' of context length). Grading mixes exact accuracy (GoEmotion/BANKING77/Discovery) and F1 computed programmatically (TacRED/DialogRE/Few-NERD).
placement_reason: Same long-context capability-probe role as RULER/Long Range Arena, one rung harder: extreme-label ICL classification forces a model to have scanned and integrated the entire demonstration set (every label needs its own examples to disambiguate) rather than locate one needle, directly targeting the shortcut RULER and NIAH both leave open -- a parse/recognize capability stress test, not a grader audit or an artificial durability wall.

title: LLM Defenses Are Not Robust to Multi-Turn Human Jailbreaks Yet
human_time: ~30 min budget per red-team jailbreak attempt (up to 2 red teamers); WMDP-Bio recoveries averaged 20.5 min per success under unlimited time.
frontier_score: multi-turn human ASR 51.7-87.9% vs automated-ensemble upper bound 0-68.3%
one_line: Multi-turn human red-teaming study + MHJ dataset (537 jailbreaks / 2,912 prompts, 7-tactic taxonomy) breaking 4 SOTA LLM defenses on HarmBench.
notes: task_shape=multi-turn: expert red teamers converse across turns (91.6% of breaks needed >1 turn), no tool/environment loop for the model. Grading: HarmBench ASR adjudicated by a GPT-4o classifier (llm-judge) inside a human-review pipeline; WMDP-Bio hand-graded (human) -> grading_all includes both. Provenance=expert-authored (Scale AI red-team conversations are the contribution); the target behaviors themselves are drawn from HarmBench (240) + WMDP-Bio (43), so 'aggregated' is arguable. items_count=537 multi-turn jailbreaks in the released MHJ artifact (2,912 prompts); the ASR eval itself ran on 240 HarmBench behaviors + 43 WMDP-Bio. saturation=open in the sense that defenses are far from robust (high attack success); not a model-capability leaderboard.
placement_reason: The object is risk/attack surface: expert multi-turn human red teamers break four SOTA defenses (RR/LAT/DERTA/CYGNET) on HarmBench, releasing the MHJ jailbreak dataset and a 7-tactic taxonomy. Jailbreak robustness against a defended model is E1-attack-surfaces; the WMDP-knowledge recovery is a secondary demonstration.

title: Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation
group: UC San Diego / Stanford / UC Berkeley / Google DeepMind
human_time: One simulated manipulation episode (e.g. pick up a coke can, open a drawer) is a single short robot task; a human demonstrator completes the analogous real task in well under a minute.
frontier_score: Real-vs-sim policy-ranking correlation (Visual Matching): Pearson r=0.976 on Pick Coke Can, with low Mean Maximum Rank Violation across 7 policy checkpoints spanning 2 robot embodiments
one_line: Simulated Gym-API manipulation suite (SAPIEN physics + system-identified control + green-screen/texture visual matching) validated to reproduce real-robot policy rankings, so RT-1/RT-2/Octo-class policies can be scored without a physical robot.
notes: 9 task environments (5 Google Robot + 4 WidowX+BridgeData V2) over the paper's stated ~1,500 evaluation episodes total; items_count uses task-environment count since there's no fixed test-item set in the VQA/MCQ sense. Domain is a least-bad fit: BENCH_DOMAINS has no robotics slot, so classified multimodal per the survey's established convention. tool_access=[none]: the simulated physics environment isn't any of the taxonomy's tool categories. Saturation=not-applicable: the headline metric is real-vs-sim correlation quality, not a model-capability ceiling to climb.
placement_reason: Ships a genuine evaluation apparatus -- a pip-installable Gym-API suite with a proposed correlation metric (MMRV) validated against real-robot trials across 7 policy checkpoints -- squarely the 'proposed evaluation methodology over an interactive environment' case (ALE's role, not OpenAI Gym's bare RL-environment-with-no-eval-apparatus case): the object evaluated is whether the simulated environment's policy rankings track real-world ones, operationalized by literally operating the interactive manipulation environment.

title: The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning
human_time: One four-choice recognition question of expert precursor knowledge; seconds to about a minute for a domain expert.
frontier_score: Yi-34B base 75.3% on WMDP-Bio (higher = more hazardous knowledge)
one_line: Public 3,668-question four-choice benchmark probing hazardous bio/cyber/chem knowledge as a malicious-use proxy; also ships the RMU unlearning method.
notes: Four-choice MCQ accuracy = exact-match; single-turn, no tools. domain_primary=safety (dangerous-capability proxy) with science (bio/chem) + knowledge (recall) secondary. Provenance=expert-authored (subject experts wrote/curated along the hazard chain), though items derive from public PubMed/GitHub. contamination_defense=none-public (fully public set, no holdout/canary; explainer flags likely pretraining exposure). Saturation semantics are inverted (higher score = more dangerous, not 'solved'): base frontier models reach ~63-75% on Bio -> mapped to closing on the raw 25-100% scale.
placement_reason: A 3,668-question proxy for hazardous bio/cyber/chem knowledge built as a measurable malicious-use-risk yardstick (plus the RMU unlearning method). The object is dangerous knowledge/capability, not a skill; WMDP is the named exemplar of E2-dangerous-capability-propensity.

title: LegalAgentBench: Evaluating LLM Agents in Legal Domain
human_time: 1- to 5-hop chained lookups (plus parallel 'writing' tasks) over real legal databases -- a few minutes to tens of minutes for a paralegal with the same database access.
frontier_score: GPT-4o + ReAct: 79.08% aggregate success rate (best); GLM-4-Plus's process rate (72.80%) exceeds GPT-4o's (71.99%) under the same scaffold despite trailing on raw success rate
one_line: 300 tool-using agent tasks (1-5 hop chains plus parallel 'writing' tasks) over 17 real Chinese legal databases and 37 tools, scored by keyword-based success/process rates rather than exact match or an LLM judge.
notes: grading_primary=proxy-metric reflects that both 'success rate' and 'process rate' are keyword-recall approximations of correctness scored against the same final-answer text, not a verified state check or a strict string match -- the paper's own critique notes this can be gamed by an answer that pads in plausible-sounding entity names. This is a Chinese-statutory-law-specific instrument, not a general legal-agent benchmark.
placement_reason: Built explicitly because getting the 'gist' right (the tolerance general agent benchmarks like AgentBench/ToolBench allow) is unacceptable in legal work -- a misread case number or filing date is a wrong answer with real consequences -- and existing legal evals stop at narrower retrieval/prediction tasks that don't chain real tools against a live legal knowledge base; professional-domain competence in a specific occupational field, the D2 case.

title: QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
human_time: Identifying the single missing fact in a grade-school-math / logic / blocks-world item takes ~1-5 min; math items are near L1, logic/planning a bit longer.
frontier_score: o1-preview 49.91% Logic-Q, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 47.32% Planning-Q; up to ~98% on GSME-Q math
one_line: Benchmark testing whether LLMs can name the one missing fact in underspecified reasoning tasks (Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q/GSME-Q) framed as 1-sufficient CSPs.
notes: Closed-set multiple-choice (pick a sufficient variable; any sufficient one counts) = exact-match, single-turn. domain_primary=reasoning (logic+planning are the discriminating domains) with math secondary. Provenance is borderline: items reframe prior benchmarks (GSM8K/GSM-Plus, SimpleLogic, BlocksWorld) -> 'aggregated' is arguable, but the underspecified 1-sufficient CSPs are program-constructed (backward search / PDDL / withholding), so called synthetic-generated. contamination_defense=none-public for the released static ~39k-item set; the templated Logic-Q/Planning-Q are procedurally generated (low contamination) while GSM-Q inherits GSM8K exposure, so 'procedural' is defensible. Saturation=open on the hard domains (40-50%) even though math is saturated (~98%). items_count=38,882 (1,150+7,500+23,642+6,590); math evaluated on subsets.
placement_reason: Probes whether a model can notice underspecification and ask for the single missing fact rather than guess. The paper explicitly shows solving does not transfer to asking, so the measured construct is the interactive clarification/information-gathering skill, not closed-form solving; among capability skills this is A7-communication (asking the right question). Reasoning-substrate MCQ format makes A3 a plausible alternative.

title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
human_time: ~15-30 min for a domain expert to draft a ~250-word cited answer covering ~7.5 rubric items (expert answers in the comparable ScholarQABench average ~289 words); borderline L3 if literature lookup is needed.
frontier_score: sonar-deep-research 75.29% rubric coverage (82% win rate over next-best gemini-2.5-pro); no parametric/retrieval system tops 70%
