one_line: Scholarly-QA benchmark of 21.4K survey-mined research questions with 160K per-query rubric items across 75 fields, LLM-judge scored.
notes: Tool access varies by tier: parametric systems run with none, retrieval/deep-research tiers get search; listed the maximal access. Provenance is synthetic (gpt-4.1-mini writes queries/rubrics) but grounded in real survey articles. items_count = 3.7K test split (21.4K total, 16.9K train). Contamination is measured (~1.1% coverage effect) and source surveys blocked from retrieval, but the set is public with no holdout.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can deep-research systems answer open-ended scholarly questions across all 75 fields of science?' — the gap is that scholarly-QA evals were pinned to a few CS-adjacent domains by the expert-annotation bottleneck. Survey-mined rubrics are the method, but the headline claim is system performance on open-ended research knowledge work (no system clears 70% coverage; best deep-research tool 75%), so it probes the research-execution skill rather than being primarily a judge protocol.

title: Organizing, Orchestrating, and Benchmarking Agent Skills at Ecosystem Scale
human_time: Not stated; producing a complete artifact-rich deliverable (a rendered video, a PPTX deck, an interactive webpage) by hand plausibly takes a human several hours per task.
frontier_score: Quality-First is top-ranked (Bradley-Terry=100 by construction) at all three ecosystem sizes (|S|=200/1K/200K); the flat, skill-free Vanilla baseline is bottom-ranked (BT=0) at every scale; Quality-First still loses more comparisons than it wins against an oracle-skill upper bound at every scale tested
one_line: A two-stage framework (LLM-built capability tree + three DAG orchestration strategies) for organizing and composing 200-to-200,000-skill Claude Agent Skill ecosystems, evaluated on an unnamed, self-authored 30-task artifact-rich benchmark scored by LLM-judge pairwise comparison and a Bradley-Terry fit; DAG-orchestrated variants beat flat skill invocation at every scale, even against an oracle skill set.
notes: This record's inclusion in the benchmarks survey is itself a borderline call worth flagging (see report): the paper's own critique states its 30-task benchmark 'is never given a name anywhere in the paper's fifteen pages... isn't released as a standalone artifact,' and is introduced twice with explicitly instrumental framing ('to evaluate the agent's ability to invoke skills, we construct a benchmark'), i.e. the paper's headline contribution is the orchestration FRAMEWORK, with the benchmark built only to evaluate it — closer to a paper that uses a benchmark than one whose primary contribution is a named, reusable benchmark. Also unresolved: the entire evaluation is closed-loop (claude-opus-4.5 builds the capability tree/DAGs AND judges the pairwise comparisons; claude-sonnet-4.5 executes), with no external orchestration-framework baseline and no human-agreement check on the judge — flagged explicitly in the page's critique. saturation='not-applicable' because Bradley-Terry scores are rescaled [0,100] separately per ecosystem-size block (a '100' at |S|=200 isn't the same absolute quality as a '100' at |S|=200K), so there's no fixed ceiling to saturate. task_shape='single-turn': each task is one instruction producing one final deliverable, even though internal DAG execution has multiple nodes.
placement_reason: The paper's own comparison set is explicit — ToolLLM, API-Bank, Gorilla, and the concurrent SkillsBench — and its benchmark exists specifically to test whether an agent can autonomously discover, select, and DAG-compose multiple Skills into an artifact-rich deliverable, the same tool/skill-orchestration question A6's other 2025/26 entries (MCP-Atlas, MCP-RADAR, MCP-Universe, SkillsBench) ask of their own augmentation channel; unlike SkillsBench's paired ablation of a single skill's marginal lift, this benchmark's headline is whether structured multi-skill composition (not just skill availability) unlocks value — its own ablation shows a flat agent handed the oracle skill set still loses to the same skills DAG-orchestrated.

title: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
human_time: Estimated human-specialist completion time per the paper's own difficulty tiers: 6 Core tasks (<60 min), 53 Extended (1-4h), 28 Extreme (>4h) — the large majority sit in the hours band.
frontier_score: OpenHands + GPT-5.5 leads at 67.3% with curated Skills; across 18 configurations mean task-macro pass rate rises 33.9%→50.5% (+16.6pp) with curated Skills, while self-generated Skills score below the no-Skills baseline on all 3 tested configurations
one_line: 87 real-world technical/professional tasks (8 domains, deterministic pytest verifiers) run under matched no-Skills / curated-Skills / self-generated-Skills conditions across 18 model-harness configurations, isolating Agent Skills' marginal contribution: curated Skills lift mean pass rate +16.6pp, while an agent's own self-authored Skills underperform not using Skills at all.
notes: confidence=medium: the page's critique shows the task-admission pipeline explicitly rejects 'low-signal' tasks with no measurable with/without-Skills separation, so the accepted 87-task population is pre-selected for Skill-sensitivity, not representative of arbitrary work; and the curated Skills used score 10.1/12 on the paper's own quality rubric against a measured 2,014,000-Skill ecosystem mean of 6.2/12 — the authors call this an 'optimistic scenario' themselves — so the headline +16.6pp is an upper bound, not a population estimate. kingdom/family judgment call: classified alongside MCP-Atlas/MCP-RADAR/MCP-Universe in A6-tool-orchestration (Skills are discovered via progressive disclosure and invoked like a tool) rather than A8-research-execution, even though the underlying task domains (natural science, cybersecurity, finance, SWE, media) more closely resemble A8's professional/technical breadth than a narrow tool-selection probe — the deciding factor is the paper's own problem statement, which is explicitly about isolating a causal marginal-contribution effect via a paired ablation, not raw open-ended-task capability. domain_secondary picks the three largest non-primary task categories (Software Engineering, Natural Science, and the broader Office/Finance/Industrial 'professional' cluster) out of 8 fairly even domains.
placement_reason: SkillsBench's own gap section is explicit that its target is isolating causal marginal contribution — 'does adding this Skill help my agent on this task, and by how much' — by holding model and harness fixed and toggling only Skill access, the same 'is this specific 2025/26-era agent-augmentation channel actually useful' question MCP-Atlas/MCP-RADAR/MCP-Universe ask of MCP tool servers, with Skills (discovered via progressive disclosure, invoked like a tool) as the augmentation channel under test rather than raw open-ended-task capability (A8) or terminal-operation skill alone (A5, though the substrate is containerized and follows Terminal-Bench's own methodology); distinguished from those MCP papers by its paired-ablation design (Δcurated vs. Δself-gen against the same no-augmentation baseline) rather than a pure selection/sequencing-accuracy metric.

title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
human_time: Seconds to ~2 min per item: typical core-scenario instances are one MC/short-QA question (MMLU, BoolQ, HellaSwag); summarization items run a few minutes but are the minority.
frontier_score: text-davinci-002 tops accuracy/robustness/fairness win-rates; e.g. 62.0% TruthfulQA, code-davinci-002 52.1% GSM8K (2022 snapshot)
one_line: The framework that standardized LM eval: 7 metrics x 16 core scenarios (42 total) for 30 models under identical 5-shot prompting.
notes: The eval artifact is an aggregation/reframing of mostly pre-existing datasets (21 of 42 scenarios new to mainstream LM eval, but drawn from prior sources). Saturation call: the explainer treats the v1 rankings as 'historical curiosities' and the constituent scenarios (MMLU, HellaSwag) are community-saturated; HELM lives on as a refreshed framework. Toxicity via PerspectiveAPI classifier binned under proxy-metric.
placement_reason: The gap is explicitly about the measurement apparatus: pre-HELM, models were evaluated on idiosyncratic 17.9%-coverage dataset patchworks with accuracy as the only metric. HELM's contribution is a holistic aggregation framework — 7 metrics x 16 core scenarios x 30 models under one standardized protocol, a taxonomize-and-name-what's-missing living benchmark. It is the named G1 exemplar; the contribution is a way of evaluating, not a new task skill.

title: Automatic Interactive Evaluation for Large Language Models with State Aware Patient Simulator
human_time: Minutes per consultation: up to 10 rounds of doctor-patient dialogue before an early diagnosis; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4 (best tested model) recalls only 38.69% of patient information (COVERAGE) and reaches 64.00% diagnostic accuracy
one_line: A doctor LLM runs a real up-to-10-round consultation against SAPS, a state-tracking patient simulator, then answers a 5-choice diagnosis MCQ.
notes: D2 (occupational-probes) chosen over D3 (collaboration-rehearsals) because AIE's whole design point is automating the human patient OUT of the loop for scalability (explicitly targeting AMIE's human-actor bottleneck); the smaller HospitalCases trial with real medical students is a validation study, not the benchmark's operating mode. provenance/contamination_defense (real-work-mined/private-holdout) describe the primary HospitalCases arm (50 real, ethics-approved cases); the parallel MedicalExam arm reuses public exam datasets instead.
placement_reason: Replaces a fixed multiple-choice medical exam with a controllable, automatically-scored multi-turn doctor-patient consultation — a professional-domain deployment rehearsal in HealthBench's own lineage (AIE explicitly targets AMIE's human-actor bottleneck and automates the patient side away). Not a D3 collaboration rehearsal: a live human is deliberately engineered OUT of the benchmark's main loop for scalability — SAPS stands in for the patient — and the smaller HospitalCases trial with real medical students validates SAPS's fidelity rather than being the benchmark's own operating mode.

title: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
human_time: ~5-10 min for a human to fully segment one image (avg 7.7 instances/image at >22 worker-hours per 1,000 masks); pure recognition would be seconds, but the artifact is per-instance masks.
frontier_score: In-paper baseline only: DPMv5-P 16.9 AP on COCO vs 29.6 on PASCAL (mAP@[.5:.95] protocol arrived later with the eval server)
one_line: 2.5M instance-segmented objects across 91 categories in 328K cluttered everyday scenes; the decade-defining detection/segmentation benchmark.
notes: Items = 328K images total (2014 test split ~40.8K); grading is IoU-threshold AP against ground-truth masks via the eval server. Saturation from own knowledge (modern detectors ~60-66 box mAP, community still uses it but treats it as aging) - the explainer only quotes 2014 DPM numbers. Test labels withheld behind eval server = private-holdout, though the server postdates the paper.
placement_reason: A classic CV capability probe: 'can detectors recognize and pixel-localize everyday objects in cluttered, non-iconic scenes?' The gap section frames it against ImageNet/PASCAL's iconic single-object images — recognition in isolation, not in context — and the DPM baseline halving from PASCAL (29.6 AP) to COCO (16.9) is the difficulty check. Headline is model performance on the perception skill, squarely A1.

title: SoftGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning for Deformable Object Manipulation
human_time: A single deformable-manipulation task (fold/spread cloth, straighten rope, pour water) that takes a person roughly a minute by hand.
frontier_score: Ground-truth-dynamics oracle (CEM) sits at/near the top of most of the 6 SoftGym-Medium tasks; image-based RL (CURL-SAC/DrQ/PlaNet) plateaus well below state-based oracles on StraightenRope, SpreadCloth and FoldCloth specifically
one_line: Ten simulated cloth/rope/fluid manipulation tasks on Nvidia's FleX particle engine with a standard Gym API -- the first shared benchmark for deformable-object RL, isolating perception vs. dynamics vs. state-dimensionality difficulty via a staged oracle/state/image baseline design.
notes: No numeric results table exists in the paper for any learned method (CURL-SAC/DrQ/PlaNet) -- every comparison is curve-reading off a 5-seed figure; every baseline, including image-only ones, trains against the ground-truth simulator reward, so the reported difficulty excludes reward estimation from pixels. items_count is the 10-task suite size (6 Medium + 4 Hard).
placement_reason: Built because deformable-object manipulation (cloth, rope, fluid) had no shared benchmark the way rigid manipulation had Meta-World/RLBench -- an interactive-environment capability probe (A5) whose staged oracle/state/image method design specifically isolates perception, state-dimensionality, and dynamics as the sources of difficulty rather than testing a fixed exam-style task set.

title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods
human_time: ~2 min per question - the paper's own human baseline averaged ~2 minutes on each of 250 questions.
frontier_score: Best 2021 model GPT-3-175B ('helpful' prompt) 58% truthful vs 94% human; the public MC variant is 'now both contaminated and largely saturated'
one_line: 817 adversarial questions targeting imitative falsehoods (popular misconceptions); showed inverse scaling of truthfulness in 2021 models.
notes: Headline generation task is human-graded; ships GPT-judge (finetuned GPT-3-6.7B, 90-96% agreement) as the automated proxy (llm-judge) and a likelihood-based MC variant (exact-match). Saturation refers to the modern public MC usage per the explainer; the original human-graded generation task was open in 2021. Primary domain borderline knowledge vs safety - it is factual QA whose point is a safety-relevant honesty axis.
placement_reason: The named B4 exemplar: it exposes that 'knows the answer' as measured by QA benchmarks (MMLU, NaturalQuestions) is not truthfulness — imitation-trained models reproduce popular human falsehoods, and inverse scaling shows bigger imitators lie more. The headline finding is about what scores really mean (imitative falsehood vs capability error), pointing at the training practice and construct, not a new skill frontier.

title: WildBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Challenging Tasks from Real Users in the Wild
human_time: One real WildChat-mined task (avg. 978.5-char query, up to 5 turns, spanning coding/info-seeking/creative-writing/reasoning/planning/math); several minutes to answer well given the multi-constraint, often long prompts.
frontier_score: WB-Reward reaches Pearson r=0.98 and WB-Score r=0.95 with Chatbot Arena's human-voted Elo (top models), vs. Arena-Hard's 0.91 and AlpacaEval 2.0's 0.87-0.89
one_line: 1,024 hard, multi-turn tasks distilled from over a million real WildChat conversations, graded with per-instance checklists via a length-penalized 3-baseline pairwise reward and a 1-10 individual score -- both closer to Chatbot Arena's human Elo than any prior automatic judge.
notes: Sampled tasks are withheld from WildChat's own public release specifically to limit contamination (coordinated with the WildChat maintainers) -> private-holdout. Saturation=not-applicable: correlation-with-Arena is the headline metric, not a model-capability ceiling (mirrors Chatbot Arena's own record).
placement_reason: The contribution is judging machinery validated against Chatbot Arena's human votes (Pearson r up to 0.98), not a task skill: real-usage-distribution task mining plus a length-penalized, 3-tier-baseline pairwise reward and a checklist-guided individual score, explicitly built to fix AlpacaEval's topic skew and Arena-Hard's coding-heavy skew -- G2's preference-protocol territory (MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena's own family), not G3 (there's no judge-vs-judge or grader-taxonomy study; the whole point is agreement with Arena's human-preference ground truth).

title: Deep Learning Face Attributes in the Wild
group: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
human_time: Seconds per image: check 40 binary attributes against one face photo.
frontier_score: LNets+ANet reaches 87% avg. attribute accuracy on CelebA / 84% on LFWA (40 attributes) vs. the best baseline PANDA-l (85%/81%, using ground-truth landmarks LNets+ANet never receives).
one_line: 202,599 celebrity face images with 40 binary attributes and 5 landmarks — the decade-long default face-attribute, verification, and GAN-generation benchmark.
notes: Saturation inferred from own knowledge (a decade as the default face-attribute/verification/GAN benchmark strongly implies later methods closed most of the 87%-average-accuracy gap), but the explainer quotes no post-2015 frontier numbers.
placement_reason: CelebA is a face-attribute recognition benchmark at scale — predict 40 binary attributes from a face image — the same recognize/parse perception construct as LFW and ImageNet, just for attributes instead of identity or object class; the paper's LNet+ANet cascade is method, but the dataset (and the fixed identity-disjoint splits it ships) is the enduring A1-style capability artifact.

title: MedDG: An Entity-Centric Medical Consultation Dataset for Entity-Aware Medical Dialogue Generation
human_time: Minutes per dialogue: read a multi-turn (avg 9.7-utterance) Chinese gastroenterology consultation and produce/rate a medically appropriate, entity-correct next response.
frontier_score: Best entity predictor (MedDGBERT) never exceeds 29.81% F1; best generator MedDGBERT-GPT leads on automatic BLEU-4/F1Ent but a simple retrieval baseline beats every trained generator on the paper's own human fluency/relevance/expertise study
one_line: 17,864 real Chinese gastroenterology consultations with 217,205 entity annotations (disease/symptom/medicine/exam/attribute), testing whether dialogue generation names the medically correct entities, not just sounds fluent.
notes: Grading blends BLEU/Distinct (proxy-metric), Hits@1/F1Ent entity-overlap (programmatic), and a 100-dialogue human fluency/relevance/expertise study. The 1,000 human-annotated dialogues used to hand-derive the auto-labeling regex rules are the same 1,000 placed entirely in the test set -- worth flagging for anyone treating MedDG's test numbers as a fully independent holdout.
placement_reason: Real gastroenterology-consultation dialogues where a wrong medical entity is not a stylistic slip but a wrong answer -- occupational (clinical) content is the design core even though the task format looks like generic dialogue generation, the same content-beats-framing rule that places MedQA and HealthBench in D2 rather than A7's general conversation family.

title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
human_time: Minutes per task: bash/SQL operations, Freebase queries, web shopping, ALFWorld household episodes - 5-50 agent rounds each, each corresponding to a few minutes of human work.
frontier_score: GPT-4 OA 4.01 (relative metric), best on 6 of 8 envs - 78% success House-Holding but 16.6 Lateral Thinking Puzzles, 29.0 Web Browsing
one_line: First multi-environment LLM-as-agent benchmark: 8 execution-graded interactive envs (OS, SQL, KG, games, web) over 5-50 rounds.
notes: Provenance borderline: 5 of 8 environments newly built by the authors (expert-authored), 3 adapted from prior benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, Mind2Web) - partly aggregated. items_count = 1,014 test (+269 dev). Headline OA is relative (cohort-normalized), so saturation judged from absolute per-env success rates, most well under 60%. KG answer-F1 has a proxy flavor but grading is env/execution-grounded overall.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can LLMs actually act?' at the height of the mid-2023 AutoGPT wave — the gap says static benchmarks (MMLU, BIG-bench, HELM) can't capture multi-round interaction with an environment that pushes back. The contribution is the environments themselves: 8 interactive execution-graded settings (OS shell, SQL, knowledge graph, games, WebShop, Mind2Web), 5 newly built, graded by what the model does. Headline = model performance operating interactive environments, the A5 definition.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on CMExam - A Comprehensive Chinese Medical Exam Dataset
human_time: ~1-2 min per multiple-choice medical-licensing item for a trained candidate, per the human-performance baseline's exam pacing.
frontier_score: GPT-4 zero-shot: 61.6% MCQ accuracy vs. 71.6% human baseline (2023); on explanation-quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) GPT-4 trails all 9 reasoning-scored CMExam-fine-tuned models
one_line: 68,119 real Chinese National Medical Licensing Examination questions, paired with a gradeable MCQ answer and a free-text explanation, plus five externally-anchored occupational taxonomies (ICD-11, clinical department, discipline, competency, difficulty).
notes: provenance judged 'exam-derived' (one real national licensing exam, matching GAOKAO-Bench/JEEBench) rather than 'aggregated' (Med-PaLM's MultiMedQA, which pools seven different QA sets); a defensible alternative given the questions were scraped from third-party exam-prep sites rather than an official source. items_count = 6,811 test-split questions (the only split carrying all five annotation dimensions), not the full 68,119-question corpus.
placement_reason: Repurposes the real Chinese National Medical Licensing Examination into a paired MCQ-plus-free-text-explanation benchmark with five externally-anchored occupational taxonomies (ICD-11 disease group, clinical department, discipline, competency, difficulty) for stratified professional-competence analysis - the Med-PaLM/CNMLE-analog occupational-domain probe (D2), not a pure knowledge-exam skill frontier, since the annotation layer's whole point is professional-domain stratification, matching D2's occupational-content tie-break.

title: Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation
human_time: A few minutes per problem - HumanEval-style single Python function synthesis from a docstring.
frontier_score: GPT-4 88.4 pass@1 on HumanEval falls to 76.2 on HumanEval+ (greedy, 2023)
one_line: HumanEval+ hardens HumanEval's 164 problems with ~80x more auto-generated tests, cutting pass@k up to ~29% and flipping rankings.
notes: Task items are the unchanged 164 HumanEval problems (hence aggregated); the contribution - the test suite - is synthetic-generated (ChatGPT seeds + type-aware mutation). Contamination explicitly 'not addressed by design'. Saturation partly own knowledge: explainer's 2023 best is 76.2 (closing then), but modern frontier models exceed 90% on HumanEval+ and the community treats it as solved.
placement_reason: The named B2 exemplar: the gap is that HumanEval's grader (9.6 hand-written tests per problem) waves through wrong code. EvalPlus manufactures 80x more tests, drops pass@k by up to 28.9%, flips model rankings, and even finds 11% of HumanEval's own ground-truths buggy. The headline finding is about the measurement apparatus — test adequacy governs what a code benchmark measures — not a new coding skill.

title: LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning
human_time: A few minutes per short-horizon manipulation episode (e.g. place a bowl, open a drawer) for a human teleoperator, per the 50 demonstration trajectories collected per task.
frontier_score: Sequential finetuning (SEQL): FWT 0.54-0.78 across 4 suites, highest of 4 algorithms tested; multitask upper bound (MTL) AUC 0.20-0.78 (2023)
one_line: 130 procedurally-generated manipulation tasks across four suites that each isolate a different kind of knowledge transfer (spatial/object/goal/entangled); plain sequential finetuning beats three purpose-built lifelong-learning algorithms on forward transfer.
notes: Task-family granularity again drives items_count = 130 tasks rather than the larger per-task demonstration count (50 human-teleoperated trajectories per task, 6,500 total).
placement_reason: The contribution is the ENVIRONMENT plus task-suite design: 130 procedurally-generated manipulation tasks split into four suites that each isolate one axis of knowledge transfer (spatial/object/goal/entangled) to ask whether a lifelong learner retains declarative vs. procedural robot knowledge - an embodied-operation capability probe (can a policy execute manipulation tasks under distribution shift), matching BEHAVIOR-1K/ManiSkill2's A5 pattern, not an audit of an existing benchmark or a hazard/deployment probe.

title: Evaluating the Logical Reasoning Ability of ChatGPT and GPT-4
human_time: A few minutes per LSAT/civil-service-style logic passage and question for a human test-taker, per the paper's own human-average baselines (56-83%).
frontier_score: GPT-4 (API): 87.20% ReClor dev, 72.25% LogiQA 2.0 test, but only 33.48% AR-LSAT and 58.49% on a newly-built OOD split (2023)
one_line: Reformats LogiQA 2.0, ReClor, AR-LSAT and six NLI datasets into a zero/one-shot prompt harness (LogiEval), plus a new OOD split from 2022 Civil Servant Exam questions.
notes: Classified as a capability probe (A3) rather than a contamination audit (B1): the paper builds a pre/post-cutoff OOD split but its own framing attributes the sharp ID-vs-OOD gap to 'difficulty' and never raises memorization as a candidate explanation (a miss the explainer's critique flags directly) - it doesn't argue or demonstrate contamination the way GSM1k does. items_count left null: multi-choice component sums to ~5,250 items but the six NLI dataset sizes aren't all stated.
placement_reason: Reformats established logical-reasoning benchmarks (LogiQA 2.0, ReClor, AR-LSAT) plus six NLI sets into a zero/one-shot prompt harness and adds one new OOD split, to ask a skill question - how good is ChatGPT/GPT-4 at logical reasoning specifically, isolated from broader ChatGPT audits - not to audit an existing benchmark's construct validity or grader; matches A3's checkable-answer (single-letter MCQ, e/c/n label) capability-probe pattern.

title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
human_time: Seconds per item — a short text-classification or short-generation NLP task (sentiment, spam, grammar, summarization) under attack.
frontier_score: Combined Attack (escape chars + fake completion + context-ignoring) reaches 0.75 avg ASV on GPT-4 (0.62 avg ASV / 0.78 MR across all 10 LLMs); ASV/MR correlate with model size (Pearson r=0.63/0.64) — more capable models are easier to hijack; none of the 10 benchmarked defenses proves sufficient.
one_line: The first formal prompt-injection framework (compromised data = A(target data, injected instruction, injected data), every existing attack a special case) plus a systematic benchmark — 5 attacks x 10 defenses x 10 LLMs x 7 NLP tasks (49 target/injected combinations, 100 held-out examples each) — finding no defense sufficient.
notes: items_count=4,900 approximates the paper's 49 target/injected task combinations x 100 held-out examples each.
placement_reason: Builds the field's first formal attack-surface taxonomy for prompt injection (every attack reduced to one function) and the first systematic attack x defense x model benchmark, headline finding 'no existing defense is sufficient' — the canonical E1 attack-surface paper for the injection sub-genre, predating and setting up the agentic instances (InjecAgent, AgentDojo, already in this taxonomy) that followed a few months later.

title: EvalCrafter: Benchmarking and Evaluating Large Video Generation Models
human_time: A few seconds to view a short generated video clip and rate it 1-5 on one aspect; the human study collected 8,647 ratings from 7 qualified raters.
frontier_score: No single system wins all four aspects — Gen2 leads Visual Quality (62.51) and Motion Quality (56.43), Show-1 leads Text-Video Alignment (62.07), PikaLab leads Temporal Consistency (65.41); the fitted human-aligned score flips motion-amplitude's raw-metric anti-correlation (avg -38.2 Spearman) to +45.0.
one_line: 700-prompt T2V benchmark scoring 8 systems on 17 objective metrics across 4 aspects, then fitting a per-aspect linear regression to human ratings (1,024 kept from 8,647 collected across 5 of the 8 systems) so the final score tracks human preference rather than averaging raw metrics.
notes: Placed in G3 (calibrated verdict engine) rather than A-capability because the paper's own 'Findings' center on which metric tracks human judgment (esp. the raw-metric-vs-human motion-amplitude inversion), not on ranking T2V models as a capability leaderboard — mirrors GenEval's placement in the same batch. The explainer flags that 3 of the 8 leaderboard systems (VideoCrafter1, Show-1, Hotshot-XL) never received a human rating; their 'human-aligned' scores are the regression extrapolated out-of-sample, and the paper's own two correlation tables disagree on several cells (e.g. VQA_A Spearman 42.1 vs. 47.8) — noted for medium confidence on exact quoted numbers, though the classification itself isn't affected.
placement_reason: The contribution is a calibrated verdict engine, not a T2V capability ranking: a 17-metric battery across four aspects, explicitly fit by linear regression to 8,647 human ratings so the automated score tracks human preference instead of naively averaging metrics that can anti-correlate with it — the G3 exemplar for a non-text, non-static-image modality, alongside GenEval for T2I in the same batch.

title: MMBench: Is Your Multi-modal Model an All-around Player?
human_time: A single 2-4-option visual multiple-choice question; seconds for a human, though CircularEval requires N repeated passes with shifted choices.
frontier_score: InternLM-XComposer2: 78.1% overall (CircularEval, MMBench-test, 2024); GPT-4v 74.3%; several abilities (Image Quality, Structuralized Image-Text Understanding) plateau at 61-68% for every model tested
one_line: A bilingual, 3,217-question multiple-choice VLM benchmark over a 20-leaf ability taxonomy, graded by CircularEval - a question only counts correct if the model survives every circularly-shifted reordering of its choices.
notes: Kingdom is a genuine judgment call between B2 (grader-hardening) and A1 (a new VQA-style capability benchmark). Placed in B-audit because the paper's own framing centers on measurement integrity - naive multiple-choice VQA scoring is corrupted by exact-match false negatives and undiagnosed guessing/positional bias (one model predicts letter 'B' 42.1% of the time against a ~25% uniform prior) - and the authors explicitly call CircularEval 'the paper's real methodological contribution', with the 20-leaf taxonomy organizing existing VQA-style perception/reasoning constructs rather than introducing a new one. Unlike EvalPlus/POPE, MMBench doesn't harden one specific NAMED prior benchmark's grader; it builds an entirely new question set with a hardened protocol from the start, which is why this call is flagged medium rather than high confidence.
placement_reason: The paper's own framing is a measurement-integrity question - objective VQA-style benchmarks are corrupted by exact-match false negatives and undiagnosed guessing/positional bias, while subjective human protocols don't scale - and CircularEval (its self-described 'real methodological contribution': answer every circularly-shifted pass or the question fails) plus GPT-4-assisted choice extraction directly harden multiple-choice VLM grading against exactly those failure modes (OpenFlamingo v2 collapses from 36.7% to 2.6% once guessing can't survive), matching EvalPlus/POPE's B2 pattern; the 20-leaf ability taxonomy is real but organizes existing VQA-style perception/reasoning constructs rather than introducing a new one.

title: ContractEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Clause-Level Legal Risk Identification in Commercial Contracts
human_time: A trained legal assistant answering one clause question over a contract (0.6k-301k chars) takes minutes to ~30 min; span lookup, not drafting.
frontier_score: GPT-4.1 mini F1 0.644 / F2 0.678; best open model Qwen3 8B (thinking) F1 0.540
one_line: Scores 19 LLMs on CUAD's clause-level legal-risk span extraction from real contracts, adding conciseness and 'laziness' lenses to F1.
notes: Provenance is borderline: a reframing of the public CUAD test split (aggregated), whose underlying items are real EDGAR contracts annotated by trained law students. Primary TP rule is binary full-span coverage (exact-match-style); Jaccard token overlap is the proxy-metric lens. Long contracts (>=128k context required) make long-context a genuine secondary.
placement_reason: Born to answer a deployment question in a professional domain: can a locally-run open model match a proprietary API at clause-level legal-risk extraction on real M&A contract review, under law-firm confidentiality constraints — junior-legal-assistant comparison, review-cost economics, and rare high-risk clause failure modes are the framing. Occupational content (law/contracts) plus deployment framing puts it squarely in D2.

title: Learn to Explain: Multimodal Reasoning via Thought Chains for Science Question Answering
human_time: Grade 1-12 multiple-choice science items; a competent adult answers most in well under a minute (humans score 88.4%).
frontier_score: few-shot GPT-3 (CoT) 75.17% vs humans 88.40% (gold-explanation upper bound 94.13%)
one_line: 21,208 multimodal grade-school science MC questions, each annotated with a lecture and explanation, as a chain-of-thought testbed.
notes: Saturation call uses own knowledge: post-2023 multimodal models exceed the 88.4% human bar and the community treats it as solved; explainer itself only quotes 2022 numbers (closing at the time). Answer accuracy is exact-match; explanation quality graded by humans and by embedding/n-gram similarity (proxy). Test split is 4,241 of the 21,208.
placement_reason: A 21k-question grade 1-12 science-curriculum multiple-choice exam, multimodal, built to probe whether models can answer (and explain) school science — the direct ancestor of the MMMU-style multimodal exam line. The rationale annotations make it a CoT testbed, but the construct is knowledge application under exam conditions, and the headline is model accuracy on the exam.

title: MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts
human_time: AMT human baseline did 5 questions in 20 minutes (~4 min/item); visually-grounded math items take a competent human a few minutes each.
frontier_score: GPT-4V 49.9% vs human 60.3% on testmini (at publication); explainer notes newer models have since largely saturated it
one_line: 6,141 visual-math problems from 31 datasets (5 tasks x 7 reasoning types) testing mathematical reasoning over figures, plots, and diagrams.
notes: GPT-4 is used only as an answer EXTRACTOR feeding a normalize-then-exact-match score, so grading stays exact-match, not llm-judge. Provenance: 28 of 31 sources are prior public datasets (12% newly expert-annotated). Contamination defense = withheld test-split labels behind an eval server; underlying public images/questions remain exposed. Saturation per the explainer's own bottom line.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can a foundation model do math when the math lives in a picture?' — an open frontier skill in late 2023, with checkable exact-match final answers (via its LLM-extractor pipeline). The gap section is explicit: text math benchmarks (GSM8K) were saturating while visual math was untested; the headline is model performance on the skill, so A3 over B3.

title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
human_time: Review one web-agent trajectory (goal, screenshots, actions, reasoning) and label success/side-effect/repetition -- several minutes per trajectory for a trained annotator.
frontier_score: No LLM judge clears 70% precision on the success question; rule-based checkers systematically undercount real agent successes
one_line: 1,302 web-agent trajectories from 5 benchmarks (WebArena, VisualWebArena, AssistantBench, WorkArena, WorkArena++), expert-labeled for success/side-effect/repetition, used to score 12 LLM judges and each benchmark's own rule-based checker; no judge clears 70% precision.
notes: Ground truth is 6 expert annotators' verdicts (3,906 binary labels, 89.3% inter-annotator agreement on a re-check); grading_primary=exact-match for judge-vs-human-verdict precision, human secondary for how the ground truth itself was produced.
placement_reason: Tests the graders, not the agents: pairs human-verified web-agent trajectories with scores from 12 LLM judges and every source benchmark's rule-based checker, scored on precision against the human verdict -- the same shape as RewardBench/JudgeBench/TRAIL, exposing that automatic web-agent evaluators (increasingly used to filter RL/finetuning data) are unreliable.

title: MCP-Universe: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Real-World Model Context Protocol Servers
human_time: Typical task (route planning, GitHub issue automation, financial lookup, Blender object) takes a competent human ~5-30 min with the same tools; agents average ~8 tool-call steps.
one_line: 231 hand-built agent tasks over 11 live MCP servers (Maps, GitHub, Finance, Blender, Playwright), graded by execution-based evaluators, no LLM judge.
notes: Contamination call is borderline: no per-eval regeneration, but 57.1% of evaluators auto-refetch live ground truth so time-varying answers can't be memorized by design - closest to live-refresh. Static evaluators compare against hand-collected facts (exact-match flavor inside a programmatic harness). Browser (Playwright) and search servers justify agentic-web secondary; long-context blow-up (~90k tokens by step 16) is a named wall.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can LLM agents actually operate real, live MCP tool servers?' — 231 tasks over 11 real servers and 133 tools, graded by execution-based (largely dynamic) evaluators. The gap is explicit: MCP adoption outran evaluation, and prior MCP benchmarks were synthetic re-skins or LLM-judged. The headline is agent skill at selecting/sequencing unfamiliar tools — the canonical A6 MCP-suite probe.

title: CRUD-RAG: A Comprehensive Chinese Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
human_time: Minutes per item to read retrieved articles and judge whether the generated continuation/answer/correction/summary is grounded; not stated by the paper.
frontier_score: Hybrid+Rerank retrieval wins 16/30 scored cells across QA+summarization; BM25 instead sweeps every metric on hallucination-correction — no single retriever/LLM wins everywhere
one_line: 36,166-instance Chinese RAG benchmark spanning four database-style operations (Create/Read/Update/Delete), with the whole pipeline (chunking, retriever, embedding, LLM) swept.
notes: A1 (retrieval-grounded knowledge capability) chosen over G-meta-evaluation because the paper's headline artifact is a capability benchmark (4 knowledge-manipulation tasks) that also runs an extensive pipeline-configuration sweep — mirroring how this taxonomy places MIRAGE (a structurally similar RAG-ablation paper) in a capability/deployment family rather than G-meta-evaluation. Recency-based contamination mitigation (news published after July 2023) doesn't map onto a distinct BENCH_CONTAM bucket, so none-public is used.
placement_reason: Asks whether an LLM+retriever pipeline can correctly touch a knowledge base across four qualitatively different operations (continue/answer/correct/summarize) — a retrieval-grounded knowledge-capability probe in BEIR's family, not a meta-evaluation protocol paper: the extensive chunk/retriever/embedding/LLM sweep is an experiment run using the benchmark (mirroring how MIRAGE's own 41-config sweep sits inside a capability benchmark, not G-meta-evaluation), not the benchmark's organizing question.

title: m&m's: A Benchmark to Evaluate Tool-Use for multi-step multi-modal Tasks
human_time: A few minutes per query to plan and (for a human) mentally trace a 1-3-step tool chain over real images/audio/text; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4 88.46% tool-F1 (set-overlap, parsing feedback only) but only 71.43% exact full-plan accuracy under multi-step+execution feedback
one_line: 4,427 auto-generated (882 human-verified, tool-balanced) multi-step multi-modal tool-use planning queries over 33 real, callable tools.
notes: saturation closing reflects GPT-4's high set-overlap tool-F1 (88.46%), but the appendix's stricter exact-match plan accuracy only reaches 71.43% — a real gap the headline metric doesn't show, flagged in the paper's own appendix.
placement_reason: The first tool-use benchmark pairing a fully executable, real 33-tool set with genuine multi-modal inputs, letting planning error and execution error be measured separately across a systematic strategy/format/feedback design space — a multi-tool orchestration capability probe (à la GAIA), not a construct audit: the strategy/format/feedback ablation is an experiment run using the benchmark, not an audit of another benchmark's broken grader (though the paper's own appendix does audit its own headline tool-F1 metric against a stricter exact-match one).

title: SpreadsheetBench: Towards Challenging Real World Spreadsheet Manipulation
human_time: Real Excel-forum questions (formulas/VBA over messy sheets); an Excel expert resolves a typical one in ~10-30 min (experts score 71.33%, no per-item time stated).
frontier_score: GPT-4o 18.35% soft / 15.02% hard; Copilot in Excel ~20% (subset); Excel experts 71.33%
one_line: 912 real Excel-forum manipulation requests over messy spreadsheets, graded online-judge style: one code solution must pass 3 input-output test sheets.
notes: Headline setting is one inference emitting code with no tools (tool_access none); a multi-round variant adds code-execution feedback and lifts most models ~10x. Contamination_defense is the closest fit, not exact: construction-time perturbations (GPT-4-rewritten instructions, twice-modified sheets, moved answer positions) defeat memorized forum solutions, but instances are fixed at release, not regenerated per-eval. Domain: work product is office/spreadsheet work but the evaluated act is program synthesis - coding primary, professional secondary.
placement_reason: Realism of real office work is the explicit design goal: 912 authentic Excel-forum questions (85.7-word real user instructions vs 9.8-27.9 synthetic), genuinely messy multi-table spreadsheets, an Excel-expert human baseline (71.33%) and shipping products (Copilot in Excel) as comparators. Spreadsheets are a named D2 domain, and occupational content beats the 'can models do it' surface framing; the code-generation medium is secondary to the professional-work rehearsal.

title: MathDial: A Dialogue Tutoring Dataset with Rich Pedagogical Properties Grounded in Math Reasoning Problems
human_time: One tutoring dialogue over a GSM8K problem runs up to ~10 turns; a teacher spends roughly 5-15 minutes guiding a student through one item.
frontier_score: human tutors Success@10 82% at 4% Telling; ChatGPT 53% success but 32% telling; finetuned Flan-T5-780M 39% at 4%
one_line: 2,861 teacher-LLM-student math-tutoring dialogues with per-turn scaffolding moves; Success@k vs Telling@k makes guide-vs-tell measurable.
notes: Grading_primary is a judgment call: the signature Success@k/Telling@k metrics are computed programmatically via interactive simulation against an LLM student (itself a soft grader - circularity flagged by the explainer); sBLEU/BERTScore are proxy, plus a small human eval. Domain: the tested skill is pedagogical restraint/scaffolding (social-moral per rubric), grounded in math dialogue. Provenance: dialogues authored by 91 recruited expert teachers with a synthetic LLM student, over crowdsourced GSM8K problems.
placement_reason: Built because LLMs that can solve grade-school math fail the tutoring job — un-prompted ChatGPT reveals the answer 66% of the time. The construct is interactive tutoring-as-service with a learner in the loop: teacher scaffolding moves, and the Success@k/Telling@k pair that scores whether the student reaches the answer themselves. That guide-vs-tell mixed-initiative framing is D3's tutoring rehearsal, not a raw communication-skill probe.

title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
human_time: A few minutes per question: given the ~9,200-token, ~300-turn, ~19-session transcript, locate the relevant turn(s) and answer one recall / temporal-reasoning question - humans reach 87.9 QA-F1 this way.
frontier_score: GPT-4-turbo 32.1 QA-F1 vs 87.9 human (best of the models tested; worst on temporal / multi-hop recall)
one_line: 50 very-long-term dialogues (avg 300 turns, 19 sessions, spanning months) with 7,512 questions plus event-summary and multimodal-generation tasks, probing cross-session memory.
notes: Provenance is machine-human: two persona- and temporal-event-graph-conditioned LLM agents generate each dialogue, then annotators edit ~15% for long-range consistency. grading_primary is the QA task's word-overlap F1 (the 32.1-vs-87.9 headline); the event-summarization and multimodal-dialogue-generation tasks add ROUGE / MMRelevance-style proxy metrics. Images are inputs, not tools (tool_access none).
placement_reason: Headline is a capability verdict - even GPT-4-turbo answers very-long-term recall/temporal-reasoning questions at 32.1 F1 against 87.9 human, so cross-session conversational memory is unsolved. A multi-turn conversation-ability probe (converse and remember across dozens of sessions), i.e. A7 'communication' extended to a months-long horizon, not a grader audit (B) or a durability wall (C).

title: OpenEQA: Embodied Question Answering in the Era of Foundation Models
human_time: One question is answered after watching a home/office video-tour episode history (EM-EQA) or exploring a scanned environment (A-EQA); a few minutes per question, close to the human ceiling of 86.8%.
frontier_score: GPT-4V (best model): 49.6% LLM-Match correctness on the 500-question EM-EQA subset vs. 86.8% human ceiling; blind (no-vision) LLMs score a surprisingly close 28.3-33.5%
one_line: 1,636 open-vocabulary embodied QA pairs over real 3D-scanned homes/offices (episodic-memory and active-exploration settings), scored by an LLM judge (LLM-Match) instead of a fixed answer list.
notes: 1,079 ScanNet-sourced (EM-EQA only, includes 10 held-out test scenes) + 557 HM3D-sourced (support both EM-EQA and A-EQA, reusing the same (Q,S,A*) triple). task_shape is a majority call: most of the benchmark (EM-EQA, given a fixed observation history) is single-turn QA; the A-EQA subset (557 questions) requires active simulator exploration and is closer to interactive-env, noted here rather than split into two records.
placement_reason: The dominant design (EM-EQA: answer from an already-observed episode history) is embodied VQA -- open-vocabulary recognition/localization/spatial-reasoning questions over a 3D-scanned scene, graded by LLM-Match the way VQA is graded by consensus string match -- the embodied extension of A1's recognize/parse/retrieve mandate, not an environment-operation benchmark (A5) where completing an arbitrary task is the object; A-EQA's exploration requirement is a secondary subset, not the headline design.

title: RewardBench 2: Advancing Reward Model Evaluation
human_time: Not applicable — the subject being tested is a reward model, not a human or generalist LLM (matches RewardBench 1's own framing).
frontier_score: Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B leads at 84.1% avg (Factuality 84.6, IF 66.3, Math 77.6, Safety 96.7, Focus 98.4, Ties 81.2); leading models fall below 40% on Precise IF and below 70% on Math
one_line: A best-of-4 (25% random baseline), majority-unseen-human-prompt reward-model benchmark across six domains (three new) that restores headroom lost by the original RewardBench and empirically checks whether RM scores predict downstream best-of-N (r=0.87) and RLHF/PPO performance (which saturates once an RM clears a 'decent-to-good' threshold).
notes: provenance='user-traffic': ~70% of prompts are previously-unreleased real WildChat queries (filtered/curated), the paper's own headline differentiator versus RM1's reused-eval-set prompts — mirrors Arena-Hard's user-traffic call for a similarly filtered live-log source; the per-domain candidate/label construction (LLM-judge agreement for Factuality, verifier functions for Precise IF, manual verification for Math/Safety) builds the GOLD LABELS, not what RM2's own exact-match accuracy metric grades, so grading_all stays ['exact-match'] only. contamination_defense='none-public': no live-refresh or private-holdout mechanism is shipped; the WildChat freshness + 20-benchmark decontamination check is a one-time construction-time safeguard, not an ongoing defense, and the paper itself flags that RM1 likely suffers 'metric capture' from repeated targeting — the same risk RM2 doesn't structurally close for itself. domain_secondary expanded from RM1's ['safety','reasoning'] to add 'instruction-following' since Precise IF is now a headline new domain.
placement_reason: RM2's own gap section states the target directly — RewardBench 1's chosen-vs-rejected pairs 'no longer separated strong reward models from weak ones,' so RM2 rebuilds the identical reward-model-grading construct with a harder best-of-4 format and fresh, decontaminated prompts to restore discriminative headroom (leading models score 20+ points lower), the same B3 pattern as SWE-Bench Pro (also a same-org-adjacent, contamination-and-saturation-driven sequel) and MMLU-Pro; kept out of G3-grader-benchmarks, where its own predecessor and JudgeBench/TRAIL live, because RM2's stated motivation is explicitly auditing/repairing RM1's measurement validity (saturation plus an unvalidated downstream-correlation assumption) rather than establishing a first grader-benchmark for a new model class.

title: Good Debt or Bad Debt: Detecting Semantic Orientations in Economic Texts
human_time: Seconds per sentence: read one financial-news sentence and judge positive/negative/neutral sentiment.
frontier_score: LPS model F1 0.739/0.861/0.813 (positive/neutral/negative) on the 100%-agreement subset vs. the SVM-MPQA baseline's 0.106/0.773/0.296; no post-2014 frontier score is quoted.
one_line: ~5,000 LexisNexis financial-news sentences labeled positive/negative/neutral by 16 finance-trained annotators — the standard financial-sentiment benchmark (FinBERT, FinBen).
notes: Saturation inferred from own knowledge — no post-2014 frontier scores are quoted in the explainer; 3-class financial sentiment classification of this kind is generally near-saturated by modern instruction-tuned LLMs. items_count uses the widest 'Gold standard' (>50%-agreement) subset, 4,840 of ~5,000 sampled sentences.
placement_reason: The construct is domain-specific text classification — parse a financial-news sentence and detect its semantic orientation (positive/negative/neutral) — the same recognize/parse/classify pattern as A1's SNLI and STS-B entries, just with financial-domain content standing in for general language. Not D2-occupational-probes: the task is a simple single-sentence 3-class classification (L1-seconds), nothing like D2's open-ended professional-judgment rehearsals (e.g. PRBench's hour-scale legal/finance analysis) — domain content (finance) rather than task complexity or economic realism is what makes this financial, and that puts it in A1 alongside the taxonomy's other domain-flavored classification probes.

title: EgoSchema: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Very Long-form Video Language Understanding
human_time: A 3-minute egocentric video clip plus a 5-way question; human accuracy barely changes from a 1-min to unconstrained time budget (67.0% to 75.0%).
frontier_score: Best zero-shot video-LM (mPLUG-Owl, 5 frames) scores 31.1% vs. 20% random baseline and ~76% human; no 2023-era model clears 33%.
one_line: 5,063 three-minute egocentric video clips with five-way diagnostic questions, introduced alongside 'temporal certificate length' — a new metric for how much video must actually be watched to verify an answer — showing prior 'long' video benchmarks often have certificates only seconds long.
notes: Placed in A1 (perception/QA over video) rather than B4 despite the temporal-certificate metric functioning as a field-wide critique of clip-length-as-proxy, because the paper's own headline contribution and lasting use ('a standard line item in multimodal model cards') is a new capability benchmark, not an audit of one existing benchmark's construct. provenance=synthetic-generated reflects the LLM-generated-then-human-filtered question pipeline (GPT-4/Bard/Claude generate, a second LLM blind-filters, two rounds of human curation) — the explainer flags this as fully public with no contamination guard.
placement_reason: A diagnostic video-QA capability probe (answer a 5-way MC question about a 3-minute egocentric clip) — the temporal-certificate metric is instrumentation that justifies the benchmark's difficulty, not an audit of a specific rival benchmark's construct; matches VQA/ImageNet's A1 pattern generalized to video.

title: SuperGPQA: Scaling LLM Evaluation across 285 Graduate Disciplines
human_time: A graduate-level MC question, now with an average of 9.67 answer options instead of the usual 4 -- a few minutes per item for a domain expert.
frontier_score: DeepSeek-R1 61.82% sample-level accuracy (top), vs. the same models' 91% (MMLU) / 84% (MMLU-Pro) / 72% (GPQA)
one_line: 26,529 graduate-level MCQs (avg 9.67 options) across 285 subfields spanning 13 disciplines -- deliberately reaching into light industry, agriculture, and service fields GPQA/MMLU-Pro skip -- via a GPQA-modeled human-LLM collaborative pipeline; DeepSeek-R1 tops out at 61.82%.
notes: Kingdom judgment call: SuperGPQA explicitly 'follows GPQA's model' for expert-only sourcing plus a Google-proof non-expert filter, and its own validity claim (87.6 correlation with Chatbot Arena, beating GPQA/MMLU-Pro/MMLU) reads as a maximally-hard, expert-authored, static summit exam (C1) scaled to 285 disciplines, rather than a B3 sequel that merely restores headroom on one prior benchmark's construct (it isn't rebuilding MMLU or GPQA item-for-item, it's building new content at much larger scope). The paper itself self-flags an unresolved science/engineering leakage signal (o1-mini/o3-mini score below o1) and a Chinese-textbook/annotator sourcing tilt, neither chased with a dedicated audit.
placement_reason: 'Question sourcing follows GPQA's model' verbatim -- PhD-only expert sourcing, a Google-proof non-expert filter, difficulty-based trimming to preserve headroom -- scaled from GPQA's narrow STEM slice to 285 subfields across 13 disciplines including deliberately unglamorous ones (light industry, agriculture, services); a maximally-hard, expert-authored, static exam built to outlast MMLU/MMLU-Pro/GPQA's saturation, the C1 pattern GPQA itself defines, not a single-benchmark desaturation sequel (B3).

title: OK-VQA: A Visual Question Answering Benchmark Requiring External Knowledge
group: University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI
human_time: Seconds per item, for someone who already has the relevant fact: one open-ended VQA question over one COCO image, hand-filtered so the image alone cannot answer it.
frontier_score: 2019 SOTA VQA models (MUTAN 26.41%, BAN 25.17%) collapse versus ~72.41% on standard VQA; fusing a naive Wikipedia-retrieval baseline (ArticleNet) only lifts MUTAN to 27.84%, with an oracle combination capping at 28.47%.
one_line: 14,055 questions over 14,031 COCO images, hand-filtered so the image alone cannot answer them, spanning 10 knowledge categories -- 2019 SOTA VQA models collapse to 26-28% vs. ~72% on standard VQA, and a naive Wikipedia-retrieval baseline barely helps.
notes: contamination_defense and saturation are judgment calls: the explainer doesn't describe a private eval server (unlike antol-2015-vqa's), so none-public is used; modern multimodal models score substantially higher than the 2019 baselines (own knowledge, not stated in the explainer), so closing rather than open or saturated. The explainer's own critique flags that OK-VQA's underlying facts (presidential trivia, animal biology) are exactly the kind of thing a modern pretrained LLM has memorized, so a high score today may reflect parametric recall of familiar stock photos rather than genuine retrieval-and-reasoning.
placement_reason: Extends VQA's perception-and-retrieval construct to require knowledge beyond the pixels -- hand-filtered so the image alone cannot answer the question -- but the headline skill tested is still recognize-then-retrieve (visual recognition triggering a knowledge lookup), the same A1 construct as VQA itself, now stress-tested against models with no external retrieval mechanism at all.

title: ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning
human_time: A couple of minutes per question: read a real chart, identify the relevant marks/legend/axis values, and perform up to a multi-step computation (sum, difference, average, comparison) to reach a numeric or short-text answer.
frontier_score: Best 2022 model (VisionTaPas): 45.52% relaxed accuracy overall (29.60% on the human-written ChartQA-H split) -- PReFIL, near-solved on older synthetic chart-QA, collapses to 4.8%
one_line: 9,608 human-written plus 23,111 machine-generated questions over 20,882 real-world charts, requiring open-vocabulary numeric answers via multi-step computation instead of a fixed label set -- models that hit 90-98% on older synthetic chart-QA fall to 29.6-45.5% here.
notes: Provenance mixed: the human half (ChartQA-H, 9,608 questions) is Mechanical-Turk-crowdsourced; the larger machine-generated half (ChartQA-M, 23,111) is auto-generated from Statista's own human-written summaries via a fine-tuned T5 pipeline -- filed as crowdsourced for the human-authored core task design. Placed in A3 rather than a pure visual-parsing framing (A1) because the benchmark's headline contribution and scoring (5%-relaxed numeric accuracy) are about checkable multi-step arithmetic over chart marks, matching its direct descendant MathVista's own A3 placement.
placement_reason: The headline contribution is open-vocabulary numeric computation over a chart -- sum, difference, average, comparison -- scored by a relaxed but still checkable numeric-match criterion, not fixed-label classification; the same closed-form arithmetic-reasoning skill its direct descendant MathVista (A3) later generalizes across visual math domains. Visual grounding is real, but 'visual and logical reasoning' in the title is earned by the multi-step arithmetic requirement (the A3 pull), not mere recognition/parsing (A1).

title: MLPerf Training Benchmark
human_time: Not applicable - this measures hardware/software training speed, not a human- or model-solvable item; one reproduced DGX-1 ResNet-50 submission is reported at 134.6 minutes (~2.2 hours) time-to-train.
frontier_score: Not a capability score - v0.5 to v0.6, fastest 16-chip result improved 1.3x on average across 5 shared benchmarks; chip count behind the best overall result grew 5.5x on average; one reproduced DGX-1 ResNet-50 run: 134.6 minutes to reach 74.9% Top-1
one_line: A 37-author industry-consortium systems benchmark measuring how fast a specific hardware+software system trains a fixed reference model (ResNet-50, SSD, Mask R-CNN, GNMT, Transformer, NCF, MiniGo) to a pre-agreed quality target - not a model-capability score.
notes: LIKELY SCOPE MISMATCH, flagged for the survey author/critic: MLPerf Training is explicitly not a capability eval (the explainer's own critique states this directly) - it measures hardware/software training speed under a fixed accuracy gate, an entirely different axis from every other facet in this schema, which was designed around AI-system capability/deployment/hazard/audit/meta-evaluation. None of domain_primary, task_shape, grading_primary, complexity, or kingdom/family have a natural fit; all five are forced choices from the closed vocabulary, made here to satisfy the required-keys schema rather than because they describe this paper well. Recommend reconsidering whether MLPerf belongs in the 'benchmarks' survey's scope at all (see also the batch report's note comparing it to the RL/robotics domain-gap cases).
placement_reason: Not a capability probe at all - MLPerf standardizes how training speed is measured and compared across hardware/software systems (timing rules, quality gates, a division/category taxonomy), the closest analogue in this taxonomy being a meta-evaluation/measurement-methodology framework (G1's 'holistic aggregation' pattern, here applied to systems performance rather than model capability) - a genuine schema/scope mismatch, not a confident placement.

title: Unifying AI Tutor Evaluation: An Evaluation Taxonomy for Pedagogical Ability Assessment of LLM-Powered AI Tutors
human_time: Read a short math-tutoring dialogue and write a one-sentence remediation turn — a human tutor needs a few minutes per instance.
frontier_score: Llama-3.1-405B most pedagogically complete (guidance 77.08%, coherence 91.67%); GPT-4 reveals the answer ~47% of the time
one_line: 192 math mistake-remediation dialogues scoring LLM tutors on eight human-annotated pedagogical dimensions (DAMR).
notes: Primary domain is social-moral per the tutoring/pedagogy-as-interpersonal rule, though several dimensions (mistake ID/location) test math understanding. Task is single-turn: one next-tutor-response given a fixed dialogue history, not live multi-turn interaction. Provenance is aggregated (dialogues from Bridge and MathDial) with newly generated LLM responses and new human annotations. LLM judges (Prometheus2, Llama-3.1-8B) ship in the eval but correlate negatively with humans, so grading is effectively human-only. Saturation is dimension-dependent (human-likeness ~96% vs tone in the teens).
placement_reason: Born to answer whether LLM tutors can actually serve a student mid-dialogue (mistake remediation) rather than just answer questions — tutoring-as-service with the human learner in the loop and human novice/expert anchors. Borderline with G3: the unified eight-dimension rubric is the headline artifact and it audits LLM judges (Prometheus2 correlates negatively with humans), but the rubric exists to measure tutoring service quality, not as a general judging protocol.

title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
human_time: One attack prompt yields one 512-token completion; a human writing an attempted harmful how-to of that length would take a few minutes.
frontier_score: Zephyr + R2D2 cuts GCG ASR from 69.5% to 5.5%; no attack or defense is uniformly effective across 18 attacks x 33 models
one_line: 510 curated harmful behaviors in a fixed attack->completion->classifier pipeline standardizing automated red-teaming comparison.
notes: Grading is a fine-tuned Llama-2-13B harm classifier (93.2% human agreement) — classified as llm-judge; copyright behaviors use a hash-based programmatic check. Saturation marked not-applicable: the metric is attack-success-rate over attack/defense pairs, with no single frontier score to saturate. Canonical val/test split defends method tuning, not training contamination — behaviors are fully public.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'which jailbreak attacks actually work and which models resist them' by standardizing the red-teaming pipeline (510 harmful behaviors, fixed 512-token budget, open harm classifier); the measured object is attack success / robust refusal — risk, not skill. Named E1 exemplar. Strong B2-ish standardization flavor (fixing incomparable ASR metrics), but there is no prior single benchmark whose grader it hardens — it founds the standard.

title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
human_time: Paper's own numbers: mean 28.9 h, median 11.5 h of professional work per project (max 450 h) — one to several working days.
frontier_score: Manus, 2.5% automation rate ($1,720 of $143,991); Elo 509.9 vs human baseline 1,000
one_line: 240 real Upwork freelance projects (video, CAD, design, games, audio...) graded by holistic human review against the paid human deliverable.
notes: Tool access varies by agent product (CLI vs computer-use scaffolds; Manus/ChatGPT agent browse) — listed the union. ~80% of the work is non-software, hence professional primary with coding/multimodal secondary. Grading tried per-project rubrics and explicitly rejected them for holistic client-acceptance judgment (94.4% agreement). 230 of 240 projects are a private holdout.
placement_reason: Built to give the automation debate an empirical price: 240 real Upwork projects worth $143,991 with gold human deliverables, dollars-earned and an 'autoflation' price index as headline metrics — real paid work with explicit economic valuation. Named D1 exemplar.

title: CALVIN: A Benchmark for Language-Conditioned Policy Learning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Tasks
human_time: A single language instruction (e.g. 'push the blue block') takes a person a few seconds to execute; the benchmark's own teleoperated 'play' data was collected at 6 hours per room with no per-instruction timing reported.
frontier_score: Best MCIL baseline: 54.2% single-instruction (MTLC, easiest single-environment setting); 0.08% on the full five-instruction chain (LH-5), 0% once training crosses environments
one_line: 24 hours of unscripted teleoperated 'play' across four structurally related PyBullet rooms, only ~1% language-labeled (34 tasks), testing whether a policy can chain up to five free-form instructions with zero-shot transfer to a held-out room.
notes: items_count is the 34 base tasks; the long-horizon challenge composes them into 1,000 five-instruction chains (LH-MTLC). The paper's own language-instruction count is internally inconsistent (main text 'over 400,' appendix '389') per the explainer's critique. Only one baseline family (imitation learning, MCIL) is evaluated despite the paper explicitly noting RL is equally applicable to the same sparse completion signal. No strong in-corpus lineage parent surfaced in the explainer's own related-work discussion (MCIL and ALFRED, its two named predecessors, are not graph nodes), so lineage is left empty rather than forced.
placement_reason: The contribution is the environment: a from-scratch PyBullet benchmark combining natural-language conditioning, multimodal sensing, 7-DOF continuous control, and long-horizon manipulation in one place for the first time, with a genuinely held-out room (D) for zero-shot transfer -- a capability probe of whether a policy can operate this environment from raw sensors and chained language (0.08% on the hardest chain), the A5 archetype extended to language-conditioned physical manipulation.

title: Terminal-Bench: Benchmarking Agents on Hard, Realistic Tasks in Command Line Interfaces
human_time: Tasks like COBOL->Python reimplementation, FEAL differential cryptanalysis, or a path tracer plausibly take an expert 1 h to a day; agents grind up to 2 h. Author-predicted difficulty, not measured human time.
frontier_score: GPT-5.2 via Codex CLI, 63% resolution rate; best open-weight (Kimi K2 Thinking) 36%
one_line: 89 hard containerized terminal tasks (SWE, sysadmin, security, scientific computing) graded by hidden tests on the final container state.
notes: Terminal agent doing software-flavored work -> coding primary per rubric, agentic-web secondary. Agents get live internet access through the terminal (folded into code-exec). Provenance: 93 community contributors wrote 229 tasks, heavily expert-audited down to 89 (~3 reviewer-hours/task) — crowdsourced with expert curation. Public repo + internet during eval; strongest shipped defense is a BIG-Bench canary string. Failure-mode taxonomies use LLM judges but do not grade the benchmark score. Authors themselves forecast saturation within a year.
placement_reason: The contribution is the interactive ENVIRONMENT: 89 containerized real-shell tasks graded on final container state, built because SWE-bench-style suites are realistic-but-narrow and computer-use suites are synthetic — 'can agents operate a real terminal across sysadmin/security/scientific work?'. Hardness is instrumental (authors expect saturation within a year), so not C; no economic valuation, so not D1.

title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
human_time: 92% human accuracy; paper doesn't report a per-task time.
frontier_score: GPT-4 + plugins: ~15% overall, 0% on the hardest (Level 3) tier
one_line: 466 human-crafted, human-validated questions that are conceptually trivial for people (92% human accuracy) but require an AI assistant to autonomously reason, browse the web, read diverse file types, and use tools to reach a single unambiguous factual answer.
notes: A single-question, single-final-answer interface (unlike WebArena/AgentBench's persistent stateful environments), even though the agent internally takes many tool-use steps — classified as single-turn on that basis.
placement_reason: Tests whether an assistant can autonomously orchestrate web search, code execution, and file reading to reach one unambiguous answer — a multi-tool general-assistant test in the same family as Gorilla/ToolLLM rather than a persistent-environment web-agent test.

title: A Diverse Corpus for Evaluating and Developing English Math Word Problem Solvers
human_time: A grade 1-6 elementary word problem; a competent adult solves most in under a minute, grade 5-6 problems (aggregative ops, external-knowledge constants) take longer.
frontier_score: Best 2020 solver (GTS, neural): 86% on low-diversity MathQA-C but only 36% on full type-diverse ASDiv; all three solvers land mid-30s% on ASDiv, collapsing to 1-7% on grade 5-6
one_line: 2,305 English elementary math word problems (24 types, 6 grade levels) built around a bidirectional-BLEU diversity metric that exposes 86%-vs-36% solver accuracy inflation from low-diversity corpora.
notes: Saturation judged from own knowledge: grade-school arithmetic word problems are trivially within reach of modern frontier LLMs, even though the 2020-era pre-neural/small-neural solvers tested here plateau in the mid-30s%. items_count is the full 2,305-problem corpus (the arithmetic-only ASDiv-A subset used for solver comparison is 1,218).
placement_reason: A checkable-answer math word-problem corpus whose real contribution is a diversity metric proving that low lexical/template diversity (not scale) is what let prior corpora overstate solver capability — the same closed-form-reasoning construct GSM8K/MATH occupy (A3), just measuring the construct's validity via corpus diversity rather than raw difficulty.

title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
human_time: Writing a paragraph-length biography of a named person takes a human a few minutes (bios average 26-41 atomic facts).
frontier_score: Search-augmented PerplexityAI 71.5% FActScore (human eval); ChatGPT 58.3%, InstructGPT 42.5%
one_line: Scores long-form factuality as the fraction of a generation's atomic facts supported by Wikipedia, with an automatic estimator within ~2% of humans.
notes: Eval-methodology paper; classified the shipped artifact (the people-biographies FActScore eval). Grading call is borderline: the automated estimator decomposes into atomic facts (InstructGPT) and validates each with retrieval+LM True/False — per-fact LLM verification filed as llm-judge; human annotation is the gold variant and the nonparametric masked-LM likelihood in the ensemble is a proxy-metric. Provenance: prompts are program-generated from 183 Wikidata entities sampled across rarity buckets. Standard subjects are tool-free LMs (PerplexityAI's search is a property of one evaluated system, not the benchmark). items_count = 183 human-eval entities; the unlabeled scaled study uses 500 prompts/model.
placement_reason: The contribution is a WAY of evaluating: atomic-fact decomposition + source-relative precision as a grading protocol for long-form output, plus an automatic retrieval+LM estimator validated against human annotators (~2% ER). Named G3 exemplar; the 13-model leaderboard is a demo of the metric, not the point.

title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?
human_time: Market payouts average ~$670/task (range $250-$32k); at freelance rates a typical Expensify bug fix is several hours to about a day.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet earns $403,325 of $1M (26.2% IC SWE pass@1 on Diamond); IC SWE pass@1 under 30% for all models
one_line: 1,488 real $1M-payout Upwork/Expensify freelance jobs: agent coding graded by human-written end-to-end Playwright tests plus manager proposal-picking.
notes: Per rubric, code-for-pay -> coding primary with professional secondary. IC SWE (the capability signal) is graded programmatically by triple-verified E2E browser tests; Manager tasks (724 of 1,488, $585k) are effectively multiple choice against the real hiring decision — exact-match. The 'user tool' (a Playwright script the agent invokes to see its work) is filed as domain-api; the Docker sandbox has no internet. $499,200 of tasks are a private holdout.
placement_reason: Born to 'anchor all of this to money': 1,488 real Upwork freelance jobs with $1M in actual market-derived payouts, dollars-earned headline and a model-first/freelancer-fallback savings formula — realism and economic value of paid work is the design goal, not just code skill (which would be A4). Named D1 exemplar.

title: NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching
human_time: Not applicable to a human in the usual sense -- one needle-question pair over a 250-32K token haystack; the paper measures models, not people.
frontier_score: 11 of 13 flagship 128K+-context models fall to half their short-context (base) score by 32K tokens
one_line: A needle-in-haystack redesign that strips literal vocabulary overlap between question and needle (ROUGE-1 0.069 vs. vanilla NIAH's 0.905), forcing latent-association retrieval instead of keyword matching; 11 of 13 128K+-context models collapse to half their short-context score by 32K.
notes: items_count=58 unique question-needle pairs; each is tested across 5 haystacks x 26 positions x multiple lengths (7,540 evaluations per context length). Kingdom judgment call: NoLiMa's headline contribution is a measured critique of what prior NIAH-family scores actually mean (Table 1's ROUGE-overlap numbers show existing benchmarks are gameable by literal string matching) rather than a plain capability leaderboard, which is the B4 construct-audit pattern (Gender Shades/TruthfulQA/OR-Bench); classified there over A1 (LRA/BEIR-style capability probe) because the exposed-shortcut finding, not the raw pass rate, is the paper's load-bearing claim.
placement_reason: The paper's own quantitative contribution is showing that near-saturated NIAH-family scores measure literal-matching, not genuine long-range association (Table 1: vanilla NIAH ROUGE-1=0.905 vs. NOLIMA's own 0.069) -- 'accuracy tells you little about whether it can actually locate and use information' is an audit of what existing long-context scores really mean, the B4 pattern, not a new raw-capability leaderboard (A1) or a fix to an existing benchmark's grader (B2).

title: ManiSkill: Generalizable Manipulation Skill Benchmark with Large-Scale Demonstrations
human_time: Not directly comparable to a human -- the ~36,000 demonstrations were RL-generated, not human-performed; a single rollout (open a cabinet door, push a chair) would take a person seconds to a couple of minutes.
frontier_score: Best baseline (BC, PointNet+Transformer): 0.37 train / 0.12 test success on object-level generalization, vs. 0.85-0.90 on a single fixed environment (Table 2)
one_line: Four full-physics manipulation tasks over 162 PartNet-Mobility objects, scored from point-cloud input with 10 held-out test objects per task -- training success exceeds test success in all 16 reported architecture x task cells.
notes: items_count is the 162 total objects across the 4 tasks (10 held-out test objects per task); the ~36,000-trajectory demonstration set is a separate figure. Direct predecessor to ManiSkill2, which the paper's own successor built to close the same three-track evaluation gap this launch paper leaves open (only the 'No Interactions' track is benchmarked).
placement_reason: The family's namesake style extended to physical manipulation: the contribution is an environment testing whether a policy trained on some cabinets/chairs/buckets generalizes to unseen instances of the same category, scored from raw point-cloud/RGB-D input with no privileged state -- a skill headline (object-level generalization collapses across all 16 reported cells), not a grader audit or hazard probe.

title: MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
human_time: Not applicable -- the subject under test is an embedding model, not a human; each of the 58 datasets' own metric (accuracy, V-measure, nDCG@10, Spearman, etc.) is computed automatically.
frontier_score: No single model wins every task: ST5-XXL tops Classification/Clustering/STS/Avg, GTR-XL Pair Classification, MPNet Reranking, SGPT-5.8B-msmarco Retrieval, multilingual MPNet Summarization
one_line: 58 datasets across 8 embedding task types and 112 languages unified into one frozen-embedding harness -- no single model wins every task, and the headline 'Avg' is a 56-dataset mean, not an equal blend of the 7 task types.
notes: Follows the BEIR precedent (thakur-2021-beir, also A1) for a single-domain aggregated-suite benchmark: MTEB explicitly reuses BEIR's own protocol for its Retrieval task. items_count is the 58 constituent datasets. Contamination is explicitly assumed away by the authors ('we ignore overlap of MTEB datasets with model training datasets'), then shown to fail at least once (MPNet/MiniLM's SciDocsRR lead attributed to training overlap) -- filed as none-public rather than a shipped defense.
placement_reason: BEIR's own precedent for A1 applies directly: MTEB is an aggregated evaluation harness unifying many existing, narrower embedding datasets (SentEval/USEB/BEIR) into one suite testing a specific representation-quality skill (can this embedding transfer across many task types), not a 'how should we evaluate at all' methodological contribution spanning the full space of AI capability (that's G1's territory, e.g. BIG-bench/HELM) -- the headline finding is a skill verdict (bifurcation between STS-tuned and retrieval-tuned models).

title: ToolComp: A Multi-Tool Reasoning & Process Supervision Benchmark
human_time: Each prompt chains several dependent tool lookups/calculations (search, weather, stocks, Python); a person with the same tools would need roughly 5-20 minutes per item.
frontier_score: o1-preview 61.83% final-answer accuracy (benchmark average 46.64%)
one_line: 485 held-out multi-tool ReAct tasks with human-verified answers plus 1,731 per-step process-supervision labels.
