notes: Prompts are model-generated few-shot then human-filtered and hand-refined, so provenance is borderline expert-authored; chose synthetic-generated. 61.83% frontier sits right at the open/closing boundary on a stale Jan-2025 leaderboard. Final-answer grading is GPT-4-Turbo judge vs a ground-truth answer (exact-match cross-check in appendix).
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can models plan and chain dependent multi-tool calls?' — the gap it names is that prior tool-use evals tested single-tool invocation or scored only final answers; headline is model skill at tool composition (majority under 50%), with per-step process labels as the grading innovation on top of that skill probe.

title: MLGym: A New Framework and Benchmark for Advancing AI Research Agents
human_time: Improving a provided non-SOTA baseline on a task like CIFAR-10 or MNLI takes an ML practitioner a few hours of iterative coding and training; agent runs are capped at 50 steps of up to 30 min each.
frontier_score: o1-preview Best Attempt AUP@4 = 1.150 (Best Submission 1.176)
one_line: Gymnasium framework + 13 open-ended ML-research tasks where agents improve baselines, scored by cross-task AUP.
notes: AUP is normalized against the best model in the pool, so the aggregate is relative with no ceiling -> saturation not-applicable (per-task metrics do have ceilings). Provenance = aggregated: all 13 tasks reframe canonical public datasets/benchmarks (CIFAR-10, MNLI, Atari), which is also the contamination weakness. BLEU on MS-COCO captioning is the proxy-metric component.
placement_reason: The gap it fixates on is that MLAgentBench/MLE-bench 'expose a benchmark you can score against, not an environment you can train against' — the contribution is the first Gymnasium step()/reset() environment for AI-research tasks so agents can be RL-trained; the 13-task bench rides on top of the training simulator, which matches F1's gym-style-environment-with-training-as-primary-use case almost verbatim.

title: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Question Answering
human_time: Seconds per item: a short generated story (a handful of sentences) plus one belief/reality/memory question.
frontier_score: None of four near-SOTA-on-bAbI models (MemN2N, Multiple Observer, EntNet, RelNet) clears the paper's own 95% success bar on the full ToM dataset; best is RelNet at 94.31%, dropping to 76.84% once test-time distractor sentences are added.
one_line: bAbI-style false-belief QA (Sally-Anne, Ice-cream-Van) with true-/false-/second-order-false-belief stories crossed with 4 question types (memory, reality, first-, second-order belief); four near-SOTA bAbI models all fail the paper's own 95% bar, with evidence of answer-pattern memorization rather than belief reasoning.
notes: items_count uses the stated training-set size (10,000 examples x 12 task/question combinations = 120,000); the paper does not state exact dev/test split sizes in the material available. Saturation ('saturated') reflects the paper's own follow-up finding that a memory-size ablation lifts the hardest task from 5.1% to 97.5% without any reasoning improvement, plus the fact that a 2019 successor (ToMi) showed the generator's story templates leak enough surface pattern for a rule-based solver ignoring belief entirely to solve it -- the construct is compromised, not durably unsolved.
placement_reason: Operationalizes the Sally-Anne/Ice-cream-Van false-belief experiments as a bAbI-style task suite with a single checkable correct answer per belief question, cross-validated against memory/reality control questions -- a closed-form belief-tracking logic-puzzle probe (A3, extending the bAbI reasoning-task lineage) rather than a conversational or perception benchmark.

title: Adversarial NLI: A New Benchmark for Natural Language Understanding
group: Facebook AI Research / UNC Chapel Hill
human_time: Seconds per item under most conditions - short premise-hypothesis NLI judgments; round-3 premises (news, fiction, court/debate transcripts, WikiHow) run longer but the task per item is still a single 3-way label.
frontier_score: Best 2020 model (RoBERTa+SNLI+MNLI+FEVER+all 3 ANLI rounds) 53.7% combined ANLI accuracy (73.8/48.9/44.4 by round) vs 33.3% chance; the round-2 adversary scores just 19.3% on its own A2 test set - below chance
one_line: 162,865-example (3,200-test) three-round adversarial NLI dataset collected via HAMLET, a human-and-model-in-the-loop loop where writers try to fool the current-best classifier and the loop retrains a stronger adversary each round.
notes: Kingdom placement is a genuine B3-vs-C3 judgment call. ANLI's 'never-ending learning' framing and iterative per-round adversarial construction resemble C3-living-walls, but the delivered artifact is a fixed, static 3-round release with no established post-publication refresh cadence - the paper's own critique concedes 'three rounds is a proof of concept, not evidence the loop stays economical indefinitely,' and tries/time per verified example roughly double by round 2-3. Classified as B3 (a repeatable desaturation method applied three times) for what was actually shipped, not the aspirational live-benchmark framing.
placement_reason: Built explicitly against SNLI/MultiNLI/GLUE saturating within about a year of a new pretrained model and encoding annotation artifacts (Gururangan et al.) rather than genuine NLU; HAMLET's iterative human-and-model-in-the-loop collection restores real headroom each round (the round-2 adversary scores below chance on its own test set) - the same construct (3-way NLI), with difficulty actively re-established three times rather than once, extending this taxonomy's usual one-shot B3 pattern (HellaSwag/WinoGrande/MultiNLI/SuperGLUE).

title: LEXTREME: A Multi-Lingual and Multi-Task Benchmark for the Legal Domain
human_time: A few minutes per legal classification/NER item for a bilingual legal-NLP annotator; long SJP/MEU documents push toward 10+ min; not stated directly.
frontier_score: XLM-R Large: 41.3 combined score (48.5 dataset-agg. / 36.0 language-agg.), 2023; zero-shot ChatGPT loses on all 8 tried validation tasks
one_line: 11 legal-NLP datasets folded into 18 task configurations across 24 European languages, scored by two separate harmonic-mean aggregates rather than one leaderboard number — the multilingual successor to LexGLUE.
notes: items_count left null: dataset sizes range from ~85K cases (SJP) to single-jurisdiction sets of a few hundred, with 24-language coverage only for 2 of 11 datasets (MultiEURLEX, MAPA); no single stated total test-item count.
placement_reason: The explicit multilingual sequel to LexGLUE (same last author, Chalkidis) — extends 'GLUE for law' to 24 European languages via two harmonic-mean aggregates (by dataset, by language) rather than a translated leaderboard, testing whether models can do the same practitioner-relevant legal work across jurisdictions/languages; the occupational content (real national/EU legal-NLU tasks) is the design core, matching D2's tie-break, not a new skill frontier or a grader audit.

title: Who did What: A Large-Scale Person-Centered Cloze Dataset
human_time: ~1-2 min to read a 325-378 token news passage and pick the correct person from 2-5 choices.
frontier_score: Best 2016 neural reader (Stanford Reader) 0.64-0.65 accuracy vs. human 84/100; all four tested readers score lower on WDW than on their own published CNN numbers.
one_line: 200K+ person-centered cloze questions built from two independent Gigaword articles, with four heuristic baselines suppressed to near-random accuracy by construction.
notes: B3 placement (not A1) because the paper is explicitly a harder, shortcut-resistant successor to CNN/Daily Mail's cloze construct — baseline suppression by optimization directly restores headroom that summary-derived shortcuts had eroded, the same 'same construct, headroom restored' pattern as MultiNLI's B3 placement. Saturation ('open') reflects the real gap the paper itself reports (0.64 best model vs. 84/100 human); no later re-evaluation is discussed in the explainer.
placement_reason: Explicitly built because CNN/Daily Mail's cloze construction 'leaves a shortcut a system can exploit without reading closely' (same-article question/passage syntactic proximity): WDW rebuilds the identical cloze-QA construct from two independent articles and actively suppresses four cheap heuristic baselines down to near-random accuracy by construction — restoring the headroom CNN/DM's shortcut had eroded, the same pattern as MultiNLI's named B3 placement (harder, shortcut-resistant successor; same task, real difficulty restored).

title: Behaviour Suite for Reinforcement Learning
human_time: Not applicable - bsuite is a diagnostic RL-agent test suite (13 named environment designs, 23 experiment instances), not a human-solvable item; each experiment is deliberately 'simple' and 'fast' (under 30 minutes on a standard CPU) by the paper's own design requirements.
one_line: 23 named diagnostic RL experiments across 7 capability categories (basic, generalization, noise, scale, exploration, credit assignment, memory), each scored [0,1] and reported as a capability radar rather than a single leaderboard rank.
notes: Domain is a forced fallback (see wang-2019-mbrl-benchmark's note on this batch's RL/robotics vocabulary gap). grading_primary 'proxy-metric' reflects each experiment's regret-normalized [0,1] summary score - an approximate stand-in for the underlying capability, per the paper's own 'quick and dirty' framing, rather than literal exact-match or code-execution grading. frontier_score/saturation both null/not-applicable since the paper explicitly states bsuite is 'not... a leaderboard to climb.'
placement_reason: Explicitly a shared, standardized diagnostic methodology - 'MNIST for RL' - trading a single leaderboard score for a holistic capability-radar profile across 7 axes; matches G1's 'holistic aggregations of the eval landscape' pattern (the RL-domain analogue of HELM/BIG-Bench in this same corpus), not a single-domain capability probe with a graded correctness score.

title: EQ-Bench: An Emotional Intelligence Benchmark for Large Language Models
human_time: Under a minute per question: read a short GPT-4 conflict dialogue and rate four emotions 0-10; the paper reports well under an hour of compute per model overall.
frontier_score: GPT-4-0613 62.52 (top score); best open model SynthIA-70B-v1.5 54.83; three legacy OpenAI completion models near/at the FAIL floor
one_line: 60 GPT-4-written conflict dialogues scored by 10-minus-summed-absolute-difference against author-set reference emotion ratings.
notes: domain_primary social-moral is a least-bad fit — BENCH_DOMAINS has no dedicated emotional-intelligence slot. The paper's own r=0.97 correlation with MMLU raises a construct-validity question (is this measuring EI or general capability?), but EQ-Bench's own thesis is a new capability benchmark fixing SECEU's specific design flaws, not an audit claiming SECEU's score is invalid, so kept in A-capability rather than B-audit.
placement_reason: Rates whether a model can infer a fictional character's unstated emotional state from a short dialogue — an inference/entailment capability probe (the same 'entail hidden state from narrative' skill VQA and NLI test for other content), not a construct audit of SECEU's validity: EQ-Bench's own thesis is a redesigned capability benchmark fixing SECEU's format flaws (crowd-compression, forced sum-to-10, narrow emotion sets), not a demonstration that SECEU's score measures something else.

title: BALROG: Benchmarking Agentic LLM and VLM Reasoning On Games
human_time: Spans seconds (a BabyAI errand) to a lifetime learning curve (NetHack takes human players years to master without a guide); a single competitive NetHack playthrough attempt can run many hours.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet leads language-only average progress (32.64%+-1.93%) across all six games; o1-preview's best-in-class NetHack score is just 1.5% average progression
one_line: Aggregates six procedurally-generated RL games (BabyAI, Crafter, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack, NetHack) behind one harness and a fine-grained 0-100 progress metric; the best model still averages just 1.5% progress on NetHack, and adding vision usually hurts rather than helps.
notes: Complexity is a forced single-bucket choice across a genuinely heterogeneous difficulty span (seconds-to-master BabyAI through years-to-master NetHack); L4-days is the closest available bucket to 'long-horizon' without claiming the taxonomy's ceiling matches NetHack's true years-scale mastery time. items_count left null since every environment is procedurally generated with no fixed task pool (episodes evaluated over a 25-seed sweep per game).
placement_reason: Explicitly targets long-horizon interactive decision-making as the next capability frontier, stitching together six procedurally-generated RL game environments behind one standardized step/reset harness so an LLM/VLM agent must act (not just answer) over up to hundreds of steps -- operating an interactive environment, the A5 case; procedural generation as the anti-memorization design mirrors AndroidWorld's own procedural contamination defense within the same family.

title: Understanding Factuality in Abstractive Summarization with FRANK: A Benchmark for Factuality Metrics
human_time: Under a minute per sentence: judge one summary sentence factual/non-factual (and, if not, which of 7 error categories apply) against its source article -- annotators reached kappa=0.86 vs. a single expert on a 201-datapoint spot check.
frontier_score: Best-correlating metrics vs. human judgment: FactCC partial Pearson rho=0.20, BERTScore Precision rho=0.27 (per the authors' bug-fixed arXiv v2); every metric tested is a weak proxy
one_line: 2,250 human-annotated summaries scored against a 7-category factual-error typology, used to benchmark 9 automatic factuality metrics by partial correlation rather than to rank the summarizers.
notes: Meta-evaluation benchmark: the object under test is the 9 automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore/OpenIE/FactCC/DAE/FEQA/QAGS), not primarily the 9 summarization systems, though system factuality rates are also reported. grading_primary filed as proxy-metric since the headline evaluation is a partial-correlation coefficient between each automatic metric's score and human judgment. Numbers here follow the authors' bug-fixed arXiv v2 for BERTScore; the officially indexed NAACL proceedings PDF still carries the pre-fix, statistically insignificant result -- see the explainer's version note.
placement_reason: FRANK's contribution is a WAY of evaluating -- a linguistically-grounded 7-category error typology plus a partial-correlation protocol for benchmarking factuality metrics against human judgment on one shared dataset, replacing each metric's own private, incomparable eval slice; the named methodological precursor its own successors (BEGIN, FActScore) explicitly build on, per the explainer's own critique section.

title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Cooperative Tasks
human_time: Roughly a minute or two per episode for a human playing manually: cooperative foraging/warehouse-delivery/matrix-game/StarCraft-unit-control tasks with short (tens-of-steps) horizons.
frontier_score: No algorithm dominates across environments; on RWARE's sparsest-reward task, on-policy actor-critic methods (MAA2C/MAPPO/IPPO/IA2C) learn while value-decomposition and off-policy methods (IQL/MADDPG/VDN/QMIX) plus on-policy COMA stay near zero
one_line: 9 deep-MARL algorithms across 3 paradigms, run on 25 cooperative tasks (2 new sparse-reward environments included), with no universal winner and value-decomposition methods collapsing under sparse reward.
notes: Complexity/human_time are rough estimates since the paper reports RL training compute (138,916 CPU-hours), not human task time, per the taxonomy's per-instance framing.
placement_reason: A systematic, controlled comparison of MARL algorithms across a shared multi-environment suite (two new open-sourced environments included) that explicitly extends single-agent RL's benchmarking-rigor tradition (Henderson et al., Wang et al.) to multi-agent cooperative control — operating a (multi-agent) interactive environment is the object being measured, not a fixed exam-style task.

title: Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs
human_time: Selecting and writing one correct fully-qualified ML-hub API call is a short documentation lookup, roughly 1-5 minutes for a practitioner.
frontier_score: Gorilla-7B zero-shot AST accuracy: 59.13 TorchHub / 71.68 HuggingFace / 83.79 TensorHub
one_line: APIBench: 1,645 ML-hub APIs with GPT-4-generated instructions, grading API-call correctness via AST sub-tree matching.
notes: tool_access is mode-dependent: the headline zero-shot setting is pure text, but the benchmark's retrieval settings feed a BM25/GPT-Index-retrieved doc; listed search-retrieval. AST sub-tree matching is a syntactic checker, not execution. items_count = 16,450 total instruction-API pairs; the eval split size is not stated. APIs scraped from real hubs but the eval items themselves are Self-Instruct synthetic.
placement_reason: The founding tool-orchestration probe (the family's named exemplar): in early 2023 no benchmark measured whether models could select and emit correct API calls at all, and APIBench plus AST sub-tree matching made tool-use hallucination measurable for the first time — headline is skill at API selection ('7B beats zero-shot GPT-4').

title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
human_time: Selecting/writing one correct function call is a short documentation lookup (~1-5 min); multi-turn and agentic-memory entries chain several such decisions across a conversation, so run longer but aren't separately timed.
frontier_score: gpt-4o-2024-11-20 (Prompt) leads at 66.4% overall; best model on the memory-management category (o1-2024-12-17, FC) manages only 12%
one_line: 5,051 function-calling tasks (single-turn, crowd-sourced-real-query, multi-turn, agentic) graded execution-free via Python AST substring matching; frontier models excel at single calls but crater to ~12% on multi-turn memory management.
notes: items_count=5,051 per Figure 1's own component sum (2,251+1,700+800+300); the paper's abstract instead claims '5,551 question-function-answer pairs' and the intro separately says 1,000 multi-turn queries vs. Figure 1's 800 — an internal inconsistency the page's own critique flags, so the figure-derived 5,051 is used here as the more load-bearing number. contamination_defense='live-refresh': the paper states BFCL is 'constantly evolving' and already on its fourth live iteration, the same continuously-updated-leaderboard pattern as Arena-Hard, on top of the one-off crowd-sourced-vs-static perplexity contamination check (which caught Salesforce xLAM-7B overfitting). task_shape majority single-turn (~78% of items by count) despite the multi-turn/agentic minority being genuinely interactive with persistent state — mirrors Gorilla/ToolLLM's own single-turn calls on this family. tool_access includes search-retrieval for the Agentic category's DuckDuckGo web-search/fetch tools.
placement_reason: The direct successor to Gorilla/APIBench (same first author) and explicit rival of ToolLLM/τ-bench, named in its own gap section as fixing exactly what each lacks (RapidAPI drift for ToolBench, only 28 functions/two domains for τ-bench) — answers 'can a model select and sequence the right external tool calls' across single-turn, crowd-sourced-real-query, multi-turn, and agentic settings, with AST-based execution-free grading as the scaling trick letting it cover thousands of heterogeneous functions; kept out of A5-embodied-operation because the object graded is the correctness of the function call itself (name + arguments), not end-to-end state change in a persistent world.

title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
human_time: Paper states tasks average ~7 hours (404 min) of expert effort, ranging up to multiple weeks -- the rubric's canonical L4 example.
frontier_score: Claude Opus 4.1: 47.6% wins+ties vs the human expert's own deliverable (50% = parity)
one_line: 1,320 real knowledge-work tasks in 44 occupations, graded by blinded expert pairwise comparison against human work.
notes: Models ran under vendor-specific tool scaffolds (web search, code interpreter, file creation UI) but the task itself is one-shot fully-specified request -> deliverable with no environment feedback loop mandated, so single-turn. Win-rate-vs-human has no fixed ceiling by design; scored open with best model at 47.6% vs the 50% parity line. Tasks authored by recruited experts from their real work product -- borderline real-work-mined.
placement_reason: The family's namesake: real paid deliverables from 44 occupations chosen top-down by U.S. GDP sector, each task dollar-valued via wage x completion time, graded pairwise against the professional's own work product — the explicit design goal is a leading indicator of economic impact, not a new skill axis.

title: Transfer Learning in Biomedical Natural Language Processing: An Evaluation of BERT and ELMo on Ten Benchmarking Datasets
human_time: Seconds-to-minutes per item: NER/relation-extraction items are sentence-length tagging or relation calls, sentence-pair STS/NLI items are one similarity/entailment judgment; document-multilabel classification (HoC, full abstracts) runs longer.
frontier_score: BERT-Base(P+M) best overall (Total 82.3 macro-avg); wins 5/10 rows; ELMo and cited SOTA* baselines never top a row
one_line: Ten pre-existing biomedical/clinical shared-task corpora (sentence similarity, NER, relation extraction, doc classification, NLI) repackaged behind one GLUE-style split and macro-averaged Total score.
notes: Domain professional (biomedical/clinical occupational NLU) with language secondary, per the LexGLUE precedent (chalkidis-2021-lexglue) for GLUE-style domain-specific NLU aggregations. items_count is the summed test-split size across all ten rows (BC5CDR contributes two label sets over the same corpus). Saturation judged from own knowledge: the field moved to BLURB and modern biomedical LLMs comfortably exceed these 2019 BERT numbers, similar to VQA's own-knowledge saturation call. Grading folds F1/Pearson/accuracy into exact-match, matching GLUE's own convention (regression/classification stats, not overlap proxies).
placement_reason: The direct biomedical analogue of LexGLUE: nine pre-existing biomedical/clinical shared-task corpora (not a novel task type) aggregated behind one GLUE-shaped harness to test whether models can do practitioner-relevant biomedical NLU across two genres (literature + clinical notes) at once. The task style is classic NLU (A1 pull), but occupational domain content (biomedical/clinical text processing) beats the skill framing per the same tie-break rule that places LexGLUE and MAUD in D2.

title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
human_time: Under a minute per agree/disagree persona statement or forced-choice behavioral probe; not stated directly in the paper.
frontier_score: Largest RLHF models (52B): >90% sycophantic answer-matching on NLP/philosophy questions; stated shutdown-avoidance peaks near 250 RLHF steps for 13B-52B models (2022)
one_line: LMs write and filter their own evaluation datasets (154 total) to discover two inverse-scaling effects: sycophancy that grows with scale, and stated shutdown-avoidance that grows with RLHF training.
notes: Measures stated propensity, not a scored capability, so saturation is not-applicable (matches the CFPD/PropensityBench precedent for E2). items_count left null: 154 datasets of heterogeneous size (133 at ~1,000 examples each, plus smaller sycophancy/advanced-AI-risk/Winogenerated sets) with no single stated total.
placement_reason: Measures stated propensity, not skill: sycophancy, self-preservation ('desire to avoid shutdown'), and instrumental-subgoal drives (survival/power/wealth) elicited via forced-choice questions the model itself helped generate — the E2 propensity-probe pattern (there is no 'good' direction on sycophancy, so no capability ceiling to climb), not an attack surface (no adversarial prompting) or a values-quality check (E3), since the headline finding is about behavioral tendency under scale/RLHF, not moral-reasoning correctness.

title: Humanity's Last Exam
human_time: Closed-ended frontier academic exam questions; a matched domain expert typically needs minutes to tens of minutes per item (math derivations at the long end).
frontier_score: o3-mini (high) 13.4% at release (text-only subset); o1 8.0% on the full set
one_line: 2,500 expert-written closed-ended academic questions kept only if frontier models fail them; 41% mathematics.
notes: 24% MC + 76% exact-match short answers, with an o3-mini judge used only for answer-equivalence calls -> exact-match primary, llm-judge secondary. Questions must not be recoverable by quick web search, and models are evaluated without tools. Explainer notes public-set scores climbed fast post-release; the 13.4% frontier number is on the easier text-only slice.
placement_reason: Built because MMLU/MATH/GPQA pinned against their ceilings — ~1,000 experts wrote closed-ended questions kept only if frontier models fail them, with a private holdout against gaming; the 'final exam at the frontier of human knowledge' wall framing (a C1 named exemplar) is the entire point, restoring headroom rather than probing a new skill.

title: LegalBench-RAG: A Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Legal Domain
human_time: Locating the exact clause answering a query inside a contract (MAUD docs average 351K chars) takes a lawyer minutes to tens of minutes with document search.
frontier_score: Best config (RCTS, no reranker): 6.41% mean Precision@1 / 62.22% Recall@64; MAUD hardest at 28.28% Recall@64
one_line: 6,889 expert-traced query-to-exact-span retrieval pairs over ~80M chars of legal documents; scores the retrieval step.
notes: Evaluates retrieval pipelines (embedder/chunker/reranker), not LLMs directly. Span-overlap Precision/Recall@k is computed against gold character spans but never formally defined in the paper; classified programmatic rather than proxy-metric. Provenance aggregated: retraces LegalBench/CUAD/ContractNLI/MAUD/PrivacyQA expert annotations back to source spans (inherited expert-authored labels).
placement_reason: Occupational content (contracts, NDAs, M&A agreements, privacy policies) with explicit deployment framing — 'production legal RAG lives or dies at retrieval' as firms ship legal RAG, lawyer-in-the-loop verifiability as a design goal; retraces LegalBench's expert clauses into the retrieval half no one scored. The construct is retrieval (an A1 skill) but occupational content plus production framing beats that.

title: DEBAGREEMENT: A comment-reply dataset for (dis)agreement detection in online debates
human_time: One comment-reply pair labeled agree/neutral/disagree; annotators judge a pair in well under a minute.
frontier_score: RoBERTa-large and DeBERTa-large (fine-tuned) tie at 64.1% accuracy; all nine 2021 encoders land in 62-64%
one_line: 42,894 real Reddit comment-reply pairs labeled agree/neutral/disagree, with a temporal user-interaction graph attached.
notes: Items mined from real Reddit threads but labels are crowdsourced (529 Scale AI workers) - real-work-mined chosen for the items themselves. social-moral secondary is borderline (reading sarcasm/partial agreement is social signal). 'Closing' at 64% is soft: only 33% unanimous labels, so the true ceiling is below 100% and no frontier LLM was ever scored.
placement_reason: Built to answer whether models can read (dis)agreement in messy socio-political online debate — the raw material for studying polarization and opinion spread — making it the corpus's disagreement/social-judgment dataset (E3 names disagreement datasets explicitly); the alternative A1 stance-classification reading is real but the birth framing is social-dynamics-first, not generic NLU.

title: Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models
group: University of Washington / MosaicML / Meta AI / AI2
human_time: Seconds per question: a 2-hop compositional trivia question (e.g. a birthplace's calling code) that a person with web access could answer in under a minute.
frontier_score: GPT-3/InstructGPT-3's compositionality gap holds ~29-64% across model sizes with no shrinkage from 0.35B to 175B parameters; self-ask+search reaches 60.0% on Bamboogle vs. 46.4% for chain-of-thought
one_line: Compositional Celebrities (8.6k template-generated 2-hop questions) plus Bamboogle (125 hand-written 2-hop questions) isolate the 'compositionality gap' -- GPT-3 answers both underlying facts correctly yet still misses the compound question 29-64% of the time, flat across model scale.
notes: Two distinct diagnostic artifacts bundled in one paper: Compositional Celebrities (CC, 8.6k template-generated questions, the instrument behind the headline scale-invariance chart) and Bamboogle (125 hand-written questions by the paper's own small author team, later cited as a standard OOD benchmark by RL search-agent papers). provenance/items_count reflect CC as the larger, primary classified artifact; Bamboogle's separate hand-authored construction is noted here rather than forcing a single provenance value. contamination_defense filed as procedural: CC was manually spot-checked against web search and Bamboogle was explicitly filtered to exclude search-engine-answerable questions, both construction-time filters against leakage.
placement_reason: A checkable, closed-book composition puzzle: no provided document to parse (unlike HotpotQA/MuSiQue's open-book multi-hop chains), just two parametric facts a model must combine into a checkable compound answer -- closer to a logic/composition puzzle over known facts (A3) than a parsing/retrieval probe (A1) or a knowledge-recall exam (A2, since the paper explicitly isolates composition failure from mere fact-ignorance). Headline is a capability verdict (the gap doesn't shrink with scale) plus a prompting-method fix, not an audit of an existing benchmark's construct.

title: LHAW: Controllable Underspecification for Long-Horizon Tasks
human_time: Variants of TheAgentCompany, SWE-Bench Pro, and MCP-Atlas tasks - multi-stage workflows of dozens-to-hundreds of actions; a competent human would need roughly 30 min to several hours per instance.
frontier_score: Opus-4.5 on MCP-Atlas: 100% base -> 47% underspecified -> 78% pass@3 with ask_user; GPT-5.2 SWE-Bench Pro recovers to 91%
one_line: 285 controllably underspecified variants of long-horizon agent tasks that test whether agents notice missing info and ask well.
notes: Cross-domain meta-benchmark: tasks span office/agentic work (85 TAC), coding (100 SWE-Bench Pro), and MCP tool-use (100) - agentic-web primary is a judgment call. Provenance is an LLM perturbation pipeline over prior benchmarks (synthetic over aggregated base). 'Procedural' defense reflects the regenerable pipeline; the shipped 285 set itself is static. Browser access in TAC subset unstated in text.
placement_reason: Built to answer whether long-horizon agents know when to stop and ask a human for clarification, and at what interruption cost — the human-in-the-loop clarification behavior (ask_user tool, Supervisor vs Busy Executive personas) is the measured construct, which is D3's literal description; the synthetic perturbation pipeline is machinery for evaluation, not a training-signal factory (no F framing).

title: Watch-And-Help: A Challenge for Social Perception and Human-AI Collaboration
human_time: A household chore (set a dinner table, put away groceries) that takes a person a few minutes; validated against 6-12 real human participants across two experiments.
frontier_score: Best non-oracle baseline (HP with true goal) helps effectively; using the model's own inferred goal degrades performance sharply on test-2's multi-activity split (recall 0.96->0.64), and a wrong inferred goal actively conflicts with the human collaborator in 40% of episodes
one_line: An AI agent watches one demonstration, infers a household task's goal, then must help a human-like (or real human) agent finish it fast in an unseen apartment -- goal-inference precision collapses under compositional generalization.
notes: items_count is the training task count (1,011); two 100-task sets are held out for test-1/test-2. Domain classified 'social-moral' (closest available label for theory-of-mind/goal-inference reasoning) with 'multimodal' secondary for the 3D VirtualHome-Social rendering -- no dedicated social-cognition domain exists in the controlled vocabulary.
placement_reason: An agent must infer another agent's goal from a single demonstration, then actively operate in a brand-new household environment alongside that agent to finish the task faster -- the active, multi-step embodied collaboration in an unseen apartment (A5) is the harder half of the benchmark, distinct from AGENT/BIB's purely passive video-judgment VoE format.

title: Generalizing Verifiable Instruction Following
human_time: Each prompt is an ordinary writing task plus 1-2 checkable constraints; a human would need a few minutes to draft a compliant response (matches IFEval's own framing).
frontier_score: OpenAI o3 leads off-the-shelf models at 69.3% (vs. 95.0% on IFEval); most others fall below 50%, e.g. Claude 4 Sonnet 42.3%, DeepSeek R1 38.0%
one_line: 58 new held-out verifiable-instruction-following constraints (7 categories, 300 prompts) exposing that frontier models scoring 80-95% on the saturated IFEval collapse — several below 50% — on unseen constraint types; ships alongside IF-RLVR, a GRPO training recipe that narrows the gap while surfacing a reward-hacking failure mode it only partially fixes.
notes: IF-RLVR (the paper's GRPO training-recipe contribution) is not itself benchmark-scored, so it's summarized in one_line but doesn't affect the taxonomy facets. grading_all stays ['programmatic'] — the auxiliary GPT-4.1 quality judge in the RLVR section scores general response quality during training analysis, not IFBench's own pass/fail. task_shape='single-turn' reflects the headline setting; a secondary multi-turn ablation (constraint isolated from task across 3 dialogue turns) also appears but isn't the reported main numbers. Lineage would also include pyatkin-2025-ifbench's own reuse by RewardBench 2's Precise-IF domain, but that edge is excluded here since RewardBench 2 (dated 2025-06) predates this paper's 2025-07 date — a real v1-vs-published-revision citation-date artifact, not an error, but excluded per the no-postdated-parent rule.
placement_reason: IFBench's own gap section names the target directly: IFEval 'quickly saturated' and technical reports now train specifically on its 25-template taxonomy, so the benchmark 'stops measuring generalization and starts measuring memorization' — IFBench rebuilds the identical construct (deterministic, judge-free verifiable-constraint compliance) with 58 disjoint held-out constraint types to restore headroom, the canonical B3 pattern (MMLU→MMLU-Pro, Arena-Hard→MT-Bench). Kept out of A7-communication, where IFEval itself lives, because the paper's headline is explicitly that IFEval's construct validity breaks down under generalization (every one of 12 models tested loses ground), not a new instruction-following skill.

title: UserBench: An Interactive Gym Environment for User-Centric Agents
human_time: Not stated; a multi-aspect travel-planning conversation (up to 20 turns, 2-5 aspects) is the kind of task a human travel agent would work through in several minutes to a few tens of minutes.
frontier_score: GPT-4o leads at 0.329 Score (single-choice) / 0.710 (multi-choice); every model actively elicits under 30% of ground-truth preferences in the single-choice setting
one_line: A Gymnasium travel-planning environment where a GPT-4o-simulated user reveals preferences only when asked well; separates task completion from preference understanding, and even GPT-4o elicits under 30% of preferences through active questioning.
notes: confidence=medium: the page's own critique flags that GPT-4o simultaneously authors the benchmark data, drives the simulated user, judges every in-episode decision (search-argument alignment, action-type classification, implicit-reveal), and is the top-scoring tested agent — no ablation swaps this backbone, so rankings are conditional on one evaluator stack. items_count=471 per Table 2's own total (118 Easy + 201 Medium + 152 Hard); the running text instead says '417 data points for testing,' an unreconciled discrepancy the page notes. provenance='expert-authored': the preferences, implicit phrasings, and five-aspect task design are hand-curated by the authors; the per-scenario option pools (correct/wrong/noise) are GPT-4o-generated under human supervision, noted here rather than driving the primary call (mirrors AgentDojo's own expert-authored call despite LLM-generated dummy data). grading_all includes llm-judge because Preference-Elicited/Action-type metrics (not the headline programmatic Score) are GPT-4o-judged in-episode.
placement_reason: The gap section explicitly separates 'did the agent finish the task' from 'did the agent ever find out what the user wanted,' and the whole environment forces incremental, implicit preference elicitation from a simulated user who never states a complete spec up front — a mixed-initiative rehearsal where the human/user must be actively queried mid-task, the move HiL-Bench (which cites this paper) later names explicitly; kept out of A6-tool-orchestration, where its nearest tool-and-user-simulator rival τ-bench sits, because UserBench's headline metric and ablations are about preference-elicitation rate and density, not domain-policy compliance — its own results show search-tool validity is uncorrelated with the benchmark's actual difficulty driver.

title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
human_time: Not stated.
frontier_score: Fine-tuned ToolLLaMA (7B) lands within a few points of ChatGPT on the paper's own ToolEval suite
one_line: An automated ChatGPT pipeline builds ToolBench — 126,486 instruction-and-solution-path traces over 16,464 real RapidAPI endpoints — plus a depth-first search decision tree (DFSDT) that finds working multi-tool solutions where ReAct gets stuck.
notes: ToolEval's own grading is ChatGPT-based pass/win-rate scoring, raising the same judge-trustworthiness question the paper's critique flags.
placement_reason: The large-scale-API peer of Gorilla: instead of one API family, orchestrates 16,000+ real RapidAPI endpoints via a synthetic ChatGPT-generated instruction/solution-path dataset and a search-based (DFSDT) planning method.

title: WorldSimBench: Towards Video Generation Models as World Simulators
human_time: Each scenario is a short embodied clip (a Minecraft action, a driving maneuver, a robot-manipulation primitive); the analogous real task takes a human seconds to a few minutes.
frontier_score: Fine-tuned Human Preference Evaluator beats a GPT-4o judge in all 3 scenarios (89.4 vs. 72.8 Acc OE; 0.60 vs. 0.28 PLCC AD; 0.43 vs. 0.07 PLCC RM); closed-loop leader Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V) tops AD Driving Score (31.054) and RM avg completed chain length (2.95/5)
one_line: A dual benchmark for video-generation models as 'World Simulators': a fine-tuned Human Preference Evaluator scores generated video on 20 embodied dimensions, while a closed loop converts video into control signals and executes them in a real simulator (MineRL/CARLA/CALVIN) to test whether the video is actually actionable.
notes: items_count left null: the paper's one clearly-stated count, the 35,701-tuple HF-Embodied Dataset, is the training data for the judge model, not a fixed evaluation-item count for the benchmark's own test protocol. task_shape=interactive-env reflects the closed-loop Implicit Manipulative Evaluation (the paper's namesake contribution); the parallel Explicit Perceptual Evaluation is closer to single-turn video scoring. The closed-loop actionability test -- the paper's central claim -- covers only 3 of 8 evaluated models in 2 of 3 scenarios (AD, RM); all 8 do appear in the OE closed loop.
placement_reason: Targets the top rung of a stated S0-S3 predictive-model hierarchy: can a video generation model's output be translated into real, working low-level control in an interactive environment (MineRL, CARLA, CALVIN)? The closed-loop Implicit Manipulative Evaluation literally executes video-derived action signals against real simulators and reads success off simulator state -- directly testing embodied-environment operation by the generative model, the A5 case; the trained Human Preference Evaluator (Explicit track) is instrumentation for judging outputs, not itself the object.

title: Towards Building Multilingual Language Model for Medicine
group: Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Shanghai AI Laboratory
human_time: A couple of minutes per item: read a medical MCQ (plus rationale, for the fine-tuned setting) in one of six languages; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4 74.27% zero-shot avg (79.43% 5-shot CoT); MMed-Llama 3 (8B, open, full fine-tuned) 67.75%
one_line: 53,566-pair, six-language medical QA benchmark (45,048 train / 8,518 test) aggregated from five existing exams, with GPT-4-generated, partially human-verified rationales.
notes: saturation closing reflects GPT-4's 74-79% average and MMed-Llama 3's 67.75%, but individual languages (French 55.63%) show real remaining headroom — a genuinely uneven picture the six-language average obscures, per the paper's own critique.
placement_reason: A shared six-language axis for medical competence, built because English-only medical evals (MedQA, MMLU-Med) leave multilingual clinical deployment unmeasured — occupational-domain competence, the canonical D2 case, not a raw A2 knowledge-exam probe: the point is cross-lingual medical-practice readiness, and the paper's three shipped artifacts (corpus, benchmark, models) are all organized around that deployment question.

title: SWE Atlas: Benchmarking Coding Agents Beyond Issue Resolution
human_time: Codebase Q&A / test-writing / refactoring in 18 real repos, requiring running the app and multi-file edits; a competent engineer would need roughly 1-4 hours per task (refactors anchor to real merged PRs up to thousands of lines).
frontier_score: GPT-5.4 (Codex) 43.49% Pass@1, Opus 4.7 (Claude Code) 41.89%; Pass3 drops to ~29% for both
one_line: 284 expert-written tasks grading coding agents on codebase Q&A, test writing, and refactoring quality, not just passing tests.
notes: Pass requires functional gate AND all must-have rubrics; rubric-judge chosen as primary since the rubric is the distinguishing gate and the Q&A split (124 tasks) is rubric-only. Ships a memorization/leakage audit (Jaccard screen, tool-call audit) but no held-out or refreshed set, so defense = none-public.
placement_reason: Built to answer whether coding agents can do the software-engineering work beyond issue resolution — codebase Q&A, test writing, refactoring across 18 real repos — i.e. a capability probe on repo-level code understanding and modification; the rubric-vs-functional-gap finding gives it a B4 flavor, but the role at birth is measuring an unmeasured skill domain, not auditing an existing instrument.

title: SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text
human_time: Read one Wikipedia paragraph and highlight an answer span - tens of seconds per question for a human.
frontier_score: Human 86.8% F1 / 77.0% EM; neural models hit 70.3% F1 within four months and the human gap was 'erased entirely by 2018'
one_line: 107,785 crowdsourced questions over Wikipedia where every answer is a passage span, gradable by exact-match and token F1.
notes: Headline metric is token F1 (proxy-metric per rubric) but EM is a co-headline and the span design is 'exact-match gradable' - borderline primary call. Private-holdout is from own knowledge (official hidden test set via Codalab leaderboard), not stated in the text; the explainer now calls it fully contaminated/saturated.
placement_reason: The canonical span-extraction reading-comprehension probe — built to answer 'can neural models read?' by threading large + human-written + auto-gradable via the answer-is-a-passage-span constraint; SQuAD is a named A1 exemplar.

title: Evaluating Protein Transfer Learning with TAPE
human_time: No direct human analogue - the tasks (secondary structure, contact prediction, remote homology, fluorescence, stability) are computational predictions from a protein sequence; determining true labels experimentally costs weeks-to-years and $200,000+ per the paper's own appendix, while a domain expert using specialized modeling tools would need hours per protein.
frontier_score: Pretrained Transformer/LSTM/ResNet improve all 15 architecture x task comparisons over no-pretrain, but still lose to hand-built alignment features on SS (0.80 vs 0.75) and Contact (0.64 vs 0.40) while winning Remote Homology (0.26 vs 0.09)
one_line: Five biologically-curated protein tasks (secondary structure, contact prediction, remote homology, fluorescence, stability) on splits filtered by sequence identity/evolutionary distance, testing whether self-supervised sequence models beat hand-built alignment features.
notes: No single items_count: five heterogeneous test sets (CB513, CASP12, a SCOP fold-holdout set, GFP variants, Rocklin stability library) with no stated combined total, so left null (same treatment as GLUE). Complexity/human_time is a genuine judgment call - there is no real 'a human solves this task' framing for protein structure prediction from sequence alone. Saturation: paper's own bottom line states its numbers are 'a historical floor, not a target' post-AlphaFold2/ESM - direct textual support, not just inference. Domain 'science' is the closest fit for computational biology; no dedicated biology/protein domain exists in the vocabulary.
placement_reason: A GLUE-shaped fixed multi-task suite (five splits, five metrics, no aggregate leaderboard) explicitly size-matched to GLUE's own architectures, testing whether self-supervised protein representations recognize/parse structural and evolutionary properties from sequence - the representation-probe pattern A1 was built to describe, transplanted from natural language to protein sequences rather than a novel occupational or frontier-wall framing.

title: Towards Empathetic Open-domain Conversation Models: A New Benchmark and Dataset
human_time: Seconds per turn: one 4-8-utterance conversational reply (avg. 15.2 words) to a partner's emotionally-grounded personal situation.
frontier_score: TopicPrepend-1 (BERT retrieval) reaches human-rated Empathy 4.03 vs. a 4.19 gold-response ceiling; simply retrieving from ED's own utterances with no fine-tuning already lifts Empathy from 2.82 to 3.45.
one_line: 24,850 crowdsourced conversations across 32 balanced emotion labels, each grounded in a Speaker's real personal situation, scoring whether a blind Listener model's reply is rated empathetic rather than merely on-topic.
notes: grading_primary set to human rather than proxy-metric because the paper's central empirical claim (does fine-tuning/retrieval make responses more empathetic) rests on Likert human ratings, not the automatic BLEU/perplexity/P@1,100 numbers reported alongside them. By 2026, ED is a common fine-tuning target, so zero-shot numbers on it are likely pretraining-contaminated -- saturated.
placement_reason: Turns 'does this response sound like it cares' into a measurable conversational-capability benchmark: a Listener model must respond to a Speaker's emotionally-grounded situation in a way a human rates as empathetic, not just on-topic -- squarely A7, explicitly built as a corrective to DailyDialog's thin, skewed emotion signal.

title: AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents
human_time: Humans succeed 80% and agents average 3.9 min per task at ~3x human speed, so roughly 1-2 minutes per task for a human; most tasks are a handful of UI steps, tail 30+.
frontier_score: M3A (GPT-4 Turbo, accessibility-tree input) 30.6% vs 80.0% human; 3-seed mean 29.0%
one_line: Android emulator with 116 tasks across 20 real apps, graded by device system state and re-parameterized per random seed.
notes: Also ships 92 ported MobileMiniWoB++ web tasks on the same interface (not counted in items_count). Procedural defense = seeded task parameterization generating fresh goals/success criteria per run; templates and apps are still public. Mobile GUI control mapped to computer-os; domain-api for the send_text_message-style function-calling APIs. 30.6% is a 2024 single-seed number on zero-shot scaffolds.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can agents operate a real phone?' — a fully functional Android emulator with execution-based reward on 116 tasks across 20 real apps, explicitly the mobile counterpart to OSWorld; the environment/agentic task is the contribution, and though parameterization enables RL training, the paper frames itself as a benchmarking environment, not a reward factory.

title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
human_time: Single-image classification into one of the ImageNet/CIFAR-10 classes - a few seconds per image for a human.
frontier_score: Best 2018 model (PNASNet) 82.9% orig -> 72.2% top-1 on ImageNetV2 MatchedFrequency (an 10.7pp drop)
one_line: ImageNetV2 and CIFAR-10.1: from-scratch replications of the classic test sets that reveal an 11-14pp accuracy drop.
notes: Methodology paper; classified artifact is the replicated test sets (10,000 ImageNetV2 + 2,000 CIFAR-10.1 = 12,000). Items scraped from Flickr/Tiny Images then MTurk-filtered - crowdsourced chosen since worker selection frequency literally defines the item set. Fresh-at-release but public and static thereafter, hence none-public. Saturation judged from the explainer's 72.2% top-1; the paper is a measurement study, not a leaderboard.
placement_reason: The archetype rebuilt-twin audit: replicates the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 test-set creation process from scratch to measure adaptive overfitting from a decade of test-set reuse — the headline finding is about the measurement apparatus (benchmark validity, 'accuracy on the line'), not a new skill; ImageNet-v2-style replication is B1's named exemplar.

title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark
human_time: One graduate-level MC science question; non-experts spent median 30 min with web, in-domain experts far less — a single hard multiple-choice item.
frontier_score: GPT-4 + search: 39.4% (Extended) at 2023 release; experts 65%, non-experts 34%, chance 25%
one_line: 448 graduate-level bio/physics/chemistry multiple-choice questions written by PhDs to be objective for experts yet Google-proof for non-experts.
notes: Canonical use is closed-book (none); paper also ran a GPT-4 + search-retrieval condition, not reflected in tool_access. Saturation marked 'closing' per the explainer's 'closing in on saturation' language for Diamond; external knowledge suggests Diamond is now near-saturated for frontier reasoning models, but the text only quotes 2023 numbers. Main-set count used (448); Extended is 546, Diamond 198.
placement_reason: Built to manufacture a 'Google-proof' expertise gap at the frontier of human knowledge: PhD-authored, expert-validated questions that skilled non-experts fail even with unrestricted web access, framed as a scalable-oversight testbed where the wall (durable expert-vs-non-expert gap) is the explicit design goal. The named C1 exemplar.

title: The MASK Benchmark: Disentangling Honesty From Accuracy in AI Systems
human_time: Reading a hand-crafted pressure scenario and answering a short factual (binary/numerical) proposition — roughly 1-5 min per item.
frontier_score: Most honest Claude 3.7 Sonnet P(Lie)=26.6%; worst Grok 2 63.0%; no model explicitly honest in >46% of cases
one_line: 1,500 pressure-scenario examples measuring whether an LLM knowingly lies (states what it doesn't believe), scored separately from factual accuracy.
notes: Grading: an LLM judge (86.4% human agreement) maps statement S and elicited belief B to proposition resolutions, then a lie is scored programmatically as S≠B. task_shape marked single-turn (belief elicitation is separate queries, not a dialogue), though 'Doubling Down'/'Continuations' archetypes are conversational. items_count is 1000 public + 500 held-out; paper reports on the combined 1500. Accuracy axis is genuinely measured, hence knowledge secondary.
placement_reason: Measures honesty-under-pressure as a propensity — whether a model knowingly states what it does not believe — cleanly split from accuracy; the object is deceptive-behavior risk, not a skill. Built explicitly against TruthfulQA-style 'honesty' evals that measure accuracy in disguise ('safetywashing'). Named E2 exemplar.

title: IntPhys 2019: A Benchmark for Visual Intuitive Physics Understanding
human_time: Roughly 10 seconds per clip: MTurk raters saw 40 short (~7s) clips per session and rated plausibility 1-6 in about 7 minutes total.
frontier_score: Two 2018-era self-supervised baselines (CNN encoder-decoder, conditional GAN) score well above chance whenever a physical violation is visible, but collapse to chance-level error (L_A ~ 0.50) the instant it happens behind an occluder, in every block and architecture tested.
one_line: Violation-of-expectation video benchmark (3 physics-concept blocks x 3,600 test clips each) scoring any vision system's single plausibility score per clip via pixel-matched possible/impossible quadruplets; 2018-era baselines collapse to chance the moment a violation happens behind an occluder.
notes: items_count = 3 blocks x 3,600 test movies = 10,800; a smaller 360-clip/block dev set also ships. Saturation ('closing') is from own knowledge, not the explainer -- Meta released a harder IntPhys 2 successor circa 2025 specifically because modern video/world models had begun to close the gap on this 2019 release; the explainer itself only reports the original 2018-era baselines at chance under occlusion. domain_primary follows the CV-benchmark convention (multimodal) since no dedicated physics/world-model domain exists in the vocabulary.
placement_reason: A model-agnostic perception/tracking probe -- object permanence, shape constancy, and spatio-temporal continuity via occlusion-resistant, appearance-robust tracking -- scored by a single plausibility score per clip; a parse-and-track capability probe (A1's occlusion-resistant tracking use case), not a symbolic-reasoning or planning benchmark.

title: XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models
human_time: Seconds per item — a single short declarative question, judged full-compliance/full-refusal/partial-refusal by a trained annotator.
frontier_score: Llama2.0 (with system prompt) fully/partially refuses ~60% of the 250 safe prompts; GPT-4 sits at 6.4%+2.0% but shows 52% full refusal concentrated in one category (T10 Privacy/Fictional); both Llama2 configs refuse ~98-100% of the 200 genuinely-unsafe contrast prompts.
one_line: 450-prompt contrast set (250 safe prompts engineered to sound unsafe + 200 minimally-edited unsafe twins) naming and measuring 'exaggerated safety' — refusing benign requests that pattern-match unsafe vocabulary.
notes: Saturation='saturated' follows the same treatment as other superseded 2023 artifacts in the taxonomy (e.g. AlpacaFarm): the explainer explicitly frames the paper's specific numbers as 'a historical snapshot of three long-superseded 2023 models,' fully public with no contamination guard, and directly superseded in scale by OR-Bench (already in the taxonomy as B4).
placement_reason: Direct predecessor to OR-Bench (already classified B4 in this taxonomy): exposes that safety evaluation had been one-sided — measuring only over-permissiveness — so a maximally-refusing model would score perfectly 'safe' by the existing yardstick. The contrast-set construction exists to prove that gap, not to rank raw capability; matches B4's construct-validity pattern exactly (cf. cui-2024-or-bench, lin-2021-truthfulqa).

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
human_time: A multi-step tool-use trajectory (ReAct loop over several turns) that a human reviewer needs a few minutes to read and judge for safety/helpfulness.
frontier_score: Best 2023 configuration (GPT-4 + explicit safety prompt) still failed 23.9% of 144 underspecified-instruction test cases (safety 2.359/3, helpfulness 1.824/3); GPT-4 basic scored 39.4% failure incidence, Claude-2 44.3%, ChatGPT-3.5 62.0%.
one_line: An LM-emulated agent sandbox — GPT-4 plays 311 tools across 36 toolkits and a second GPT-4 scores safety/helpfulness on 144 underspecified-instruction (non-adversarial) test cases, validated by human annotation (72.5% identified-failure precision) and a 6-of-7 real-terminal-sandbox reproduction.
notes: Placed in E2 (dangerous-capability & propensity) rather than E1 (attack surfaces) because the paper's own chosen threat model is explicitly non-adversarial — 'a benign user who omits a critical detail... as opposed to an adversarial user trying to jailbreak the model' — measuring an agent's propensity to cause harm through underspecification rather than resistance to attack, closer to PropensityBench's would-do framing (already E2 in this taxonomy) than AgentDojo/InjecAgent's attack-surface framing.
placement_reason: Measures an agent's propensity to take harmful actions under benign, underspecified instructions (no adversarial user in the threat model) — the would-do-under-pressure pattern PropensityBench later formalizes (E2), not an attack-surface probe (E1, which requires an adversarial actor) or a values/judgment probe (E3).

title: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
human_time: Labeling one image (classify among 1000 classes) takes seconds; the trained human annotator did 1500 images after a short training phase.
frontier_score: GoogLeNet 6.7% top-5 error (2014); trained human A1 5.1% on the same sample
one_line: 1000-class ImageNet image-classification challenge (plus single-object localization and 200-class detection), scored by top-5 error on a withheld test set.
notes: Classification top-5 error is label exact-match; localization/detection use box-IoU/mAP (programmatic), hence grading_all includes programmatic. Provenance crowdsourced (web images labeled via Amazon Mechanical Turk with QC voting). items_count ≈ 100,000 test images; training set is ~1.2M. Treated as saturated: 2014 machine error already near the single-human baseline and long since surpassed.
placement_reason: Role at birth: give the ImageNet database the protocol it lacked — a fixed 1000-class task, withheld test set, evaluation server, and one metric — so 'is visual recognition getting better?' became answerable. The canonical perception capability probe of the deep-learning era.

title: EmoBench: Evaluating the Emotional Intelligence of Large Language Models
human_time: A minute or two per item: read a short scenario and choose the best emotion/action; the paper's 48 recruited participants were screened out if they failed a 6-question quiz.
frontier_score: GPT-4 59.75%/54.12% EU (EN/ZH), up to 75.88%/73.75% EA — still below the 48-person human baseline on both tasks
one_line: 400 hand-crafted bilingual MCQs (200 Emotional Understanding + 200 Emotional Application) engineered so surface pattern and correct answer diverge.
notes: domain_primary social-moral is a least-bad fit — no dedicated emotional-intelligence slot in BENCH_DOMAINS. The paper's own Limitations concede GPT-4-generated scenario seeds are an unquantified bias risk it never resolves.
placement_reason: Engineers scenarios so the correct emotional read requires inferring an unstated cause or value (a shirt's sentimental worth, a culture's punctuality norm) rather than pattern-matching an explicit label — a perception/inference capability probe explicitly extending ToM's 'entail hidden state from narrative' paradigm (its own perspective-taking category is directly borrowed from FANToM/Hi-ToM), not an audit of an existing EI benchmark's construct: EmoBench's own thesis is a broader, harder capability test, not a demonstration that EQ-Bench's score is invalid.

title: Complex Sequential Question Answering: Towards Learning to Converse Over Linked Question Answer Pairs with a Knowledge Graph
human_time: A few minutes per dialog: track 15.9 avg. linked turns over a KG subgraph, resolving coreference/ellipsis and composing logical/quantitative/comparative queries -- longer than a single-tuple factoid lookup.
frontier_score: HRED + key-value-memory hybrid reaches 15.83% recall / 6.7% precision overall on entity-retrieval questions; 0.29% recall / 0.44% precision on Quantitative Reasoning (All), vs. 40.2% F1 on its count-producing sibling.
one_line: 200K dialogs (1.6M turns) requiring logical, quantitative, and comparative reasoning over a 21.2M-tuple Wikidata subgraph, with dialog-linked coreference/ellipsis/clarification -- a 2018 HRED+KV-memory hybrid manages only 15.83% recall overall.
notes: domain_primary is a genuine judgment call between reasoning, knowledge, and conversation -- the paper explicitly frames CSQA as sitting at the intersection of dialog and complex KG-QA; classified as reasoning because the headline evaluation breaks accuracy down by reasoning type (logical/quantitative/comparative) and the near-zero score on quantitative-reasoning entity retrieval is the paper's central finding. grading_all folded to proxy-metric even though the paper uses three distinct metric families (recall/precision, F1, BLEU-4 for clarification NLG) across different answer types -- none of them is a literal exact-match despite recall/precision approaching one for simple lookups.
placement_reason: Tests whether a system can decompose logical/quantitative/comparative multi-set queries over a large KG into checkable structured answers (entities, counts, booleans) rather than just retrieve one fact -- a closed-form multi-hop reasoning probe (A3), with conversational turn-linking (coreference, ellipsis, clarification) as the delivery mechanism rather than the tested skill itself.

title: WinoGrande: An Adversarial Winograd Schema Challenge at Scale
human_time: Seconds per item: one two-option pronoun-resolution sentence pair; humans reach 94.0% via a 3-worker majority vote.
frontier_score: RoBERTa (2019 best) 59.4-79.1% depending on training size vs 94.0% human; modern frontier LLMs are widely known to exceed 90% (own knowledge, not in the explainer)
one_line: 44k crowdsourced Winograd-schema pronoun-resolution problems, adversarially debiased via AFLITE (a RoBERTa-embedding-ensemble filter) to 12,282 hard instances; cuts state-of-the-art from ~90% (biased WSC) to 79.1% against 94.0% human.
notes: Saturation via own knowledge: WinoGrande has been a standard eval-suite entry since 2019 (GPT-3, PaLM, LLaMA-2 and beyond per the explainer) and modern frontier models are known to score well above the 2019 79.1% ceiling. No lineage edge to HellaSwag added despite topical similarity - the paper's actual cited AFLITE precursor is Zellers et al.'s original SWAG adversarial filter (2018), which is not a node in this corpus (only the later HellaSwag paper is), and WinoGrande's own text does not cite HellaSwag directly.
placement_reason: Neural LMs had reached ~90% on WSC variants, but Trichelair et al. showed 13.5% of WSC problems carry detectable word-association bias; WinoGrande rebuilds the same construct (pronoun-resolution commonsense) at 44k scale and applies AFLITE to algorithmically strip embedding-level shortcuts, restoring a genuine 79.1-vs-94.0 headroom - the taxonomy's own de-saturation pattern, alongside MultiNLI/SuperGLUE/HellaSwag in this same corpus.

title: The StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge
human_time: A few minutes per scenario: one real-time StarCraft II micromanagement battle against the scripted AI.
frontier_score: QMIX leads aggregate self-play win rate across 14 maps but 'makes meaningful progress' on only 2 of 5 Super Hard maps (27m_vs_30m 49%, MMM2 69%); the other three Super Hard maps stay at 0-3% for every 2019 algorithm tested.
one_line: 14 partially-observable StarCraft II micromanagement scenarios (Easy/Hard/Super-Hard tiers), each unit its own decentralized RL agent battling the game's scripted AI, released with the PyMARL framework implementing QMIX, QTRAN, COMA, VDN, and IQL.
notes: domain_primary follows the same reasoning fallback as Hanabi -- no dedicated multi-agent/tactical-control domain exists in the controlled vocabulary. The Easy/Hard/Super-Hard difficulty tiers were defined post hoc from the same lab's own algorithms' scores (QMIX's authors largely overlap with SMAC's authors), a benchmark-design caveat worth flagging even though it doesn't change the facet values.
placement_reason: Ports the 'ALE for single-agent RL' idea to cooperative multi-agent RL: 14 partially-observable combat scenarios where each unit is its own decentralized agent operating a real-time tactical action space (move/attack/heal) -- the archetypal interactive-environment capability probe (A5), with its headline result (three of five Super-Hard maps unsolved by every 2019 algorithm) about tactical coordination skill within an operated environment, not knowledge or conversation.

title: ARB: Advanced Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Models
human_time: Graduate-level exam items (PhD qualifying exams, MCAT/bar-exam prep, contest-math problem books) take a few minutes each for multiple-choice/numerical items; open-ended proofs run longer.
frontier_score: GPT-4 leads every subset (~80-87% MCAT, ~60-63% Law) but collapses under 20% on Physics Numerical and under 5% on Math Numerical (1%-relative-error threshold); rubric-based GPT-4 self-grading correlates with human graders at Pearson r=0.78-0.91.
one_line: 1,207 graduate-level math/physics/law/MCAT problems (MC, numerical/symbolic short-answer, open-ended proof) deliberately sourced from low-web-visibility exam/problem-book material, plus a GPT-4 rubric-grading pipeline for open-ended answers.
notes: Domain split across math/physics/law/MCAT; classified reasoning primary since the benchmark's own framing and title center on testing genuine reasoning vs. memorized recall, not knowledge recall per se (contrast A2-style MMLU/AGIEval). contamination_defense=private-holdout reflects the paper's API-gated (not public-download) access, explicitly chosen over canary-text after weighing both.
placement_reason: Explicitly built because GSM8K/MATH/MMLU/BIG-bench/HELM were 'increasingly favored' by models over benchmarks: sources problems from PhD qualifying exams, contest-math books, and professional-exam prep specifically because they're harder and less scraped, with GPT-4 staying under 20%/5% on the hardest numerical subsets — durable headroom is the explicit design goal, the C1 pattern (cf. OlympiadBench, HLE in the existing taxonomy), not a knowledge-exam capability probe (A2).

title: AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments
human_time: A simulated clinical encounter is capped at 20 patient/measurement interactions before a diagnosis is due; a physician conducting an analogous real history-taking interview needs roughly 10-20 minutes.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet leads AgentClinic-MedQA at 62.1% (n=11 doctor models), ahead of 3 human physicians at 54% (n=3, high variance); GPT-4 trails humans at 51.6%
one_line: Four-LLM-agent simulated clinical encounter (doctor/patient/measurement/moderator) replacing static medical MCQs with sequential history-taking under a fixed interaction budget, across 5 case sources and bias/tool ablations.
notes: items_count = 215 (MedQA) + 200 (MIMIC-IV) + 120 (NEJM) + 260 (Spec) + 749 (7-language MedQA translations incl. English) -- paper doesn't total these itself. Provenance mixes GPT-4-populated JSON templates from five existing sources (USMLE, MIMIC-IV, NEJM, MedMCQA) with manual validation -> aggregated. Family placement (D2 vs A5 interactive-env) is a judgment call: classified D2 because the design intent is explicitly 'is MedQA accuracy a good guide to real clinical competence,' mirroring Med-PaLM/HealthBench's argument-past-the-exam framing, rather than a generic environment-operation headline.
placement_reason: Directly extends Med-PaLM's own critique -- static MedQA accuracy climbed from 38% to 90% while saying nothing about whether a model can gather the right information in the right order -- into a simulated four-agent clinical encounter with a finite question budget, cognitive/implicit bias injection, and multilingual/multi-specialty coverage; the object is occupational medical competence under realistic constraints (D2's mandate), not human-in-the-loop collaboration (D3: no real human counterpart, all four roles are LLM agents) or bare environment-operation (A5: the interactive loop is a vehicle for the professional-competence question, not the headline).

title: Ignore This Title and HackAPrompt: Exposing Systemic Vulnerabilities of LLMs through a Global Scale Prompt Hacking Competition
human_time: Seconds per submitted injection attempt; competitors could submit up to 500 attempts/day over the multi-week competition.
frontier_score: 9 of 10 designed challenges solved within days; 83.2% success rate on the refined Submissions Dataset (34,641/41,596) vs. 7.7% on raw Playground exploration (43,295/560,161); ChatGPT's extra defenses only marginally reduced success rate (7% vs. FlanT5-XXL's 8%, GPT-3's 7%).
one_line: A global prompt-hacking competition (2,800+ competitors, 50+ countries) against GPT-3, ChatGPT, and FlanT5-XXL produced 600K+ adversarial prompts and the first data-driven taxonomy of 29 hierarchically-related prompt-hacking techniques, showing prompt-based defenses reliably fail.
notes: items_count=601,757 sums the Submissions Dataset (41,596) and Playground Dataset (560,161) the explainer states; the paper's own headline rounds this to '600K+.' saturation='saturated' reflects that 9 of the 10 designed challenges fell within days of the competition opening.
placement_reason: A large-scale, human-crowdsourced attack-surface study — 600K+ real prompt-injection/jailbreak attempts against production LLMs, yielding a data-driven 29-technique attack taxonomy and the empirical finding that prompt-based defenses don't work — the E1 pattern at competition scale, complementary to the formal attack/defense benchmark (liu-2023-open-prompt-injection, same batch) but sourced from real human adversaries rather than five heuristic attack functions.

title: PropensityBench: Evaluating Latent Safety Risks in Large Language Models via an Agentic Approach
human_time: The underlying task τ is a short multi-step tool operation; a scenario runs up to 156 agent interactions across 12 pressure levels, but the equivalent human work per instance is minutes (synthetic agentic task).
frontier_score: Avg propensity 46.9% at max pressure; safest OpenAI o3 10.5%, worst Gemini 2.5 Pro 79.0% (near-zero at zero pressure)
one_line: 5,874 agentic scenarios that rig the safe tool to always fail and escalate operational pressure, measuring an LLM's propensity to grab a forbidden dangerous-capability tool.
notes: Headline propensity is a mechanical/programmatic check (did the agent ever call the misaligned tool?); LLM judges are used in scenario generation and the justification taxonomy (hence llm-judge in grading_all). Contamination: scenarios are freshly synthesized and the metric is behavioral (low exposure), but no explicit held-out/canary/live-refresh mechanism is described and templated pressure prompts are Goodhart-able, so marked none-public — low confidence on this dimension. Saturation 'open' interpreted as the safety target (near-zero propensity) being far from met; could be argued not-applicable since it's a lower-is-better propensity metric. Complexity is a judgment call on synthetic agentic tasks.
placement_reason: Shifts frontier-safety evaluation from can-do to would-do: hands an agent a forbidden proxy tool and escalating operational pressure to measure its propensity to knowingly cross a line across bio/chem/cyber/self-proliferation risk domains. The object is latent risk, not skill. Named E2 exemplar.

title: ASPI: Seeking Ambiguity Clarification Amplifies Prompt Injection Vulnerability in LLM Agents
human_time: Same office-chore tasks as AgentDojo (delete a file, book travel, send a Slack message) that a human finishes in a few minutes with the same tools; ASPI doesn't add new task complexity beyond AgentDojo's own.
frontier_score: Attack success rate rises sharply from execution to clarification for most models (o3: 1.8%→34.0%, Gemini-3-Flash: 2.2%→35.7%, Kimi K2.5: 11.1%→63.1%); Claude-Opus-4.7 is the lone model staying flat (2.1%→2.2%)
one_line: 728 paired task-attack scenarios built on AgentDojo, isolating the causal effect of an agent transitioning from task execution to clarification-seeking on prompt-injection vulnerability: the same attack that fails during execution succeeds 12-63% of the time once delivered through the agent's own ask_user channel, across 10 frontier models.
notes: provenance='synthetic-generated': base scenarios (domains, tools, user tasks, attacker goals, scoring) are inherited verbatim from AgentDojo (expert-authored), but ASPI's own novel content — the ambiguity-construction pipeline that removes one slot and writes the clarification question — is Gemini-3.1-Pro-proposed then quality-control-verified, with human validation on a 200-sample check finding 99% correctness (AC1≈0.99). grading_all includes llm-judge for the behavioral mechanism analysis (CONFUSED/PERSUADED state labeling) that explains WHY the effect happens, distinct from the deterministic AgentDojo ASR scoring that IS the headline metric. Noted circularity (not scored as a flaw here, but relevant to confidence in absolute numbers): Gemini-3.1-Pro generates the ambiguous prompts, is the primary judge, and is one of the 10 evaluated models, partially mitigated by GPT-5.4 + human cross-validation (kappa_bin=0.905).
placement_reason: Directly measures an attack surface — indirect prompt injection succeeding through a newly-identified delivery channel (the agent's own clarification-seeking ask_user call) — built explicitly on AgentDojo's environment/scoring and reporting attack success rate as the headline metric, the same object InjecAgent/AgentDojo/BrowserART/FORTRESS measure; the paper's contribution is isolating a state x channel interaction within that same risk space (clarification reopens an injection path execution-time defenses had closed), not a new agent-capability skill.

title: SciPredict: Can LLMs Predict the Outcomes of Scientific Experiments in Natural Sciences?
human_time: Reading one fully-specified experimental setup and predicting its outcome — an expert reasoning task of roughly minutes to tens of minutes per item.
frontier_score: Gemini 3 Pro best at ~25.3%; range 14-26% across 15 models, vs ~20% human-expert baseline
one_line: 405 post-training-cutoff physics/chemistry/biology experiment-outcome prediction tasks testing predictive accuracy and, centrally, calibration.
notes: Grading is a composite: MCQ (~40%, exact-match), numerical (~28%, expert tolerance-band check — treated as numeric exact-match), free-form (~32%, LLM rubric-judge). Primary set to exact-match as the plurality/headline format, but rubric-judge is central — this dimension is a judgment call. Contamination is live-refresh by design (post-March-2025 papers, web search disabled; rubric names SciPredict as the example). Provenance marked expert-authored (recruited PhD experts write tasks/rubrics/tolerance bands over 7,380 expert-hours), though items are grounded in real recent papers (real-work-mined flavor). Domain science with strong forecasting/calibration character (secondary).
placement_reason: Post-cutoff sourcing is the stated core design, not an add-on: every task comes from papers posted after every evaluated model's training cutoff with web search disabled, so 'prediction' can never collapse into recall — unsaturable-by-construction outcome prediction. The taxonomy's own C3 style exemplar ('SciPredict-style').

title: PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action
human_time: Each case is a short vignette-driven agent trajectory (e.g. send an email/Slack message using gathered context) -- a human doing the same task takes a few minutes.
frontier_score: GPT-4: 98.99% trajectory-level probing accuracy yet 25.68% adjusted leakage rate (LRh, Privacy-Enhancing Prompt); Claude-3-Sonnet: 100% probing accuracy, 37.74% LRh
one_line: 493 Contextual-Integrity-grounded seeds/vignettes/agent trajectories showing that near-perfect privacy-QA probing accuracy does not predict whether an LM agent actually leaks sensitive info when it acts.
notes: task_shape is a judgment call: the model under test generates one final action given a fixed, pre-built multi-step trajectory context rather than acting turn-by-turn itself, so classified single-turn (the same logic used elsewhere for InjecAgent's borderline case, though that record went the other way). grading_primary=llm-judge reflects the headline leakage-rate metric; the 3-level probing questions are exact-match ('No'/'Yes'). Every headline number is the helpfulness-adjusted LRh, whose judge only reaches Fleiss kappa=0.56 against humans per the paper's own validation.
placement_reason: Points at the measurement apparatus, not a skill: shows that near-perfect probing-question accuracy (GPT-4: 98.99%-100%) does not predict real in-action privacy behavior (25-39% leak rate on the identical underlying cases), exposing that a model's score on the standard privacy-QA construct means something different from what it's assumed to mean -- the canonical B4 audit move, paired with a dynamic red-teaming extension rather than itself being the object.

title: MedicalAgentsBench for Complex Medical Reasoning: Comparing Internalized Reasoning Models versus Externalized Agent-based Frameworks
human_time: A single hard medical MCQ (avg 147.4 tokens) drawn from USMLE-style/board exams -- a few minutes for a physician.
frontier_score: o3-mini + MDAgents (best combination of internalized reasoning + agent framework): 35.1% overall accuracy
one_line: 862-question hard set built by filtering 8 medical QA benchmarks (MedQA, PubMedQA, MedMCQA, MedBullets, MedExQA, MedXpertQA, MMLU, MMLU-Pro) to items fewer than half of 10 base models answer correctly, then MELD-screened and clinician-reviewed; the best combination (o3-mini + MDAgents) reaches only 35.1%.
notes: Contamination_defense: the paper runs MELD (a Levenshtein-based memorization probe) to screen candidate questions and states it has 'high precision but unknown recall' -- a real but partial screening step, not a formal holdout/canary/procedural-regeneration defense, so coded none-public with this caveat (same convention as DS-1000's perturbation defense). Kingdom judgment: same construct (medical MCQ), headroom restored via cross-benchmark difficulty filtering rather than new item authorship -- the B3 pattern applied across benchmarks instead of within one.
