placement_reason: Standard medical QA is 'solved from the top down' (GPT-4o 88-91% on the full sets) so the paper filters 8 existing benchmarks down to only the questions models actually disagree on -- the same headroom-restoration move as MMLU-Pro, just applied across a whole family of saturated medical exams at once rather than rebuilding one from scratch; its real contribution (does reasoning-model depth and agent-framework breadth stack) rides on top of that harder set.

title: ResearchRubrics: A Benchmark of Prompts and Rubrics For Evaluating Deep Research Agents
human_time: Producing one well-researched 5k-50k-token report on an open-ended prompt via multi-source web research — several hours of expert work.
frontier_score: Gemini DR 0.677 (ternary) / 0.615 (binary); OpenAI DR 0.664 / 0.597; no system tops 70%
one_line: 101 open-ended Deep-Research-agent prompts paired with 2,593 expert-written weighted rubric criteria, LLM-judged for compliance.
notes: domain_primary is a judgment call: the evaluated systems are web-research (Deep Research) agents (agentic-web), but the graded skill is implicit reasoning + cross-document synthesis of a written report (reasoning/knowledge secondary). task_shape marked interactive-env because DR agents run a live multi-step web-browse/retrieve loop, though the human-facing prompt is single-turn and the harness only grades the final report. Grading is rubric-judge (LLM over per-criterion weighted rubrics); human annotators validate the judge but don't score systems. No private held-out set, live-web retrieval is non-reproducible, prompts adapted from public forums — hence none-public. Best systems ~62-68% → closing.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'how good are Deep Research agents at open-ended, multi-source research?' — the headline is agent skill (no system clears 70%; failures concentrate in implicit reasoning and cross-document synthesis), with the 2,593 hand-written rubrics as the instrument. The binary-vs-ternary grading findings pull toward G3, but they are secondary lessons, so per the tie-break the skill headline wins.

title: TaskBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Task Automation
human_time: A few minutes to read a multi-tool instruction and manually work out the correct tool sequence, dependency wiring, and parameters.
frontier_score: GPT-4 leads tool-selection Edge-F1 in every domain (54.70/69.27/80.53 across Hugging Face/Multimedia/Daily-Life) and parameter v-F1 (60.86/72.31/71.14), though CodeLlama-13B beats it on Daily Life APIs task decomposition (R1 89.86 vs. 85.07); edge/dependency prediction trails node/tool-selection by roughly 20 F1 points across every model tested.
one_line: A three-stage task-automation benchmark (decomposition, tool selection under explicit resource/temporal dependency graphs, parameter prediction) across 3 domains (Hugging Face Tools, Multimedia Tools, Daily Life APIs), built by sampling Tool Graphs and having GPT-4 back-instruct them into 17,450 verified instructions, correlating with human judgment at Kendall's tau=0.89.
notes: The paper's own audit found ~12% of generated samples contain errors (mostly incorrect tool dependencies) — a caveat on fine-grained rankings, but doesn't affect classification.
placement_reason: Tests the full task-automation pipeline (decompose, select tools under explicit resource/temporal dependency graphs, fill parameters) as one scored capability, the dependency-graph structure being the stated gap every prior tool benchmark (APIBench, ToolBench, MetaTool, API-Bank) lacked — the A6 tool-orchestration pattern shared with MetaTool in the same batch, distinguished by making tool dependencies (not just selection) a first-class scored target.

title: Language Models are Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoners
human_time: 1-5 min per item: a GSM8K-style grade-school word problem needing 2-8 reasoning steps (paper's own step counts).
frontier_score: PaLM-540B 55.0% avg (TRANSLATE-EN best setting; 2022 numbers)
one_line: 250 GSM8K math problems hand-translated into 10 languages to test multilingual chain-of-thought reasoning.
notes: Provenance borderline: items are GSM8K (crowdsourced) problems re-rendered by hired professional translators; could also read as aggregated. items_count = 250 x 11 languages incl. English. Saturation from own knowledge (frontier models score ~90%+ by 2024); explainer only quotes 2022 numbers.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can step-by-step reasoning that works in English survive in Swahili/Bengali/Telugu?' — the first multilingual multi-step arithmetic benchmark, literally 250 GSM8K problems hand-translated into ten languages with checkable numeric answers. Headline is model performance on a frontier reasoning skill, so A3 (GSM8K family), not A2: the object is math reasoning, not exam knowledge.

title: Retrieval Models Aren't Tool-Savvy: Benchmarking Tool Retrieval for Large Language Models
human_time: Not applicable in the usual sense -- ToolRet scores retriever models automatically; a human shortlisting relevant tools for one query from a pool would need a couple of minutes.
frontier_score: Best off-the-shelf retriever (NV-Embed-v1, 7B) reaches only 33.83 nDCG@10 zero-shot
one_line: Reformats 7.6k tool-retrieval tasks and 43k tools from 30+ existing tool-use datasets into an MTEB-style test bed; even the strongest embedding model clears only 33.83 nDCG@10 zero-shot, and the shortfall measurably drags down downstream ToolBench pass rates.
notes: grading_primary judgment call: headline metrics are nDCG@10/Recall@10/Precision@10/Completeness@10, all automatically computed -- coded programmatic (primary) with proxy-metric secondary for the ranking-quality nature of nDCG, mirroring the call made for MMTEB in this same batch.
placement_reason: Explicitly modeled on MTEB/BEIR's retrieval-benchmark methodology, transplanted to a new corpus type (tool descriptions instead of documents): can a general-purpose IR model find the right tools for a query from a large heterogeneous pool -- the A1 retrieval capability question, not A6 (tool orchestration/sequencing, which presumes the right tools are already found).

title: AGENT: A Benchmark for Core Psychological Reasoning
human_time: Watch a short TDW-rendered familiarization + test video pair (each video 5.6-25.2s) and rate which of two outcomes is more surprising; human-validated via 300 MTurk raters on 240 of 960 test trials.
frontier_score: Given oracle 3D state: hand-engineered BIPaCK holds at 0.94-0.96 across in-distribution and both generalization tests; learned ToMnet-G scores a comparable 0.90 in-distribution but collapses to 0.65-0.71 under held-out generalization, vs. an estimated 0.91 individual-human accuracy
one_line: A TDW-rendered 3D violation-of-expectation video benchmark testing whether machine agents share infants' core intuitive psychology (goal preference, efficiency, hidden constraints, cost-reward trade-offs) -- a hand-engineered Bayesian planner holds under generalization where a learned Theory-of-Mind network collapses.
notes: items_count is the 960-trial held-out test set (480 matched expected/surprising pairs); 1,920 training + 480 validation trials are separate and contain only expected videos. All headline numbers use oracle ground-truth 3D state, not raw perception -- perception-based results are relegated to a supplementary appendix outside the main text. Domain 'social-moral' is the closest available label; no dedicated theory-of-mind domain exists.
placement_reason: Explicitly scopes itself to the 'core' pre-verbal psychological reasoning infants already have (not false-belief ToM), scored purely by whether a model's surprise rating on a passively-observed video pair matches the design intent -- perceiving and parsing an agent's goals/rationality from behavior alone (A1), the same slot BIB occupies, since neither model ever acts in the environment.

title: CORE-Bench: Fostering the Credibility of Published Research Through a Computational Reproducibility Agent Benchmark
human_time: Capsules are selected to run in under 45 minutes, but Hard-tier tasks additionally require finding the run command and installing dependencies from a README alone -- plausibly an hour or more of active researcher work per paper.
frontier_score: CORE-Agent+GPT-4o: 60.00% Easy / 57.78% Medium / 21.48% Hard (test-set accuracy per tier)
one_line: 270 tasks (90 published CodeOcean papers x 3 scaffolding tiers -- output given / Dockerfile given / README only) asking an agent to reproduce a paper's own results from its own code, graded against a 95% prediction interval from 3 manual reruns.
notes: Complexity is a borderline L2/L3 call: the explicit 45-minute runtime cap is L2-ish, but Hard-tier's dependency-install-from-README-alone step plausibly pushes real human effort into the hours range, matching MLE-bench/MLAgentBench's L3 precedent in the same family. Grading via a 95%-prediction-interval from 3 manual reruns (rather than a single brittle ground truth) is unusually rigorous for stochastic code output.
placement_reason: Built as a narrower, checkable precursor to 'AI automates science' claims: can an agent reproduce a published paper's own results from its own code, at three scaffolding tiers -- reproducing existing research end-to-end is the A8 case, distinguished from A4 program synthesis since nothing is written from a spec, only executed, diagnosed, and reported against the paper's own numbers.

title: SciRepEval: A Multi-Format Benchmark for Scientific Document Representations
group: Allen Institute for AI / Northwestern / Yale
human_time: Not stated; a human doing the equivalent classification/regression/search-matching task per paper would need a few minutes (BEIR-style estimate).
frontier_score: Adapters + MTL CTRL ensemble: 71.2 average (62.9 in-train / 74.1 out-of-train), 2023
one_line: 24-task, four-format (classification/regression/proximity/search) benchmark for scientific document embeddings; absorbs SciDocs as a subset and shows per-task-format embeddings beat one shared embedding.
notes: domain_primary 'long-context' follows the BEIR precedent (label covers 'long context & retrieval'); tool_access 'search-retrieval' for the same reason (ad-hoc search is one of the four task formats, corpus is the task substrate). grading_primary judged 'programmatic' (F1/MAP/nDCG/correlation against fixed ground-truth labels, à la COCO's IoU-AP) rather than 'exact-match', a genuinely close call given BEIR itself used exact-match for a similar mix. items_count left null: 8 in-train tasks each 200K+ instances, 16 held-out tasks of varying size, no single stated total.
placement_reason: Absorbs SciDocs (whose four nearest-neighbor tasks the paper's own Appendix G shows correlate >0.99, collapsing to one signal) into a broader 24-task, four-format representation-quality suite asking whether an embedding actually generalizes across realistic scientific-document uses — a representation/retrieval capability probe (A1, BEIR/COCO's family), not a construct audit: the SciDocs-redundancy finding is a secondary result, not this paper's headline contribution (a bigger benchmark plus a multi-format training method).

title: Large Language Models Encode Clinical Knowledge
human_time: ~1-2 min per USMLE-style vignette; several minutes for a long-form consumer health answer.
frontier_score: Flan-PaLM 540B 67.6% on MedQA (USMLE), +17 over prior SOTA
one_line: MultiMedQA: seven medical QA sets plus clinician-rated axes (consensus, harm) pushing medical eval past multiple choice.
notes: Classified artifact = MultiMedQA benchmark + clinician human-eval framework (Med-PaLM the model is the vehicle). Headline metric is MC accuracy; the 12-axis human panel is the lasting methodological piece. items_count (~11k across the seven sets) and saturation (MedQA >90% for current frontier) from own knowledge, not the explainer.
placement_reason: The gap is explicitly clinical-deployment readiness: exam accuracy 'says nothing about whether a free-text answer is factual, complete, or dangerous' and 'medicine is the wrong domain to evaluate sloppily.' MultiMedQA plus the 12-axis clinician harm/consensus/bias framework asks whether answers are safe enough for the clinic — occupational medical competence, the HealthBench-precursor role the D2 rubric names. Not A2: the multiple-choice exams are the thing it argues past; not G3: the human-eval axes serve the medical question, the protocol isn't the headline.

title: CLUTRR: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Inductive Reasoning from Text
human_time: Expert annotators given unrestricted time take ~6 min per puzzle on average and solve 100% correctly (k=2-6); time-limited Turkers score 0.848 to 0.406 as clause length k rises from 2 to 6, with perceived difficulty (1-5 Likert) rising from 1.49 to 4.46.
frontier_score: GAT (given the symbolic graph) reaches 1.0 accuracy at k=2, degrading with chain length; best text model (BERT-LSTM) ~0.9 at k=2, all models converge to 0.15-0.3 by k=10; human (unrestricted time) solves 100% at k=2-6
one_line: Procedurally generated kinship-inference benchmark: backward-chains a 16-rule KB for k reasoning steps then crowd-paraphrases the result into natural-language stories, isolating systematic generalization from pattern matching as held-out reasoning-chain length k varies from 2 to 10.
notes: items_count left null - CLUTRR is a generator, not a fixed dataset (5,000 training / 100 test stories per clause length in the paper's own released runs, but the total is unbounded by design, same treatment as Reasoning Gym).
placement_reason: A dial-able K-way relation-classification puzzle with a checkable, ground-truth answer (kinship inference via a 16-rule symbolic KB) - the closed-form reasoning family's core pattern (matches fabbri-2025-multinrc), distinguished by held-out reasoning-chain length as the systematic-generalization axis rather than static per-item difficulty.

title: MultiChallenge: A Realistic Multi-Turn Conversation Evaluation Benchmark Challenging to Frontier LLMs
human_time: A few minutes: read a ~1,232-word, ~5-turn conversation and answer the final turn (paper's own averages).
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Jun 2024) 41.42% human-eval average
one_line: 273 adversarially-mined multi-turn conversations testing instruction retention, memory, editing, and self-coherence.
notes: Multi-turn by content but the model answers only the final turn of a frozen history (no live user simulation) - borderline single-turn. Provenance is MMSE multi-agent synthesis, then heavy human editing (~25% rewritten). A held-private hard split exists but isn't scored, so contamination defense counted as none-public (the 273 are on GitHub).
placement_reason: The gap opens with saturation: 'MT-Bench and MT-Eval — once the standard — are saturated... A benchmark that everyone passes measures nothing,' and the design gate keeps only examples that break >=3 of 6 frontier models. Same construct (multi-turn conversation ability) rebuilt 'deliberately un-saturated' for discriminative power — the exact Arena-Hard-vs-MT-Bench pattern B3 names. The skill isn't new; the restored headroom is the point.

title: TutorBench: A Benchmark To Assess Tutoring Capabilities Of Large Language Models
human_time: ~5-15 min: read the tutoring exchange plus (often) handwritten student work and craft a pedagogically sound response.
frontier_score: Gemini 2.5 Pro 55.65% overall; GPT-5 55.33%
one_line: 1,490 STEM tutoring conversations (half with handwritten-work images) rubric-graded on explanation, feedback, hints.
notes: Tutoring/pedagogy -> social-moral per rubric (the tested skill is interpersonal teaching, not STEM solving - the difficulty filter enforces that). Frozen-conversation final-response grading makes the multi-turn shape borderline single-turn. The 3-of-5-models difficulty filter is an anti-saturation device, not a contamination defense; 30 samples public, full release planned, no private holdout.
placement_reason: The gap is a shipping question: 'LLMs are already de-facto tutors for millions of students... If we are going to deploy these systems as teachers, we need to measure how good they actually are at teaching.' The construct is tutoring-as-service with a student in the loop — adapt to confusion, give feedback, hint without revealing — exactly the tutoring/teacher-assist benchmark D3 names. Not A7: the framing is deployment of a teaching service, not conversational skill per se; not A3: solving the problem is explicitly what it is NOT measuring.

title: BEHAVIOR: Benchmark for Everyday Household Activities in Virtual, Interactive, and Ecological Environments
human_time: Roughly 1.5 minutes on average per VR demonstration (758.5 min / 500 demos), though individual household activities range from seconds (pick up trash) to many minutes (cook a meal).
frontier_score: SAC/PPO score Q=0 on all or nearly all of the 12 simplest activities under realistic sensing+physics; removing physics alone lifts 9/12 off zero (up to Q=0.92)
one_line: 100 household activities grounded in the American Time Use Survey, defined declaratively in BDDL so a simulator can generate unlimited instances and grade partial progress -- SAC/PPO score Q=0 on nearly all of even the 12 simplest activities under realistic physics and sensing.
notes: Activity definitions were crowdsourced via Upwork annotators using a live feasibility-checking interface against iGibson 2.0; contamination_defense filed as procedural since BDDL's declarative initial/goal conditions let the simulator generate a 'potentially infinite' set of concrete instances per activity rather than a fixed, memorizable set. Only the 12 simplest of 100 activities are actually RL-benchmarked in this launch paper.
placement_reason: BDDL turns 'success' into a declarative logic check over a simulator anyone can generate unlimited instances from -- the operate-an-interactive-environment archetype extended to full household physics (temperature, wetness, cleanliness, not just position). Headline is a capability verdict: SAC/PPO score essentially zero on even the easiest activities under realistic sensing+physics.

title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and Extrapolating the Capabilities of Language Models
human_time: Typically <1 min: one MC or short-answer item; some tasks (logic puzzles, multi-step arithmetic) run a few minutes.
frontier_score: best 2022 models < 20 on 0-100 human-normalized scale (experts ~100); PaLM ~42 on BIG-bench Lite
one_line: 204 community-contributed tasks designed to outpace models and chart which capabilities emerge with scale.
notes: items_count = 204 tasks (per-task example counts vary widely; total examples not stated). Provenance: open GitHub community contributions, though mostly by researchers. A minority of programmatic Python tasks are multi-turn. Saturation from own knowledge - community treats BIG-bench/BBH as solved (BBEH built to replace it); the <20 headline is a 2022 number.
placement_reason: The G1 archetype by name: a 204-task collaborative compendium from 450 authors across 132 institutions, whose contribution is a WAY of evaluating — evaluation as capability forecasting (linearity vs breakthroughness, canary contamination guard, human-normalized aggregation) — not any single task skill. The gap section is about benchmarks themselves (SuperGLUE's two-year saturation treadmill, smooth aggregates hiding emergence), and the point 'is not to crown a winner but to chart what models can't yet do.'

title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
human_time: Days-plus: ML PhDs reached only 41.4% after 48 h and were still climbing; a full replication is plausibly 1-2 weeks.
frontier_score: o1 IterativeAgent 24.4% (26.0% at 36 h); Claude 3.5 Sonnet BasicAgent 21.0%
one_line: Agents replicate 20 ICML 2024 papers from scratch, graded on 8,316 author-co-written rubric criteria by an LLM judge.
notes: Provenance: task items are real published ICML papers (real-work-mined), with rubrics expert/author-co-written. Explainer mentions an internal held-out paper set -> private-holdout, though the scored 20 are public with a self-acknowledged contamination clock. reproduce.sh executes in a fresh env but every leaf is judge-scored, so grading stays rubric-judge.
placement_reason: Asks 'can an AI agent read a fresh ML paper and autonomously reproduce it — build the codebase, run the experiments, match the numbers?' — open-ended ML research work end-to-end, the MLE-bench-style skill A8 names. The gap is that CORE-Bench/MLE-bench/RE-Bench don't capture the full from-scratch loop. Preparedness/RSP autonomy tracking is a motivation, but the headline (best agent 21.0% vs PhDs 41.4%) is skill performance, not a risk finding, so A8 over E2.

title: Reasoning Gym: infinite, verifiable reasoning environments for RLVR
human_time: A typical procedurally generated puzzle/math item (algebra, ListOps-style logic, small Rubik's cube) takes a human a few minutes; hard configs longer.
frontier_score: o3-mini 63.51% avg on hard RG configs (DeepSeek-R1 59.52%); hardest per-task configs top out under 8%
one_line: 100+ procedural generators of algorithmically verifiable reasoning puzzles with tunable difficulty, for RLVR and eval.
notes: Doubles as an RLVR training environment; item count is unbounded by design (100+ generators, infinite instances). Verifiers are algorithmic checkers over final answers, many reducing to exact match.
placement_reason: The gap section is explicit: RLVR's bottleneck is the supply of checkable problems, and RG is 'a library of procedural generators rather than a frozen dataset' built to emit unlimited verifiable training data at tunable difficulty. Training on it is the headline use (RL-training Qwen2.5-3B with GRPO on generator output); the eval leaderboard is secondary. Generator-as-contribution with explicit training intent is the F1 definition verbatim.

title: BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
human_time: One query (a StackExchange question, LeetCode/Pony problem, or math-competition problem) requires a human to recognize the underlying theorem/algorithm/mechanism connecting it to a relevant document; a few minutes of expert reasoning per query.
frontier_score: Every one of 13 retrievers does badly; MTEB's leaderboard-topping SFR-Embedding-Mistral falls from 59.0 to 18.3 nDCG@10, best overall (gte-Qwen1.5) averages 22.5
one_line: 1,384 real queries (StackExchange, LeetCode/Pony, math-competition problems) paired with documents relevant only through a shared theorem, algorithm, or causal mechanism -- retrieval that requires reasoning, not lexical or semantic overlap.
notes: 12 datasets across 3 source types (7 StackExchange, 2 coding, 3 theorem-based). The paper's own headline ceiling claim ('24.3 nDCG@10') doesn't match its own Table 2 max of 22.5, per the source explainer -- flagged there, not corrected here.
placement_reason: BEIR's own explicit foil: BEIR's 'level 1/2' keyword-and-semantic retrieval is exactly what BRIGHT argues is solved and insufficient, building instead a 'level 3' reasoning-gated retrieval suite where query and relevant document share almost no lexical or topical overlap -- still fundamentally a retrieve capability probe (A1, BEIR's own family), with reasoning as the differentiator rather than a distinct construct-audit (B) of an existing retrieval benchmark's validity.

title: Challenging BIG-Bench Tasks and Whether Chain-of-Thought Can Solve Them
human_time: Under a minute per item for most tasks (multiple-choice or short answer); the average human rater across the 23 tasks scored 67.7% (max rater 94.4%).
frontier_score: Codex + chain-of-thought: 73.9% avg accuracy, beating the average human rater on 17/23 tasks (vs. 56.6% / 5-of-23 with answer-only prompting)
one_line: A hand-curated 23-task (27-subtask), 6,511-example subset of BIG-Bench -- specifically the tasks where no prior model had beaten the average human rater -- used to show that chain-of-thought prompting flips that outcome on most of them.
notes: Curation is itself a judgment call the paper is upfront about: 13 of 36 candidate hard tasks were dropped as 'extremely difficult for authors of this paper' to solve by hand, and the CoT condition got hand-engineered per-task exemplars while answer-only got only a one-time generic strengthening -- a prompt-engineering-effort confound per the explainer's critique.
placement_reason: The literal desaturation-sequel pattern: same construct (BIG-Bench's multi-task suite) rebuilt as a curated hard subset to restore headroom exactly where standard prompting had left it -- the taxonomy's own de-saturates relation to srivastava-2022-big-bench captures it precisely, the same operation SuperGLUE performed on GLUE. Unlike a fresh A-family capability probe, BBH's whole reason to exist is 'BIG-Bench already exists and scored X on this filtered slice; is that filtered slice still hard?' -- a construct-headroom question, not a new skill question.

title: CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge
human_time: Seconds per item: one five-way multiple-choice commonsense question.
frontier_score: Best 2018 baseline (BERT-LARGE) reaches 55.9% accuracy vs. 88.9% human on the primary random split; the paper's own SANITY check (curated distractors swapped for random ones) pushes the same model to 92.3%.
one_line: 12,247 five-way multiple-choice commonsense questions generated by grounding crowd-worker prompts in ConceptNet subgraphs, forcing background knowledge the question itself never states -- BERT-LARGE reaches 55.9% vs. 88.9% human, but 92.3% once curated distractors are swapped for random ones.
notes: Modern LLMs solve CommonsenseQA well past the 2018 human ceiling; saturated is from own knowledge, since the explainer only reports 2018-era numbers.
placement_reason: Tests whether a model can apply background commonsense knowledge never stated in the question -- a multiple-choice, exam-style knowledge-application probe (A2) scored against a human ceiling, distinct from the paper's own SANITY ablation showing much of the measured difficulty traces to adversarial distractor selection rather than a new skill or a benchmark-auditing purpose.

title: JudgeBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Judges
human_time: Not applicable — the subject being tested is an LLM judge, not a human.
frontier_score: Vanilla-prompted GPT-4o: 50.86% (near-random); best reasoning-heavy judge (o3-mini-high): 80.86%
one_line: 350 objectively correct-vs-incorrect response pairs across knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding, sampled from a single strong model so pairs are style-matched — vanilla-prompted GPT-4o scores just 50.86% at telling right from wrong.
notes: Dual-tagged benchmarks+evaluations for the same reason as RewardBench: a named benchmark whose headline contribution is testing judges' factual/logical correctness rather than style-preference.
placement_reason: The LLM-judge peer of RewardBench: instead of testing whether a judge's verdict matches human style preference (MT-Bench, Arena-Hard), it tests whether the judge can tell objectively correct from incorrect at all — most vanilla judges can't beat chance.

title: Long Range Arena: A Benchmark for Efficient Transformers
human_time: One instance is a classification over a 1K-16K-token input (byte-level review, nested ListOps expression, pixel image); a human needs minutes to read/resolve, though Pathfinder rendered visually is seconds.
frontier_score: BigBird 55.01 five-task avg vs vanilla Transformer 54.39; every 2020 model fails Path-X (16K) at chance
one_line: Six 1K-16K-token from-scratch tasks ranking efficient-Transformer architectures on long-range sequence modeling.
notes: Evaluates architectures trained from scratch, not LLMs. Saturation call uses outside knowledge: state-space models (S4 lineage, Mega) later solved Path-X and pushed averages to ~86-90, and the community treats LRA as retired; the explainer's own 2020 numbers read as open. Contamination is moot since the protocol forbids pretraining.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'which architecture can actually model long context?' — six encoding tasks from 1K to 16K tokens, trained from scratch so the score isolates long-range inductive bias. A long-context stress test / architecture capability probe, the A1 exemplar named in the taxonomy. Its in-corpus cites (NQ, MultiNLI, HotpotQA) are incidental; its real ancestry is the GLUE-style averaged multi-task suite method transplanted to the efficient-transformer subfield.

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
human_time: One instance is retrieving relevant documents for a single query from a large corpus; a human with search tooling would need minutes per query.
frontier_score: BM25+CE re-ranker beats BM25 on 16/18 datasets, +11% avg nDCG@10 (2021 snapshot); 0.757 on TREC-COVID
one_line: 18-dataset, 9-task zero-shot retrieval benchmark scoring retrievers out-of-domain by nDCG@10.
notes: Evaluates retrieval systems, not generative LLMs; tool_access = the retrieval corpus is the task substrate. Grading is automatic nDCG against human-pooled relevance labels (labels are provenance, not eval-time human grading). Saturation is ambiguous: nDCG ceiling is nominal (annotation holes), modern embedders reach ~0.55 avg, and the benchmark became a training target - 'open' is a loose call.
placement_reason: 'BEIR-style retrieval' is A1's named exemplar. Role at birth: can neural retrievers generalize zero-shot to unseen corpora? — a skill headline (BM25 vs dense out-of-domain), not an audit of a grader or a durability wall. It extends in-corpus component datasets (NQ, HotpotQA) into a unified 18-dataset zero-shot retrieval suite. The Hole@10 annotation-bias study is a B-flavored aside, but the paper's contribution and headline are the heterogeneous capability benchmark itself.

title: MMInA: Benchmarking Multihop Multimodal Internet Agents
human_time: Tasks average 2.85 hops (up to 10) and 12.9 actions across up to 14 real sites; a human clears these in a few to ~15 minutes (near the 96.3% human ceiling).
frontier_score: GPT-4V (best multimodal model): 21.8% overall task success rate vs. 96.3% human ceiling; collapses to 1.13% at 5+ hops
one_line: 1,050 multihop tasks chaining across up to 14 live, real-world websites (avg. 2.85 hops), requiring both image and text reasoning at every hop -- unlike prior web-agent sets that stay within one site.
notes: Grading mixes a strict keyword must_include check (programmatic) and a lenient GPT-3.5 fuzzy_match judge (llm-judge); the paper's headline task-success-rate number is the strict all-hops-correct metric. Tasks built via GPT-4V generation (108 WebQA-adapted) plus human-authored additions, both cross-validated -> synthetic-generated.
placement_reason: Extends the single-site limitation shared by WebArena/VisualWebArena/Mind2Web (all averaging ~1.0-1.06 hops) to genuine cross-site chains (2.85 avg, 10 max) -- the interactive multi-site browsing environment itself is the contribution, A5's operate-a-real-environment mandate stretched from one website to a chain of them, not a new grading protocol (G) or a hazard probe (E).

title: MuSiQue: Multihop Questions via Single-hop Question Composition
human_time: Roughly a few minutes: read up to 20 paragraphs (gold evidence plus positive distractors), chain 2-4 hops of single-hop facts, and extract a span -- harder than HotpotQA's 2-hop reading given more paragraphs and hops.
frontier_score: Best multihop model: 49.8 answer F1 vs. 78.0 human (MuSiQue-Ans, dev); DiRe cheatability score 37.8 vs. 68.8 (HotpotQA) / 63.4 (2WikiMultihopQA)
one_line: 2-4 hop questions built bottom-up by composing filtered, connected single-hop question pairs, explicitly engineered to close HotpotQA/2WikiMultihopQA's shortcut loopholes -- DiRe cheatability drops from 68.8/63.4 to 37.8.
notes: contamination_defense filed as procedural: the Disconnection Filtering (DF) and leakage-minimizing split (RL) pipeline stages are explicit construction-time steps against shortcut answerability and train/test overlap, ablated in Table 6 to show both are load-bearing. items_count is MuSiQue-Ans's 24,814 questions (MuSiQue-Full roughly doubles this with unanswerable twins).
placement_reason: Same construct (multi-hop reading-comprehension QA), headroom restored by construction: MuSiQue is built explicitly because HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA don't actually require the intended hop (a 2019-2020 run of shortcut-audit papers proved it), so it composes and filters single-hop pairs until a strong model provably can't skip the dependency -- the taxonomy's own de-saturates relation, not a fresh A-family capability probe of an unaudited construct.

title: AppWorld: A Controllable World of Apps and People for Benchmarking Interactive Coding Agents
human_time: Solutions average 50 lines (max 134) of multi-app API code with control flow; a competent dev with the docs needs roughly 20-60 min per task - borderline L2/L3.
frontier_score: ReAct + GPT-4o: 48.8% TGC normal / 30.2% challenge (32.1/13.0 SGC), mid-2024 snapshot
one_line: 750 interactive coding tasks over 9 simulated apps and 457 APIs, graded on database end-state incl. collateral damage.
notes: 250 author-written scenarios x 3 programmatically instantiated variants; generators exist but the shipped set plus gold solutions is public on GitHub, so contamination defense = none-public (Test-C unseen-app split is a generalization guard, not a holdout). Complexity is borderline L2/L3. Saturation judged from the 2024 numbers; live leaderboard likely higher now.
placement_reason: The contribution is the ENVIRONMENT: a simulated world of 9 apps / 457 APIs / ~100 people with mutable database state, where agents operate the world through interactive code and are graded on the resulting state (collateral-damage clause). Built explicitly against trace-graded tool benchmarks (Gorilla, ToolLLM) and porting the WebArena/OSWorld interactive-environment style from web/GUI surfaces to a personal-app ecosystem — A5's app-environment case, not A4 plain code-writing or A6 tool-selection.

title: VeRO: An Evaluation Harness for Agents to Optimize Agents
human_time: One instance = iteratively editing an agent codebase across a budget of 8 gated evaluations, reading traces between edits; a human engineer would spend hours to a day per optimization run.
frontier_score: VeRO-Agent Default (Sonnet 4.5) lifts avg target score 0.50 -> 0.61 (+8 pts); GEPA and prompt-only variants ~0.54
one_line: Budget-gated, permission-controlled harness + 5-task benchmark measuring how well coding agents optimize another agent's code.
notes: Meta-benchmark: the optimizer is graded by the target agent's lift on 5 aggregated public benchmarks (MATH, TAU-Bench Retail, GAIA, SimpleQA, GPQA), whose own grading is exact-match/programmatic. 'Private-holdout' = harness access-controls the test split, though the underlying data is public and only SimpleQA is contamination-hardened. Saturation call is loose - no natural ceiling for 'optimization lift'.
placement_reason: The question at birth: how good are coding agents at the open-ended engineering task of optimizing another agent's program (edit, evaluate, version under budget)? That is ML/agent-engineering knowledge work, MLE-bench-adjacent — A8. The harness (versioning, budget gating, permission control) is infrastructure to measure that skill fairly, mirroring how SWE-bench's Docker harness serves its skill probe (the paper says so explicitly). Borderline with G (the title says 'evaluation harness' and the protocol is the deliverable), but the headline claims are about optimizer-agent performance on the task, so A wins the tie-break.

title: PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Planning and Reasoning about Change
group: Arizona State University / Colorado State University
human_time: A trained person can generate a short Blocksworld/Logistics plan (a handful of actions) in a couple of minutes; formal verification against the plan validator (VAL) is instant.
frontier_score: GPT-4 solves 34.3% of plan-generation instances (Blocksworld), collapsing to 4.3%/2% once object/action names are obfuscated (Mystery Blocksworld)
one_line: A PDDL-grounded, planner-and-validator-graded test harness spanning eight reasoning-about-action tasks over two domains -- GPT-4 solves only 34.3% of plan-generation instances, collapsing to 2-4.3% once the domain vocabulary is obfuscated.
notes: contamination_defense filed as procedural: the obfuscated 'Mystery' domain variants (misleading or fully randomized object/action names over the identical underlying PDDL problem) are a built-in probe for vocabulary-pattern-matching vs. genuine domain-general planning, though it sits in an appendix rather than the headline table. Only two 2023-era models tested, single greedy sample, no chain-of-thought or agentic scaffolding.
placement_reason: Formal PDDL planning is a checkable-answer reasoning domain by construction -- a real planner and plan validator grade every instance mechanically, no partial credit, no judge -- squarely A3's 'logic puzzles with checkable answers' (planning is a classical AI logic problem), extended into an LLM capability probe. The Mystery-domain obfuscation is a built-in contamination check on that skill, not itself the design center (unlike B-family construct audits, whose whole point is auditing an existing benchmark's validity).

title: The AI Productivity Index (APEX)
human_time: Paper states mean 2.7 hours of real professional work per case (range 0.5-20h), per expert estimate.
frontier_score: GPT-5 (thinking=high) 67.0% of rubric criteria met; Gemini 3 Pro 64.3%; law easiest (77.9%), banking hardest (63.0%)
one_line: Expert-authored deliverables from banking, consulting, law and medicine, graded on Pass/Fail rubrics by an LLM judge.
notes: 137 vetted practitioners author source-grounded cases (~14.8 binary criteria each); single Gemini 2.5 Flash judge grades all criteria including Google's own models. n=400 scored set private, n=100 devset public; forced single-turn with attached source documents (up to 100K tokens) but no tools.
placement_reason: Named 'The AI Productivity Index' and framed against GDPval: does frontier work deliver real-world value on realistic deliverables from four high-paid jobs (banking, consulting, law, medicine), with tasks valued at ~2.7 expert-hours each. Explicit economic/productivity framing puts it in D1 rather than D2 despite the occupational content; its corpus neighborhood (cites GDPval + HealthBench, cited by RLI/UpBench/PRBench) is the economic-rehearsal cluster. The rubric-as-unit-tests grading imports HealthBench's physician-rubric method across occupations.

title: HEAD-QA: A Healthcare Dataset for Complex Reasoning
human_time: ~1-3 min per multiple-choice item at typical professional-licensing-exam pace (4-5 answer options); real exam-takers spend a year or more preparing beforehand, which is study time, not per-item solve time.
frontier_score: Best 2019 baseline (cross-lingual English IR) 34.6% avg accuracy (unsupervised) / 37.2% (test split) - below the official pass mark in every one of six subject areas; 10-best-human POINTS average far exceeds the model in all six.
one_line: 6,765 real Spanish healthcare-specialization licensing exam questions (medicine, nursing, pharmacology, psychology, biology, chemistry), in Spanish plus a machine-translated English version; the best 2019 baseline misses the real pass mark in every subject.
notes: Kingdom placement (D2 vs A2) is a judgment call: unlike MMLU/AGIEval's broad multi-domain sweep (which stay A2-knowledge-exams), HEAD-QA is 100% one occupational vertical (a real government healthcare-licensing exam battery), so the 'occupational content beats skill framing' tie-break used for LexGLUE/MAUD/Med-PaLM was applied here too. Saturation 'closing' is inferred from general knowledge that frontier LLMs now handle graduate-level professional MC exams well, not from a number in the explainer - the paper predates the audit era entirely.
placement_reason: A real professional-licensing exam battery (Spain's MIR/EIR/FIR/PIR/BIR/QIR) scraped wholesale and scored with the exam's own POINTS rule, gating entry to specific hospital jobs - occupational credentialing content, not a broad multi-subject knowledge sweep (contrast MMLU/AGIEval, which stay A2 for spanning many unrelated fields); the D2 tie-break (occupational content over skill framing) places single-vertical professional exams here, alongside Med-PaLM's MedQA-style precedent.

title: Building a Question Answering Test Collection
human_time: ~10-30s per candidate answer string for a human assessor to judge correct/incorrect; the paper doesn't state a figure.
frontier_score: Best 1999 run (50-byte) MRR .660, 250-byte MRR .646, 73% found-rate on the best run; no post-1999 scores are quoted.
one_line: The founding QA-benchmark methodology study: 200 fact questions, three independent assessors, MRR scoring — stable system rankings despite ~6% judgment disagreement.
notes: Grading is fundamentally human relevance judgment of each answer string (no fixed answer key drives the primary scoring) reduced to MRR; the paper's own pattern-matching answer-key experiment is a secondary reusability attempt, not the primary evaluation — hence grading_primary='human' rather than 'exact-match'. Saturation judged from own knowledge (simple factoid recall of this style is trivial for modern LLMs); the explainer quotes no post-1999 scores.
placement_reason: The founding QA-as-benchmark artifact: 200 closed-class fact questions scored by MRR over a ranked [doc-id, answer-string] list is a straightforward capability probe (can 1999 IR/IE systems find and rank correct short answers?), the same retrieve-and-answer construct A1's other QA members (SQuAD, TriviaQA) share. Not G3-grader-benchmarks: the paper studies whether *human* relevance-judging methodology transfers to QA, not whether an AI judge/grader can be trusted — no model or system is ever cast as the grader here, three NIST assessors are.

title: BridgeData V2: A Dataset for Robot Learning at Scale
human_time: One pick-and-place-style manipulation trial, judged success/fail by a human observer in well under a minute; each reported cell averages 10-20 such trials.
frontier_score: RT-1 leads language-conditioned unseen tasks (0.50 avg over 6 unseen); GCBC leads image-goal seen tasks (0.49); LCBC (language-only, no RT-1 extras) is the weakest, 0.08 unseen (zero on 4 of 6 tasks); zero-shot transfer to a second lab drops the 6-method aggregate from 0.215 to 0.165.
one_line: 60,096-trajectory real-robot manipulation corpus (84% human-teleoperated/16% scripted) collected on a $4,000 publicly-reproducible WidowX rig, with an 8-seen/6-unseen evaluation task suite that six structurally different offline-learning methods must be trained on this same data before being scored against.
notes: Placed in F1 (reward-factories) rather than A5 (embodied-operation) because, unlike A5's members (all pretrained-agent-vs-fixed-task-suite benchmarks — Mind2Web, WebArena, OSWorld), every one of BridgeData V2's six evaluated methods must first be TRAINED from scratch on the shipped 60k-trajectory corpus before it can be scored — the AlpacaFarm/MLGym pattern (train-on-the-shipped-resource, then measure), not a zero-shot capability probe. domain_primary has no dedicated robotics bucket in the closed vocabulary; 'multimodal' (vision-conditioned control) is the closest fit, with 'agentic-web' as secondary for the operate-an-environment flavor. items_count=14 reflects the eval task suite (8 seen + 6 unseen), following the MLGym precedent of counting the shipped eval tasks rather than the training-corpus scale. grading_primary='human' because success/fail is judged by a human observer per real-robot trial, with zero reported error bars across every 10-20-trial cell (an explicit critique in the explainer).
placement_reason: The title and framing are dataset-first ('A Dataset for Robot Learning at Scale'), and its six evaluated offline-learning methods must all be trained on this exact corpus before being scored — unlike A5's plug-in-a-pretrained-agent pattern, here training on the shipped data is the mechanism that produces a scoreable policy at all, matching F1's 'generators/sandboxes meant to be trained on' definition (cf. AlpacaFarm, MLGym).

title: A Dataset for Research on Short-Text Conversations
human_time: Seconds per pair: read a short Weibo post and a candidate reply, judge suitability on 3 criteria.
frontier_score: Best 2013 config (P2R+P2P+MATCH) MAP 0.621 / P@1 0.574, rising to P@1 0.81 when the system is restricted to the most-confident 25% of posts.
one_line: 628,833 naturally-occurring Weibo (post, response) pairs with a pooled, human-judged evaluation subset — the first at-scale short-text-conversation dataset.
notes: Saturation is uncertain — the paper reports only its own 2013 baselines (MAP 0.621) with a real ceiling well below 1.0, and no later re-evaluation is discussed in the explainer, so 'open' is a default rather than an evidenced call. grading_primary=proxy-metric reflects that MAP/P@1 are IR-style ranking proxies computed over a human-labeled candidate pool.
placement_reason: Built to make retrieval-based, single-round social-media response selection trainable and testable at scale — a communication-skill capability probe (pick a natural, relevant, human-like reply), matching A7's verb list ('follow instructions, converse, clarify') and its existing conversation-domain members. Not F1: the paper's own validation model (a two-stage matching-then-RankSVM baseline) is built to demonstrate the dataset is usable for training and testing, but the framing throughout is an evaluation benchmark (MAP/P@1 scored against a pooled, human-labeled candidate set), not a training-signal generator with unlimited/procedural instances the way F1's exemplars are.

title: GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding
human_time: Seconds to ~1 min per item — single-sentence or sentence-pair classification judgments (acceptability, sentiment, paraphrase, NLI).
frontier_score: BERT-class models pushed past the human baseline (~87) within a year; best 2018 baseline (BiLSTM+Attn+ELMo multi-task) 70.0
one_line: Nine recycled English NLU classification tasks macro-averaged into one leaderboard score, with private test labels on four tasks.
notes: Grading folded to exact-match: STS-B is scored by Pearson/Spearman correlation and CoLA by Matthews correlation, which are aggregate classification/regression statistics rather than overlap proxies. Test-set item count not stated in the text. The ~550-pair expert-authored diagnostic is a secondary artifact within an otherwise aggregated benchmark.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can one model do general language understanding across tasks?' — nine recycled NLU tasks (entailment, paraphrase, acceptability) collapsed into one model-agnostic leaderboard; the gap it fills is siloed per-dataset NLU evaluation, a classic parse/entail capability probe (the taxonomy's own A1 exemplar).

title: Benchmarking Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
group: University of Toronto / Vector Institute / UC Berkeley
human_time: Not reported - this is a classic continuous-control RL benchmark (18 OpenAI-Gym physics environments), not a human-solvable item; episodes run hundreds of thousands of simulator steps of agent training, with no human baseline anywhere in the paper.
frontier_score: No single best algorithm across 18 environments (Table 5); best mean/median rank tie: PETS-CEM & SLBO (4.0/10 mean), SLBO best median (3.5/10); model-free SAC/TD3 keep climbing past 200k steps while nearly all learned-dynamics MBRL methods plateau below them at 1M steps (Hopper's SLBO is the one exception)
one_line: 18 continuous-control OpenAI-Gym environments and one shared training/eval protocol comparing 11 model-based RL algorithms against 4 model-free baselines, isolating three named failure modes (dynamics bottleneck, planning-horizon dilemma, early-termination dilemma).
notes: SCHEMA GAP: this and four sibling papers in this batch (PHYRE, bsuite, RLBench, Meta-World) are classic 2019-era deep-RL/robotics benchmarks with no good home in BENCH_DOMAINS (no control/robotics/continuous-control category exists) - domain_primary 'reasoning' is a forced least-bad fit here, not a genuine claim that this is a reasoning benchmark. Flagged for the survey author/critic's attention; see also the batch report's note on whether these five predate the survey's own 'LLM & agent benchmarks' scope. items_count is the environment count, not a question/item count. grading_primary 'programmatic' reflects automated cumulative-reward/simulator scoring, matching the convention used for other interactive-env benchmarks.
placement_reason: Explicitly benchmarks whether model-based RL agents can operate 18 simulated continuous-control physics environments as capably as model-free rivals under one shared protocol - an operate-the-environment capability probe (task_shape=interactive-env); A5 is the closest family fit even though its other members are web/computer-use agents rather than physical control, since no domain/family combination in this taxonomy was built around classic robotics/control RL (a vocabulary gap, not a confident placement).

title: SuperGLUE: A Stickier Benchmark for General-Purpose Language Understanding Systems
human_time: Under a minute per item — short-passage QA/NLI/coreference/WSD designed to be solvable by college-educated non-experts (MTurk human baseline protocol).
frontier_score: T5-11B scored 88.9 within a year vs the 89.8 human estimate; models soon passed the human baseline outright (BERT++ launch baseline 71.5)
one_line: GLUE's harder sequel: eight difficulty-screened NLU tasks (QA, coreference, WSD) with crowd human baselines and a held-out test server.
notes: reasoning secondary for COPA causal reasoning and WSC/ReCoRD commonsense. Total test-item count not stated (per-task sizes range 146 to ~10k). Aggregated: all eight tasks recycle pre-existing public datasets chosen via open call.
placement_reason: Built explicitly because BERT/XLNet pushed GLUE past its human baseline within a year — same construct (multi-task NLU macro-average), rebuilt with difficulty-screened tasks to restore headroom; the taxonomy's canonical B3 case (SuperGLUE vs GLUE).

title: A Large-Scale Chinese Short-Text Conversation Dataset
human_time: Seconds per turn: rate one short (avg ~7-8 word) open-domain Weibo-style chit-chat response for fluency/relevance/informativeness on a 0-2 scale.
frontier_score: CDialGPT_LCCC-large: best PPL (18.23) and best human score (1.217/2) among 7 systems fine-tuned and evaluated on STC, but worse BLEU-2 than a plain non-pretrained Transformer baseline
one_line: A 6.8M/12.0M-dialogue cleaned Chinese Weibo pretraining corpus (two release tiers) plus four GPT-style checkpoints, validated by fine-tuning on the older STC benchmark rather than a novel held-out eval.
notes: Likely mis-tagged for this survey: LCCC's primary, novel contribution is a pretraining CORPUS (79M raw -> 6.8M/12.0M cleaned dialogues) plus released model checkpoints, not a new evaluation artifact — its only 'eval' is fine-tuning every checkpoint on STC (an existing 2013 corpus this paper doesn't introduce) and scoring with BLEU/human rating. Classified here as the closest-fitting capability construct (open-domain Chinese dialogue generation quality) rather than excluded, since the batch requires a record for every tagged paper; flagging for survey-owner review. items_count uses LCCC-base's 6.8M dialogue count as the representative release size. Saturation 'not-applicable': no fixed ceiling metric, evaluated entirely on the noisy corpus (STC) it was built to replace.
placement_reason: Insofar as it functions as a benchmark at all, LCCC's fine-tune-on-STC-and-rate protocol tests general open-domain Chinese chit-chat generation quality (fluency/relevance/informativeness) — a conversational-capability construct (A7), not an occupational one; but the paper's real contribution is the pretraining corpus itself, which is why this placement is lower-confidence than the rest of this batch.

title: MAUD: An Expert-Annotated Legal NLP Dataset for Merger Agreement Understanding
human_time: ~2-10 min per item for a trained M&A attorney to read a deal-point clause (half exceed 512 tokens; MAE clauses much longer) and answer the ABA-standardized multiple-choice question; estimated from task descriptions and the 10,000-hour/$500-per-hour annotation effort.
frontier_score: BigBird-base 57.8% overall AUPR (best single-task encoder baseline) vs 16.8% random; hardest categories near 48-51%
one_line: Expert-annotated legal reading comprehension: 144 ABA-standardized multiple-choice questions over deal points in 152 real merger agreements.
notes: Provenance is borderline: clause texts are mined from real EDGAR merger agreements and questions derive from the ABA's existing deal-point study, but the defining effort is 10,000+ hours of recruited expert annotation, so expert-authored over real-work-mined. items_count is the derived test split (~20% of the 35,551 main+abridged examples), not stated verbatim. Headline metric is minority-class AUPR over classifier scores, folded to exact-match (MC classification). Saturation judged from 2023 encoder baselines only — no frontier LLM was evaluated.
placement_reason: Expert-annotated M&A contract-review benchmark ($5M of lawyer time, ABA deal-point questions) probing the interpretive judgment M&A attorneys are paid for — occupational law/contracts content beats its 'can models read legal prose' skill framing per the tie-break ladder.

title: CMB: A Comprehensive Medical Benchmark in Chinese
group: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
human_time: ~1-2 min per licensing-exam MC question (CMB-Exam); several minutes per multi-turn clinical-case consult round (CMB-Clin).
frontier_score: HuatuoGPT-II-34B leads CMB-Exam at 76.82% (Qwen-72B-Chat 74.38%, GPT-4 59.46% answer-only/60.22% 3-shot); on CMB-Clin (GPT-4-judge, 1-5 scale), Yi-34B ties GPT-4 at 4.67, but every other domestic general model trails ChatGPT (4.53).
one_line: A two-part Chinese medical benchmark: CMB-Exam (11,200-question licensing-exam test set spanning physicians/nurses/technicians/pharmacists, incl. Traditional Chinese Medicine) and CMB-Clin (208 multi-turn diagnostic questions from 74 real clinical cases), the latter scored by a GPT-4 judge validated against 320 expert-scored responses (Spearman 0.93).
notes: task_shape and grading_primary reflect the paper's dual instrument: CMB-Exam (11,200 items, single-turn, exact-match) dominates by volume but CMB-Clin's multi-turn clinical dialogue is the paper's stated methodological differentiator ('use both CMB-Exam and CMB-Clin'), so task_shape is coded multi-turn to capture that novel half. items_count=11,408 sums the CMB-Exam test set (11,200) and CMB-Clin (208); most of the taxonomy's single-instrument medical benchmarks (e.g. Med-PaLM) report only one component's count.
placement_reason: Explicit occupational-coverage complaint (pharmacist-only prior sets say nothing about nurses/technicians) plus a measured cultural-localization argument (TCM's zero-keyword-overlap with MedQA-USMLE) — the object is deployment-readiness across China's actual medical licensing structure, pairing a knowledge exam with a multi-turn clinical-case component the way HealthBench pairs USMLE-style recall with realistic conversation (D2's HealthBench-precursor role). Not A2: MC knowledge testing is explicitly one half of a two-instrument design built to go past exam recall into applied clinical dialogue.

title: GTA: A Benchmark for General Tool Agents
human_time: Tasks need 2-4 solution steps across 14 real deployed tools (OCR, calculator, image tools, search); a person using the same tools by hand needs a few minutes per task.
frontier_score: End-to-end AnsAcc tops out at 46.59% (GPT-4-1106-Preview) and 41.52% (GPT-4o); the other 14 of 16 tested models all score below 25%
one_line: 229 human-written, tool-implicit tasks over 14 real deployed tools and authentic multimodal inputs, scored both step-by-step (diagnostic) and end-to-end (the agent actually calls the tools) -- the only prior-work comparison table with every property checked.
notes: 252 images, 557 total tool calls, mostly 2-3 tools per task. AnsAcc uses whitelist/blacklist term matching for objective queries and best-cosine-similarity against 3 references for subjective ones (proxy-metric); step-by-step InstAcc/ToolAcc/ArgAcc/SummAcc and end-to-end tool-selection F1 are programmatic.
placement_reason: The named gap is queries that never name a tool (unlike ToolBench/m&m's AI-generated queries that hand over the tool list up front), scored against a real, deployed 14-tool platform with human-annotated ground-truth chains -- a tool-selection-and-sequencing capability probe, A6's mandate, distinguished from A8 by task grain (discrete tool calls to a fixed platform, not an open-ended research workflow) and from G3 by object (agent tool-use skill, not a judge/grader protocol).

title: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark
human_time: ~1-10 min per item — ten-option exam questions where the added STEM material (stemez/TheoremQA/SciBench) demands multi-step CoT derivations rather than recall.
frontier_score: GPT-4o 72.6% overall (best at launch, vs ~88.7% on MMLU); reasoning models (o1, R1) already climbing it by 2025
one_line: The reasoning-era rebuild of MMLU: 12,032 ten-option questions across 14 domains, filtered for difficulty and expert-reviewed twice.
notes: Aggregated: 56.6% reworked MMLU plus STEM-website/TheoremQA/SciBench items, with GPT-4-Turbo-authored distractors under expert review (synthetic-generated is only the distractor pool, not the stems). Fully public and 56.6% derived from the most-leaked benchmark ever, so none-public despite the expert cleanup.
placement_reason: MMLU had flatlined at 86-87% for every frontier model; MMLU-Pro rebuilds the same construct (broad multi-task MC knowledge exam) with 10 options, easy-item filtering and harder STEM material to restore discriminative headroom — the taxonomy's named B3 case (MMLU-Pro vs MMLU).

title: EnigmaEval: A Benchmark of Long Multimodal Reasoning Challenges
human_time: Typical Normal puzzle ~15-60 min (88% are PuzzledPint, whose guideline is an inexperienced team finishing the whole event under 2 hours); Hard puzzles take experienced teams hours to days, i.e. L3+.
frontier_score: o1 solves 7.0% of Normal and 0.0% of Hard; all nine models score 0% on Hard, next-best (Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking) 1.4%
one_line: 1,184 instruction-free multimodal puzzle-hunt problems requiring lateral, cross-domain inference, graded by exact string match.
notes: Complexity is bimodal: Normal (949 items, dominated by beginner PuzzledPint) is L2-minutes, Hard (235) is L3-hours-plus; classified by the typical instance. Contamination defense combines a private unreleased set with continuous updates — live-refresh is the strongest mechanism; private-holdout also applies. exam-derived: items come from existing real puzzle-hunt competitions.
placement_reason: Framed as joining HLE in 'a new class of deliberately unsaturated benchmark' — puzzle-hunt problems where the best model scores 7%/0%, kept private and continuously refreshed; durable headroom at the frontier is the explicit design goal (a named C1 exemplar).

title: MultiFileTest: A Multi-File-Level LLM Unit Test Generation Benchmark and Impact of Error Fixing Mechanisms
human_time: ~1-4 hours for a competent developer to write a runnable, high-coverage unit-test suite for a 2-15-file, <1,600-LOC project.
frontier_score: Gemini-3.0-Pro 77% vanilla correctness on Python (90 after manual fixing); GPT-o1 87% on JavaScript; Java hardest with several 7B models at 0
one_line: Unit-test generation over 60 whole multi-file Python/Java/JS projects, scored by real execution, with a vanilla vs error-fixed comparison.
notes: Task shape: headline (vanilla) scenario is one-shot generation with execution only for grading, so single-turn; the self-fixing scenario adds one execution-feedback round, edging toward interactive-env but not the primary protocol. Human manual fixing is an intervention scenario, not a grading mechanism. Saturation 'closing' judged on best vanilla correctness (62-87% by language).
placement_reason: Asks 'can models write runnable unit tests for whole multi-file projects?' — the gap is that HumanEval/ClassEval/TestGenEval grade test-gen on single functions/files; headline is model skill at cross-file code understanding and test writing (the error-fixing study is a diagnostic within the skill probe, not the object).

title: Long-form factuality in large language models
human_time: Minutes to draft a long-form factual answer to one prompt; grading a single response against Google Search cost SAFE $0.19 versus $4.00 for a human annotator.
frontier_score: GPT-4-Turbo leads at F1@64=95.0%, F1@178=66.4%; SAFE agrees with humans 72.0% of the time, wins 76% of adjudicated disagreements
one_line: 2,280 GPT-4-generated long-form fact-seeking prompts, graded by SAFE (an LLM search agent decomposing responses into atomic, search-verified facts) via a precision/recall F1@K metric.
notes: grading_primary llm-judge reflects SAFE's per-fact verdicts (a search-augmented LLM agent); F1@K is the aggregate proxy-metric built on top of those verdicts. Only 250 of the 2,280 LongFact-Objects prompts are actually run in the 13-model benchmark study.
placement_reason: FActScore's direct generalization: the same atomic-fact-decomposition grading idea, broadened from single-domain biographies to 38 broad topics and upgraded from a fixed knowledge source to live search. Its central contribution (SAFE, F1@K) is a grading protocol for open-ended long-form generation — the G3 case FActScore itself already establishes — not a new capability probe: the 13-model leaderboard is downstream evidence the grader works, not the paper's organizing question.

title: Measuring short-form factuality in large language models
human_time: Seconds to under a minute per item: one short single-answer fact question (lookup-style long-tail trivia).
frontier_score: o1-preview 42.7% correct (F-score 44.8); GPT-4o 38.2%, all frontier models under 50%
one_line: 4,326 short single-answer fact questions, adversarially filtered to stump GPT-4-class models, scoring abstention as a first-class outcome.
notes: Grading is a prompted ChatGPT equivalence check against a short gold string — coded exact-match primary with llm-judge in grading_all. Hired OpenAI AI trainers coded as expert-authored rather than crowdsourced.
placement_reason: The gap section is explicit: TriviaQA and Natural Questions are 'saturated — too easy for frontier models to be discriminative', and SimpleQA rebuilds the same short-form factual-QA construct adversarially (every question stumps at least one GPT-4-class model) to restore headroom. The calibration/abstention framing adds a B4 flavor, but the stated reason for building is de-saturation of the short-form factuality construct.

title: BrowseComp: A Simple Yet Challenging Benchmark for Browsing Agents
human_time: Human trainers solved only 29.2% within a 2-hour cap and gave up on 70.8%; solved items often took 2-3 hours — hours per question.
frontier_score: Deep Research 51.5% (best-of-64 confidence voting ~78%); GPT-4o 0.6%, o1 9.9%
one_line: 1,266 inverted-fact questions — trivial to verify, brutal to find — probing persistent web-browsing agents.
notes: Coded interactive-env/browser for the intended browsing-agent setting, though non-browsing baselines were also run (they score ~0-10%). Short-string LLM equivalence grading (HLE prompt) coded exact-match primary + llm-judge. 51.5% single-sample keeps it open; best-of-N ~78% is a nonstandard protocol.
placement_reason: The defining C2 exemplar: inverted questions engineered so the answer is a trivially verifiable short string but agonizingly hard to locate — vetted to stump GPT-4o/o1/early Deep Research, resist five Google searches, and defeat the human trainers themselves (70.8% gave up after two hours). Durable difficulty via the find/verify asymmetry is the explicit design goal, built because HotpotQA/TriviaQA-style 'findable' QA had saturated.

title: FollowIR: Evaluating and Teaching Information Retrieval Models to Follow Instructions
human_time: Minutes per query for a professional TREC assessor to apply a detailed narrative's inclusion/exclusion criteria to a candidate document; these are the same narratives written for real relevance judging.
frontier_score: Most retrieval/embedding models score ≤0 avg p-MRR; FollowIR-7B (fine-tuned Mistral-7B-Instruct) reaches +12.2 avg p-MRR, the highest in Table 2
one_line: 102 TREC queries (Robust04/Core17/News21) with deliberately altered professional-assessor narratives, scored via a new pairwise instruction-sensitivity metric (p-MRR).
notes: grading_primary proxy-metric reflects p-MRR (a custom rank-change score), the paper's actual novel instrument; standard MAP/nDCG (programmatic) is also reported per query but isn't the paper's contribution.
placement_reason: Tests whether a retrieval model actually changes its rankings when a TREC-grade narrative instruction is deliberately altered — an instruction-following capability probe for IR, the same construct IFEval/AdvancedIF test for chat models, just applied to rerankers — not a construct audit of an existing IR benchmark's relevance labels: FollowIR's alterations and re-annotations are new data built to answer a new question, not a re-measurement of TREC's own validity.

title: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Limited LLM Benchmark
human_time: Not stated.
frontier_score: o1-preview (top model at release): 64.7%
one_line: A monthly-refreshed, 18-task LLM benchmark spanning math, coding, reasoning, data analysis, instruction following, and language comprehension, scored entirely by objective ground truth rather than an LLM judge.
notes: Direct multi-domain generalization of LiveCodeBench's live-refresh, contamination-resistant design to six categories at once.
placement_reason: LiveCodeBench proved a monthly-refreshed, exam-derived question stream keeps a coding benchmark contamination-free; LiveBench is the same living-wall design generalized across six task categories at once.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating Frontier AI R&D Capabilities of Language Model Agents against Human Experts
human_time: 61 human ML experts across 71 runs, matched to 8-hour agent budgets, with some human runs extended to 32 hours
frontier_score: Agents score ~4x humans at a 2-hour budget, but plateau; humans reach ~2x the best agent's score by 32 hours
one_line: METR's benchmark pitting frontier AI agents against 61 real ML experts on 7 hand-crafted AI-research-engineering tasks under matched time budgets — agents win early but plateau while humans keep improving.
notes: Time-horizon plateau finding directly informs kwa-2025-time-horizons' cross-model trend analysis.
placement_reason: The human-anchored peer of MLAgentBench/MLE-bench: instead of scoring agents against a fixed leaderboard, it runs matched-budget agent-vs-expert trials on real ML R&D tasks to measure where agents' time-scaling curve diverges from humans'.

title: A Broad-Coverage Challenge Corpus for Sentence Understanding through Inference
human_time: Seconds per premise-hypothesis pair — crowdworkers label 3-way entailment in well under a minute.
frontier_score: BERT hit 86.7% within a year; later models low-90s — SuperGLUE retired it as near-solved (human agreement ~88.7%)
one_line: 433k premise-hypothesis NLI pairs across ten genres with a matched-vs-mismatched split testing cross-genre generalization.
notes: Test labels withheld on Kaggle → private-holdout, though the premises come from public corpora. items_count is the 20k test set (plus 20k dev; 433k pairs total including train).
placement_reason: Born as the harder, broader successor to SNLI: the gap names 'no headroom — the best models were already within a few points of human accuracy' and single-genre narrowness as the two limits, and rebuilds the identical three-way NLI construct across ten genres to restore ~15 points of headroom (ESIM 86.7 on SNLI falls to 72.3). Exactly the SuperGLUE-vs-GLUE de-saturation pattern, one generation earlier.

title: Sequential Matching Network: A New Architecture for Multi-turn Response Selection in Retrieval-Based Chatbots
human_time: Seconds per candidate: read a short multi-turn chat context and judge whether one candidate response fits.
frontier_score: SMN's best variant: Ubuntu R10@1 0.726, Douban P@1 0.397 / R10@1 0.236, vs. the best 2017 baseline (Multi-View/Multi-Channel) at 0.662 / 0.349 / 0.203.
one_line: Multi-turn response-selection architecture (match-then-accumulate) plus the Douban Conversation Corpus, the first human-labeled multi-turn retrieval benchmark.
notes: Saturation ('open') is a default rather than a directly evidenced call — the explainer's own critique notes BERT-based rerankers later outperformed SMN by a wide margin, but doesn't quote a specific post-2017 frontier score on Ubuntu/Douban. Borderline tagging call: SMN's title-level contribution is the architecture, with the Douban Conversation Corpus as a co-released, explicitly named first-class benchmark ('the first human-labeled multi-turn response-selection dataset') that went on to become one of the field's two standard multi-turn benchmarks — judged in scope per the survey's 'benchmark is a first-class named contribution' rule.
placement_reason: A multi-turn response-selection capability probe — pick the response that fits an entire conversation history, not just the last turn — matching A7's communication definition; the Douban Conversation Corpus it co-releases is explicitly positioned as filling a real-data, human-labeled gap in exactly this skill (the paper's own gap section: no public human-labeled multi-turn dataset existed to test a realistic retrieval-candidate setting).

title: Human Preference Score v2: A Solid Benchmark for Evaluating Human Preferences of Text-to-Image Synthesis
human_time: Ranking multiple generated images per prompt across 4 style categories; a few minutes per prompt-group for a trained contract annotator.
frontier_score: HPS v2: 65.7% (ImageReward's external test) / 83.3% (HPD v2 test) preference-prediction accuracy, ahead of PickScore/ImageReward/HPS v1/Aesthetic/CLIP (2023); community Stable-Diffusion fine-tunes top the 20-model Table 7 leaderboard, ahead of official SD releases
one_line: A CLIP-based scorer fine-tuned on 798,090 professionally-annotated preference comparisons across 9 held-out-tested generator families (5 unseen in training), shipped as a static 20-model/4-style-set benchmark table.
notes: Third of a genuinely three-way judgment call (F1 vs. G2 vs. G3) across the T2I reward-model trio in this batch. Placed in G3 (not F1, since no generator-weight training is demonstrated in this paper; not G2, since it's a fixed, one-time-collected dataset and static leaderboard, not an ever-growing live platform like Pick-a-Pic) - matches the FActScore/TIFA 'build + validate an automated scorer, ship a benchmark table' pattern most closely. items_count = 3,200 prompts (Table 7's actual 20-model benchmark: 4 style sets x 800 prompts), not the larger 798,090-comparison HPD v2 training/test dataset.
placement_reason: The contribution is a WAY of grading text-to-image quality: a CLIP-based scorer fine-tuned on 798,090 professionally-annotated preference comparisons spanning 9 generator families (4 in training, 5 held out to test cross-generator generalization), validated against human agreement and an external test set (ImageReward's own), then shipped as a static 20-model/4-style-set benchmark table - the FActScore/TIFA pattern, not a live, ever-growing preference PLATFORM (Pick-a-Pic, G2) or a reward signal demonstrated for training a generator's weights (ImageReward's ReFL, F1).

title: SmartPlay: A Benchmark for LLMs as Intelligent Agents
human_time: A single playthrough of one game — from a few rounds of Bandits/RPS to a full up-to-10,000-step Crafter episode; the paper's own human baseline is just 3 players, unevenly sampled (3 rounds on easy games, 1 round on hard ones).
frontier_score: Best model (GPT-4 variants) trails the human baseline by roughly 10 points on 3-Disk Hanoi (0.90), ~40 on Minecraft (0.61, tied with llama-2-13b), and ~70 on Crafter (0.32); vicuna-13b scores below its own untuned base (llama-13b) on 6 of 7 settings.
one_line: Six games (Bandits, Rock Paper Scissors, Tower of Hanoi, Messenger, Crafter, Minecraft creative-navigation) behind one Gym-style text API, scored against 9 named agent capabilities via a degree-weighted radar, normalized to a small (n=3) human baseline.
notes: items_count=20 reflects the paper's stated 'up to 20 distinct evaluation settings' across the 6 games; the quantitative Table 2 run only covers 7 of them. contamination_defense='procedural' reflects that 3 of 6 games (Crafter, Minecraft, Messenger) are procedurally generated, which the paper argues (with one concrete Hanoi memorization-boundary anecdote, not a systematic check) resists memorization — not a formal shipped defense mechanism. The explainer flags a formula bug in the paper's own printed normalization equation (the appendix formula's sign is inverted relative to what actually reproduces Table 2) — doesn't affect classification.
placement_reason: Ships a real evaluation apparatus — a human-normalized score plus a degree-weighted 9-capability radar (planning, spatial reasoning, learning-from-interaction, etc.) built explicitly to diagnose *why* an agent fails, not just whether — across six turn-by-turn interactive game environments behind one unified Gym-style text API. Matches ALE's precedent in the same family: a proposed evaluation methodology, not merely a trainable environment (contrast OpenAI Gym in F1).

title: FlowBench: Revisiting and Benchmarking Workflow-Guided Planning for LLM-based Agents
human_time: One multi-turn business-workflow session (e.g. book a flight, handle a failed reservation); a trained customer-service agent following the same written procedure needs a few minutes per session.
frontier_score: GPT-4o's best configuration reaches 43.2% single-scenario / 40.9% cross-scenario session-level success rate; every model does better with some workflow knowledge (any format) than none
one_line: Hands an LLM agent the identical business workflow three ways -- prose, pseudocode, Mermaid flowchart -- across 51 scenarios in 6 domains, isolating which knowledge representation actually helps planning rather than each system inventing its own format.
notes: items_count=51 scenarios (22 roles, 6 domains); the paper doesn't report a single total session count. Static turn-level grading (tool-invocation/parameter F1) is programmatic; session-level success/response-preference scoring uses a GPT-4-based user simulator and a GPT-4 judge (llm-judge).
placement_reason: Isolates the one variable prior work never isolated -- hold the task and underlying procedure fixed, vary only whether workflow knowledge is given as text, code, or flowchart -- and measures tool-invocation precision/recall/F1 at both static and simulated-session granularity across 6 business domains; a tool-sequencing capability probe (A6, tau-bench's own family), not a hazard or grader-audit paper.

title: PIXIU: A Large Language Model, Instruction Data and Evaluation Benchmark for Finance
group: Wuhan U. / U. Florida / ChanceFocus AMC
human_time: A few minutes per financial NLP item (sentiment/NER/headline) or QA question for a financial analyst; stock-movement items require domain judgment despite a quick factual-lookup surface.
frontier_score: FinMA-30B: 0.88 F1 FPB sentiment (best), but FinQA EM only 0.06-0.11 (GPT-4 0.63); stock movement prediction MCC ~0.00-0.04 for every model tested, indistinguishable from chance (2023)
one_line: The first open financial-LLM stack: FIT (136K instructions), FinMA (LLaMA fine-tuned on it), and FLARE (a benchmark pairing financial NLP with financial prediction) - every model tested is near chance at stock-movement prediction.
notes: items_count left null: FLARE's own per-dataset eval-set sizes aren't summed to one total in the explainer, and the paper's arXiv preprint (5 tasks/9 datasets/136K FIT samples) and NeurIPS camera-ready (8 tasks/15 datasets/128K samples) describe different final scope, per the critique's own version note. saturation judged 'open' from the paper's own most-emphasized, most 'real-world' task (stock movement prediction), which is unsolved by every model including the benchmark's own fine-tuned FinMA, despite several financial-NLP sub-tasks (sentiment, headline) being much closer to ceiling.
placement_reason: The first open financial-LLM stack: FIT (instruction data) + FinMA (fine-tuned model) + FLARE (the benchmark pairing financial NLP with financial PREDICTION, e.g. stock movement) - explicitly built because prior financial benchmarks like FLUE 'don't include financial prediction tasks... critical for evaluating the model's performance applied to real-world scenarios'; occupational-domain competence (can a model do an analyst's actual predictive job) is the design core, matching FinQA/FinanceBench's D2 family, which FLARE explicitly extends (FinBen builds directly on it).

title: FinBen: A Holistic Financial Benchmark for Large Language Models
human_time: Typical item is a short financial classification/extraction (seconds) up to numeric QA over filings (a few minutes); the trading-agent episodes run much longer but are a small subset.
frontier_score: GPT-4 leads (FinQA EM 0.63, ConvFinQA 0.76; trading Sharpe 1.51) but forecasting MCC ~0 and many tasks score 0.00
one_line: 36-dataset, 24-task financial suite spanning extraction to forecasting, plus the first agent-graded stock-trading eval.
notes: Heterogeneous multi-task suite: grading spans F1/EM/MCC (exact-match), ROUGE/BERTScore (proxy), and simulator-scored trading returns (programmatic); most tasks are pure zero-shot text but the RAG and FinMem trading-agent subsets add retrieval/agent tooling, reflected in tool_access. Test sets are 100-4,000 items each across 36 datasets; total not stated.
placement_reason: A professional-finance competence suite: 36 datasets over the seven things 'financial LLMs are asked to do' — extraction, sentiment, numeric QA, risk management, forecasting, and agent-graded stock trading scored in money metrics (Sharpe, drawdown). Occupational content is the whole design ('measuring the actual job', not the easy 20%); the holistic-taxonomy shape gives a G1 pull, but domain-occupational competence beats framing per the ladder, and trading-for-profit is deployment-realism, not aggregation.

title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
human_time: Median human completion 111.94 s per task; the hard tier is >180 s — a few minutes each.
frontier_score: best 2024 agent (GPT-4 + a11y tree) 12.24% vs human 72.36%; screenshot-only ~5%
one_line: VM-backed real-computer environment: 369 execution-graded OS/app/multi-app tasks with per-task end-state checks.
