notes: Task ideas mined from public tutorials/forums but configs and 134 eval scripts authored by the team → expert-authored. No shipped defense (none-public), though execution grading on a fresh VM inherently resists answer memorization.
placement_reason: The family's namesake style: the contribution is the ENVIRONMENT — a VM-backed real OS with 369 execution-graded tasks over a raw keyboard/mouse action space, built because static demonstration sets (Mind2Web) can't grade alternative solutions and executable environments (WebShop/WebArena) were boxed into the web. Headline is skill: can agents operate a real computer yet (humans 72.36% vs best agent 12.24%, grounding is the wall).

title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine
human_time: A minute or so per question: a zero-shot medical MCQ/yes-no answered with up to 32 retrieved snippets; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4+MedRAG 79.97% avg (up from 73.44% CoT-only); GPT-3.5+MedRAG 71.57% (+17.9% relative over CoT)
one_line: 7,663 zero-shot, question-only-retrieval medical QA questions from five source datasets, paired with a 5-corpus x 4-retriever x 6-LLM MedRAG toolkit.
notes: tool_access is search-retrieval since MedRAG's whole point is retrieval augmentation; the model receives retrieved snippets rather than browsing live, matching the BEIR precedent's tool_access convention.
placement_reason: Builds the first medical RAG stress test combining zero-shot, multiple-choice, retrieval-augmented, and question-only-retrieval conditions at once — testing whether retrieval genuinely helps real clinical/biomedical question-answering, the professional-deployment rehearsal this taxonomy's LegalBench-RAG precedent already establishes as the D2 pattern for RAG evaluation, not a raw A2 exam-recall probe: no model is ever scored on knowledge alone without the RAG apparatus being the point.

title: CLUE: A Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation Benchmark
human_time: Seconds to a couple minutes per item across nine short classification/similarity/MRC tasks; two-stage human annotation (practice + majority-of-3) set the human row on five of nine tasks.
frontier_score: Best 2020 baseline RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large Avg 74.90 vs. human Avg 85.09 (widest gap on C3, 22.72 pts); modern Chinese LLMs far exceed this fine-tuning-era ceiling
one_line: The GLUE-for-Chinese: nine NLU tasks (classification/similarity/MRC), a 214GB pre-training corpus, and a 514-item linguistic diagnostic set, explicitly modeled on GLUE/SuperGLUE.
notes: items_count is the approximate sum of the nine tasks' test splits (~54.6K); the suite's own headline Avg score blends 8 accuracy tasks with 1 EM task unweighted. Saturation judged from own knowledge (pre-ChatGPT fine-tuning benchmark; modern Chinese LLMs clear it easily).
placement_reason: A 32-author consortium builds the first general-purpose Chinese NLU suite explicitly on the GLUE/SuperGLUE template — nine classification/similarity/MRC tasks plus a from-scratch linguistic diagnostic set — the archetypal parse/entail/retrieve capability corpus (A1, the same family SNLI anchors), just ported to Chinese rather than a domain-specific occupational suite.

title: Beyond Goldfish Memory: Long-Term Open-Domain Conversation
human_time: A few minutes: read the up-to-5-session (~1,600-token) history and produce or judge one context-appropriate next utterance.
frontier_score: Retrieval- and summary-memory-augmented BST 2.7B beat plain encoder-decoder fine-tuning on validation perplexity and human preference (no single accuracy ceiling - perplexity/preference-graded)
one_line: First public multi-session dialogue-memory dataset: crowdsourced human-human chats over up to 5 sessions (hours-to-days apart) with per-turn persona summaries.
notes: Dataset-plus-modeling paper: it introduces the Multi-Session Chat crowdsourcing protocol (~5,001 collected episodes; session 1 is a PersonaChat conversation, personas from Zhang et al. 2018) and the retrieval-/summary-memory models built on it. Graded by validation perplexity (proxy) and human preference, with no fixed accuracy ceiling, so saturation is not-applicable and items_count is null. Effectively superseded as a memory probe by LoCoMo (2024), which is ~9x longer.
placement_reason: First public probe of whether a dialogue model can hold a coherent conversation across multiple sessions using earlier context - a conversation-ability question (A7 'communication'), not an audit of a grader or a frontier wall. Its retrieval-/summary-memory models are the paper's proposed fix to that capability gap, not the object being classified.

title: ImageReward: Learning and Evaluating Human Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation
human_time: Rating an image on 3 Likert scales plus ranking 4-9 images into 5 preference slots per prompt; a few minutes per prompt for a trained annotator, not stated exactly.
frontier_score: ImageReward: 65.14% pairwise preference accuracy (own test set, 2023); independent re-evaluations find 61.1% (Pick-a-Pic's test set) and a rank collapse to second-worst of six models (HPS v2's nine-generator test set)
one_line: 137k expert rate-and-rank comparisons (ImageRewardDB) train a BLIP-backed T2I preference scorer, plus ReFL, a method that back-propagates its gradient through a diffusion model's late denoising steps.
notes: Kingdom is the most contestable call in this batch: placed in F1 (reward factory) rather than G2 (preference protocol, like Pick-a-Pic) specifically because ReFL explicitly back-propagates ImageReward's gradient into a diffusion model's weights - a genuine 'train on the generated signal' loop matching AlpacaFarm's F1 precedent, which Pick-a-Pic/HPS v2 (inference-time re-ranking or a static leaderboard only) don't attempt. items_count = the 466-prompt/6,399-pair held-out test set used for the headline 65.14% accuracy, not the 136,892-pair training set. Lineage excludes kirstain-2023-pick-a-pic despite v4's own references to it: this paper's `date` (2023-04) predates Pick-a-Pic's (2023-05), so a lineage edge in that direction would be chronologically reversed even though the camera-ready text discusses it.
placement_reason: Builds a reward model (ImageReward) AND explicitly demonstrates training on its output: ReFL back-propagates the reward's gradient through a randomly-sampled late denoising step directly into a diffusion model's weights, beating three indirect baselines (Dataset Filtering, Reward Weighted, RAFT) in every pairwise human comparison - the AlpacaFarm-style 'generates its own training signal' pattern F1 names, not merely a proposed evaluation metric (G2/G3), since the training-loop demonstration is a first-class, equally-weighted half of the paper.

title: OpenToM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Theory-of-Mind Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models
group: King's College London / Huawei London Research Centre
human_time: A couple of minutes per narrative (194-492 words) to read and answer its 23 associated questions; not stated exactly, but a 3-annotator agreement on a 100-narrative subsample stands in for the human reference.
frontier_score: Zero-shot GPT-4-Turbo 0.643 F1 (Loc-coarse, 1st-order) vs. 0.990 human agreement; Attitude 0.544 vs. 0.862 human agreement
one_line: 696 LLM-personified-character narratives (596 standard + 100 extra-long), 23 questions each across location/multi-hop/attitude genres.
notes: contamination_defense procedural reflects OpenToM's generative personality/preference/intention pipeline (parallel to MMToM-QA's simulator-based generation), even though the final prose is GPT-drafted and human-revised rather than purely algorithmic.
placement_reason: Builds narratives from a generative personality/preference/intention model — rather than a fixed Sally-Anne template — specifically so location, multi-hop, and a new psychological Attitude question type test genuine belief/desire inference instead of a memorizable template. A from-scratch capability probe in the ToMi/FANToM lineage, not primarily an audit paper: its faithfulness/role-gap analyses are real second-pass scrutiny of its own leaderboard, but that's a secondary contribution layered onto a new capability benchmark, not the paper's organizing question.

title: HotpotQA: A Dataset for Diverse, Explainable Multi-hop Question Answering
human_time: Roughly 1-3 minutes: read ~10 short Wikipedia paragraphs (2 gold + 8 distractors), chain two facts, extract a span; borderline with L1 for easy items.
frontier_score: baseline 58.28 distractor answer F1 vs human 91.40; leaderboard hit high-70s/80s joint-F1 within ~2 years — effectively solved
one_line: 113k crowd-written Wikipedia questions requiring two-document multi-hop chains, graded jointly on answer and supporting-fact evidence.
notes: Primary domain is a judgment call: classic NLU-era extractive QA (language, per the SQuAD precedent) with multi-hop reasoning and world knowledge secondary. tool_access reflects the fullwiki retrieval setting; the distractor setting is pure provided-context text. Hidden-test leaderboard (private-holdout) is from own knowledge of the paper, not stated in the explainer. items_count is one 7,405-item test set (distractor and fullwiki each; 112,779 pairs total).
placement_reason: A classic NLU capability probe at birth: QA had a 'depth problem' — SQuAD answerable from one span — so HotpotQA asks whether models can chain facts across two documents (plus retrieval in fullwiki) and justify the answer with supporting sentences. Multi-hop reading comprehension / retrieval / span extraction is squarely the SQuAD-family parsing skill, extended; the open frontier skill is the headline (58.28 F1 vs human 91.40), not durability or auditing.

title: SUPERB: Speech processing Universal PERformance Benchmark
human_time: Not applicable in the usual sense -- every task scores a lightweight probe's output (accuracy/F1/WER/EER/DER/MTWV) against existing dataset labels; no human baseline is run through the harness.
frontier_score: HuBERT Large wins 8/12 scored metric columns; no representation wins every column (wav2vec 2.0 Large takes KS/SD, HuBERT Base takes QbE/ASV)
one_line: Ten speech tasks across content/speaker/semantics/paralinguistics, scored with every SSL representation frozen and only a minimal task head trained, so the score isolates representation quality from downstream capacity.
notes: domain_primary has no dedicated 'speech' value in the controlled vocabulary; filed as multimodal (audio, a non-text modality) with language secondary since several tasks (ASR, slot filling) are speech-to-text. items_count left null: the ten tasks each draw from a different existing dataset (LibriSpeech, VoxCeleb1, IEMOCAP, etc.) with no single combined item count reported. Domain overlap between LibriSpeech-pretrained encoders and LibriSpeech-derived tasks (PR/ASR/SD) is a real, undiscussed confound per the explainer's critique.
placement_reason: The GLUE playbook transplanted into speech: a multi-task suite spanning many facets with a shared frozen-representation-plus-lightweight-head protocol, testing whether a pretrained representation can be recognized/parsed into ten different downstream signals -- a capability probe of representation reusability, not an audit of an existing grader or a hazard probe.

title: InterCode: Standardizing and Benchmarking Interactive Coding with Execution Feedback
human_time: A single bash/SQL/Python instruction-completion task with iterative execution feedback; a few minutes for a competent programmer, per the paper's own human-in-the-loop framing.
frontier_score: GPT-4 + Try Again (n=10): 73.7% InterCode-SQL (from 9.1% single-turn), 48.5% InterCode-Bash (from 34.0%); Python/MBPP environment never quantitatively benchmarked (2023)
one_line: Frames interactive coding as a POMDP (code as actions, execution output as observations) and wraps NL2Bash, Spider, and MBPP in Docker-sandboxed Bash/SQL/Python environments so execution-feedback methods can finally be compared on one benchmark.
notes: items_count = 200 (Bash) + 1,034 (SQL) + 117 (Python) = 1,351 task instances across the three environments; the critique flags that Python/MBPP is defined but never quantitatively benchmarked despite counting toward this total.
placement_reason: Recasts interactive coding as a standard POMDP (code as actions, execution output as observations) and wraps existing static code datasets (NL2Bash, Spider, MBPP) in Docker-sandboxed environments so execution-feedback methods can be compared on one benchmark - a program-synthesis capability probe extended to the interactive-env shape (matching RefactorBench/SWE-Atlas's A4 pattern), not an audit of an existing benchmark's grader or a tool-orchestration suite (the 'tools' here are language runtimes themselves, not external APIs).

title: SWE-bench Multimodal: Do AI Systems Generalize to Visual Software Domains?
human_time: Gold patches average 27 lines across 2 files in a 549K-line/1,799-file codebase -- similar order of engineering effort to SWE-bench, roughly an hour or more per issue for a competent JS/TS developer.
frontier_score: SWE-agent (GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet): 12.2% Resolved, vs. Agentless 3.9% / RAG 5.5%, against SWE-bench Lite's contemporaneous ~43% Python state of the art
one_line: 619 real GitHub issue->PR task instances from 17 JavaScript/TypeScript libraries where every task requires reading at least one embedded image (83.5% judged image-necessary); agentic scaffolds (11.5% avg.) badly outperform fixed localize-then-repair pipelines (Agentless 3.9%, RAG 5.5%).
notes: task_shape/tool_access mirror SWE-bench's own precedent (single-turn/none) despite the paper's headline evaluation being about agentic scaffolds (SWE-agent) vs. fixed pipelines -- RAG is the direct single-turn analogue to original SWE-bench's retrieval-augmented baseline. A date-segmented contamination check (Appendix C.3) finds no test-set advantage, one of the more rigorous such checks in this batch.
placement_reason: Keeps SWE-bench's exact execution-graded, real-GitHub-PR formulation and changes only two variables -- Python to JavaScript, and every task now requires reading an image -- as a generalization stress test of the same repo-level patch-writing construct; A4's program-synthesis case (same family as its parent), not a B-family desaturation sequel, since the point is domain/modality transfer, not restoring headroom on a saturating benchmark.

title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents
human_time: Humans averaged ~815 s (~14 min) per live-Amazon episode; a typical sandbox shopping task is minutes of search/compare/choose.
frontier_score: IL+RL agent 62.4 task score / 28.7% success vs 59.6% human-expert success
one_line: Simulated Amazon (1.18M real listings) where agents search, pick options, and buy; auto-graded by attribute/option/price spec match.
notes: Instructions crowd-written on MTurk over scraped real products (provenance crowdsourced, not real-work-mined). items_count is the full 12,087-instruction set; the standard test split is 500. Explainer only quotes 2022 pre-LLM agents (~29%); later LLM agents improved but the benchmark stayed unsaturated.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can grounded agents operate a realistic web environment?' — prior interactive benchmarks were toy vocabularies (MiniWoB) or human-graded (WebGPT), so WebShop supplies a 1.18M-real-product e-commerce environment with an automatically computable reward. The environment/agentic task is the contribution; the taxonomy's A5 archetype is literally 'WebShop-style'. RL training inside it exists but the paper's headline is the human-agent capability gap (29% vs 60%), not a reward factory.

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
human_time: Minutes per conversation: a handful of dialogue turns plus a handful of tool calls per task; paper doesn't state a human baseline time.
frontier_score: gpt-4o function-calling agent: 48.2% average success (τ-retail/τ-airline); pass^8 reliability falls below 25%
one_line: A customer-service benchmark forcing agents to extract intent from a simulated human user, obey a written domain-policy document, and reproduce their own success across repeated trials — gpt-4o clears under half the tasks and its pass^8 reliability collapses below 25%.
notes: Introduces pass^k as a new reliability statistic (fraction of tasks solved on ALL of k independent trials) distinct from Codex's pass@k (at least one of k) — the reason this paper is dual-tagged benchmarks+evaluations.
placement_reason: Existing tool-use benchmarks (Gorilla, ToolLLM) hand the model a fully-specified task upfront; τ-bench instead makes information-gathering-from-a-human and written-policy compliance first-class parts of the tool-orchestration problem, closer to how service agents are actually deployed.

title: RoTBench: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Evaluating the Robustness of Large Language Models in Tool Learning
human_time: A minute or two per query for a human to select the right (noise-renamed) tool and fill its parameters; the paper's 3-student human baseline barely moves under noise (88.57%→85.71%).
frontier_score: GPT-4 tool-selection accuracy falls 80.00% (Clean) → 58.10% (Union) while 3 human graders fall only 88.57%→85.71% on identical items
one_line: Six LLMs scored on tool selection/parameter identification/content filling across five levels of tool-and-parameter naming noise (Clean to Union).
notes: B4 (construct audit) chosen over A-capability because the paper's headline finding is that clean-environment tool-selection accuracy is a fragile surface-cue score that collapses under noise a human wouldn't even notice — closer to TruthfulQA's 'a score means something else' pattern than a new capability probe. E1-attack-surfaces was the nearest rival call but the noise here is benign robustness testing (renamed but functionally identical tools), not an adversarial jailbreak/injection/hijack.
placement_reason: Doesn't ask whether models can select tools (already near-solved on clean ToolEyes-style environments) but whether that skill survives trivial character-level renaming a human wouldn't even notice — GPT-4's tool-selection accuracy falls 21.9 points while three human graders move 2.86 on identical items. That's a construct audit (a score means something else: clean-environment accuracy is a fragile surface-cue measurement, not a stable competence signal), not an attack-surface/jailbreak paper (E1): the noise is benign robustness testing, not an adversarial exploit, and not a new capability probe since RoTBench adds no new task, only noise on an existing one.

title: ToolEyes: Fine-Grained Evaluation for Tool Learning Capabilities of Large Language Models in Real-world Scenarios
human_time: Minutes per query: a domain professional's real request resolved via a multi-round (avg 2.8-7.0 turns) tool-use trajectory; not stated exactly.
frontier_score: GPT-4 70.31% overall (best in every one of 7 scenarios); best tool-tuned open model ToolLLaMA-2-7B-v2 56.30%; even GPT-4 manages only 35.70% on behavioral planning
one_line: 382 real user queries over 568 genuinely invocable tools across 7 real-world scenarios, scored on five separable process capabilities, not just outcome.
notes: grading_primary rubric-judge reflects the 5-dimension score (3 GPT-4-graded sub-scores, 2 rule-based) blended into an overall mean, validated against human raters (kappa up to 0.96, GPT-4/human agreement >83.5%).
placement_reason: Asks whether an agent can complete real user requests end-to-end using genuinely invocable, live real-world tools across seven authentic scenarios — a direct tool-orchestration capability probe (568 real tools, not simulated or emulated), scored on five separable capability dimensions rather than auditing whether an existing benchmark's rule-based grader is broken (that's ToolEyes's critique target, not its own design).

title: HELMET: How to Evaluate Long-Context Language Models Effectively and Thoroughly
human_time: Not stated; individual items span short QA/retrieval-style questions to a full document summary, at up to 128K tokens of context.
frontier_score: No single headline number (7 categories reported separately); open-source models lag closed ones by 30-40 absolute points on citation generation and re-ranking specifically at 128K
one_line: Evaluates 59 long-context LLMs across seven application-centric categories (RAG, citations, re-ranking, many-shot ICL, long-document QA, summarization, synthetic recall) at up to 128K tokens, replacing ROUGE with a validated model-based metric, and shows needle-in-a-haystack correlates with real downstream performance at only rho<=0.68 across 35 models.
notes: items_count left null: HELMET aggregates many pre-existing datasets of varying size into 7 categories rather than shipping one fixed item pool. grading_primary reflects that most of the 7 categories use exact-match/accuracy-style scoring; the paper's own methodological innovation (GPT-4o replacing ROUGE) applies only to 2 of 7 categories (LongQA's NarrativeQA subset, both Summ datasets), and the paper reports no same-family-judge-bias check for GPT-4o grading GPT-4o's own outputs.
placement_reason: The paper's own diagnosis is about measurement, not capability: existing long-context reports lean on needle-in-a-haystack and ad hoc dataset handfuls that don't correlate with real downstream use (rho<=0.68-0.8), and long-document scoring still leans on unreliable ROUGE. HELMET's contribution is a standardized, holistic protocol across seven genuinely distinct application categories (cross-category correlation ranges 0.92 down to 0.34) with a validated model-based metric replacing ROUGE -- the G1 panorama move (a way of evaluating, in the HELM/BIG-bench tradition), not a new capability construct.

title: UpBench: A Dynamically Evolving Real-World Labor-Market Agentic Benchmark Framework Built for Human-Centric AI
human_time: Real fixed-price single-milestone Upwork gigs (web dev, data science, writing, translation); estimated hours to ~a day each — the text gives payouts, not hours.
frontier_score: Claude Sonnet 4: 39.8% first-attempt strict completion (51.2% after one human-feedback pass)
one_line: 322 real paid Upwork jobs graded by expert freelancers against 5-20 labeled acceptance criteria, with human-in-the-loop re-attempts.
notes: Grading is per-criterion rubrics scored by HUMAN experts, so human (not rubric-judge, which the taxonomy reserves for LLM graders). Agents run a plan-act-reflect loop with only attachment-read/artifact-store tools (no web/retrieval) — borderline interactive-env. 'Dynamically evolving' refresh is the design claim; the released 322-job snapshot is static. Complexity L3 is an estimate; some jobs may be L4.
placement_reason: 322 real, paid Upwork contracts with actual client payouts, an explicit economic breakeven model (E(V)=sV−c, AI/HITL/human regimes), and a continuously refreshed live-marketplace stream — squarely 'real paid work with explicit economic framing/valuation (live freelance feeds)'. The human-in-the-loop rescue axis gives it a D3 collaboration flavor, but the substrate and valuation framing are economic rehearsal.

title: AssistantBench: Can Web Agents Solve Realistic and Time-Consuming Tasks?
human_time: 214 tasks each take a person 'several minutes' of open-web browsing by explicit design (e.g. checking nearby gyms' class schedules, tracking a real-estate listing).
frontier_score: No configuration tops 26.4 accuracy (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, SPA-to-CB ensemble); the paper's own SOTA web-agent baseline, SeeAct alone, scores 2.2-4.1
one_line: 214 hand-collected, automatically-verifiable open-web tasks that take a person several minutes to answer, plus SPA (a planning-and-memory upgrade to SeeAct) -- exposing that closed-book guessing can out-score a real web agent on raw accuracy alone once answer-rate and precision aren't reported separately.
notes: 'Expert-authored' would also be defensible for the domain-expert-sourced 42/214 subset, but the majority pipeline (172/214) is personally-contacted-participant + crowd-worker template expansion, so classified crowdsourced overall. Scoring is per-answer-type: word-F1 for strings, DROP-style alignment for lists, a log-ratio decay for numbers, precision/recall-F1 for dict answers -> proxy-metric primary, with a separate strict exact-match also reported.
placement_reason: Targets the open web specifically (unlike Mind2Web/WebArena's fixed sandboxed sites), with a realistic/time-consuming/automatically-verifiable filter and closed-form scoring immune to answer drift -- the interactive open-web-navigation environment operated end-to-end (SPA's planning+memory loop on top of SeeAct) is the contribution, A5's mandate, not a grader audit (the paper's own critique of collapsing four different mechanisms into one 'accuracy' column is a reading of the results, not the benchmark's construct).

title: Spider: A Large-Scale Human-Labeled Dataset for Complex and Cross-Domain Semantic Parsing and Text-to-SQL Task
human_time: A couple of minutes per item: read a multi-table schema (avg. 27.6 columns, 8.8 foreign keys) and compose a correct multi-clause SQL query.
frontier_score: Best 2018 baseline (SQLNet) reaches 12.4% exact-match on the cross-domain database-split test set; by 2026, years of public exposure have pushed fine-tuned model scores well above 85%.
one_line: 10,181 questions / 5,693 hand-written SQL queries across 200 multi-table, cross-domain databases, split by database so a test-time schema is always unseen in training -- 2018 SOTA (SQLNet) reaches only 12.4% exact-match under that split.
notes: Provenance is expert-authored rather than plain crowdsourced: 11 Yale CS students spent ~1,000 person-hours under a strict five-stage annotation protocol, not open MTurk collection. contamination_defense follows Spider's original design intent (a held-out test set, historically gated behind a leaderboard/eval server) though the explainer's own critique notes the dataset has since become fully mirrored and public -- treat this facet as the launch-time defense, not the current state.
placement_reason: Tests whether a model can synthesize a correct, schema-grounded SQL program for a genuinely unseen database -- the database split specifically defeats the template memorization that inflated prior single-database text-to-SQL scores -- a program-synthesis capability probe (A4, matching BIRD's own placement in this taxonomy), not a semantic-similarity or retrieval task.

title: Meta-World: A Benchmark and Evaluation for Multi-Task and Meta Reinforcement Learning
human_time: Not reported - a simulated RL benchmark, not human-timed; each task episode is a short Sawyer-arm manipulation sequence (reach/push/grasp) that would take a human teleoperator well under a minute per attempt.
frontier_score: Best 2019 baselines: MT-SAC 68.3% (MT10) / 38.5% (MT50); RL2 86.9% train / 35.8% test (ML10, the largest train-test collapse of any method); MAML 39.9%/33.3% (ML45 train/test) - no method comes close to solving even 10 training tasks jointly, let alone held-out ones
one_line: 50 simulated Sawyer-arm manipulation tasks (non-parametrically distinct, each with parametric object/goal variation) with 5 evaluation protocols (ML1, MT1, MT10/MT50, ML10/ML45) of increasing difficulty; seven 2019 baselines all struggle to learn even 10 tasks jointly.
notes: Domain is a forced fallback (see wang-2019-mbrl-benchmark's note on this batch's RL/robotics vocabulary gap).
placement_reason: A shared-arm, shared-format multi-task manipulation suite explicitly built to force meta-/multi-task RL methods to prove generalization past narrow parametric task families - an 'operate an interactive environment across many distinct tasks' case, even though (like RLBench, PHYRE, bsuite, and the MBRL benchmark in this same batch) its domain content is physical robotics rather than the family's usual web/computer-use exemplars.

title: MMMU: A Massive Multi-Discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
human_time: One college-exam question with image(s) requiring domain knowledge plus deliberate reasoning; ~1-5 min for a subject expert.
frontier_score: GPT-4o 69.1 (validation) vs 88.6 human experts; GPT-4V 55.7 test at launch
one_line: 11.5K college-exam questions across 30 subjects and 30 image types (diagrams, scans, scores) testing expert multimodal reasoning.
notes: Contamination call: 10.5K test-split answers are withheld behind a leaderboard (private-holdout-ish), but questions are public and textbook-sourced — explainer stresses this defense is weak. 94% MC scored by regex extraction with random fill on parse failure.
placement_reason: Explicitly the multimodal MMLU: 11.5K college-exam questions across 30 subjects testing expert knowledge + deliberate reasoning under exam conditions, framed against 'Expert AGI' (90th-percentile skilled adult). A2 names MMMU as an example. Born because VQA-style suites were saturated (~90%) while text exam suites (MMLU, AGIEval) showed no images.

title: MMMU-Pro: A More Robust Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding Benchmark
human_time: Same underlying exam-style questions as MMMU (college-exam multi-discipline items); approximated human performance (reused from MMMU's own study) stays high (88.6%->85.4%) across the harder formats.
frontier_score: GPT-4o (0513): 54.0% Standard-10 / 49.7% Vision (~51.9% overall), down from 69.1% on MMMU Val; VILA-1.5-40B falls 26.9 points to 25.0%
one_line: Rebuilds MMMU by filtering out text-solvable questions, widening 4 options to 10, and adding a vision-only setting that embeds the question in a photo/screenshot; every model falls, some by more than 25 points, and reasoning errors -- not OCR -- now dominate.
notes: items_count=3,460 is 1,730 unique post-filter questions x2 presentations (Standard-10 and Vision); provenance stays exam-derived (same underlying MMMU exam-question base) even though the 10-option distractors are GPT-4o/Claude-generated additions on top.
placement_reason: Explicitly rebuilds MMMU's exact construct (multi-discipline multimodal exam questions) to close two demonstrated leaks -- text-solvability and a guessable 4-way option set -- restoring headroom (GPT-4o falls from 69.1% to roughly 52%) without changing what's being measured; the canonical B3 desaturation-sequel move, not a new construct the way a C-family fresh summit exam would be.

title: Social-IQ: A Question Answering Benchmark for Artificial Social Intelligence
human_time: A ~13-second in-the-wild video clip with 6 questions (4 correct + 3 incorrect candidate answers each, nearly double the answer length of prior VQA-style sets) - a minute or two to watch and answer; human binary accuracy 95.08%.
frontier_score: Best 2019 model (Tensor-MFN, a TFN+MFN hybrid) 64.82% binary / 34.14% four-way accuracy vs 95.08% human binary ceiling - a 30.26-point gap; an answer-only (no video) baseline already clears random by 7 points (57.02%)
one_line: 7,500 open-ended social-intelligence questions (52,500 correct/incorrect candidate answers) over 1,250 in-the-wild YouTube clips, built via a 6-stage annotation pipeline testing judgment of social situations, mental states, and intentions.
notes: domain_secondary is a judgment call: 'social-moral' is the closest available bucket for social-cognition/theory-of-mind-adjacent content even though the taxonomy's social-moral domain is mainly used for ethics/values benchmarks elsewhere. Saturation 'saturated' reflects the explainer's own framing of Social-IQ as 'a fair historical marker' now superseded by interactive benchmarks (SOTOPIA) for behavior rather than passive judgment - own-knowledge inference, not a measured modern number.
placement_reason: Direct lineage descendant of VQA/COCO-QA/MovieQA/TVQA (named explicitly in the paper's own gap section), swapping numeric sentiment/emotion labels for open-ended multiple-choice QA about social situations and mental states over naturalistic video - a recognize/comprehend capability probe over multimodal content, not an ethics/values benchmark (E3, since the construct is situational judgment not moral valence) nor a conversational-communication task (A7, since the model judges others' interactions rather than participating in one).

title: Multi-SWE-bench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Issue Resolving
human_time: A real GitHub issue with a human-verified regression-tested fix, in Java/TS/JS/Go/Rust/C/C++; annotator-estimated resolution time spans <15 min to 4h+ per issue.
frontier_score: Agents resolving ~half of SWE-bench Verified's Python issues clear well under a quarter of Java's and under 12% of TypeScript/JavaScript/Go/C/C++'s
one_line: SWE-bench's issue-resolving task ported to 7 languages beyond Python: 1,632 human-verified GitHub issues (Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C, C++), built via a five-phase pipeline with dual-annotator verification; agent resolve rates collapse from ~50% on Python to under 12% on most other languages.
notes: Same construction bar as SWE-bench Verified (a real fix, zero regressions, human-verified) reproduced across a Docker build pipeline per language -- a direct generalization test of whether coding-agent skill transfers past the language it was built and measured on.
placement_reason: Same repo-level patch-generation construct as SWE-bench, ported to seven new language ecosystems to test whether the capability generalizes past Python -- a direct A4 sequel (ports-to-new-domain), not a desaturation of Python SWE-bench itself (which the paper explicitly isn't retiring or replacing).

title: PhotoChat: A Human-Human Dialogue Dataset with Photo Sharing Behavior for Joint Image-Text Modeling
human_time: Seconds per turn: read the dialogue so far and judge whether a photo will be shared next, or which of 1,000 candidate photos the conversation is about; no human baseline is reported for either task.
frontier_score: Intent prediction: T5-base 58.1% F1 (T5-3B 58.9%); Image retrieval: SCAN 10.4% R@1 out of 1,000 candidates
one_line: 12,286 human-human dialogues, each paired with one of 10,917 photos visible to only one side until at least five turns have passed -- predicting when a photo will be shared tops out at 58.1% F1, and retrieving which photo tops out at just 10.4% R@1.
notes: No human performance ceiling or inter-annotator agreement is reported for either task, so 58.1% F1/10.4% R@1 have no denominator for 'how hard is this really.' Filed under A7-communication rather than a pure multimodal-retrieval family since the paper's own framing is dialogue behavior (when/whether a photo gets shared during an ordinary conversation), with retrieval as the second of two tasks built on that same asymmetric-photo-sharing protocol.
placement_reason: The object under test is conversational behavior around photo-sharing -- does a system know when a photo is about to be shared and which one -- extending the WoW/PersonaChat dialogue lineage with an asymmetric photo-holding protocol (only one side can see the photo for the first 5 turns), closer to A7's conversational-ability probes (cf. LoCoMo, MSC) than to a pure image-retrieval benchmark; retrieval is one of two tasks built on the same dialogue substrate, not the benchmark's sole design center.

title: HellaSwag: Can a Machine Really Finish Your Sentence?
human_time: One four-way sentence-completion choice; humans answer near-instantly (95.6% accuracy).
frontier_score: GPT-4 95.3% (10-shot) vs 95.6% human
one_line: Adversarially-filtered commonsense sentence completion: GPT-generated wrong endings BERT can't catch, trivial for humans.
notes: Provenance is mixed: real ActivityNet/WikiHow contexts and gold endings, but the defining task items (distractors) are GPT-1-generated via Adversarial Filtering with crowd validation — classified synthetic-generated. Fully public, in modern pretraining corpora, treated as saturated/retired.
placement_reason: Born the moment BERT 'solved' SWAG overnight; the paper shows the predecessor was gamed via distributional artifacts (ending-only 74.8%, shuffled 60.4%) and rebuilds the same commonsense-completion construct with adversarial filtering against BERT-Large to restore a >50-point human-machine gap — the textbook SuperGLUE-vs-GLUE desaturation sequel. SWAG is not a corpus node, so lineage is empty.

title: AIR-Bench 2024: A Safety Benchmark Based on Risk Categories from Regulations and Policies
human_time: One risky prompt yields one response scored 0/0.5/1 (harmful compliance / ambiguous / refusal); a human writing a comparable response takes a couple of minutes.
frontier_score: Claude 3 Sonnet/Haiku tie for highest average refusal rate at 89% across 45 level-3 categories; DBRX Instruct refuses only 15%
one_line: 5,694 prompts across a 314-category risk taxonomy decomposed directly from 8 government regulations and 16 corporate AI policies, graded by 314 bespoke category-specific autograders -- the first safety benchmark whose taxonomy maps onto actual regulatory text rather than researcher intuition.
notes: AIR 2024 taxonomy itself (4->16->45->314 tiers) is the paper's other headline artifact; a coverage audit shows HEx-PHI/HarmBench/SALAD-Bench cover only 51%/26%/71% of the 45 level-3 categories. Category-specific judge prompts (70% GPT-4o-drafted, 30% human-edited) reach Cohen's kappa 0.86 vs. a fixed-prompt approach's 0.69.
placement_reason: Same object as HarmBench -- refusal/compliance on risky prompts -- but grounds the risk taxonomy directly in 8 regulations and 16 corporate policies rather than researcher intuition, and shows the field's existing benchmarks (HEx-PHI, HarmBench, SALAD-Bench) cover as little as 26% of the resulting categories; a broader, compliance-grounded hazard probe in the same E1 family as its own comparison targets, not a B4 construct audit (it doesn't re-measure an existing benchmark's scores, it replaces the taxonomy those benchmarks were built against).

title: INJECAGENT: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
human_time: One decision point: read a tool response with an embedded malicious instruction and choose the next action — seconds for a human.
frontier_score: fine-tuned GPT-4: 6.6% ASR (base); ReAct-prompted GPT-4 hijacked 23.6% (47.0% enhanced)
one_line: 1,054 indirect-prompt-injection cases testing whether tool-using agents execute malicious instructions hidden in tool outputs.
notes: task_shape borderline: nothing executes — the benchmark inspects the parsed next action, with at most a 2-step GPT-4-simulated tool loop for data-stealing; could be argued single-turn. Saturation inverted metric: 'solved' would be ~0% ASR; fine-tuned models reach 4-8% but prompted frontier agents remain highly vulnerable — called open. Cases GPT-4-synthesized over ToolEmu schemas (low leak by construction but no ongoing defense).
placement_reason: First benchmark to formalize and measure indirect prompt injection against tool-integrated agents (1,054 cases, ASR as the metric) — the object is the attack surface a tool-calling agent exposes, not a skill. E1 names InjecAgent explicitly. Built in response to the tool-use agent wave whose action-level safety no benchmark measured; AgentDojo is its corpus descendant.

title: Personalizing Dialogue Agents: I have a dog, do you have pets too?
human_time: Seconds per turn: pick or write one short next-utterance (15-word cap) given a persona and dialogue history.
frontier_score: KV Profile Memory reaches the best next-utterance hits@1, 0.511 (original persona) vs. 0.349 with no persona; the paraphrased 'revised' persona condition cuts every ranking model's hits@1 roughly in half (e.g. 0.509 -> 0.354).
one_line: 1,155 crowdsourced personas (162,064 utterances, 10,907 dialogues) -- the first large chit-chat dataset conditioning both speakers on an explicit, human-readable persona instead of a latent per-speaker embedding, with a paraphrase-defended 'revised' persona set to block lexical shortcuts.
notes: Public dataset with no held-out private test labels found in the explainer; by 2026 the corpus is described as 'almost certainly contaminated' for any post-2019 LLM and the original leaderboard is effectively retired -- saturated.
placement_reason: The classic conversational-persona capability probe: can a dialogue model maintain a consistent, explicitly-given personality across a conversation instead of defaulting to bland, inconsistent replies -- tested by next-utterance selection/generation, squarely a communication skill (A7), with the paraphrased 'revised' persona condition specifically defending against a lexical-overlap shortcut rather than changing the tested construct.

title: CBLUE: A Chinese Biomedical Language Understanding Evaluation Benchmark
human_time: Well under a minute per item for most tasks (NER tag, relation label, similarity judgment); amateur trained annotators, following SuperGLUE's human-baseline protocol, reached 77.1 average vs. the best model's 70.0.
frontier_score: Best single model (RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large): 70.0 Avg vs. 77.1 amateur-human majority-vote Avg -- every one of 11 models trails humans on every one of 8 tasks
one_line: Eight Chinese biomedical NLU tasks built from real clinical trials, EHRs, medical forums, and search logs, left in their natural long-tailed distribution -- 11 fine-tuned Chinese PLMs, including a purpose-built medical BERT, all trail amateur human annotators on every task.
notes: First Chinese biomedical language-understanding benchmark, modeled explicitly on GLUE/SuperGLUE/CLUE's multi-task-leaderboard paradigm (human baseline follows SuperGLUE's protocol exactly) but applied to real, non-i.i.d. clinical text. items_count left null: the 8 tasks' train/dev/test sizes range from ~1.6k to ~24k each with no single combined figure reported. The one domain-specific baseline (PCL-MedBERT) finishes below plain general-domain BERT-base, a result the paper flags but doesn't explain.
placement_reason: Real clinical-trial, EHR, medical-forum, and search-log text, deliberately left long-tailed rather than balanced, testing whether Chinese PLMs can handle biomedical text the way it actually appears in practice -- occupational medical-domain competence (the Med-PaLM/MultiMedQA precedent), not a general Chinese-NLU capability probe; GLUE/SuperGLUE's multi-task-leaderboard mechanics are the method transplanted in, not the classifying axis.

title: Evaluating the Performance of Large Language Models on GAOKAO Benchmark
group: Fudan University / East China Normal University
human_time: 1-3 min per objective item; longer (10-20 min) for open-ended essay/derivation items under real exam pacing.
frontier_score: GPT-4-0314: 485/750 (humanities) / 447/750 (sciences) converted score (2023); ERNIE-Bot-0615 upsets on chemistry/politics/history
one_line: Converts the real Chinese college-entrance exam (2010-2022, 9 subjects, 2,811 questions) into an LLM benchmark, auto-grading objective items and human-grading subjective ones, on the exam's own 750-point scale.
notes: grading_primary judged 'human' rather than 'exact-match' since the paper's actual headline metric (Figure 1's converted totals) is dominated by two-teacher subjective grading for the five closed-source models compared; the seven open-source models are objective-only and don't receive a converted total. contamination_defense 'live-refresh' reflects the paper's explicit GAOKAO-Bench-2023 supplement, built and stated to be extended annually to mitigate leakage - though the critique flags this check as incomplete (misses 3 of 5 headline models, can't distinguish contamination from genuine difficulty).
placement_reason: Repurposes the actual Chinese national college-entrance exam (2010-2022, 9 subjects) into an LLM benchmark scored on the exam's own 750-point scale - 'how does the model perform against a real, high-stakes human exam' is the headline question, matching AGIEval-style A2 exemplars; unlike LEXTREME/LexGLUE (D2) the content spans general secondary education rather than one professional occupation, and unlike AGIEval it uniquely mixes objective auto-grading with two-teacher subjective essay grading.

title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents
human_time: Each scenario is a short agentic task (e.g. an e-commerce or IT-admin chore) a human would complete in a few minutes with the same tools; attacks add no extra legitimate work.
frontier_score: Mixed Attack averages an 84.30% success rate across 13 backbones (only 3.22% refusal); the best DPI defense (Dynamic Prompt Rewriting) still leaves a 44.45% ASR
one_line: Formalizes four LLM-agent attack surfaces (direct/indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, a novel Plan-of-Thought backdoor) across 10 scenarios, 400+ simulated tools, 13 backbones, and 11 defenses, finding an 84.30% average success rate for combined attacks that current defenses barely mitigate.
notes: items_count=50 is the base task count (10 agent personas x 5 user tasks); the full evaluated instance count is far larger once the 5 attack families, escalating injection techniques, and 13 backbones are all crossed, which the paper doesn't total in one number. domain_secondary=tool-use reflects that all four attack surfaces (system prompt, user prompt, tool response, memory) route through a ReAct-style tool-using agent loop. The entire scenario/tool/task corpus was generated by GPT-4, and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini are then evaluated inside that same-family-authored world -- an unaudited stylistic-familiarity confound the paper doesn't test.
placement_reason: Formalizes the LLM agent's full attack surface end-to-end (system prompt, user prompt, tool response, memory) under one shared threat-model notation and pairs each with a matched defense -- explicitly built to unify InjecAgent's IPI-only and AgentDojo's prompt-injection-only coverage into one benchmark; the object is agent attack surface / hijacking risk, the E1 case, not model skill.

title: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
human_time: ~3-4 min per problem: annotators solved 4.36 problems per 15-minute timer in the paper's own solve-rate check.
frontier_score: GPT-4o 92.9% on GSM1k (5-shot, fixed harness)
one_line: 1,205 hand-written, difficulty-matched private twin of GSM8k measuring how much contamination inflates public math scores.
notes: Provenance borderline: written by paid Scale annotators under a three-layer QA gauntlet (not domain experts, not an open crowd) - counted as expert-authored. The artifact is a math benchmark, but its lasting contribution is the private difficulty-matched twin methodology for contamination measurement. Classified manually by the lead agent after the batch-19 classifier skipped it (it classified mt-bench, batch 20's paper, instead).
placement_reason: Built to answer 'is GSM8k measuring reasoning or memorization?' — a hand-written, difficulty-matched, deliberately-withheld twin of GSM8k whose headline finding (overfit families drop up to 8 points, frontier models flat) is about the measurement apparatus, not a new skill; the explainer names Recht et al.'s CIFAR-10/ImageNet rebuilds as the imported template. The archetypal contamination twin.

title: Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models
human_time: First-solve-time spans 2 minutes to 24h54min across the 40 tasks (a 747x range, roughly log-linear) -- grounded in how long the fastest real competitive human team took in the original competition, not an estimate.
frontier_score: Claude 3.5 Sonnet leads unguided performance (17.5%, 7/40 tasks); OpenAI o1-preview leads subtask/partial-credit performance (46.8%)
one_line: 40 professional-level CTF tasks from 4 real 2022-2024 competitions, difficulty-calibrated to real teams' first-solve times (2min-24h54min) and partial-credit-gradable via subtasks.
notes: domain_secondary 'tool-use' covers the bash-driven agentic loop; no better single BENCH_DOMAINS fit exists for offensive-cyber capability than 'safety'. Contamination explicitly flagged as unresolved by the authors for the top-scoring model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet's later cutoff overlaps more of the task pool); by 2026 the whole 40-task set is a plausible pretraining-contamination risk for any newer model, hence none-public over a stronger label.
placement_reason: Built explicitly to quantify offensive-cyber capability as a named AI risk (2023 US Executive Order, frontier-safety frameworks), replacing subjective CTF point values with real human first-solve-time calibration -- a dangerous-capability probe measuring how far an LM's own hacking skill extends, the E2 case; not E1, since the object measured is the model's offensive capability itself, not an attack surface exposed by or against an agent.

title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
human_time: Read a full multi-agent failure log, reconstruct the reasoning chain, and often re-verify external evidence -- the paper's own annotators spent 23-31 hours per system across 127 systems.
frontier_score: Best of three LLM-based attribution methods: 53.5% agent-level accuracy, 14.2% step-level accuracy (several method/setting cells score below the paper's own random baseline)
one_line: 184 expert-annotated failure logs across 127 GAIA/AssistantBench-derived and hand-crafted multi-agent systems, formalizing 'automated failure attribution' via a counterfactual decisive-error definition; the best LLM-based method reaches only 53.5% agent-level / 14.2% step-level accuracy.
notes: domain_primary is a judgment call: the failure logs come from GAIA/AssistantBench-style general-assistant multi-agent systems (web browsing, file navigation, research), so reasoning (matching TRAIL's own domain choice for judging agent traces) fits better than agentic-web, which would overstate the web-specific share.
placement_reason: Builds a judge benchmark, not a skill benchmark: given a failed multi-agent trajectory, can an automated method (LLM-based attribution) correctly name the responsible agent and decisive step, scored against expert ground truth -- the same 'judge protocols and error taxonomies' pattern as TRAIL/Agent-as-a-Judge, applied to failure attribution specifically rather than general trace quality.

title: DataSciBench: An LLM Agent Benchmark for Data Science
human_time: A prompt bundling data cleaning, model fitting, a calculation, and a file-format/chart deliverable -- tens of minutes for a competent data scientist; borderline L2/L3.
frontier_score: GPT-4o tops every column (SR 66.31%, CR 68.44%, composite Score 64.51%); completion rate falls from 37.76% (easy) to 3.83% (hard) averaged across all 23 models
one_line: 222 data-science prompts and 519 hand-verified test cases graded by a Task-Function-Code framework that auto-generates and executes a partial-credit checker per prompt; GPT-4o leads every metric but caps out at 64.51% composite, and completion collapses to 3.83% on hard prompts.
notes: items_count=222 prompts (519 derived test cases). Models only generate code in response to a prompt -- the TFC grading harness executes and checks it afterward, not the model itself -- so tool_access=none rather than code-exec despite the 'LLM Agent' title.
placement_reason: Asks whether models can write real, multi-deliverable data-science code (clean data, fit a model, save a chart, write a report) -- the DS-1000 question taken further with partial-credit, multi-criteria grading instead of DS-1000's simpler execution tests; a program-synthesis capability probe with data-science domain content, not an occupational-deployment rehearsal (the interface is still one-shot code generation, not a workplace simulation).

title: Ape210K: A Large-Scale and Template-Rich Dataset of Math Word Problems
human_time: A Chinese elementary-school word problem; abstract states 'the gap is still significant between human and our baseline model' but no numeric human ceiling is reported.
frontier_score: Best 2020 baseline (copy-augmented seq2seq): 70.20% on Ape210K's own test set vs. two re-run open-source solvers (52.28%/56.56%); modern LLMs would trivially clear this elementary-arithmetic ceiling
one_line: 210,488 Chinese elementary-school math word problems and 56,532 equation templates (9x/25x Math23K's scale/diversity) -- but the paper was withdrawn by its own authors, and the dataset never went officially public.
notes: Genuinely unusual contamination/provenance case: arXiv 2009.11506 carries an author withdrawal notice stating the dataset 'is not going public' and calling the paper's own experiments 'irreproducible without access to the dataset'; a third-party copy has circulated since days after the withdrawal with no verified chain of custody. contamination_defense is none-public since there is no structural defense and the mirror is unverified, not because it's cleanly released. Equations are heuristically extracted from human rationales with no reported audit. Saturation judged from own knowledge (elementary arithmetic, pre-LLM baselines only).
placement_reason: A large-scale, template-diverse Chinese math word-problem corpus explicitly built to push past Math23K's low template diversity (0.80% vs. 37.70% requiring external constants) -- the same checkable closed-form-reasoning construct as GSM8K/ASDiv (A3), with diversity rather than raw difficulty as the design axis, though its since-withdrawn status is a real caveat on how load-bearing any specific reported number should be treated.

title: Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences? Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs
human_time: Read a stated preference and a later, topically-unrelated query buried under real multi-session chat stretching up to 100k tokens; a few minutes to locate and judge for a human.
frontier_score: Zero-shot accuracy falls below 20% within 10 turns for 9 of 10 models (o1-preview the outlier at ~50%), keeps sliding toward single digits by 100k tokens
one_line: 3,000 manually curated preference-query pairs bury a stated user preference under real multi-session chat (up to 100k tokens); 9 of 10 models fall below 20% preference-following accuracy within 10 turns.
notes: Provenance is mixed: the 3,000 preference-query pairs (the graded items) are manually authored by the team across three difficulty tiers, but the interleaved background conversation is real LMSYS-Chat-1M user traffic -- coded expert-authored for the graded artifact, per the same logic as HealthBench. grading_primary=llm-judge for the headline generation-task metric (4 Claude-3-Sonnet binary checks aggregated into an error taxonomy); the cheaper classification-task variant is exact-match and correlates with it at Pearson r=0.73.
placement_reason: Distinct from retrieval-style long-context QA (LongBench, needle-in-haystack) by design: the model must not just locate a stated preference in a long transcript but proactively apply it to a later, topically-unrelated query -- a conversational capability probe (can the assistant converse coherently with a persistent user state) in the same family as LoCoMo/MSC, not a construct audit or an occupational deployment test.

title: AgentDAM: Privacy Leakage Evaluation for Autonomous Web Agents
human_time: A short web task (a Reddit post, a GitLab issue, a shopping purchase) seeded with sensitive but task-irrelevant data -- a couple of minutes for a person to complete without over-sharing.
frontier_score: GPT-4o-mini leaks in 45.9% of runs before any defense; even the best mitigation tried still leaks in 6-18% of cases while task success drops
one_line: 246 realistic web-navigation tasks on self-hosted Reddit/GitLab/shopping replicas, each seeded with task-irrelevant sensitive data; every agent tested leaks some of it, and directly probing a model about privacy norms diverges sharply from watching it act (e.g. gpt-4o 0.915 probed vs. 0.646 in action).
notes: Utility is a programmatic binary reward against final environment state; the privacy score is a gpt-4o LLM-judge verdict per action (98% match to 4 human annotators on one checked configuration) -- coded llm-judge primary since that's the paper's headline metric.
placement_reason: Measures a real-world agent risk (does the agent leak sensitive data it didn't need) during ordinary task execution in a full multi-step web environment -- the same 'object is risk, not skill' pattern as AgentDojo/InjecAgent/WebGuard, just for data minimization rather than an active attacker; not E3 (values/judgment on moral dilemmas) since the construct is action-level information leakage, not a judgment quality score.

title: MiniF2F: a cross-system benchmark for formal Olympiad-level mathematics
human_time: Competition-level problems (IMO/AIME/AMC) typically take a skilled human competitor tens of minutes to a few hours to prove formally; the paper reports ~15 min for a trained practitioner to *formalize* (not solve) one statement.
frontier_score: GPT-f/PACT (Lean): 24.6% Pass@1 / 29.2% Pass@8 on test; GPT-f (Metamath): just 1.3% Pass@1 on the same underlying problems
one_line: 488 competition-math problem statements (AMC/AIME/IMO plus a formalized MATH subset) manually formalized across Metamath, Lean, and partially Isabelle/HOL Light, graded by kernel-verified proof search rather than string match.
notes: Grading is strictly binary kernel verification -- no partial credit, no learned judge -- so grading_all has only one member. The Metamath/Lean gap (1.3% vs 24.6% Pass@1, identical model and method) is the paper's headline finding, attributed to tactic access rather than a controlled ablation; per the explainer's critique, Appendix B's MATH-Algebra counts disagree with the Discussion prose and Figure 1 by one solve per baseline.
placement_reason: The C2 archetype: proofs are hard to find but trivially easy to verify by a kernel -- no partial credit, no learned judge, just Pass@N against a formal checker. The paper's whole point is cross-system comparability under this verification-not-generation asymmetry, not a durable expert-vs-model gap (C1, static exam) or a living, ever-refreshing wall (C3).

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
human_time: One two-turn open-ended chat question (writing, roleplay, math, coding); a few minutes to answer well.
frontier_score: GPT-4 8.99/10 at release; explainer: modern scores 'cluster near the ceiling'
one_line: 80 hand-written two-turn chat questions graded 1-10 by a GPT-4 judge; shipped alongside the Chatbot Arena human-vote leaderboard.
notes: Eval-methodology paper shipping two artifacts; classified the MT-bench set (per slug). Chatbot Arena would differ: user-traffic provenance, human/Elo grading, not-applicable saturation, live-refresh by design — human grading and its user-traffic character are reflected only in grading_all.
placement_reason: The contribution is preference machinery, not a task skill: LLM-as-a-judge validated against human votes, plus MT-bench (80 pairwise-judged questions) and Chatbot Arena (crowdsourced Elo battles). Born because MMLU/HELM could not distinguish aligned chat models from their bases; the headline claim (GPT-4 judge agrees with humans 85%) is about the evaluating method itself.

title: WebGuard: Building a Generalizable Guardrail for Web Agents
human_time: Judging one proposed web action's SAFE/LOW/HIGH label from a screenshot or A11y tree takes well under a minute; annotation collection took longer but the per-instance task is a single classification.
frontier_score: GPT-4o best zero-shot at 57.5% average three-class accuracy; fine-tuned WebGuard-VL-7B reaches 80.4%
one_line: Action-level web-agent safety dataset: classify 4,939 real-website actions as SAFE/LOW/HIGH by reversibility and blast radius.
notes: Provenance is borderline: actions are harvested from 193 real live websites but the items/labels are created by trained, pilot-qualified annotators, so expert-authored over real-work-mined. Evaluated model gets page state as input only (no browsing), so tool_access none.
placement_reason: An action-level unsafe-action-guard dataset: 4,939 real-website actions graded SAFE/LOW/HIGH by reversibility and blast radius, built to train/measure a guardrail that blocks harmful web-agent actions before execution — E1's 'unsafe-action guards / refusal-of-harmful-web-actions' exactly. The object is risk of consequential actions, not task skill; guardrail fine-tuning serves the safety instrument.

title: AGIEval: A Human-Centric Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models
human_time: One exam item (SAT/LSAT/Gaokao MC or fill-in) takes a human test-taker roughly 1-3 minutes, per standard exam pacing.
frontier_score: GPT-4 zero-shot CoT all-task average 58.4 (few-shot CoT 61.3); 95.0% on SAT-Math
one_line: 8,062 bilingual multiple-choice/fill-in questions repurposed from 20 official high-stakes human exams (Gaokao, SAT, LSAT, bar, AMC/AIME).
notes: Saturation call uses own knowledge beyond the 2023 numbers quoted (modern frontier models score well above GPT-4's 61.3, but sub-90 on the hard subsets) -> closing. F1 on fill-in-blank counted as proxy-metric in grading_all.
placement_reason: Repurposes 20 official high-stakes human exams (Gaokao, SAT, LSAT, GRE/GMAT, Chinese bar) into 8,062 bilingual objective questions to ask 'how does the model stack up against a person under exam conditions?' — headline is model-vs-human exam performance. Built against MMLU's opaque provenance and English-only scope and against GLUE-era single-skill curation; a named A2 exemplar.

title: A Dataset for Document Grounded Conversations
human_time: Seconds per turn: one conversational reply grounded in a just-revealed ~143-word document section.
frontier_score: Conditioning a seq2seq generator on the current document section (SEQS) beats a section-blind baseline (SEQ) on every axis: test perplexity 10.11 vs. 21.8, pairwise engagement 43.9% vs. 36.4%, fluency 3.84 vs. 2.88 (1-4 scale).
one_line: 4,112 crowdsourced two-party conversations grounded in 30 Wikipedia movie articles (4 sections each), every turn-range mapped to the document section that prompted it; conditioning generation on the current section beats a section-blind baseline on perplexity, human engagement, and fluency.
notes: Saturation set to not-applicable: this is a small (30-document) resource used mainly as an ablation-style demonstration (SEQ vs. SEQS) rather than a tracked leaderboard with a single frontier score. The paper never states whether its 0.8/0.05/0.15 split holds documents constant across partitions -- a real generalization concern given only 30 underlying documents, flagged in the explainer but unconfirmable from the text.
placement_reason: Built to give conversational generation a real, checkable source of information to talk about -- unlike scripted movie dialogue or narrow tech-support logs -- pairing turns with an explicit document section so grounding can be tested directly; a document-grounded conversational-generation capability probe, squarely A7, explicitly positioned as going beyond PersonaChat's handful of one-line persona facts.

title: KdConv: A Chinese Multi-domain Dialogue Dataset Towards Multi-turn Knowledge-driven Conversation
human_time: Minutes per dialogue: 19.0 turns on average across three knowledge-graph-grounded domains (film/music/travel), each utterance tied to specific knowledge triples.
frontier_score: Knowledge-aware BERT (retrieval) leads on Hits@1/3 in every domain; best knowledge-aware generators (Seq2Seq+know / HRED+know) sweep BLEU/Distinct per domain but no automatic metric checks knowledge faithfulness directly
one_line: 4,500 open-ended Chinese multi-domain (film/music/travel) dialogues with sentence-level annotation tying every utterance to the exact knowledge-graph triples it draws on.
notes: items_count is the released dialogue count (450 held out as test, 150/domain). Grading mixes BLEU/Distinct/PPL (proxy-metric) with Hits@1/3 retrieval ranking (exact-match) and a human fluency/coherence study. Saturation 'open': no automatic metric directly measures whether a response used the correct knowledge triple, so headroom on the construct KdConv actually cares about is real and unmeasured by its own metrics.
placement_reason: Built to test open-ended, multi-topic, knowledge-grounded conversation with explicit sentence-level triple supervision — a general conversational-capability probe (converse, clarify, stay grounded) rather than occupational content, unlike D2's professional-domain suites; the knowledge graph is the scaffolding for the conversation skill being measured, not the object of study itself.

title: Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models
human_time: Each prompt is an ordinary writing task plus checkable constraints (e.g. 400+ words in JSON); a human would need several minutes to draft a compliant response.
frontier_score: GPT-4 (Nov 2023) 76.89% prompt-level strict accuracy
one_line: 541 prompts with deterministically verifiable constraints (word counts, JSON, keywords, casing) scoring instruction compliance judge-free.
notes: Saturation judged from the explainer's own framing ('now easy to saturate and partly contaminated', sits in post-training mixes) plus community knowledge of >90% frontier scores, not from the 2023 numbers quoted.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can models actually follow instructions precisely?' via 541 prompts of deterministically-verifiable directives (word counts, JSON, casing) — the headline is model compliance on the instruction-following skill (GPT-4 fails ~1 prompt in 4). The judge-free verifier design is the method, but the object measured is the skill; the taxonomy's own A7 exemplar ('IFEval-style').

title: SOTOPIA: Interactive Evaluation for Social Intelligence in Language Agents
human_time: A few minutes to read and score a full up-to-20-turn social-interaction transcript against the 7-dimension rubric; the human study covers 200 double-scored episodes plus 40 human-GPT-4 and 20 human-human interactions on a hard subset.
frontier_score: GPT-4 leads every SOTOPIA-EVAL dimension (GOAL 7.62 vs. GPT-3.5's 6.45, Llama-2-70b-chat's 5.38, MPT-30b-chat's 4.10), but every model averages negative on social-rule-following/secret-keeping (GPT-4 SOC -0.07, SEC -0.14), and GPT-4 trails humans on SOTOPIA-hard's 20 toughest scenarios (GOAL 4.85 vs. 5.95-6.15).
one_line: Two LLM agents with private, possibly conflicting social goals act freely across up to 20 turns in one of 450 GPT-4-generated scenario/character/relationship combinations, scored post-hoc on a 7-dimension rubric (goal completion, believability, knowledge, relationship, financial benefit, secrets, social rules) instead of one accuracy number.
notes: Placed in A7 (communication) rather than A5 (embodied-operation) because every action (speak, non-verbal, physical, leave) is realized purely as free text with no external tool_access — a social-conversation capability probe, not a software/OS-operation environment; task_shape scored multi-turn rather than interactive-env on the same basis. The explainer flags that GPT-4 authors the scenarios, plays one of the four evaluated models, and grades the automated Table-2 results — a structural self-preference risk the paper doesn't rule out.
placement_reason: Built to test social intelligence under interaction, not static QA: two agents with private, conflicting goals converse and act freely across turns, scored on 7 human-motive dimensions (goal, believability, relationship, secrets, norms) rather than accuracy — the capability under test is holding a goal-driven social conversation, all realized in free text with no external tool_access, the A7 pattern rather than A5's software-environment operation.

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
human_time: Human baseline 78.24% task success; paper doesn't report a per-task time.
frontier_score: GPT-4 + chain-of-thought: 14.41% task success vs. 78.24% human baseline
one_line: Four fully-hostable, real-world-scale websites (e-commerce, forum, GitLab, CMS) with 812 long-horizon tasks scored by functional correctness rather than reference-trajectory matching — GPT-4 with chain-of-thought closes only 14.41% of tasks.
notes: Foundational ancestor of the modern web-agent benchmark family (VisualWebArena, OSWorld, AndroidWorld, WebVoyager all extend its design).
placement_reason: The founding realistic, persistent-state web environment: agents act against fully-hostable clones of real sites and are scored by post-hoc functional-correctness checks on environment state, not by matching a reference action trajectory — the template every later web-agent benchmark in this family (VisualWebArena, OSWorld, AndroidWorld) reuses.

title: robosuite: A Modular Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot Learning
human_time: A single manipulation task (block lifting/stacking, pick-and-place, nut assembly, door opening, two-arm peg-in-hole) that a person could complete in well under a minute by teleoperation.
frontier_score: Paper's only reported result (SAC, 2 robots): qualitatively 'solves' 3 of 9 tasks (Block Lifting, Door Opening, Two Arm Peg-in-Hole) by curve-reading, no printed numeric table, 'slow progress' on the rest
one_line: A modular MuJoCo simulation framework (10 robots, 9 grippers, 6 controller types) plus a small, fixed 9-task manipulation benchmark; its own results section reports one algorithm (SAC) on two robots with no printed score table.
notes: robosuite is genuinely two artifacts (a research framework and a benchmark) under one title; classified on the benchmark half (9 standardized tasks) per this survey's rubric. No 'robotics' domain exists in the controlled vocabulary; 'multimodal' stands in for RGB-D/proprioceptive embodied state. items_count is the fixed task-suite size (9), not the framework's much larger capability catalog (10 robots etc.).
placement_reason: Ships a modular robot-manipulation simulator plus nine standardized, randomized benchmark tasks specifically because prior manipulation research was hard to compare across incompatible hardware/simulators -- the object measured is operating a (physical, simulated) interactive environment end-to-end, the same construct RLBench/Meta-World occupy, not a fixed exam-style item set.

title: TAT-QA: A Question Answering Benchmark on a Hybrid of Tabular and Textual Content in Finance
human_time: A few minutes per question: read a real financial-report table plus its surrounding paragraphs, locate relevant cells/spans across both modalities, and compute a correctly-scaled numeric answer -- sampled human annotators (301 questions) reached 90.8 F1 this way.
frontier_score: TAGOP: 50.1 EM / 58.0 F1 vs. 90.8 F1 human estimate (301-question sample) -- an 11.1-point jump over the next-best adapted baseline; 84% of errors from wrong/missing evidence, not bad arithmetic
one_line: 16,552 questions over 2,757 real financial-report table+paragraph pairs, requiring numerical reasoning plus a correctly-scaled answer -- the paper's own TAGOP model trails the human estimate by 32.8 F1 points, mostly on evidence retrieval rather than arithmetic.
notes: Domain judged like its close sibling FinQA (chen-2021-finqa, also D-deployment/D2): the measured skill is checkable extract-then-compute reasoning (an A1/A3 pull -- hybrid table+text parsing plus arithmetic), but the benchmark's design center is real financial-analyst work (annual-report tables + prose, scale-aware scoring), so D2's occupational-content-beats-framing rule places it here rather than A1. The 90.8 human-F1 ceiling rests on a 301-question (18%) sample with no reported inter-annotator agreement.
placement_reason: Asks whether a model can do the real work of a financial analyst: extract and combine numbers from a real annual-report table and its surrounding prose, get the scale right (thousand/million/billion/percent), against a human estimate (90.8 F1) as the bar -- the same occupational-content-beats-framing logic that places its close sibling FinQA here, not the general SQuAD-family parsing skill (A1) the underlying mechanics resemble.

title: DyVal: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks
human_time: A single generated DAG-based problem (arithmetic chain, logic puzzle, or graph-reachability query) takes a recruited evaluator a few minutes at the hardest (D4) level.
frontier_score: GPT-4 leads overall (e.g. Abductive Logic ~89% at D1 falling to ~58% D3); GPT-3.5-Turbo's Arithmetic score falls 97.3% (D1) to 71.5% (D4); 4 of 8 tested models (Flan-T5-large, phi-1.5, WizardMath-13B, Xwin-13B) score exactly 0% on every task at every complexity level.
one_line: A dynamic-evaluation protocol (A_T = F(G(C))) that generates fresh math/logic/algorithm problems from directed acyclic graphs on every run, with complexity set by graph depth/width — avoiding contamination by construction (~10^-15 collision-probability bound) rather than by detection after the fact.
notes: items_count left null: DyVal is a generative protocol, not a fixed corpus — the paper's own study used 500 generated samples/task x 7 tasks x 4 complexity levels x 3 seeds x 3 description orders as its running experiment, but no single 'dataset size' exists (cf. Chatbot Arena's null items_count for the same reason). Placed in C3 (living-walls) over F1 (reward-factories) because the paper's own title and framing are explicitly about dynamic EVALUATION responding to static-benchmark staleness/contamination; the fine-tuning-on-DyVal-data experiment is a secondary finding (one figure), not the headline the way it is for reasoning-gym (F1). The explainer flags real internal inconsistencies in the paper's own tables (a missing D4 row, a backwards order-effect claim, a demographics-count mismatch) that don't change the classification but temper confidence in exact quoted numbers.
placement_reason: The paper's own problem statement is durability of measurement, not depth of a static wall: static, public, scraped test sets get memorized and can't keep discriminating as models improve, so DyVal generates a fresh problem from a DAG on every call and proves (not just claims) a near-zero collision probability — unsaturable and uncontaminated by construction, the C3 pattern (cf. LiveCodeBench, LiveBench), distinguished from C1's fixed-but-hard exams by never shipping a static answer key at all.

title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures
human_time: Not stated precisely; annotating a multi-step agent trajectory (ALFWorld runs cluster around steps 6-15, some to 29) for root-cause step/module/error-type takes real expert time, similar order to TRAIL's own reported 30-40 min/trace for a comparable trace-debugging task.
frontier_score: AgentDebug (GPT-4.1 detector) reaches 45.0% Step / 31.3% Step+Module / 24.3% All-Correct detection accuracy vs. the strongest baseline's 28.0% / 10.0% / 0.3%
one_line: A 5-module/17-type agent-failure taxonomy plus 200 human-annotated failed trajectories (ALFWorld/GAIA/WebShop, Cohen's kappa=0.55) for scoring root-cause error detection, paired with AgentDebug, a corrective-feedback debugging framework reaching 24.3% all-correct detection against a 0.3% strongest baseline.
notes: confidence=medium: the page's critique documents a genuine internal contradiction — Algorithm 1's own comment labels Stage 2 'via LLM (no rollout/counterfactuals)' while §3.2's prose describes literally re-executing corrected actions ('via Counterfactuals') — so which mechanism AgentDebug actually runs at inference time is undisclosed; also flags kappa=0.55 mislabeled 'substantial' (Landis-Koch 'moderate' band) and two of three headline 'consistently outperforms' claims being ties on the paper's own figures. domain_primary='reasoning' (diagnosing/localizing a trajectory's causal root-cause error is a reasoning-over-traces task) mirrors TRAIL's own domain_primary call for the same trace-debugging construct; domain_secondary reflects the three source environments (GAIA=tool-use/agentic-web, WebShop=agentic-web). grading_all includes programmatic for the separate task-success recovery experiment (Self-Refine/Best-of-N/ToT comparisons on live ALFWorld/GAIA/WebShop success rates), distinct from the exact-match Step/Module/ErrorType/All-Correct detection metrics against human ground truth. Paper doesn't state which model(s) generated the original 500-trajectory failure pool before curation to 200.
placement_reason: AgentErrorBench is a step-level agent-failure taxonomy plus 200 expert-annotated failed trajectories built to score whether an automated method can localize a trajectory's root-cause error — the trace-debugging judge-benchmark peer of TRAIL (traces from ALFWorld/GAIA/WebShop vs. TRAIL's GAIA/SWE-bench) and the explicit rival of Who&When (zhang-2025-failure-attribution, discussed at length in the critique); the paper's own headline metrics (Step/Module/ErrorType/All-Correct accuracy against human ground truth) grade a diagnostic method, not agent task-completion skill, so it stays out of A5/A8 despite the underlying trajectories coming from capability-probe environments.

title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
human_time: A team task like co-authoring a five-question research proposal, building a Minecraft structure, diagnosing a database anomaly, or playing a full Werewolf game -- tens of minutes to an hour for a human team.
frontier_score: gpt-4o-mini highest average Task Score across the six scenarios (~52.7%); no model's Coordination Score reliably predicts its Task Score outside 2 of 6 scenarios
one_line: Six scenarios (Research, Minecraft, Database, Coding cooperative; Werewolf, Bargaining competitive) score LLM-based multi-agent teams on both task completion and a separate LLM-judged coordination quality, with topology (star/tree/graph-mesh/chain) and planning strategy as explicit experimental axes.
notes: domain_primary=reasoning is a least-bad fit: BENCH_DOMAINS has no multi-agent-coordination or MARL slot, and per the batch's stated convention that's the bucket for MARL/game-style multi-agent environments (Werewolf/Bargaining are explicitly game-theoretic; Research/Minecraft/Database/Coding are task-oriented). Family is likewise a least-bad fit: A5 (environment operation) fits the four task-oriented scenarios but not perfectly the two competitive-game ones; no dedicated multi-agent-coordination family exists in the taxonomy. items_count left null -- six heterogeneous scenarios with different per-scenario counts (Research=100, Werewolf=100 archives, others unspecified in the explainer), no single total given.
placement_reason: The object under test is whether a team of LLM agents can jointly operate shared, mutable environments (a Minecraft world, a Postgres instance, a codebase, a negotiation) to a working end-state -- environment operation extended from one agent to a coordinated team, with coordination quality scored as an explicit secondary axis rather than the primary deliverable (Communication/Planning scores don't predict Task Score outside 2 of 6 scenarios per the paper's own tables), so A5 over A7 (communication as the deliverable).

title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
human_time: One DevAI task is a small end-to-end AI build (load data, train a model, report, visualize) kept 'small enough to run cheaply' - a competent ML engineer would need roughly 1-4 hours.
frontier_score: GPT-Pilot / OpenHands satisfy ~29% of requirements with dependencies enforced; task solve rate 1.81%
