one_line: DevAI: 55 realistic AI-app development tasks with 365 DAG-structured requirements, graded per-requirement by an agentic judge.
notes: Eval-methodology paper: classified the shipped artifact, DevAI + the Agent-as-a-Judge grader. Headline grading is the agentic judge checking per-task requirement checklists (rubric-judge); the human panel is the gold standard and LLM-as-a-Judge the baseline, hence grading_all. 55 tasks but 365 gradable requirements.
placement_reason: The contribution is a judging protocol for other systems' outputs: an agentic evaluator that reads workspaces and grades per-requirement DAG milestones, validated against a human panel (~90% alignment at ~2% cost), with DevAI shipped as the substrate for the judge. Born against SWE-bench's final-resolve-rate-only scoring and LLM-as-a-judge's blindness; explicitly named in the G3 family definition.

title: BigCodeBench: Benchmarking Code Generation with Diverse Function Calls and Complex Instructions
human_time: One task is a ~1,100-char spec with a ~10-line multi-library reference solution; the authors' own expert annotators solved sampled tasks blind - roughly 10-20 minutes each.
frontier_score: GPT-4o ~60% Pass@1 on Complete, <50% on Instruct (vs 97% human pass rate)
one_line: 1,140 Python tasks composing 723 real library calls under complex specs, execution-graded by unit tests at 99% branch coverage.
notes: tool-use secondary is borderline: it tests composing library function calls inside generated code, not BFCL-style API emission. Provenance: GPT-4-synthesized from ODEX seeds under year-long human curation -> synthetic-generated. Contamination per explainer: 'private held-back test answers' + HF gating -> private-holdout. Saturation: ~60% quoted is 2024-dated and explainer notes frontier has since climbed -> closing.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'can a model read a rich spec and orchestrate many real library calls?' — 1,140 execution-graded Python tasks over 723 calls/139 libraries, headline being frontier skill (GPT-4o ~60% vs 97% human). The gap section frames a new construct (function-call composition + complex instructions) that HumanEval/MBPP never tested, not the same construct rebuilt for headroom, so A4 over B3.

title: MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding
human_time: A few minutes per item: a licensing/specialty-board vignette (149.35 avg tokens) with labs, ECG crops or images, 10 (Text) or 5 (MM) options.
frontier_score: o1 49.89% average (44.67% Text/56.28% MM), only narrowly above the paper's own pre-licensed-human baseline of 43.92%
one_line: 4,460 medical-licensing/specialty-board exam questions (text + multimodal) built to escape MedQA/MMLU-Medical's saturation; o1 leads at 49.89%, barely clearing a pre-licensed-trainee baseline.
notes: Contamination_defense judgment call: Appendix A's 'Leakage Prevention Statement' withholds original data sources and asks readers not to share items publicly, and the paper states this blocks outside re-verification -- closest fit is private-holdout, though the paper never states the item set itself is access-gated (unlike VCT). domain_primary=professional (medical) rather than knowledge, matching Med-PaLM/HealthBench convention for clinical-competence content; multimodal is secondary for the MM subset's 10 image categories. 10-option Text format vs 4-option MMLU/MedQA is a guessing-floor confound the paper itself doesn't normalize for (noted in the explainer's critique).
placement_reason: The paper's own gap statement is a saturation complaint -- MedQA/MMLU-Medical/MedMCQA are 'running out of headroom' (o1-preview already 96-99%) -- and its fix keeps the MCQ-exam construct (now exam-derived from real licensing/specialty boards, harder options, added multimodal cases) rather than proposing a new open-ended clinical-safety task; a same-construct, headroom-restored sequel like MMLU-Pro vs MMLU, not a D2 clinical-deployment rehearsal (it never leaves the exam format the way HealthBench/Med-PaLM's free-text grading does).
